Kelly gives many examples of “the appeal to the Fathers” in the early Church to affirm traditional beliefs and doctrines:
a. Writing to the Egyptian monks in defense of the blessed Virgin’s claim to be called

“Mother of God,” St. Cyril of Alexandria counseled them to follow in the steps of the holy Fathers, since it was they who had preserved the faith handed down from the apostles and taught Christians to believe aright. Again, he was prepared to affirm that the correct doctrine of the Holy Trinity had been expounded by “the wisdom of the holy Fathers.” As against Nestorius, he appealed to “the holy catholic Church and the venerable Fathers themselves,” claiming that the Holy Spirit spoke in them.

For the more formal justification of his Christological position, he prepared elaborate arguments from patristic quotations, inserting them in his controversial writings and producing them at the council of Ephesus. St. Cyril states, “I am a lover of sound doctrines, treading in the religious footsteps of the Fathers.”

b. Theodoret, the Antiochene Father, speaks of the orthodox faith as having been transmitted to us, not only by the apostles and prophets, but also by those who interpreted their teachings. These include Ignatius, Eustathius, St. Athanasius, Basil, Gregory, John Chrysostom, and other luminaries of the world as well as the holy Fathers who assembled before them at Nicaea. He added that any who deviated from their collective teaching must be labeled as an enemy of the truth. Elsewhere, he explained that the Holy Spirit inspired the Fathers to make clear the more difficult passages of the Scriptures.
It is worth noting that according to our Orthodox Church no single Father can alone comprehend the Truth in its fullness — only the Church as a whole can do this.
What is the role of the laity in preserving the traditional life of the Church?

The laity play a role in preserving tradition by practicing it in their daily lives and in their worship. Church life cannot be preserved only by canons or through books, but through practice and life.

Every true believer represents a living stone in the spiritual temple of God, laid upon other living stones that came before him. That is, he receives the traditional life of the Church from past generations. And at the same time, he bears other living stones. That is, he transmits this life to future generations. Thus, he becomes a living member of the Church of Christ, transmitting her life by practicing it daily. We can therefore identify “traditional believers” not as those who carefully study Church canons, are well acquainted with the details of the rites, or just recite the church hymns; but rather as those who discover their unity with God in Christ Jesus by the Holy Spirit through preserving and practicing the canons, rites, hymns, etc., of the Church.
Source: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Fr. Tadros Y. Malaty (2023), Book 1: Introduction to the Coptic Catechism.
More on Holy Tradition — Part 3
How can we hold fast to the tradition of the Church in contemporary life?

Some assume that “tradition” means “conservation” or “solidification,” as if it prevents any progress in the life of the Church. From our Orthodox point of view, tradition is the life of the Church throughout history, which is guided and renewed by the Holy Spirit. The Church will never be satisfied until the perfection of all mankind. Sergius Bulgakov declares, “Tradition is not a book which records a certain moment in the development of the Church and stops itself, but a book always being written by the Church’s life. Tradition continues always and now not less than formerly; we live in tradition and create it. And nevertheless the sacred tradition of the past exists for us as present; it lives in our own life and consciousness … Ecclesiastical tradition does not put the voice of the past in the place of the voice of the present; in it the past does not kill the present, but gives it full force.”

Tradition must be creative and at the same time conservative. There is no contradiction between these two elements, but they are essential and are indispensable to each other. Tradition cannot be conserved unless it is continually developing, and it cannot develop unless it stands on the shoulders of the past. Conservation and development are two facets of the same process, which we call tradition.
What does tradition mean in the ecumenical movement of the Church?
As theologians today explore the ecumenical movement that strives to attain the global unity of the Church, they face this question: What is the true tradition received by the

Church, whose principles can guide her life everywhere in the whole world? If we return to the apostolic age, we find “many local church traditions” reflecting a variety of cultures. However, all these traditions are bound together by one mind, the mind of Christ; one spirit, the Spirit of the Lord; and one aim, our salvation.

For this reason, the bishops of Alexandria did not hesitate to participate with the bishops of Rome, Antioch, and Jerusalem, in one service and on one altar, even if they differ in the details of their rites and traditions. For all of them received a single form of worship, in one spirit and one Tradition.

So did all the apostles live in one open spirit of preaching. “For though I am free from all men, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might win the more” (1 Cor. 9:19). When St. Mark preached in Egypt, he spoke about the One Christ. The Egyptians worshiped through their culture but in true apostolic spirit, and with the same spirit of worship as other bishoprics. For instance, the Coptic hymns differ from the Syrian and Latin ones … but all have the quiet and meek spirit, the spirit of the new heavenly hymn, reflecting the deepest true dogmatic and spiritual concepts and teachings.

The Lights in the House of the Lord are another example. All the apostolic Churches in the world use lights during worship by day and by night, especially during the reading of the Gospel. This is the spirit of tradition, which declares that “Christ is the Light of the world.” However, Egyptian art emerged in the crafting of their oil lamps —kanadeel — peculiar to the Coptic Church, while the Syrians, Latins, Greeks, etc., embody their own artistic traditions in the particular styles of their own lamps.

Thus, while all who are called Christians across the world share a unity of faith and preserve the true, living tradition, every local church expresses this one faith through her own language, her liturgical rites, hymns, sacred clerical vestments, etc., without losing the unity of faith. The local character of Churches does not obscure the character of the Universal Church. In other words, the differences between traditions, in detail and not in essence, do not stop the realization of the unity of the Universal Church, as long as those traditions have all been established upon the unity of faith and life.
Finally, we conclude this section with the following observations:

a. The Orthodox Church, especially the Church of Alexandria, has more than others, preserved the holy tradition, both in its details and in its spirit. Perhaps this is because our Church has neither worldly authority nor does it interfere in politics. She lives in her spirituality far from the spirit of the world. The emergence of the monastic movement in Egypt has preserved the reverent, biblical, and ascetic spirit of the tradition of the Church.

b. The unity that exists between the Non-Chalcedonian (Ephesian) Orthodox Churches in our time provides a very practical case study for theologians interested in the ecumenical movement of how the concept of unity can be implemented. While these Churches differ in some details in their local traditions, they are blessed in sharing a single Faith and a single Tradition. More than once in recent years, the whole world has witnessed the cooperation of the patriarchs, bishops, presbyters, deacons, and laymen from these Churches in one service, partaking in one offering for all.

It behooves these Churches to play an active role with their sisters, the Chalcedonian Orthodox Churches, so that together, the Orthodox Church can devote all her power to evangelism across the whole world.

c. As an Orthodox Church, we need to think seriously about what we can offer to the world through our evangelism. When a French man, for instance, accepts the Orthodox faith, it is the heart of our mission that we should offer him the opportunity for genuinely Orthodox, patristic, divine worship with one spirit, yet through the culture he finds familiar. In a speech to Orthodox Church leaders in Melbourne in June 1977, H.E. Metropolitan Gregorius, of New Delhi, India said that we must sow the seeds of Orthodoxy in Australian soil, so that an Australian Orthodox tree may grow and flourish.

d. As the Church of Alexandria has opened up to the outside world, and millions of her faithful have emigrated to the diaspora, the Mother Church needs to re-examine her mission. She must guide and help them to present Orthodox thought to others without deviating from the spirit of tradition or rites. She must never enclose herself within an ethnic community nor make a particular language compulsory; she must bear a worldwide responsibility. This is a very delicate mission, to offer this living tradition to the world with an open heart, while at the same time avoiding deviation or negligence! This is the most important work of theologians today.
Source: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Fr. Tadros Y. Malaty (2023), Book 1: Introduction to the Coptic Catechism.
BOOK 3

The inspired and authoritative Word of God contained in the Old and New Testaments. Scripture reveals God's plan of salvation, teaches divine truth, and serves as a foundation for Christian faith and practice.
Authenticity & Reliability of the Holy Bible

subsections.heading: PROOF OF THE UNIQUENESS OF THE HOLY BIBLE
paragraphs: The Holy Bible is one of a kind in its continuity. It was written over a stretch of about 1,600 years, across roughly 40 generations, by more than 40 different writers who came from every walk of life: kings and peasants, philosophers and fishermen, poets, statesmen, and physicians, among others. It was written in a wide range of places, from the sands of the Sinai desert to the prison cell where St. Paul sat in chains. It was written in times of peace and in times of war, in moods of great joy and deep sorrow. It was written across three continents (Asia, Africa, and Europe) and in three languages (Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek). It deals with hundreds of separate subjects. And yet, in spite of all these differences, the Holy Bible tells one single, unbroken story with remarkable agreement from start to finish: the story of God rescuing the human race.
To see this unity, simply compare the first three chapters of the Holy Book of Genesis with the last three chapters of the Holy Book of Revelation:
• In Genesis we read, "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth" (Gen 1:1), and in Revelation we find "a new heaven and a new earth" (Rev 21:1).
• Genesis 2 shows us the first wedding, that of Adam and Eve, and Revelation 21 speaks of the final wedding, the marriage of the Lord Jesus Christ and His Church (Rev 21:2, 9).

• Genesis 3 tells of the short-lived victory of the serpent (Satan), and Revelation 20 describes his final and everlasting defeat, "the dragon, that serpent of old, who is the Devil and Satan" (Rev 20:2-10).

• Genesis 3 shows us the sin that cut us off from God, and Revelation 21 announces our restoration: "Behold, the tabernacle of God with men, and He will dwell with them, and they shall be His people. God Himself will be with them and be their God" (Rev 21:3).

• In Genesis 3 God keeps Adam away from the tree of life, while in Revelation 22 the tree returns for all: "the tree of life, which bore twelve fruits, each tree yielding its fruit every month. The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations" (Rev 22:2).
• Genesis opens with paradise lost through the first Adam, and Revelation closes with paradise regained through Christ, the "last Adam" (1 Cor 15:45).

This deep unity is not just a matter of a few matching bookends. The whole Bible is tied together by an enormous web of connections. Scholars who have carefully studied the text have counted more than 60,000 cross-references linking one passage to another, threads running back and forth between the Old Testament and the New Testament, tying promise to fulfillment and shadow to reality. A promise made in the Law is answered in the Gospels; a figure hinted at in the Psalms steps into the light in the Epistles. No committee planned this. It arose naturally as more than 40 writers, most of whom never met one another, were each moved by the same Holy Spirit to write one coherent message. No other book in human history shows this kind of woven, self-connected unity across so many centuries and so many hands.

The Holy Bible is also one of a kind in its SURVIVAL. It was written on materials that decay, and it had to be copied by hand, again and again, for hundreds of years before the printing press was ever invented. None of this wore down its style, its accuracy, or its very existence. Set beside other writings from the ancient world, the Holy Bible rests on more manuscript evidence than any ten works of classical literature put together. It has outlasted not only the wearing down of time, but also fierce persecution, both from governments and from scholars. It survives daily under a storm of criticism. No other book has been so cut apart, sifted, picked over, and attacked. And still it remains the most read, most quoted, most printed, most translated, and most loved book on earth. If all this criticism had really worked, the Bible would long ago have faded into something the critics no longer bothered with. The plain fact that they keep aiming at it, century after century, only shows that every past attack has done nothing but make faith in the Holy Bible stronger.

subsections.heading: OLD TESTAMENT MANUSCRIPTS
paragraphs: We do not have nearly as many surviving Old Testament manuscripts as we do for the New Testament, and the ones we do have were, for a long time, copied far from the date of the original writings. The Old Testament itself was written somewhere between 1500 and 400 BC. Until fairly recently (before the Dead Sea Scrolls turned up), the oldest complete Old Testament manuscript we possessed dated to around 900 AD. That left a gap of about 1,300 years between the finishing of the Old Testament (around 400 BC) and the earliest full copy we could hold in our hands.
At first, this shortage of very old copies might worry someone, until he learns just how carefully the Hebrew scribes did their copying:
1. A synagogue roll had to be written on the skins of clean animals, prepared by a Jew.
2. The skins had to be joined together with strings taken from clean animals.
3. Every skin, or page, had to hold a set number of columns, kept equal throughout the whole book.
4. Each column had to run no fewer than 48 lines and no more than 60, and its width had to be thirty letters.
5. The whole copy had to be ruled with lines first; if even three words were written without a line, the copy was thrown out.
6. The ink had to be black and mixed according to a fixed recipe.
7. A trusted master copy had to serve as the pattern, and the scribe was not allowed to stray from it in the smallest detail.
8. Not a single word or letter, not even the tiny yod, could be written from memory; the scribe had to keep his eyes on the copy in front of him.
9. The copyist had to wash his whole body and sit dressed in full Jewish dress.

10. He could not begin the name of God (YHWH) with a pen freshly dipped in ink; and if a king spoke to him while he was writing that holy name, he was to pay the king no attention at all. (Samuel Davidson, "Hebrew Text of the Old Testament," 2nd ed., Samuel Bagster & Sons, 1859)

subsections.heading: GREEK SEPTUAGINT
paragraphs: There is an important point here that many people overlook. The Hebrew text we lean on so heavily today, the "Massoretic" text, was not fixed in its final form by ordinary Jewish scribes; it was shaped and standardized by the Massoretes, a group of Jewish scholars who did their work between roughly AD 500 and 900, long after the coming of Christ. That is to say, the "standard" Hebrew Bible in common use was settled by men who did not accept the Lord Jesus as the Messiah, and who were reading and editing the text in the middle of the long dispute between the Synagogue and the Church. This matters, because in a number of places the Massoretic wording drifts away from the older reading that the early Church knew and quoted. The Massoretic text, for all the care of its copyists, was locked into place too late and by the wrong hands to be treated as the final word.

Long before the Massoretes ever set to work, the Jewish people themselves had already produced a Greek translation of the Old Testament known as the **Septuagint**, often written as "LXX" after the tradition that about seventy scholars carried it out. This translation was made in Alexandria roughly 250 to 150 years before Christ was born, at a time when no one had any reason to twist the text to argue against Christianity, because Christianity did not yet exist. The Septuagint was the Bible of the Greek-speaking Jewish world, and it became the Old Testament of the early Church. When the writers of the New Testament quote the Old Testament, they very often quote it in the words of the Septuagint, not the later Hebrew wording of the Massoretes. This is exactly why the Orthodox Church has always held the Septuagint in the highest honor: it preserves, in many places, a reading older and purer than the Massoretic text.

The importance of this shows up sharply in the Messianic prophecies. Take Isaiah 7:14. The Septuagint, translated centuries before Christ, reads that "the virgin shall conceive," using the Greek word *parthenos*, which plainly means a virgin. The later Massoretic tradition favored a Hebrew word that can be softened to mean only a "young woman." Since the Septuagint was written long before the argument over Jesus ever began, it stands as an honest witness, untouched by that later dispute, that the ancient Jewish understanding of the prophecy was indeed a virgin birth. In this way the Septuagint quietly convicts the later text and confirms the faith of the Church.

subsections.heading: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR AND THE EARLY WITNESS
paragraphs: We are not the first to notice this. As far back as the second century, the Christian teacher and philosopher **St. Justin Martyr** (who lived roughly AD 100 to 165, only a generation or two after the Apostles) was already defending the authenticity of the Scriptures and pointing to the Old Testament prophecies as proof that Jesus is the Christ. In his writings, especially his "Dialogue with Trypho the Jew" and his "First Apology," St. Justin argued at length that everything foretold about the Messiah, His birth from a virgin, His place of birth, His suffering, His death, and His resurrection, had already been written down in the Hebrew Scriptures centuries in advance and had come true in Jesus.

St. Justin made two things very clear. First, that these prophecies were far too old to have been faked after the fact, since they were on record in books the Jews themselves guarded and read publicly. Second, that some among the Jewish teachers of his own day were already altering or explaining away certain readings of Scripture precisely because those readings pointed so obviously to Christ. He specifically accused them of tampering with passages like Isaiah's prophecy of the virgin, trading the clear word for a weaker one to escape its force. Coming so close to the time of the Apostles, St. Justin's testimony is powerful: it shows that the Church was reading these prophecies as fulfilled in Christ from the very earliest days, and that the older Greek text he relied upon already carried the very readings the later Massoretic tradition tried to soften.

subsections.heading: DEAD SEA SCROLLS
paragraphs: The finding of the "Dead Sea Scrolls" at Qumran has been called the greatest archaeological discovery of the twentieth century. The scrolls showed that a community of monk-like farmers lived in that valley from about 150 BC to 70 AD. It is thought that when they saw the Roman armies coming into the land, they tucked their treasured leather scrolls into jars and hid them in the caves along the cliffs to the northwest of the Dead Sea. This find gave us powerful proof of how genuine and reliable the ancient Old Testament manuscripts really are. Among the complete books recovered from Qumran cave 1 were two copies of Isaiah, dating from a thousand years before the oldest Hebrew manuscripts known up to that point. The scrolls confirmed the astonishing care with which the text had been handed down, and in several places they actually agree with the older Septuagint reading against the later Massoretic wording, another quiet confirmation that the text the Church has always trusted goes back to the earliest times.

subsections.heading: NEW TESTAMENT MANUSCRIPTS
paragraphs: For the New Testament, we now have more than 24,000 manuscript copies of some part of the text. No other writing from the ancient world comes anywhere close to that number or that level of support. By comparison, the "Iliad" of Homer sits in second place with only 643 surviving manuscripts. Other works, such as the writings of Plato and Herodotus, survive in no more than about 20 copies each. (F. F. Bruce, "The Books and the Parchments," rev. ed., Westwood: Fleming H. Revell Co., 1963)

On top of the number of copies, the New Testament stands out because the gap between when it was written and the date of its earliest surviving copy is astonishingly small compared to other classical works. For most of the New Testament, that gap is only about 100 to 125 years. Set that next to gaps of 1,000 to 1,600 years for the classical writings of Caesar, Plato, Aristotle, Tacitus, Aristophanes, Euripides, Herodotus, and many more.

There is one more remarkable support. Imagine that every copy of the New Testament had been wiped out and lost by the end of the third century, a full 100 years before the Synod of Hippo settled the New Testament canon. How much of it could we piece back together just from the quotations found in the writings of the Church Fathers of the second and third centuries? The answer is astonishing: all of it, except for 11 verses. (C. Leah, "Our Bible: How We Got It," Chicago: Moody Press, 1998)

subsections.heading: MESSIANIC PROPHECIES
paragraphs: These are the prophecies about the anointed one ("Messiah" in Hebrew) who was promised to come. There are more than 300 of them, and every one was fulfilled with great accuracy in the person of our Lord Jesus Christ. What makes this so striking is that these prophecies were written down centuries before He was born, so no one could have arranged their fulfillment after the fact. And as we have seen, they were preserved in the ancient Septuagint and defended by teachers like St. Justin Martyr long before anyone could accuse the Church of inventing them.
One of the clearest examples is Psalm 22, in which King David paints a picture of the crucifixion almost 1,000 years before it took place:
• "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" (Ps 22:1)
• "All those who see Me ridicule Me; they shoot out the lip, they shake the head, saying, 'He trusted in the Lord, let Him rescue Him; let Him deliver Him, since He delights in Him!'" (Ps 22:7-8)
• "My tongue clings to My jaws." (Ps 22:15)
• "They pierced My hands and My feet." (Ps 22:16)
• "They divided My garments among them, and for My clothing they cast lots." (Ps 22:18)
But Psalm 22 is only one of many. The Old Testament is filled with details about the Messiah that came true in Christ, for example:
• He would be born of a virgin: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a Son, and shall call His name Immanuel" (Is 7:14), fulfilled in Matthew 1:22-23.

• He would be born in Bethlehem: "But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of you shall come forth to Me the One to be Ruler in Israel" (Micah 5:2), fulfilled in Matthew 2:1-6.
• He would come from the line of David: "I will raise to David a Branch of righteousness; a King shall reign and prosper" (Jer 23:5).
• He would enter Jerusalem humbly, riding on a donkey: "Behold, your King is coming to you… lowly and riding on a donkey, a colt, the foal of a donkey" (Zech 9:9), fulfilled in Matthew 21:1-11.
• He would be betrayed for thirty pieces of silver: "So they weighed out for my wages thirty pieces of silver" (Zech 11:12-13), fulfilled in Matthew 26:14-15.
• He would be silent before His accusers: "He was oppressed and He was afflicted, yet He opened not His mouth" (Is 53:7), fulfilled in Matthew 27:12-14.
• His bones would not be broken: "He guards all his bones; not one of them is broken" (Ps 34:20), fulfilled in John 19:33-36.
• He would suffer and die for our sins: "He was wounded for our transgressions, He was bruised for our iniquities… and by His stripes we are healed" (Is 53:5).
• He would be buried with the rich: "They made His grave with the wicked, but with the rich at His death" (Is 53:9), fulfilled in Matthew 27:57-60.
• He would rise from the dead: "For You will not leave my soul in Sheol, nor will You allow Your Holy One to see corruption" (Ps 16:10), fulfilled in Acts 2:29-32.

When we remember that these words were set down hundreds of years in advance, and that so many of them were completely outside any one person's control (where He would be born, how He would die, what would be done with His body), the odds of all of them landing on a single man by chance are beyond imagining. They point clearly to a God who knows and shapes the future.

subsections.heading: PROPHECIES DEALING WITH NATIONS
paragraphs: Archaeologists have found solid evidence that these prophecies were written down long before the events they describe took place, which rules out the idea that they were faked documents pretending to be prophecies after the fact. In truth, the discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls put an end to most of that kind of talk. It would take a whole lecture to treat this subject properly, so we will offer just one example that should hit close to home for most of us. Every one of you carries proof of a fulfilled prophecy right on your ID card. The simple fact that your last name is not "Mohamed," or some other Muslim name, is a fulfillment of what Isaiah spoke concerning Egypt: "In that day there will be an altar to the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to the Lord at its border… Then the Lord will be known to Egypt, and the Egyptians will know the Lord" (Is 19:19-21).

subsections.heading: EVIDENCE OF PEOPLE LIVING AT THE TIME OF OUR LORD
paragraphs: The New Testament carries a special kind of proof, because the early Christians were harshly persecuted by both the Jewish leaders and the Roman government. If the New Testament accounts had been made up, these two powerful groups would have rushed to produce evidence against them to choke off the growth of this new "sect." Yet no such evidence exists anywhere. On top of that, the New Testament writings were circulating while thousands of people who had personally seen our Lord's miracles and lived through those events were still alive. Not one of them ever stepped forward to expose the New Testament accounts as fairy tales, and it would have been easy to do so if they were false.

subsections.heading: EVIDENCE OF HISTORIANS
paragraphs: History written outside the Church also backs up the Holy Bible. For example, in "The Antiquities of the Jews," book 18, chapter 3, paragraph 3, the well-known Jewish historian Flavius Josephus writes: "Now, there was about this time Jesus, a wise man, if it be lawful to call him a man, for he was a doer of wonderful works, a teacher of such men as receive the truth with pleasure. He drew over to him both many of the Jews and many of the Gentiles. He was the Christ; and when Pilate, at the suggestion of the principal men among us, had condemned him to the cross, those that loved him at first did not forsake him, for he appeared to them alive again the third day, as the divine prophets had foretold these and ten thousand other wonderful things concerning him; and the tribe of Christians, so named from him, is not extinct to this day."

subsections.heading: EVIDENCE OF SCIENCE
paragraphs: The Holy Bible is not a science textbook, and yet whenever it touches on the natural world, it turns out to be accurate. To feel the difference between the Bible and a science book, try picking up a science textbook that is only 50 years old and see how much of it is now out of date. Science is like a child who is still learning and growing, while the Holy Bible is like a wise old elder, already full of knowledge. The statements below line up with facts that science confirmed only much later, in many cases hundreds or even thousands of years after the Bible had already recorded them.
IN LINE WITH GEOLOGY: "It is He who sits above the circle of the earth" (Is 40:22). Isaiah wrote this hundreds of years before Aristotle ever proposed that the earth might be a sphere.

IN LINE WITH HYDROLOGY: "He causes the vapors to ascend from the ends of the earth; He makes lightning for the rain; He brings the wind out of His treasuries" (Ps 135:7); and "When He utters His voice, there is a multitude of waters in the heavens; and He causes the vapors to ascend from the ends of the earth. He makes lightning for the rain; He brings the wind out of His treasuries" (Jer 10:13). In these verses you can trace several stages of the water cycle: evaporation, movement through the air, and condensation with lightning and rainfall. The Bible even describes how water keeps circling back around: "All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full; to the place from which the rivers come, there they return again" (Ecc 1:7).

IN LINE WITH ANTHROPOLOGY: "They were driven out from among men, they shouted at them as at a thief. They had to live in the clefts of the valleys, in caves of the earth and the rocks" (Job 30:5-6). Here the Bible describes people living in caves. Note that these were not ape-men, but descendants of those who scattered from Babel. They were pushed out by other tribes who won the better land, and afterward they declined in mind, body, and spirit.

IN LINE WITH ASTRONOMY: "He stretches out the north over empty space; He hangs the earth on nothing" (Job 26:7). The Bible describes the earth hanging freely in space at a time when many "learned" people believed the earth rested on the back or between the horns of some great animal.

IN LINE WITH PSYCHOLOGY: "A merry heart does good, like medicine, but a broken spirit dries the bones" (Prov 17:22). It is now well established that a person's mental and spiritual health is closely tied to physical health.

IN LINE WITH BIOLOGY: The phrase "according to its kind" appears again and again in the Holy Book of Genesis, underlining how each kind of animal and plant reproduces true to its own type. Today we understand that this happens because every one of these reproductive systems is programmed by its own genetic code.

IN LINE WITH PHYSICS: "You laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the work of Your hands. They will perish, but You will endure; yes, they will all grow old like a garment" (Ps 102:25-26). Long before modern science, King David's words capture the idea of entropy, the slow wearing down of the universe over time.

Taken all together (the sweeping unity across 1,600 years, the tens of thousands of cross-references binding the two Testaments into one, the ancient witness of the Septuagint, the early defense of teachers like St. Justin Martyr, the flood of surviving manuscripts, the hundreds of fulfilled prophecies, the support of outside historians, and the quiet scientific accuracy), the evidence points in one direction. This is no ordinary book, and it did not come from human wisdom alone.
"All Scripture is given by inspiration of God [Theopneustos, God-breathed]." (2 Tim 3:16)
Inspiration of the Holy Scriptures

When we look at history, one thing stands out clearly: Jews and Christians alike have always believed that the books of the Bible are inspired by God. These books are treated as sacred and as part of the canon, not because a group of people wrote them and the Church later stamped them with approval, but because they were written under the guiding breath of the Holy Spirit. God Himself is their true author, and for that reason they were handed down to the Church as a guide that cannot lead her astray.

Our Lord Jesus Christ Himself treated the Scriptures, just as everyone in His day did, as the very word of God. Some of the strongest passages showing this are found in the Holy Gospel of John (5:39; 10:34-36). In the words and writings of the Apostles, the terms "Scripture," "Word of God," and "Spirit of God" are used almost as if they mean the same thing (Rom 4:3; 9:17; Acts 20:27; 1 Thess 2:3; 2 Cor 2:17; 13:3). St. Paul by himself points more than eighty times to "the Oracles of God," meaning the divine words that God entrusted to Israel to guard. Both St. Paul and St. Peter tell us plainly why Scripture was received as it was: because all of it is breathed out by God (2 Tim 3:16; 2 Pet 1:20-21).

Over and over in the first five books of the Bible we meet phrases like, "Now the Lord spoke to Moses, saying" (Ex 13:1; Lev 4:1; Num 4:1; Deut 32:48). Moses was told directly to write down in a book what God had spoken to him (Ex 17:14; 34:27). The prophets speak the same way: "For the Lord speaks" (Is 1:2), "The Lord said to Isaiah" (Is 7:3), "Thus says the Lord" (Is 43:1), "The word which came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying" (Jer 11:1), and "The word of the Lord came expressly to Ezekiel" (Ezek 1:3). Phrases like these appear more than 3,800 times across the Old Testament. So the Old Testament plainly presents itself as a message that comes from God.

The New Testament writers make the very same claim about themselves: that they are passing on God's message, not their own. St. Paul insists that what he wrote came as the commandments of the Lord (1 Cor 14:37); that what he preached was to be received as nothing less than the word of God (1 Thess 2:13); and that believing the teachings he handed on is necessary for salvation. That is why he can say, "But even if we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel to you than what we have preached to you, let him be accursed" (Gal 1:8). These are not the words of a man who thinks he is merely sharing his own opinions.

subsections.heading: TERMS RELATED TO THE DOCTRINE OF INSPIRATION
paragraphs: Before we go further, it helps to be clear about a few key words that come up whenever people talk about inspiration. Four of them stand out: revelation, authority, inerrancy, and illumination.

1. Revelation: "God is love" (1 Jn 4:8). Because love is part of who God is, He has always reached out to those of His creatures who have even a little power to understand, to love, and to share in His plans. This reaching out, this communication of God to human beings, is what we call revelation. It comes to us in two forms.

a) General Revelation: This is the way God shows Himself through nature, through history, and through the human conscience. It comes to us through the ordinary things we see happening in the world around us and in the flow of events. It is meant for everyone and is open to everyone. Its purpose is to meet a basic need in the human heart and to gently push the soul to go looking for the true God. As the Psalmist says, "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament shows His handiwork" (Ps 19:1). Yet general revelation can only take us so far. It can tell us that God exists and that He is great, but it cannot, on its own, tell us the full story of how He saves us.

b) Special Revelation: This is God making Himself known in more direct and particular ways: through miracles and prophecy, through the person and work of our Lord Jesus Christ, through the Scriptures, and through personal experience. It is this special, direct revelation that we are mainly concerned with here, as opposed to the general, indirect kind.

At this point, it is worth pausing to notice an important difference. Revelation is about God making known a truth that we could never have discovered on our own. Inspiration, on the other hand, is about the writing down of that revealed truth. The two do not always go together. A person can receive revelation without inspiration. This happened many times to godly people in the past. St. John, for example, heard the seven thunders speak, but he was not allowed to write down what they said (Rev 10:3-4). St. Paul, too, tells us that he was caught up into Paradise and heard words so holy that a man is not permitted to repeat them (2 Cor 12:4). It can also work the other way: a person can be inspired without receiving a fresh, direct revelation. This is what happens when a writer records what he himself saw, or what he carefully looked into and checked (Lk 1:1-4; 1 Jn 1:1-4). St. Luke worked like a careful historian, going through written records and testing the oral accounts as he composed his Gospel, and he was himself an eyewitness to much of what he later wrote in the Holy Book of Acts. St. John, by contrast, received much of the Holy Book of Revelation straight from God. Both men were inspired as they wrote, even though the material reached them in very different ways.

2. Authority: The Holy Bible carries God's own authority. Because of this, it has a real claim on us: on our minds, our consciences, our wills, and our hearts. Every person, every creed, and even the Church herself stands under the authority of the Holy Bible. God has spoken, and our part is to bow and obey. The unchanging "thus saith the Lord" is the standard by which everything is measured. Usually, whatever is inspired is also authoritative, meaning it can be used to teach us how to believe and how to live. But there is a subtle point here that is easy to miss. Not everything recorded in Scripture is meant to be followed. Satan's words to Eve are written down in the Holy Book of Genesis under inspiration, yet they are lies. The same goes for St. Peter's mistaken advice to Christ (Mt 16:22). These words were faithfully recorded, but since they do not express God's mind, they are not authoritative for us. And the same is true whenever a verse is yanked out of its setting and twisted to mean something else: the words themselves are still inspired, but the false meaning forced onto them carries no authority at all.

3. Inerrancy: Holy Scripture is not only inspired and authoritative; it is also inerrant and infallible. What we mean is that, in the original manuscripts as they first came from the writers, it contains no error. It tells the truth in everything it affirms, whether the matter is historical, scientific, moral, or doctrinal. This freedom from error covers the whole of Scripture, not just the parts that deal directly with faith and salvation. God does not make mistakes, and neither does the record He gave through His chosen writers.

4. Illumination: The same Holy Spirit who inspired the sacred writers also lights up the minds of those who read what they wrote. Sin has darkened the human understanding, and because of this no one can grasp the true meaning of Scripture by his own power alone. But the Holy Spirit is able to open the eyes of the believer's heart so that he can understand the Scriptures (1 Cor 2:6-16; Eph 1:18; 1 Jn 2:20-27). This is why prayer and humility matter so much in reading the Bible: we come needing the Author Himself to be our teacher.

subsections.heading: BIBLICAL DOCTRINE OF INSPIRATION
paragraphs: We can put it simply: inspiration is the supernatural working of the Holy Spirit upon the minds of the sacred writers, so that what they produced was not merely their own words but the word of God. The Holy Spirit so guided and watched over these writers, while still using each one's own personality, that they wrote down exactly what He wanted, with nothing added, nothing left out, and nothing mistaken. This is why the inspired writings are at one and the same time fully divine and fully human. They carry unshakable authority because every part of them is breathed out by God, and yet they are perfectly understandable because they are written in the ordinary language of men.

The push to write came from God, who moved the will of each writer. Sometimes He did this directly, and sometimes He did it by placing certain reasons and motives in the writer's mind. He could stir up circumstances, or simply make use of things already happening, to work upon the will of the sacred writer. According to an early tradition, both St. Mark and St. John wrote their Holy Gospels because the faithful asked them to. Some parts of Scripture came straight from God and are called "apocalypse" or "revelation," such as the visions given to St. John and to St. Paul (2 Cor 12:1; Rom 16:25). Other parts, like the historical accounts, rest on human testimony. But here is a point that is easy to overlook: inspiration was just as necessary for recording well-known facts as it was for revealing brand-new truths. After all, why were certain events chosen to be written down while countless others were left out? The very act of selecting is itself the work of the Spirit. So an inspired silence is every bit as much a miracle as an inspired word. If the Gospel writers had been left to their own instincts, they surely would have filled their pages with all sorts of details about our Lord's childhood, the very things our curiosity longs to know. But God's wisdom held those things back, so that all our attention would rest where it belongs: on Christ's ministry, His saving death, His glorious resurrection, His ascension, and the hope of His coming again.

subsections.heading: GUIDING PRINCIPLES OF THE DOCTRINE OF INSPIRATION
paragraphs: 1. Inspiration cannot be fully explained. It is the work of the Holy Spirit, and for all that we can say about what inspiration is, we still do not know exactly how the Spirit's power carries it out. Some mysteries belong to God alone.

2. Inspiration, in the strict sense, belongs only to the writers of the Bible. No other books are inspired in this same way. A book put together purely from human effort does not turn into an inspired text just because the Holy Spirit later approves of it. Such approval might confirm that what the book says is true, even worthy of belief, but it can never give the book itself a divine origin. There is a real line between the Scriptures and every other good and holy book ever written.

3. Inspiration is essentially guidance. The Holy Spirit lifted up and directed the abilities of the sacred writers, overseeing both the material they chose and the words they used to write it. We do not need to know the exact method God used; what matters immensely is the result: that their writings are a trustworthy guide for us. As Scripture itself says, "no prophecy of Scripture is of any private interpretation [origin], for prophecy never came by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke as they were moved [literally, carried along] by the Holy Spirit" (2 Pet 1:20-21). The image is of a ship's sails being filled and carried along by the wind.
4. The Holy Spirit kept the sacred writers from every error and from every wrong omission. They neither wrote what was false nor left out what needed to be there.

5. Inspiration is claimed only for the original text as it first left the hands of the sacred writers. It is not claimed for any translation, old or new, nor for any Hebrew or Greek copy now in existence, nor for any ancient text we know of, since none of these can be shown to be completely free of copying errors. But this should not trouble anyone. The small differences found among manuscripts do not overturn the truth that Scripture is inspired word for word. Even though the original documents are no longer in our hands, God has preserved such a huge number of ancient copies, quotations in the writings of the Fathers, and early translations, that we can rebuild the original text almost perfectly for every practical purpose. The number of words still genuinely in question is tiny, and not a single teaching of the faith hangs in the balance because of them.

6. The inspiration of Scripture is plenary and verbal. It reaches down to the actual words, not just the general ideas. It is "plenary," meaning full and complete, because it covers all of Scripture without exception (2 Tim 3:16). It is "verbal," meaning it reaches every word (1 Cor 2:13). Caiaphas is a striking example that even the words were governed by God. Through his office as high priest of Israel, he was granted the ability to speak a prophecy, and though he had no idea of the deep meaning of what he was saying, "he spoke not of himself" (Jn 11:49-52).

Our Lord Jesus Christ Himself believed in the word-for-word inspiration of the Old Testament. He showed His view of it when He said, "until heaven and earth pass away, not one jot [the smallest letter] or one tittle [the tiniest stroke of a letter] shall pass away from the law, until all is accomplished" (Mt 5:18; Lk 16:17). "Law" here surely takes in the whole Old Testament, just as (Jn 10:34) uses the word "law" even for the Psalms. On another occasion, Christ rested an entire argument for His own divinity on a single word, "my": "The Lord said unto my Lord" (Ps 110:1); and if David calls Him "Lord," how can He simply be David's son (Mt 22:41-46)? Our Lord laid down as a firm rule that "the Scripture cannot be broken," right down to one word (Jn 10:35). St. Paul, in the same spirit, leans confidently on the exact wording of particular texts: on "seed" rather than "seeds" (Gal 3:16), on "all" (Heb 2:8), on "brethren" (Heb 2:11), on "today," and on "My rest" (Heb 4:1-11). And to top it all off, the very close of the Bible warns, "If any man shall take away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God shall take away his part out of the book of life" (Rev 22:19).

There is one more point that is often misunderstood. In (1 Cor 7:5-6), St. Paul carefully separates what he says "by permission" from what he says "of commandment"; and in verses 25-38 he offers his "judgment," his considered opinion, as a faithful man who admits he has "no commandment of the Lord" on that particular question. Some people wrongly take this to mean Paul is confessing that parts of his letter are not inspired. But that is not it at all. His inspiration actually shows itself precisely here, in the fact that he knows, as an Apostle, exactly when he is passing on a direct command of the Lord and when he is instead giving wise counsel as a Christian brother. In verses 12-15 (compare verse 10) he says of a certain case, "I, not the Lord," while on the main matter he had said, "not I but the Lord." The Lord had already given commands about divorce (Mt 5:31); so now Paul, speaking with the authority handed to him, says "I, not the Lord," meaning simply that he has no earlier word or tradition from the Lord on this exact point, and so he gives his own judgment, still under the steady inspiration that guided the Apostles in all their canonical writings (1 Cor 7:40; 14:34; 1 Thess 4:15). Paul is not marking off an "inspired" part of his letter from an "uninspired" part. He is claiming full authority to lay down doctrine and practice, because, as he says, he too has "the Spirit of God" (1 Cor 7:40).

subsections.heading: INADEQUATE THEORIES OF INSPIRATION
paragraphs: Down through the years, people who were unwilling to accept the full truth about inspiration have offered various watered-down versions of it. Each one falls short, and it is worth seeing exactly where each goes wrong.

NATURAL INSPIRATION, OR THE INTUITION THEORY: This idea says that inspiration is nothing more than an unusually sharp insight belonging to ordinary human genius. On this view, the biblical writers were simply men with especially strong and elevated religious feelings, no different in kind from the passion that stirred poets like Homer or thinkers like Plato. This is really a flat denial of anything supernatural, both in the Bible and in religion as a whole. It ends up putting some of the Church's great hymns on the very same level as the Holy Bible. The mistake at its heart is confusing two different things: the Spirit's work of illumination, which He gives to all believers, and His special work of inspiration, given to the sacred writers alone. Illumination only helps us understand a truth already revealed; it does not deliver that truth in the first place.

DYNAMIC, OR PARTIAL INSPIRATION THEORY: This theory grants that the writers of Scripture were kept from error in matters of faith and practice, but claims they could still slip up in things that are not directly religious. In other words, they might make mistakes in history or science while being reliable in doctrine. This view is common in many Protestant circles and was held by Luther, Calvin, Baxter, Doddridge, and others. It treats the Bible as a revelation of God's will, but leaves the door open for human error in the details, allowing (or at least admitting the possibility) that the writers got some historical or scientific facts wrong. Luther, for all his high regard for St. Paul, once accused the Apostle of faulty reasoning, and he spoke rather dismissively of the Holy Book of Esther. (P. Schaff, "A Religious Encyclopedia…," vol. II, p. 1105) The problem is plain: this theory runs straight against the Bible's own claim that all Scripture, every part of it, is breathed out by God (2 Tim 3:16). You cannot carve Scripture into an inspired zone and an error-prone zone once God has called the whole of it His own.

THEORY THAT THE BIBLE MERELY "CONTAINS" THE WORD OF GOD: This view holds that the Bible is basically a human book, which God can turn into His word in the moment of a personal encounter with the reader. On this theory, the writers were simply recording their own experiences of God, using the ideas and imagination of their own time, and they wove into their accounts all sorts of myths and miracle-stories in order to get across spiritual lessons. Their writing, it is said, only becomes God's word to us in that flash of experience when God breaks through and meets us. This is not a small or harmless view; it is not merely soft on inspiration but flatly denies it. Those who hold it insist the Bible must be "demythologized," so that the reader's task becomes stripping away the supposedly mythical decorations to dig out the spiritual kernel underneath. The strange result is that inspiration gets moved off the text and onto the reader: the Bible is no longer inspired, but the person reading it somehow is.

DICTATION THEORY: Those who defend this idea argue that there is nothing shameful in dictation, especially between God and man, and they point out that even the writers themselves rarely describe such a thing actually happening. They suggest that people who recoil at the word "dictation" are usually thinking too little of God and too much of man, and so they conclude it makes no real difference if the Holy Spirit used the sacred writers as mere instruments, like a pen in a hand or a flute played by a musician. But this theory stumbles badly, because it simply cannot account for the obvious differences in style between Moses, David, Isaiah, James, John, Peter, and Paul. If God had merely dictated word by word to passive scribes, why do these writers sound so distinctly different from one another? We have to hold on to both truths at once: Holy Scripture is at the same time fully divine and fully human. God worked through living men, not lifeless tools. He never erased their personalities, nor stripped away their individual ways of writing, for "where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty" (2 Cor 3:17). Their wills were brought into harmony with God's will, and His Spirit worked upon their spirits in such a way that their own individuality was given free play within the sphere of His inspiration.

subsections.heading: A CLOSING WORD
paragraphs: When we gather all of this together, a clear picture emerges. The Bible is not a human book that talks about God, nor a divine book that swallows up the human writers. It is both fully God's and fully man's at once. God guarded every word without silencing a single personality. He revealed truths we could never have reached on our own, and He saw to it that those truths were written down without error. And the same Spirit who moved the writers still moves in the hearts of readers today, opening the meaning of the sacred page. This is why we come to Scripture not as critics standing over it, but as humble students sitting under it, asking the Author Himself to teach us.
St. Philip: "Do you understand what you are reading?" Ethiopian Eunuch: "How can I, unless someone guides me?" (Acts 8:30-31)
THIS WAS ADAPTED FROM "THE INSPIRATION OF THE HOLY SCRIPTURES" BY FR. SHENOUDA MAHER.
Biblical Interpretation

Every text has to be interpreted, and the Holy Scripture is no exception. In the Holy Book of Nehemiah, we read that the Levites "helped the people to understand the law" (Neh 8:7), and that they "gave the sense, and helped them to understand the reading" (Neh 8:8). Our Lord Jesus Christ interpreted many Old Testament passages for His disciples: "And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, He expounded [explained] to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning Himself" (Lk 24:27). He also challenged the views of the Pharisees about the Sabbath by presenting the correct interpretation of the commandment (Mt 12:7-12). In a real sense, the whole history of Christian theology can be seen as the history of how the Bible has been interpreted.

subsections.heading: THE GOLDEN RULE FOR INTERPRETING HOLY SCRIPTURE
paragraphs: The early Church faced a serious threat from a movement called Gnosticism. This mixed and complicated movement, not unlike today's New Age phenomenon, gained a good deal of influence in the late Roman Empire. The finer points of Gnostic belief need not concern us here; what matters is that Gnosticism looked very much like Christianity at many points. Because of this, many early Christian writers, and St. Irenaeus above all, saw it as a grave danger. On top of that, the Gnostic writers had a habit of twisting New Testament passages in ways that alarmed the Christian leaders and raised the whole question of how Scripture ought rightly to be read.

In that setting, an appeal to tradition became very important. The word "tradition" literally means "that which has been handed down," though it can also refer to "the act of handing down." Irenaeus insisted that the Apostolic Church had faithfully kept the "rule of faith," and that this rule found its expression in the canonical books of Holy Scripture. From the days of the Apostles right up to the present, the Church had preached one and the same Gospel. The Gnostics could make no such claim of unbroken connection with the early Church. They had simply cooked up new ideas and were wrongly labeling them "Christian." Irenaeus therefore stressed the continuity of the teaching and preaching of the Church and its officers.

Tertullian took a related line. Scripture, he argued, can be understood clearly enough, so long as it is read as a whole. Yet he admitted that arguments over the meaning of certain passages were bound to happen. Heretics, he noted grimly, can twist Scripture to say just about anything they wish. For this very reason, the tradition of the Church carried great weight, because it showed how Scripture had been received and understood within the Church from the beginning. The right reading of Scripture, then, was to be found where the true Christian faith and way of life had been kept. St. St. St. Athanasius held a similar view, arguing that Arius' errors about Christ would never have arisen had he stayed faithful to the Church's interpretation of Scripture. Tradition, in this sense, was seen as an inheritance from the Apostles, by which the Church was guided toward a correct reading of Scripture. It was not treated as some "secret extra source of revelation" alongside Scripture; rather, it was the safeguard that kept the Church faithful to the Apostles' teaching instead of drifting off into private, oddball interpretations of the Bible. (Adapted from Alister E. McGrath, "Christian Theology," 1997, Blackwell Publishers)

It is truly sad to watch people who confess the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ, and so are called Christians, twist the word of God and fall into all sorts of heresies. The very word of God that is meant to be food for our souls becomes, for them, a stumbling block on the road to salvation. As Scripture warns, "Now the works of the flesh are evident, which are… dissensions, heresies… those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God" (Gal 5:19-21). St. John Chrysostom captured this sad situation in his introduction to the homilies on the Holy Epistle to the Galatians, where he said, "Diseased persons are injured even by healthy food."

In the sixteenth century, Martin Luther opened the door to the chaotic state of Western Christianity we see today. He put forward his doctrine of Sola Scriptura, or "Scripture alone," as a reaction against the distorted idea of tradition then found in the Roman Catholic Church. He claimed that every individual had the right to interpret Scripture however he or she pleased, without holding to tradition. This threw the door wide open to individualism, lifting the private judgment of each person above the shared judgment of the whole Church. In 1530, Sebastian Franck wrote, "Foolish Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Gregory, of whom not even one knew the Lord, so help me God, nor was sent by God to teach. Rather, they were all apostles of the Antichrist." And what has this so-called "Reformation" produced? Look around and you will find thousands of rival Protestant groups, each claiming to understand the Bible correctly, yet unable to agree on the basic things it says, or even on what it means to be a Christian. Some will even argue fiercely over the very verses that speak of love.

As one writer puts it, "Taken from its context within Holy Tradition, the solid rock of Scripture becomes a mere ball of clay, to be molded into whatever shape its handlers wish. It is no honor to the Scriptures to misuse and twist them, even if this is done in the name of exalting their authority. We must read the Bible; it is God's Holy Word! But to understand its message, let us humbly sit at the feet of the saints who have shown themselves 'doers of the Word and not hearers only' (Jam 1:22), and have been proven by their lives worthy interpreters of the Scriptures. Let us go to those who knew the Apostles, such as Saint Ignatius of Antioch and Polycarp, if we have a question about the writings of the Apostles. Let us inquire of the Church, and not fall into self-deluded arrogance." (Fr. John Whiteford, "Sola Scriptura," 1996, Conciliar Press)

Consider the following verses: "Therefore, brethren, stand fast and hold the traditions which you were taught, whether by word or our epistle" (2 Thess 2:15); and "Now I praise you, brethren, that you remember me in all things and keep the traditions as I delivered them to you" (1 Cor 11:2). The truth is that every Protestant sect has developed its own tradition for interpreting the Bible. "Thus, the question is not really whether we will just believe the Bible or whether we will also use tradition. The real question is, which tradition will we use to interpret the Bible? Which tradition can be trusted: the Apostolic Tradition of the historic Church, or the modern and divergent traditions of Protestantism, which have no roots deeper than the advent of the Protestant Reformation?" (Fr. John Whiteford, "Sola Scriptura," 1996, Conciliar Press)
(Also see Acts 15:27; 2 Thess 3:6; Phil 4:9; 2 Tim 2:2.)

subsections.heading: THE OLD TESTAMENT INTERPRETATION BETWEEN THE CHURCH AND THE SYNAGOGUE
paragraphs: The theologians of the School of Alexandria embraced the allegorical interpretation of the Old Testament, comparing the literal sense of Scripture to the shadow that a body casts, and finding the deeper, truer meaning in the spiritual reality that the shadow points to. They did not wish to belittle or throw out the literal or historical meaning; rather, they regarded it as they would a man's body, worthy of full respect. Origen points out that if the Holy Book of Leviticus were taken only literally, Christians would be obliged "to sacrifice calves and lambs and to offer fine wheat flour with incense and oil." (Allegory means saying one thing while pointing to something beyond what is plainly said.)
── In the New Testament ──

Some scholars believe St. Paul introduced the allegorical reading of the law with his question, "Is it oxen God is concerned about? Or does He say it altogether for our sakes?" (1 Cor 9:9-10). Our Lord interpreted the bronze serpent allegorically (Num 21:9; Jn 3:14-15) as a type of the salvation won by His cross. In (Mt 12:40-42), we recognize Jonah the prophet in the belly of the whale as an allegory of our Lord's burial. Allegory is applied to the cleaning out of the old leaven at Passover to signify the purity of the Christian community (1 Cor 5:6-8). In (Rom 5:14), St. Paul presents Adam as a "type" of our Lord. In (1 Cor 10:6-13), St. Paul teaches that events recorded in the Holy Books of Exodus and Numbers (Ex 13:21-22; 14:22-29; 16:4-35) prefigure the Holy Sacraments.
── In the Sayings of the Fathers ──

1. "Rebecca came to draw water from the well, and because she went every day, it was possible for her to be found by Abraham's servant and be married to Isaac. You think that these are myths, and that the Holy Spirit only records history in the Scriptures. Here is an instruction for the soul and a spiritual teaching, which instructs you to come daily to the wells of the Scriptures… All that has been written points to mysteries: Christ wishes to wed you too, and for that reason sends His servant to you. This servant is the word of the prophets. You cannot be wed to Christ if you have not first received them." (Origen)
2. Chapter 22 of the Holy Book of Genesis is interpreted typologically in the fraction of the Divine Liturgy of Great Thursday (Coptic Liturgy of St. Basil, p. 298).

3. The death of Joseph as a figure of the death of our Lord Jesus Christ: "Joseph, the text says, 'died, and all his brothers and all that generation. But the sons of Israel increased and were multiplied and were extended into a great multitude and became very strong, for the land multiplied them' (Ex 1:6-7). While Joseph was living, it is not reported that the sons of Israel were multiplied, nor is anything at all mentioned about increases and multitudes in those times… If, therefore, Joseph dies in you also, that is, if you take on the dying of Christ in your body and make your members dead to sin, then 'the sons of Israel' are multiplied in you. 'The sons of Israel' are interpreted as good and spiritual senses. If, therefore, the senses of the flesh are put to death, the senses of the spirit increase; and while the vices in you are dying daily, the number of virtues is being increased." (Origen)

4. "We can take the windows (Song 2:9) as meaning the bodily senses, through which life or death gains entrance to the soul; for that is what the prophet Jeremiah means when, speaking of sinners, he says, 'Death is come up through your windows' (Jer 9:21). How does death come up through the windows? If the eyes of a sinner should look on a woman to lust after her; and because he who has thus looked upon a woman has committed adultery with her in his heart, then death has gained entrance to that soul through the windows of the eyes… And likewise, when the soul listens to the Word of God and takes delight in the reasoning of His wisdom and knowledge, the light of wisdom enters her through the windows of her ears." (Origen)

5. "This, then, is why it is said, 'Catch the little foxes.' Fittingly indeed he bids them to be caught and taken while they are still little. For as long as a bad thought is only beginning, it is easily driven from the heart. But if it comes again and again, and goes on for long, it surely leads the soul to agree with it; and once agreed to and settled in the heart, it is certain to result in the committing of sin. It must, therefore, be caught and driven out while it is still small and just beginning; otherwise, once it has grown up and become a matter of habit, it can no longer be driven out. Thus Judas too had a beginning of evil in his love of money, and that was for him a 'little fox.'" (Origen)
"You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God." (Mt 22:29)
THIS WAS ADAPTED FROM "THE SCHOOL OF ALEXANDRIA — BOOK I" BY FR. TADROS Y. MALATY.
Alleged Discrepancies of the Holy Bible

Before we look at any specific example, it would be wise to speak first about the burden of proof. It is a basic rule in philosophy that the one who makes a claim is the one who has to explain and defend it. If someone declares that "X exists," then the responsibility falls on that person to build a case for the existence of "X." The responsibility does not fall on the person who denies it, for how could anyone ever prove a negative? In this matter, it is the critics who are making the claim. They assert that the Holy Bible is riddled with contradictions, and they often present a long list of supposed examples.

Now, as Christians, we cannot prove that something is NOT a contradiction (that is, no one can prove that "X," the contradictions, simply do not exist). All that is asked of us is to offer a reasonable explanation, so that what is claimed to be a contradiction is shown not to be necessarily a contradiction at all. If we manage this, then the critics' confident assertion that "X" and "Y" clash is no longer an obvious fact; it becomes merely one possible opinion that a person may hold.

At this point the critics might cry "foul" and point out that it is really the Christians who are making a claim, since we are the ones who say the Holy Bible is without error, and so we ought to prove it. But how? How can anyone demonstrate that a whole document contains no error? Here the Christian need only borrow a page from the playbook of modern atheism. Many atheists do not argue outright that God does not exist, because they know one cannot prove the non-existence of something. Instead, they take a more agnostic stance and simply argue that there is no proof for God's existence, and so they hold no belief in God. In the very same way, the believer in inerrancy cannot prove the non-existence of contradictions in the Holy Bible. After all, the Holy Bible contains 31,173 verses. If we compared them two at a time, setting any one verse against any other, we could form more than 971 million pairs. So, looking at pairs alone, there are nearly one billion possible "contradictions"! Surely it is not reasonable to demand that a believer in inerrancy trudge through a billion potential pairs, proving a negative in every single case. Instead, the believer can simply say that there is no proof for the existence of contradictions in the Bible, and therefore he does not believe the Bible errs; which is to say, he believes it is inerrant, without error.

subsections.heading: ERRONEOUS ASSUMPTIONS EMPLOYED BY CRITICS
paragraphs: a) Taking things out of context. A very common mistake is to lift a passage out of its setting. It is easy to manufacture contradictions where none exist by ignoring the context of the passages in question. Even more important is the context of belief. Christian understanding is a woven-together whole made up of many beliefs, and biblical teachings are usually read against this background. That background may include other facts, not directly tied to the supposed contradiction, but still relevant to it. When a critic proposes a contradiction, he ought to argue from within this background; when he fails to do so, he is simply forcing in foreign ideas as if they belonged. For example: suppose Joe is recorded saying that Sam is not his son, while elsewhere he is recorded saying that Sam is his son. An obvious contradiction, right? But what if the background includes the fact that Sam is Joe's adopted son? By ignoring the context that this fact supplies, a person sees a contradiction where there is none.

b) Assuming the accounts are exhaustive and exact. The critics often take it for granted that the biblical accounts record every detail and are meant to be precise. This is rarely so. Building on this faulty assumption, they see contradictions that are not there. It ties in with the context problem. Suppose the only records of Joe speaking about Sam are the two statements where he affirms and denies that Sam is his son. Of course Joe said countless other things in his life that were never written down, including the fact that he adopted a boy and named him Sam. Consider a real-life case: a newspaper reported the birth times of twin babies, the first born at 1:40 AM and the second at 1:10 AM. Without the added detail that the births happened on the very night when daylight saving time ended, this would LOOK like a plain contradiction. But it was not; you simply have to know the whole story. Since the accounts in the Holy Bible are rarely meant to be exhaustive and exact, it is wise to check whether different accounts complete one another rather than contradict.

c) Assuming the Bible is written in a single genre. The critics often treat the whole Bible as if it were one kind of writing, a flat, literal report. While the Holy Bible certainly contains literal and descriptive accounts (which, again, are not exhaustive in detail), it also contains many other styles: the Psalms speak through poetry, many teachings and prophecies come in the form of hyperbole and metaphor, parables carry deeper messages, and so on. Since the Holy Bible is really a whole library of books in different genres, the critics' one-size-fits-all assumption leads them astray when they use it to hunt for contradictions.

d) Depending on a particular interpretation. This point is related to the last. Many so-called contradictions exist only under one specific interpretation. The clash appears only if the critic reads the passage a certain way, and often that reading is not the correct one. For instance, critics frequently take particular incidents or general rules of thumb and treat them as though they were absolute, universal principles.

e) Equivocating. Sometimes the critics play on words. They use a single sense of a word across two sets of verses, when in fact the word carries two different meanings. For example, "peace" can mean the absence of war, or it can mean an inner sense of calm and tranquility. (See example 8 below.)

f) Reading contradictions into the text. The critics often read clashes into the accounts that are not really there. This is frequently a byproduct of the errors already listed, but sometimes it is simply due to ignorance. In other cases, it happens because features of Hebrew idiom do not always carry over cleanly into English translations.

g) Assuming inerrancy means the copyists were flawless. The critics suppose that anyone who believes in biblical inerrancy must also believe that no copyist ever made a mistake. But that is not our position. We believe that the original documents were without error, and that they were then copied as faithfully as humanly possible. Copyist slips, therefore, are a minor matter and are very unlikely to have produced any significant change in meaning.

h) Black-and-white thinking. Finally, the critics often fall into rigid "either/or" thinking when a "both/and" approach is what the passage actually calls for. This one can be subtle, so see the first example below. (Adapted from Andrew Tong, "Intro to Contradictions")

subsections.heading: EXAMPLES OF PURPORTED CONTRADICTIONS
paragraphs: 1. "Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you also be like him" (Prov 26:4). "Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes" (Prov 26:5).

The first thing to notice is that these seemingly clashing sayings sit right next to each other. Could the Holy Spirit contradict Himself within a single breath? Of course not. In fact, it is very telling that these two verses are placed so closely together. They show that some biblical instructions are not meant to be read as "either/or," but as "both/and." When debating various non-Christians or non-Orthodox, you may run into foolish replies and name-calling. Sometimes you will choose not to respond and simply let the foolishness pass; at those times you are following (Prov 26:4). At other times you will answer the foolishness of your opponent, hoping that when you refute it he may see the folly of his own approach; at those times you are following (Prov 26:5). In every case, you need the guidance of the Holy Spirit to know which path to take.
2. "All the persons of the house of Jacob who went to Egypt were seventy" (Gen 46:27). "Joseph sent and called his father Jacob and all his relatives to him, seventy-five people" (Acts 7:14).

In (Gen 46:26-27) we read, "All the persons who went with Jacob to Egypt, who came from his body, besides Jacob's sons' wives, were sixty-six persons in all. And the sons of Joseph who were born to him in Egypt were two persons. All the persons of the house of Jacob who went to Egypt were seventy." Notice that in the Holy Book of Genesis the wives are not counted, but Jacob, Joseph, and his two sons are. This gives a total of 66 + 4 (Jacob, Joseph, and his 2 sons) = 70. In (Acts 7:14) we read that Joseph sent and called his father and all his relatives. Here, Joseph, his wife, and his two sons are not counted, since they were already in Egypt, and Jacob is not counted, as the verse implies; but the wives are now added, giving a total of 66 + 9 (Judah's and Simeon's wives had already died, according to Gen 38:12; 46:10) = 75. The two numbers simply count different groups.
3. "And those who died in the plague were twenty-four thousand" (Num 25:9). "Nor let us commit sexual immorality, as some of them did, and in one day twenty-three thousand fell" (1 Cor 10:8).

This one is straightforward. The Holy Book of Numbers gives the TOTAL number of those who died in the plague, while St. Paul gives the number who fell on one single day. There is no conflict between a total and a daily count.
4. Some claim there is a contradiction in the order of the three temptations of our Lord Jesus Christ as recorded in the Holy Gospels of St. Matthew and St. Luke (Mt 4:1-11; Lk 4:1-13).

St. Matthew lists the temptations in the order in which they happened, while St. Luke arranges them according to where they took place. So St. Luke groups together the temptations that occurred in the wilderness before mentioning the one that occurred in Jerusalem. The difference is one of arrangement, not of fact.

5. "Then he threw down the pieces of silver in the temple and departed, and went and hanged himself. But the chief priests took the silver pieces and said, 'It is not lawful to put them in the treasury, because they are the price of blood.' And they took counsel and bought with them the potter's field, to bury strangers in" (Mt 27:5-7). "Now this man (Judas) purchased a field with the wages of iniquity; and falling headlong, he burst open in the middle, and all his entrails gushed out" (Acts 1:18).

Two questions arise from these verses. First, what happened to Judas? The two accounts do not clash but complete each other: Judas hanged himself, as St. Matthew tells us, and afterward his body fell and burst open, as the Holy Book of Acts tells us. Second, who bought the potter's field? The chief priests physically went, paid the money, and bought the field, as St. Matthew says; but St. Luke links Judas to the purchase because Judas, through his betrayal money, was the real cause of it in the first place. (A similar way of speaking appears in the next example.)

6. "Now it was the Preparation Day of the Passover, and about the sixth hour. And he said to the Jews, 'Behold your King!'… So he delivered Him to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus and led Him away" (Jn 19:14-16). "Now it was the third hour, and they crucified Him" (Mk 15:25).

When exactly was our Lord crucified? St. John says the sixth hour, and the Church has us remember the crucifixion every time we pray the prayer of the sixth hour; so why does St. Mark say the third hour? At the third hour, the Jews were crying out, "Crucify Him! Crucify Him!" And even though the Roman soldiers physically nailed our Lord to the cross at the sixth hour (as St. John records), St. Mark wanted to lay the blame on the Jews who handed Him over to Pilate. In other words, St. Mark is saying, "Now it was the third hour, and they [the Jews] crucified Him."

7. "Very early in the morning, on the first day of the week, they came to the tomb when the sun had risen" (Mk 16:2). "On the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark…" (Jn 20:1).

Had the sun risen, or was it still dark? St. John describes the start of the journey, when it was still dark, while St. Mark describes the end of it, once the sun had risen. Others have suggested that St. John speaks of a first visit to the tomb and St. Mark of a second. Either way, there is no real contradiction.

8. "The men who journeyed with him stood speechless, hearing a voice but seeing no one" (Acts 9:7). "Now those who were with me indeed saw the light and were afraid, but they did not hear the voice of Him who spoke to me" (Acts 22:9).

The word "hear" in the second verse carries the sense of "understand." We see this same usage elsewhere: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear" (Mt 11:15); and "Those who heard it, being convicted by their conscience, went out one by one, beginning with the oldest even to the last" (Jn 8:9). So the men traveling with St. Paul on the road to Damascus heard a voice but did not grasp what was being said. And of course there is no clash between "seeing the light" in the second verse and "seeing no one" in the first, since they refer to different things.
"Speak, Lord, for Your servant hears." (1 Sam 3:9)
Practical tips on reading the Holy Scriptures

subsections.heading: INTRODUCTION
paragraphs: There are three main ways to read the Holy Bible. First, you can read it just to learn what it says: its stories, commandments, and teachings. Second, you can stop at a verse or story and think about it slowly, for spiritual benefit. Third, you can study it closely, using helps like Bible dictionaries, atlases, and encyclopedias, and most of all the writings of the Church Fathers.

It is important to keep a steady, ongoing relationship with God's word. Keep a regular reading plan that covers both the Old and New Testaments. Try to combine these three ways of reading as much as you can, or at least the first two.
