But kings can act unfairly and not always look out for their people. So calling God a "King" might wrongly suggest He is harsh or unfair. But the Bible also says a father is tender toward his children (Psalm 103:13-18), and a good shepherd is fully devoted to his flock (John 10:11). These show that God's authority is meant to be gentle and wise, not harsh.
── METAPHOR ──

People still debate the exact difference between an analogy and a metaphor. Here is one way to think about it: an analogy feels natural and expected, while a metaphor feels surprising or even shocking at first. Compare these two statements:
• God is wise.
• God is like a thief (Revelation 3:3; 16:15)

The first statement feels natural, since we already connect the idea of "wisdom" with God. The second one feels strange, since it doesn't seem right to compare God to a thief. So a metaphor mixes together things that are alike and things that are not alike, showing both similarities and differences at the same time.

subsections.heading: THE SOURCES OF THEOLOGY
paragraphs: Like most fields of study, Christian theology draws on several sources. There are four main ones:
1. Holy Tradition 2. Holy Scripture 3. Reason 4. Experience
── REASON ──

Since humans are rational beings, it makes sense that reason plays a big part in theology. But Christianity is not limited to only what reason alone can figure out. Faith goes beyond reason. It gives us access to truths that reason could never discover on its own. So faith doesn't fight against reason. It builds on it and adds to it. Reason's job is to build on what God has revealed and explore what it means.

In this way, theology is a reasonable, logical field of study that uses reason to build on what has been revealed. Christian theology is like a cathedral. It stands on the solid ground of human reason, but its towers rise far above what reason alone could reach. It rests on a rational base, but the building itself goes beyond what reason alone could build.
── EXPERIENCE ──

We can talk about God's existence using Scripture, Tradition, and reason (Romans 1:20). But eventually, like Job, we will say, "I have said things I did not understand, things too wonderful for me to know" (Job 42:3). Still, once a person who speaks about God actually experiences God in their own life, their words take on new depth. They can say to God, "I heard about You before [through Tradition], but now my eyes have seen You [through experience]" (Job 42:5).

The early Church Fathers who taught us about God had a deep personal relationship with Him. Their theology was backed up by real, personal experience. This is why they were able to stand firm against false teaching.

subsections.heading: WHY SPEAK ABOUT GOD?
paragraphs: We speak about God because we love Him, and talking about Him brings joy to our souls (Saturday Psali). We also love our Orthodox Christian faith, so we defend it and explain it to others. We love the people around us, and we want to share the true teaching about God so they can come to know and experience Him too. Finally, we reject false teachings and heresies (Revelation 2:6,15), so we speak the truth about God and all Christian teaching to expose the lies of the devil, who is the source of all heresy.

subsections.heading: ORTHODOXY AND HERESY
paragraphs: The word "Orthodoxy" literally means "correct belief" (Greek: *orthos*, correct + *doxa*, belief). "Heresy" (Greek: *hairesis*, meaning "choice" or "sect") is defined as a religious belief that goes against the accepted teachings of a church.

Since "theology" means "speaking about God," it's important to remember that God does not accept false theology, or heresy. God told Job's friend, "My anger burns against you and your two friends, because you have not spoken the truth about Me" (Job 42:7). St. Paul also warns that those who follow heresies will not inherit God's kingdom, listing heresy among sins like idolatry, hatred, and jealousy (Galatians 6:19-21).

The Existence of God

subsections.heading: FAITH AND REASON
paragraphs: People often discuss whether God's existence can be proven, and whether such proof would be enough to bring a non-believer to faith. Reason alone may not bring someone to faith in God. Still, believers can give reasonable explanations for their faith. Our knowledge of God, and our certainty that He exists, comes through personally experiencing Him in our lives. Rational reasons can help us appreciate that God is real. The reasons below are meant to strengthen the faith of those who already know and worship God. They are also meant to help those who are still searching.

subsections.heading: THE THREE TYPES OF ATHEISTS
paragraphs: 1. The Absolute Atheist: This is someone who denies that God exists at all.

2. The Providential Atheist (also called a "Deist"): The word "deism" (from the Latin *deus*, meaning "god") is generally used for the view that God created the world but does not stay involved in it or continue to be present within it. This type of atheist denies that God cares for or acts within the world. This differs from "theism" (from the Greek *theos*, meaning "god"), which holds that God stays actively involved in the world.

3. The Practical Atheist: This person does not deny that God exists, but through their actions, sin, and neglect of God, they live as if He does not exist. "They claim to know God, but their actions deny Him. They are detestable, disobedient, and unfit for any good work" (Titus 1:16).

In every atheist, there is a moral flaw. "The fool has said in his heart, 'There is no God.' They are corrupt, they do detestable things, there is no one who does good" (Psalm 14:1). People deny God because they want to be free from responsibility for their sins, like those who avoid the light because their actions are evil (John 3:19-20).

subsections.heading: ARGUMENTS FOR GOD'S EXISTENCE
paragraphs: ── 1. PASCAL'S WAGER ──

Blaise Pascal (1623 to 1662) was a French philosopher, scientist, and mathematician. He argued for God's existence using the idea of a bet. His reasoning was based on the fact that a rational person, given two choices, will pick the one with the best chance of a reward. For example, if someone tells you your house is on fire, it might be true or it might not be. Checking costs you very little, but not checking could cost you everything if the house really is burning. It would be foolish not to check.
In the same way, God either exists or He does not.
• If we believe in God and He exists, we gain eternal life in heaven.
• If we believe in God and He does not exist, at worst we only miss out on some sinful pleasures.
• If we do not believe in God and He exists, we face eternal punishment.
• If we do not believe in God and He does not exist, our sins go unpunished either way.

If we bet that God exists and we are right, we gain everything. If we bet that God exists and we are wrong, we lose nothing. But if we bet that God does not exist and we are wrong, we lose everything.

Would a reasonable gambler ever place a bet where they can only lose everything and gain nothing? The only sensible choice is to bet that God exists. With this bet, we have everything to gain and nothing to lose. As Scripture says, "The fool has said in his heart, 'There is no God'" (Psalm 14:1; 53:1).
── 2. THE ARGUMENT FROM MOTION ──
The world is not still. It is always changing. Rain falls, stones roll downhill, the earth moves around the sun. So how did nature start moving in the first place? Why isn't everything still?
• Every motion has a cause. Things do not move on their own. They are moved by something else.
• Each cause of motion must have its own cause, and that cause must have a cause too.
• Eventually there must be one first cause that is not moved by anything else. All other motion comes from this first cause.
This first, unmoved cause is God.
── 3. THE ARGUMENT FROM THE CAUSE OF EXISTENCE ──

Common sense tells us that nothing creates itself. Something else must have caused it to exist. So there must have been one first, uncaused cause, which is God, that started the chain of everything that exists. If a child comes home with a black eye, we assume something caused it. We would not accept "it just happened" as an answer. The same logic applies to the universe. Like the black eye, it did not just happen. It had a cause, and that cause was God.

The second law of thermodynamics states that the amount of usable energy in a system is always decreasing. As usable energy decreases, disorder (called entropy) increases. In other words, things naturally move toward disorder, not order, and useful energy is lost along the way. Eventually the universe will run down, and all life and motion will stop. This is the natural direction of all things. Batteries run down, machines break, buildings fall apart, roads wear out, living things die.
• The universe cannot be infinitely old, because it has not yet reached total disorder.
a. If it were infinitely old, it would have reached total disorder long ago. b. Since it has not, the universe must have had a beginning.
• Because the universe had a beginning, it cannot be infinite in size.
a. Becoming infinite in size would take infinite time. Since the universe has not had infinite time, it must be limited in size.
• All events have causes.
a. There cannot be an endless chain of causes going back forever, because that would mean the universe is infinitely old, which we already showed it is not.
• Since the universe is limited in size, had a beginning, and cannot have an endless chain of causes, there must be one single cause that itself has no cause.

a. This first cause must be greater, in both size and duration, than the universe it created. Otherwise, it could not have caused something equal to or greater than itself. b. Anything that is a natural part of the universe cannot cause the whole universe to exist, since it is only a part of what needs a cause. c. So the first, uncaused cause cannot be a natural part of the limited universe. It must be infinite in both space and time, since it is greater than everything it caused.
• This uncaused cause must be supernatural, meaning completely different from the universe itself.
a. This uncaused, supernatural cause is God.
── 4. THE ARGUMENT FROM DEPENDENT AND NECESSARY BEINGS ──

There are two kinds of things in the universe: dependent beings and necessary beings. A dependent being is something that cannot exist unless something else, a necessary being, causes it to exist. Human beings are like this. We are not here out of necessity. Our existence needs an explanation. Why are we here? What caused us to exist?
Because dependent beings exist, there must be something that exists on its own and does not depend on anything else. This necessary being is what we call God.
── 5. THE ARGUMENT FROM HUMAN VALUES ──

Where do human values like truth, goodness, and honor come from? Something must exist that is itself fully true, good, and honorable, and that gives rise to our ideas of these things. God is the source of these ideas. For any quality, such as goodness, beauty, or knowledge, there must be a perfect standard that all examples of that quality are measured against. These perfect standards exist in God.

We also know deep down that doing good is right and doing evil is wrong. Even in a society focused on material things, almost everyone, whether Christian or atheist, feels a sense of duty to do good. This sense of duty only makes sense if there is a basic moral standard, God, that exists beyond human life and has the authority to require moral behavior from us.
── 6. THE ARGUMENT FROM INTELLIGENT DESIGN ──

If you found a clock and looked closely at how it worked, you would likely conclude that something this detailed was designed, not the product of random chance. No reasonable person believes that great works of art, like Michelangelo's David or Beethoven's symphonies, came from random accidents. We know from experience that such beautiful creations come from an artist, not from chance.

Now look at the universe. Could something this complex, from the paths planets take around the sun to the cells in your fingernails, really happen by accident? This enormously complex system must have been designed, and the one who designed it is God. Anyone who does not believe God created the universe must instead believe the laws that govern it appeared by pure chance. The odds of that happening are so incredibly small that it defies reason.
• Human-made objects are the result of intelligent design.
• The universe resembles human-made objects, but on a far greater scale.
• Therefore, the universe is also the result of intelligent design.
• Since the universe is far more complex and massive than anything humans make, its designer must be extremely powerful and intelligent.
• That designer is God.
"Since the creation of the world, God's invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen and understood through what He has made" (Romans 1:20).
The Attributes of God

subsections.heading: THE DIVINE ATTRIBUTES
paragraphs: We have already established that a Personal First Cause exists on His own, separate from everything He created. In this section, with God's grace, we will look at some of His attributes, focusing on questions that have come up throughout history and in modern times.

subsections.heading: 1. GOD IS SPIRIT
paragraphs: "God is Spirit" (John 4:24), meaning He has no physical body or form. St. Paul said, "We should not think that the Divine Nature is like gold, silver, or stone, something shaped by human hands and imagination" (Acts 17:29). He also said, "the Lord is the Spirit" (2 Corinthians 3:17). God commanded the people of Israel, "You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything in heaven above, on the earth below, or in the water under the earth" (Exodus 20:4). This command teaches us that God's nature is far above any physical form we can see.

Even though God is Spirit, He has appeared in physical forms to communicate with His creation. For example, He appeared to Moses in a flame of fire coming from a bush (Exodus 3:2), and to Abraham as a man (Genesis 18:2). In the New Testament, God appeared to John the Baptist as a dove (Luke 3:22), and at Pentecost as tongues of fire (Acts 2:3).
── WHAT IS ANTHROPOMORPHISM? ──

Anthropomorphism is a false belief that pictures the eternal, spiritual God as having a human body, with a mouth, eyes, hands, and feet, reducing His Divine Nature down to a human form. This comes from wrongly reading the many biblical comparisons and word pictures too literally, images God has graciously used to help us understand Him in a way we can grasp.

Still, God clearly said, "Be very careful, for you saw no form when the Lord spoke to you at Horeb out of the fire. Do not act wrongly and make for yourselves a carved image, in the shape of any figure, whether male or female" (Deuteronomy 4:15,16). This kind of thinking leads people to act wrongly and to build a false mental image of God.
── IS GOD MALE? ──

Modern feminism has often come into conflict with Christianity, partly because Scripture uses mostly male language and male comparisons for God. Does this mean God is male? God is Spirit, and spirits are beyond gender, which belongs to the physical body. For example, there are no male or female angels, as Jesus Christ pointed out to the Sadducees in Matthew 22:30, because angels are spirits (Psalm 104:4). Deuteronomy 4:16 also makes clear that God is not "in the likeness of male or female."

Even though Scripture mostly uses male language for God, it also uses some female images. For example: "As a mother comforts her child, so I will comfort you" (Isaiah 66:13), and "Can a mother forget the baby at her breast and have no compassion on the child she has borne? Even if she should forget, I will not forget you" (Isaiah 49:15). The Wisdom of God, which refers to Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 1:24; Colossians 2:3), is also described using feminine language in the Book of Proverbs.

Since "the letter kills" (2 Corinthians 3:6), none of these male or female images should lead us to think God is literally male or female. For example, St. Paul writes to the whole Corinthian church, both men and women, married and unmarried, saying, "I have promised you to one husband, so that I might present you as a pure virgin to Christ" (2 Corinthians 11:2), calling the entire church a "bride."

subsections.heading: 2. GOD IS ETERNAL
paragraphs: Moses wrote, "Before the mountains were born, before You brought forth the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting You are God" (Psalm 90:2). To say God is eternal means He is beyond all limits of time. He has no beginning, no end, and no sequence of moments passing one after another.

This does not simply mean God lasts for an unlimited amount of time. It means He is completely outside of the limits that time itself creates. God's eternity is tied to the fact that He exists on His own and is infinite. Since time only measures limited, finite things, whatever is truly infinite must be beyond it. Even though God is present alongside time, His own existence is timeless.

We sometimes talk about "infinite" time or space, meaning a length of time or amount of space so large we can't set a fixed limit on it. But since this kind of "infinite" time or space is still made up of countable parts, it is actually still finite compared to God's true infinity.

subsections.heading: 3. GOD IS EVERYWHERE PRESENT
paragraphs: King David said to God, "Where can I go from Your Spirit? Where can I flee from Your presence? If I go up to the heavens, You are there. If I make my bed in the depths, You are there. If I rise on the wings of the dawn, if I settle on the far side of the sea, even there Your hand will guide me" (Psalm 139:7-10).

Space, like time, is a measure of limited things. Just as God's eternity means He is beyond all limits of time, His presence everywhere means He is beyond all limits of space. This means two things: first, that God is truly present everywhere, actively sustaining everything that exists, and second, that He is not contained, measured, or divided by space the way physical things are.
── WHAT IS PANTHEISM? ──

Pantheism is a false teaching that claims God and the universe are the same thing. It focuses only on the idea that God is present everywhere, but denies that God is a Person or that He exists beyond and above the universe. It claims God is simply the sum of everything that exists. Hinduism is built on this belief. Christianity, on the other hand, teaches that God is present everywhere while also existing beyond and above the created world.

subsections.heading: 4. GOD IS UNCHANGEABLE
paragraphs: St. James said that with God "there is no change or shifting shadow" (James 1:17). King David also said to God, "Like a robe You will roll them [the heavens] up, and like clothing they will be changed. But You remain the same, and Your years will never end" (Psalm 102:26,27).

To say God is unchangeable means His nature never changes. If God's nature could change, it would mean either a move away from perfection, meaning He is no longer perfect, or a move toward perfection, meaning He was not perfect before. Neither is possible.
── DID GOD STOP BEING UNCHANGEABLE DURING THE INCARNATION? ──

Change only applies to the human nature of Jesus Christ, as Scripture says, "Jesus grew in wisdom and stature" (Luke 2:52). His Divine Nature did not change because of the Incarnation. We confess that His Divine and Human Natures were joined together without mixing, confusion, change, or separation.
── CAN GOD SUFFER? ──

God's Divine Nature cannot suffer. This is called God's "impassibility," meaning He cannot experience anything we would call suffering. Even so, during the Incarnation, His Divine Nature was joined, without mixing, confusion, change, or separation, with the human nature of Jesus Christ, including during His suffering on the cross.

This can be compared to fire joined with iron. As the iron is hammered and bends, the fire stays joined to it without being changed itself. In the same way, when Jesus Christ died, His human spirit was separated from His human body, but His Divine Nature, which cannot die, was never separated from either one.
── DID THE DIVINE NATURE ITSELF SUFFER? ──

St. Cyril of Alexandria explained, in his first letter to Nestorius, that Christ suffered and rose again, but not because God the Word suffered wounds or pain in His own Divine Nature, since the Godhead cannot suffer and has no body. Rather, because the body that had become His own suffered these things, He is said to have suffered for us, since the One who cannot suffer was present within the body that did suffer. The same is true of His death. God the Word is by nature immortal and gives life to all things, but because His own body, by God's grace, tasted death for everyone, He Himself is said to have suffered death for us. This does not mean He experienced death in His own Divine Nature, but that His flesh tasted death. In the same way, when His flesh was raised, the resurrection is credited to Him, not because His Divine Nature had decayed, but because His body was raised.

We confess one Christ and Lord. We do not worship a man alongside the Word as if they were two separate beings joined together. We worship one and the same Person, since the body with which He now sits at the Father's right hand truly belongs to the Word Himself. It is not that two sons sit with the Father, but one Son united with His own flesh. If we reject this personal union, we end up saying there are two sons: one who is simply a man given the honor of being called "son," and another who is the Word of God, who alone truly has the nature and title of Son.

St. Cyril is saying that the Divine Nature cannot suffer and cannot die, but since the body Christ took on is mortal and capable of suffering, and since His Divine Nature was joined with that body, the Word is rightly said to have suffered and to have died. St. Cyril stresses that this does not mean the Word experienced death in His own Divine Nature.

St. Cyril also wrote, in his twelfth point of correction, that whoever does not recognize that the Word of God suffered in the flesh, was crucified in the flesh, tasted death in that same flesh, and became the first to rise from the dead, since as God He is life and gives life, is mistaken. St. Cyril's focus is on the phrase "in the flesh." He is not saying the Divine Nature itself suffered or died after the union, but that the Word suffered and died in the flesh. His Divine Nature remained joined with His human nature without change, and stayed incapable of suffering even after the union, yet the suffering is rightly credited to Him.

This becomes clearer when we compare it to what Nestorius argued in response: that if anyone, while confessing the sufferings of the flesh, also credits them to the Word of God as though they belonged to the flesh He appeared in, without properly distinguishing the two natures, that person is mistaken.

St. Cyril is saying the sufferings of the flesh are rightly credited to the Word of God because the Word was joined with that flesh, not because His Divine Nature itself suffered. Nestorius, who wanted to keep the two natures more separated, objected to this way of speaking.

Notice that neither St. Cyril nor Nestorius claimed that the Divine Nature suffered in itself. St. Cyril says the Word suffered "in the flesh," while Nestorius says the Word "never suffered at all." The Word cannot suffer physically, emotionally, or psychologically, yet He took on a complete human nature, with real emotions and a real human personality. This is how the prophecy of Isaiah was fulfilled: "it pleased the Lord to crush Him, and He caused Him grief" (Isaiah 53:10), fulfilled in the Incarnation of the Word.
── THE EXAMPLE OF THE LORD'S CIRCUMCISION ──

This event is celebrated as a feast because the Lord, the Word made flesh, accepted circumcision in His body. No one would say His Divine Nature was circumcised, yet this act of the flesh is credited to the Word, because He was fully joined with that flesh. The same applies to His suffering and death. He suffered and died in the flesh, while His Divine Nature remained incapable of suffering and unable to die.

The Word is Spirit, yet He took on flesh, and circumcision is credited to Him. The Word is immortal, yet He took on flesh, and death is credited to Him. The Word cannot suffer, yet He took on flesh, and suffering is credited to Him. None of this lessens the reality of the Lord's suffering. As St. Cyril taught, the suffering happened "in the flesh" and is rightly "credited" to Him. At the same time, we hold firmly that His Divine attributes were not changed by the Incarnation.

In the Church's prayers for the Lord's feasts, we say of the Incarnate Word that "He grew little by little," as it is written, "Jesus grew in wisdom and stature" (Luke 2:52). The Divine Word, who is Spirit, clearly does not grow physically. The Divine Word, who is "the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24), does not grow in wisdom, since His Divine Nature cannot change. Yet this growth in wisdom and stature is credited to the Divine Word, since His Divine Nature was joined with His human nature in the Incarnation, so the unchangeable Word grew in wisdom and stature in the flesh.

subsections.heading: 5. GOD IS ALL-POWERFUL
paragraphs: God said to Moses, "I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob as God Almighty" (Exodus 6:3), and the Nicene Creed says, "We believe in one God, the Father, the Almighty." Belief in God as almighty, or all-powerful, is a core part of the Orthodox Christian faith. But what does it actually mean to say God is all-powerful? The simple answer is that God can do anything.
── CAN GOD CREATE A STONE TOO HEAVY FOR HIM TO LIFT? ──
If God cannot create such a stone, it seems His power has a limit. But if He could create it, then there would be something He could not do, lift that stone, and again His power would seem limited.

The real meaning of God's all-powerful nature is that He can do anything that does not involve a logical contradiction. For example, God cannot make a square circle or a round triangle, since these are contradictions in terms, not real things. Once God chooses to act in a certain way, other conflicting options are automatically excluded. Saying something like "God can give a creature free will while also withholding free will from it at the same time" is not actually saying anything meaningful about God. Empty, self-contradictory phrases do not become meaningful just because we put the words "God can" in front of them.

It remains true that all real things are possible for God. Logical impossibilities are not "things" at all. So God cannot do what is logically impossible, and He cannot do anything that goes against His own nature and character. For instance, sin is a failure to be perfect. Being able to sin would mean being able to fall short, which cannot be true of an all-powerful, perfect God. In fact, it is precisely because God is all-powerful that He cannot sin.
• "He cannot deny Himself" (2 Timothy 2:13)
• "It is impossible for God to lie" (Hebrews 6:18)
• "God cannot be tempted by evil" (James 1:13)
── THE PROBLEM OF EVIL AND SUFFERING ──

If God is good, He would want His creatures to be fully happy. If God is all-powerful, He would be able to make that happen. Yet His creatures are not always happy. Some argue this means God must lack either goodness, power, or both. This is the basic shape of the problem of evil and suffering. Can evil and suffering really be reconciled with a God who is both good and all-powerful?

God, in His goodness, created everything good (Genesis 1:12,25,31). Free will is itself a good gift God gave His creatures. Evil is the direct result of creatures misusing that freedom. Even so, evil is temporary, and goodness will win out forever: "I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away" (Revelation 21:1). St. Paul wrote that "creation itself will be set free from its slavery to decay and brought into the glorious freedom of God's children" (Romans 8:21).

God's power and goodness can even turn evil into good. For example, Joseph told his brothers, "You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring about what is happening today, the saving of many lives" (Genesis 50:20). Indeed, "all things work together for the good of those who love God" (Romans 8:28). Regarding suffering, St. Paul wrote, "I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed in us" (Romans 8:18), and, "our light and momentary troubles are producing for us a far greater and eternal glory, as we fix our eyes not on what is seen, but on what is unseen. For what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal" (2 Corinthians 4:17,18).

Question: If God created everything good, as Genesis records, then what do these verses mean? "I form the light and create darkness, I bring prosperity and create disaster; I, the Lord, do all these things" (Isaiah 45:7). "When disaster comes to a city, has not the Lord caused it?" (Amos 3:6). Is disaster a "good" thing?

Answer: First, the verse in Isaiah is meant to stress that there is only one God, since some ancient nations believed in separate gods for good and evil: "so that from the rising of the sun to the place of its setting, people may know there is none besides Me. I am the Lord, and there is no other. I form the light and create darkness, I bring prosperity and create disaster; I, the Lord, do all these things" (Isaiah 45:6,7).

Second, neither verse means that God is the direct cause or source of disaster. Rather, they mean that no disaster happens without God's permission. This is clear from the story of Job, where Satan caused Job's suffering, but only by God's permission. Even so, Job said to his wife, "Shall we accept good from God, and not trouble?" (Job 2:10), treating the hardship as coming from God even though it was really Satan's doing.

Finally, hardship can genuinely lead to something good, as in the story of Lazarus and the rich man (Luke 16:19-30). Lazarus's earthly suffering led to his eternal comfort, as Abraham told the rich man, "Son, remember that in your lifetime you received your good things, while Lazarus received bad things, but now he is comforted here and you are in agony" (Luke 16:25). As Scripture says, "we must go through many hardships to enter the kingdom of God" (Acts 14:21). Another example is St. Paul's illness (2 Corinthians 12:7), which kept him from becoming proud because of the great revelations he had received.

subsections.heading: 6. GOD IS ALL-KNOWING
paragraphs: Scripture says of God, "Nothing in all creation is hidden from God's sight. Everything is uncovered and laid bare before the eyes of Him to whom we must give account" (Hebrews 4:13). God is all-knowing. His knowledge of everything is complete and perfect.
── DOES GOD'S FOREKNOWLEDGE CONTROL OUR DECISIONS? ──

We need to separate God's knowledge from God's will. For example, God "wants all people to be saved" (1 Timothy 2:4), yet not everyone will be saved, and God knows this. Those who are ultimately lost will lose their salvation because they misused their own free will, not because God simply knew about it ahead of time.
"Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory" (Isaiah 6:3).
Biblical Foundations of the Trinitarian Faith

subsections.heading: THE HOLY TRINITY
paragraphs: Some people who question the doctrine of the Holy Trinity say it really teaches three gods, not one. They argue that God the Father, plus the Son, plus the Holy Spirit, equals three gods. But this is not the only logical way to look at it. Instead of adding, why not think of it as multiplying? God the Father times the Son times the Holy Spirit equals one God. There is no requirement that addition is the only way to judge this doctrine. In truth, the doctrine should stand or fall based on what the Bible actually teaches, not on human logic alone.

Because the word "Trinity" never appears in the Bible itself, some wonder whether this is really a biblical teaching. But just because a word used to describe a doctrine is missing from Scripture does not mean the doctrine itself is unbiblical. The real question is whether the term accurately describes what Scripture teaches. For example, words like "Omniscient" (all-knowing), "Omnipotent" (all-powerful), and "Omnipresent" (present everywhere) also never appear in the Bible. Yet we use these words to describe God's nature, and no one argues that God is not all-knowing simply because the word "Omniscient" isn't in Scripture. So saying the doctrine of the Trinity is false just because the word "Trinity" isn't in the Bible is not a valid argument.

subsections.heading: HINTS OF PLURALITY: OLD TESTAMENT
paragraphs: The most common Hebrew name for God in the Old Testament is *Elohim*, which is always translated "God." This word is technically a plural form of *Eloah*, which also appears in Scripture, though far less often. Even though *Elohim* is plural in form, it is almost always paired with singular verbs and pronouns, as in "In the beginning Elohim [God] created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1). This is the usual pattern throughout the Hebrew Bible. But sometimes the plural form is matched with plural verbs and pronouns as well, and sometimes singular and plural forms appear together:
• "God [plural] caused me to wander" (Genesis 20:13)
• "Heard the voice of the living God [plural]" (Deuteronomy 5:26)
Similar plural patterns show up even without the word *Elohim*:
• "Let Israel rejoice in his Maker [plural]" (Psalm 149:2)
• "For your Maker [plural] is your husband [plural]" (Isaiah 54:5)
• "Remember now your Creator [plural]" (Ecclesiastes 12:1)

What deserves our attention is that *Elohim* is used constantly to name the one true God. It is striking that within the sacred writings of a people set apart specifically to reject polytheism, the ordinary word for the one true God takes a plural form. Was this because the language had no other option? Not at all. Hebrew was a rich language. Besides the unique and sacred name "Jehovah," there was also the singular form *Eloah* of this very word. Yet in the central statement, "Hear, O Israel, Jehovah, our Elohim, one Jehovah!" (Deuteronomy 6:4), the singular form *Eloah* was not used, even though it was available. If the point had simply been to declare an absolute, simple oneness with no hint of plurality at all, we would expect the verse to read "Hear, O Israel, Jehovah, our Elohim, one Eloah." Instead, the actual wording seems deliberately chosen to convey that, even though *Elohim* carries a real sense of plurality, Jehovah is still one. (Summarized from Dr. P. Smith)

"For with You is the fountain of life; in Your light we see light" (Psalm 36:9)
Trinitarian Analogies

In lecture I (Theological Preliminaries) of this section, we have discussed how analogies are not perfect and that they break down at certain points. Indeed it is written, “To whom then will you liken God? Or what likeness will you compare to Him?” (Is 40:18), “To whom will you liken Me, and make Me equal and compare Me, that we should be alike?” (Is 46:5) Nevertheless, Holy Scripture has used many analogies about God, which in their totality complement each other and make up for any deficiencies or limitations that a single analogy may have. St. Cyril of Alexandria once said, ‘when things concerning God are expressed in language used of men, we ought not to think of anything base, but to remember that the wealth of divine Glory is being mirrored in the poverty of human expression.’

E Examples & Analogies: 1. The Human Being: Pope Shenouda said that man who is created “in the image of God” (Gen 1:26) is one of the best analogies for the Truth of the Holy Trinity; man is of one humanity possessing a mind and a spirit. Personality, mind, and spirit comprise just one human being. In the same way, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is One Self. No one can say that God has no Mind or Spirit. God, in His Mind and Spirit is One God not three gods. The Mind is also called the Logos or the Son. God created the world by His intelligent mind, or by His Son, or by His Logic or Wisdom – all of which mean the same. For God and His Mind are the same Being. An example of this is when we say, “you solved the problem with your mind.” Is it you who solved the problem or your mind? Both are the same being. The distinction between you and your mind does not mean separation. If God were without His Mind He would not be God, or if He were without His Spirit He would not be God either. Thus, God, of necessity has to be with His Mind and Spirit a Trinity of Unity. 2. The Fire: It is written, “Our God is a consuming fire” (Heb 12:29) Fire can be used as an analogy for the Holy Trinity for fire generates light and heat. Nevertheless, the flame, its light and its heat are one entity. From the moment the flame begins, from that moment light and heat also begin. 3. The Sun: It is written, “The Lord God is a sun…” (Ps 84:11) The sun has been used as an analogy for the Holy Trinity in much the same way fire was used; the sun has ray and light. You cannot separate the light from the ray and you cannot separate either from the sun. 4. The Spring of Water: It was written, “The wellspring of wisdom is a flowing brook” (Prov 18:4) The well, spring and stream have been used also as an analogy for the Holy Trinity: Just as the spring and the stream produced from a well are not separate and yet there are in fact three visible objects and three names yet they all have the same water. àà Even though St. Gregory of Nazianzus used some of the above analogies to explain the relation between

the Father and the Son, he said: “I have very carefully considered this matter in my own mind, and have looked at it in every point of view, in order to find some illustration of this most important subject, but I have been unable to discover anything on earth with which to compare The Nature of The Godhead. For even if I did happen upon some tiny likeness it escaped me for the most part, and left me down below with my example. I picture to myself an eye, a fountain, a river, as others have done before, to see if they first might be analogous to The Father, the second to The Son, and the third to The Holy Spirit. For in these there is no distinction in time, nor are they torn away from their connection with each other, though they seem to be parted by three personalities. But I was afraid in the first place that I should present a flow in The Godhead, incapable of standing still; and secondly that by this figure a numerical unity would be introduced. For the eye and the spring and the river are numerically one, though in different forms. Again I thought of the sun and a ray and light. But here again there was a fear lest people should get an idea of composition in the Uncompounded Nature, such as there is in the sun and the things that are in the sun. And the second place lest we should give Essence to The Father but deny Personality to the others, and make Them only Powers of God, existing in Him and not Personal. For neither the ray nor the light is a sun, but they are only effulgence [radiance] from the sun, and qualities of its essence. And lest we should thus, as far as the illustration goes, attribute both Being and Not- being to God, which is even more monstrous.” (Adapted from the 5th Theological Oration on The Holy Spirit, Articles XXXI and XXXII) “They have forsaken Me, the fountain of living waters, and hewn themselves cisterns – broken cisterns that can hold no water.” (Jer 2:13)
Trinitarian Heresies

subsections.heading: ANALOGIES FOR THE HOLY TRINITY
paragraphs: In the earlier section on theological basics, we discussed how analogies are never perfect and always break down at some point. Scripture itself says, "To whom then will you liken God? Or what likeness will you compare to Him?" (Isaiah 40:18), and "To whom will you liken Me, and make Me equal and compare Me, that we should be alike?" (Isaiah 46:5). Even so, Scripture uses many different analogies for God, and together they support each other and make up for what any single analogy lacks on its own. St. Cyril of Alexandria once said that when we describe God using human language, we should not think of it as something lowly, but should remember that the richness of God's glory is being reflected, however imperfectly, through the limits of human words.

subsections.heading: EXAMPLES AND ANALOGIES
paragraphs: ── 1. THE HUMAN BEING ──

Pope Shenouda taught that humanity, created "in the image of God" (Genesis 1:26), is one of the best analogies for the truth of the Holy Trinity. A human being is one person, yet has a mind and a spirit. Personality, mind, and spirit together make up just one human being. In the same way, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one single Being.

No one would say that God has no mind or spirit. God, together with His Mind and His Spirit, is one God, not three gods. God's Mind is also called the Word, or the Son. God created the world through His intelligent Mind, or through His Son, or through His Wisdom, all different ways of describing the same reality, since God and His Mind are the same Being.

Think of it this way: when we say, "you solved the problem with your mind," did you solve it, or did your mind solve it? Both answers point to the same person. Distinguishing between "you" and "your mind" does not mean they are separate beings. In the same way, if God did not have His Mind, He would not be God, and if He did not have His Spirit, He would not be God either. So God, by His very nature, must exist as a Trinity that is still fully one.
── 2. FIRE ──

Scripture says, "Our God is a consuming fire" (Hebrews 12:29). Fire can serve as an analogy for the Trinity because fire produces both light and heat. Yet the flame, its light, and its heat are all one and the same reality. The moment the flame begins, its light and heat begin as well.
── 3. THE SUN ──

Scripture says, "The Lord God is a sun" (Psalm 84:11). The sun works as an analogy for the Trinity in a similar way to fire: it has both rays and light. You cannot separate the light from the rays, and you cannot separate either one from the sun itself.
── 4. THE SPRING OF WATER ──

Scripture says, "The wellspring of wisdom is a flowing brook" (Proverbs 18:4). A well, a spring, and a stream have also been used as an analogy for the Trinity. The spring and the stream that come from a well are not separate from it, yet we can point to three distinct things, with three different names, all sharing the very same water.

subsections.heading: A WORD OF CAUTION FROM ST. GREGORY OF NAZIANZUS
paragraphs: Even though St. Gregory of Nazianzus used some of these same analogies to explain the relationship between the Father and the Son, he also gave a strong warning about their limits. He explained that he had thought carefully about this subject from every angle, searching for something on earth that could truly compare to the nature of God, but found nothing adequate. Even when he found a small likeness, it quickly fell short and left him without a full answer.

He considered images like an eye, a spring, and a river, hoping the first might represent the Father, the second the Son, and the third the Holy Spirit, since none of these are separated by time and all remain connected, even though they appear as three distinct things. But he grew concerned that this image would suggest God is like a constant flow that can never stand still, and that it would wrongly suggest a kind of numerical oneness, since an eye, a spring, and a river are really just one thing appearing in different forms.

He then considered the sun, a ray, and light, but worried this might suggest that God's simple, undivided nature is somehow made of separate parts, the way a sun has visible features. He also worried this image might give real existence and personhood to the Father alone, while reducing the Son and the Holy Spirit to mere qualities or powers belonging to God, rather than full Persons in their own right, since neither a ray nor light is itself the sun. They are only a radiance or a quality coming from it. He was concerned that, in trying to illustrate the Trinity this way, we might end up implying that some Persons of the Trinity fully exist while others do not, which would be an even greater error. (Adapted from the Fifth Theological Oration on the Holy Spirit)
"They have forsaken Me, the fountain of living waters, and hewn themselves cisterns, broken cisterns that can hold no water" (Jeremiah 2:13).
The Triunity of God

subsections.heading: INTRODUCTION: ST. AUGUSTINE AND THE CHILD
paragraphs: One day, St. Augustine was walking along a sandy beach by the sea. His mind was turning over the mystery of the Holy Trinity. He was talking to himself: "One God, but three Persons. Three Persons, not three gods, but one God. What does this mean? How can it be explained? How can my mind ever grasp it?"

As he wrestled with this question, he noticed a young boy on the beach. He walked over to see what the boy was doing. The child had dug a small hole in the sand and, using his hands, was carrying seawater and pouring it into the hole. Augustine asked him, "What are you doing, child?" The boy answered, "I want to fit all the water of the sea into this hole." Augustine asked again, "But how could all the water of this vast sea ever fit into such a small hole?" The child replied, "If the water of this limited sea cannot fit into this little hole, then how could the infinite, Triune God ever fit into your mind?" Then the child vanished. He had actually been an angel.

The doctrine of the Holy Trinity is not simply a "belief" that Christians are told to accept, nor a rule handed down by the Church for people to take on faith. It is not something invented by scholars through pure reasoning or philosophy. Instead, the doctrine of the Trinity comes directly from God revealing Himself to us. Since God is God, everything we know about Him comes only through His own choice to be known. We cannot know God unless He makes Himself known to us, through His Word and His Spirit, both of whom reveal and save.

subsections.heading: GOD REVEALS HIMSELF THROUGH CHRIST
paragraphs: God has revealed Himself through Himself: through the Incarnation of His Son among us as our Savior, and through the power of His Spirit. Because of this, the Christian understanding of God centers entirely on Christ. It turns on the fact that God revealed and gave Himself to us directly in the Incarnation, an actual, visible expression of God's own nature, which is identical to God's own Being.

This does not mean everything we know about God can be reduced only to the study of Christ. Rather, it means that since there is only one Mediator between God and humanity, who is Himself both God and man, and only one true revelation of God in which God Himself is the actual substance of what is revealed, all real knowledge of God flows from and is understood through God's revelation of Himself in the flesh, in the Lord Jesus Christ. Any statement we make about God is only true if it is grounded in Christ. Only in Jesus Christ do we truly encounter a real, personal, visible revelation of God, one that closes the gap between God and us, and is identical with God's own Being.

subsections.heading: THE DIVINITY OF THE HOLY SPIRIT
paragraphs: The same is true of our knowledge and worship of God through the Holy Spirit. The Father sends the Spirit through the Son to live within us and open our minds to God, completing God's movement of revealing and giving Himself to us, and enabling us to respond to Him with faith and understanding. The Holy Spirit is fully God, no less than the Son.

How could the Spirit pour God's love into our hearts? How could the Spirit bring Christ near to us, and how could Christ be present to us through the Spirit, unless the Spirit Himself were fully divine, sharing the very same Being (*homoousios*) as the Father and the Son? Like the Son, the Holy Spirit is not simply some cosmic force standing between God and the world. He is God's own Spirit, who lives eternally within God and through whom God knows Himself. So to know God through His Spirit is to know Him in the deepest depths of His Triune Being, as Holy Spirit, Father, and Son together. Without the presence of the Holy Spirit, we could not experience the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ or the love of God the Father.

We can only speak about God this way because He has truly made Himself known to us. God revealing Himself to us as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit gives us solid ground, in real human history, to actually know God as He truly is in His Triune reality. The ground on which we know God through His revelation in history is the very same ground as God's own eternal Being, because in Jesus Christ and in the Holy Spirit, God is completely one with what He reveals and gives.

God reveals Himself through Himself. What God gives us is not just something about Himself, it is His very own Self: true God from true God. In Him, the One who reveals and what is revealed, the Giver and the Gift, are one and the same Being. In Jesus Christ, God has fully revealed and given Himself to us, holding nothing back, in such a way that what He reveals and gives is rooted in His own ultimate Being as God.

This is the central truth on which the Christian understanding of God, and of His saving work, depends: the full Divinity of Jesus Christ. This is what the great theologians and Church councils of the fourth century worked to defend, formulating the key concept of *homoousios* (same Being) to describe the Son and the Spirit, defending it against every threat to the Gospel.

subsections.heading: THE IMMANENT TRINITY AND THE ECONOMIC TRINITY
paragraphs: At this point, it helps to introduce two terms: the "immanent" or "theological" Trinity, and the "economic" Trinity. The first refers to how we understand God in His eternal Being. The second refers to how we understand God as He reveals Himself and saves us throughout history.

In the Gospel, God does not merely appear to us as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. He truly is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in Himself, and He reveals Himself exactly as He is. So the economic Trinity (God as He acts in history) and the theological Trinity (God as He eternally is) cannot be separated from one another. They are joined together in God's one act of revealing and giving Himself to us as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. St. St. St. Athanasius taught that while we can distinguish between God's saving actions in history and God's eternal nature, we can never separate the two.

If the economic Trinity and the theological Trinity were actually different from one another, it would raise doubt about whether God Himself was truly the content of His own revelation, and whether Jesus Christ was truly God reconciling the world to Himself. This is exactly why the term *homoousios* ("of one Being" with the Father) mattered so much at the Council of Nicea in 325 AD. If there were no real connection between God's saving acts in history and God's eternal Being, then the saving events described in the Gospel would carry no real divine weight, and the doctrine of the Trinity would lack any ultimate divine truth.
The Trinitarian message of the Gospel tells us the opposite is true. In Jesus Christ and in the Holy Spirit, we are truly dealing with the Lord God Himself as our Savior.

subsections.heading: ONE BEING, THREE PERSONS - ONE OUSIA, THREE HYPOSTASES
paragraphs: When we look closely at how God reveals Himself as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one Being (*Ousia*), three Persons (*Hypostases*), we see just how unique and singular this truth is. Believing that God is a Trinity in His eternal Being means rejecting both the idea that God is a single Person with no real distinctions (Unitarianism), and the idea that there are many gods (polytheism).

In fact, understanding God as both truly One and truly Three, at the same time, is the most distinct way of understanding God possible. This is not only because there is no simple human way to explain how three can be one and one can be three, but also because of God's unique nature as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit within His one eternal Being.

Even so, we must say that the three Persons exist fully within the one Being, and the one Being exists fully within the three Persons. There is no "one Being" apart from the three Persons, and there are no three Persons apart from the one Being. The Holy Trinity is a unity, and that unity is a Trinity, because God is triune within Himself, and it is precisely in this triune way that God makes Himself known to us.

subsections.heading: THE LIMITS OF OUR UNDERSTANDING
paragraphs: When we try to understand the Triune nature of God, we naturally move back and forth between the "whole" and the "parts," understanding the parts in light of the whole, and the whole in light of the parts. But this language of "whole" and "parts" doesn't perfectly fit God's Triune revelation of Himself as Unity and Trinity, since the three divine Persons are not "parts" of the Trinity, and the Trinity is not a "whole" made up of separate "parts." This language doesn't fully capture how we come to understand the Trinity either, though it may work better when we're simply talking about Church teaching as a whole, versus the specific teachings about the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit individually.

At the same time, even though God reveals Himself to us as a whole, and even though it is God as a whole that we come to know, this does not mean we can know Him completely or fully understand Him. In His greatness, God is always beyond our full understanding. What God allows us to grasp of Himself always breaks past the limits of our understanding, so that even as we grasp something real about Him, we recognize we cannot fully take Him in. Even in His kindness in revealing Himself to us, God is always far greater than what we can grasp or imagine. So our knowledge of God can only ever be partial, as St. Paul said, "Now I know in part, but then I shall know fully, just as I am fully known" (1 Corinthians 13:12).

All of this means that any honest attempt to explain the doctrine of the Holy Trinity must move back and forth continually between Unity and Trinity, and between Trinity and Unity. We cannot speak of the whole Trinity without also speaking of the three individual Persons, and we cannot speak of any one Person without already assuming knowledge of the whole Trinity, because God is only fully God as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together.

We said earlier, with some caution, that understanding God's Triune nature involves moving from "whole" to "parts" and back again. The reason for this caution is that the oneness of the Holy Trinity is a "three-in-oneness," meaning a wholeness that includes three divine Persons, where each Person is fully God in Himself. So our usual way of thinking about wholes and parts simply doesn't apply here.

As St. Gregory of Nazianzus said, "As soon as I think of the One, I am surrounded by the brightness of the Three. As soon as I distinguish the Three, I am brought back to the One. When I think of any one of the Three, I think of Him as complete. My sight is filled, and yet the greater part still escapes me. I cannot grasp the greatness of the One in a way that makes the others any less great. And when I consider the Three together, I see only one brightness, and I cannot divide or measure that one light" (Oration 40, On Holy Baptism).

The Fathers and theologians of the early Church understood that, since the truth of something beyond our full understanding shows itself through the basic trust and conviction it produces in people, the way to truly grasp a completely new realm of truth is through faith. This is why the Church has long taught the principle: "Unless you believe, you will not understand." This holds true whenever we are dealing with the deepest realities, ones that carry their own authority and call for real, thoughtful commitment, and that form the very foundation on which all rational knowledge and theological understanding is built.
"God said to Moses, 'I AM WHO I AM'" (Exodus 3:14).
Trinitarian Terminology & Vocabulary

subsections.heading: INTRODUCTION
paragraphs: Before reading further, understand that grasping the words and ideas behind the doctrine of the Holy Trinity is one thing. Knowing the living reality of God behind those words and ideas is something else entirely. We must work and pray so that we can move beyond every word and concept about God, and come to actually know Him for ourselves, in living union with Him: the Father, through the Son, by the Holy Spirit.

subsections.heading: IMPORTANT TRINITARIAN TERMS
paragraphs: Many people find the doctrine of the Holy Trinity to be the most confusing part of the Christian faith, mostly because of its complicated vocabulary. A clear, working understanding of the following terms will help us grasp, as best we limitedly can, the mystery of the Holy Trinity.

subsections.heading: BEING, ESSENCE, SUBSTANCE, OR NATURE
paragraphs: (Latin: *Substantia*; Greek: *Ousia*)

The Greek-speaking Church Fathers used the word *ousia* to describe God's Being. This word was already familiar from Greek philosophy, but the Fathers used it very differently in Christian theology, shaped by God's saving actions in history as recorded in the Old and New Testaments. In other words, they did not treat God's Being as something still and lifeless, but as living, speaking, and personal.

So God's Being is not some cold, impersonal idea. It is a dynamic, personal Being. St. St. Athanasius, from the very beginning, described God the Creator as far beyond any human idea of "being," beyond anything we could imagine using ordinary categories. He was not starting from some borrowed definition of "being" and then applying it to God. Instead, he built his understanding of God's Being directly from the living God Himself, as God speaks to us personally through His Word and reveals Himself through His work of creation and salvation.

So when St. St. Athanasius used the word *ousia* to describe the Being of God the Creator, and of God the Father of Jesus Christ, he used it in its simplest sense of "being," but transformed by the biblical truth of God stepping into human history to save humanity. This "being" only makes sense in light of the truth that the Son and the Spirit share the very same Being as the Father, expressed by the word *homoousios* ("same Being"). Or put another way, the full Being of the Father is also fully the Being of the Son and of the Spirit.

Because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit share one identical Being, the word "being" or "*ousia*" should not be used the way certain Greek philosophers, like Aristotle, used it: as something fixed, abstract, and impersonal. Unfortunately, this more abstract sense crept into Western thinking about the Trinity through the Latin words *Substantia* and *Essentia*. St. Hilary, who wrote in Latin himself, once noted how much confusion is caused simply by translating Greek terms into Latin, since being overly literal in translation sometimes makes things less clear rather than more.

This does not mean the early Church Fathers completely rejected the idea of "being" as something that exists and stands on its own. They used this idea appropriately to express the truth that God's Being is infinite, without limit, without origin, and fully grounded in Himself alone, since God and His Being are one and the same. But this idea was reshaped by the Church's effort to understand God's nature, not through outside speculation, but through God's own specific self-revelation in Jesus Christ, within the story of our salvation.

It is only through Christ, the only Son, truly born of the Father's own Divine Nature, that God's Nature can be known at all. So God's Being can only be properly defined through the relationship between Father and Son, or rather, God defines His own nature for us through that relationship. As St. St. Athanasius put it, it is more accurate and reverent to understand God through the Son and call Him "Father," than to define God only by His works and call Him simply "the Uncreated One."

It is especially important to see how radically the Greek idea of "being" (*ousia*) was transformed when applied to God, shifting from an impersonal, pre-Christian idea to a deeply personal one. This transformation was rooted in God's own self-revelation to Israel as "I AM," a name Jesus Christ applied to Himself when He said, "I AM" (John 8:58). Neither the Old nor the New Testament ever treated God's nature as impersonal, and Orthodox Christian theology refused to use the term *ousia* the impersonal way it was used in non-Christian Greek philosophy.

The theological phrase "One Being (*Ousia*), Three Persons (*Hypostasis*)," agreed upon at the Council of Alexandria in AD 362 under St. St. Athanasius, should not be understood as three Persons existing separately from, or different from, God's one Being. Rather, the three Persons together are precisely the one Being of God. So God's Being was never understood through some outside definition, but only in light of how God named Himself: "I AM WHO I AM" in the Old Testament, and Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in the New Testament, as reflected in the baptismal formula. Within this New Testament revelation, the Old Testament name "I AM" is taken up again in Christ's own "I AM" sayings. Through Him, the true offspring of God's Nature, and through the Spirit, God has made Himself more fully known to us through the personal communion that is His very Being.

St. St. Athanasius explained that when we hear phrases like "I am who I am," "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth," "Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord," and "Thus says the Lord Almighty," we understand nothing other than the simple, blessed, and ultimately incomprehensible Being of the One who exists. Though we cannot fully grasp what God is, when we hear the words "Father," "God," and "Almighty," we understand these to point to nothing other than the very Being of the One who is. And when we say of Christ that "He is the Son of God," we are also saying that He comes from the very Being of the Father. Since Scripture itself declares that the Son comes from the Father, and the Father Himself said, "This is My beloved Son," and since a son is, by definition, the offspring of his father, it becomes clear why the Fathers at Nicea rightly declared that the Son comes from the very Being of the Father.

So in the doctrine of the Holy Trinity, the one Being of God, who exists as three Persons, does not point to some abstract essence. It refers to the eternal, living Being that God truly is as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, both fully Triune and fully Personal at the same time. God's Being and God's communion of Persons must always be understood together, in light of one another.

subsections.heading: PERSON
paragraphs: (Latin: *Persona*; Greek: *Hypostasis* or *Prosopon*)

Based on the New Testament's witness to God's self-revelation, "the Father," "the Son," and "the Holy Spirit" are unique, proper names referring to three distinct Persons, or real *Hypostases*. These three cannot be swapped or exchanged for one another, yet they share one and the same Divine Being.

There is one Person who is always the Father, distinct from, but not separate from, the Son and the Spirit. There is another Person who is always the Son, distinct from, but not separate from, the Father and the Spirit. And there is another Person who is always the Holy Spirit, distinct from, but not separate from, the Father and the Son. In this threefold, tri-personal revelation of God, no single Person is more or less God than the others, since all three are equally eternal and equally God. They are perfectly one in their shared Nature, and perfectly of one and the same Being.

Each of the three Persons is fully Lord and God, and yet there are not three Lords or three Gods, only one Lord God, and only one eternal Being shared by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. St. St. Athanasius said that we confess God to be one through the Trinity, and that our understanding of one Godhead existing as Trinity is far more godly than the false, fragmented ideas of God found among heretics.

The precise wording used to express this truth did not appear all at once. It developed gradually as the Church worked to guard the faith against error on two sides: the error of teaching there are three separate gods (tritheism), and the error of teaching that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are just three different masks or roles worn by a single divine Person (modalism). In the time of St. St. Athanasius and the early pro-Nicene theologians, the words *ousia* (essence, or being) and *hypostasis* (concrete, real existence) were often still used as if they meant nearly the same thing. Because of this overlap, saying "three *hypostases*" could easily sound, to early Alexandrian and Western Christians, like a claim that there were three separate gods. For this reason, the earliest formula used by St. St. Athanasius and his contemporaries was one *hypostasis*, meaning one single divine reality, together with three *prosopa* (the plural of *prosopon*), meaning three "faces" or "persons" as they are presented to us. St. St. Athanasius insisted on speaking of one *hypostasis* in order to protect the truth that the Father and the Son are completely united within a single Godhead, guarding against the Arian error of treating the Son as somehow less than or subordinate to the Father. Meanwhile, the word *prosopon*, borrowed from everyday language for a face or a role someone plays, allowed theologians to explain the real distinctions between Father, Son, and Holy Spirit without splitting God's one divine substance into separate parts.

The Holy Trinity, three divine Persons, is thus completely unified, both in how God acts and in His eternal, unchanging personal Being. The key word eventually used to express this reality was *hypostasis*, taken from the New Testament's description of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, as "the exact representation of His being" (Hebrews 1:3). As the Church's understanding of the Gospel deepened, the word *hypostasis* came to express the real, objective self-revelation of God's Son and Word, who took on human flesh in Jesus Christ as the incarnate "I AM" of the living God. But it was only once this was worked out further, in light of God's threefold revelation as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, that the specific concept of "Person" fully took shape, and only within the relationships of the Holy Trinity as one Being, three Persons. It was St. Basil the Great and the other Cappadocian Fathers who later refined and standardized this vocabulary into the form still used today. They settled on using *ousia* to describe what is one in God, His single divine essence, and *hypostasis* to describe what is three in God: the distinct, real Persons of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. This fixed the meaning of *hypostasis*, shifting it away from its earlier, looser overlap with *ousia*, and gave the Church the lasting formula "one *ousia*, three *hypostases*." Once it became clear that "three *hypostases*" meant three distinct, concrete ways in which the one divine Being exists, rather than three separate divine substances, St. St. Athanasius himself came to accept this way of speaking. This shows that the real point of agreement was never really about which specific words to use, but about protecting the same underlying truth: one God, truly three, and three, truly one.

St. St. Athanasius explained that the Nicene Fathers could confidently speak of Jesus Christ as the true and natural Son of the Father, belonging to the Father's own Being, truly God Himself, and of one Being with the true Father (*Homoousios*). This is because He is "the exact representation of the Father's Being," light from light, and the true expression and image of the Father's own Being.

In precise theological terms, as the vocabulary settled, *ousia* came to refer to being in terms of its inner nature, what something actually is. *Hypostasis* came to refer to being in terms of its distinct, individual existence, how it stands apart as its own reality. As one scholar put it, *ousia* points to being's "inward" quality, while *hypostasis* points to being's "outward" distinctness.

It's also worth noting that these terms carry a deeply personal meaning in Christian theology that they did not have in earlier, non-Christian Greek thought. No divine Person is who He is apart from His essential relationship to the other two, and yet each divine Person remains distinct and different from the other two. They are fundamentally connected, not only because they share one common Being, so that each is fully God in Himself, but also because of their distinct identities as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, identities that are woven together and belong to their unbreakable unity within the Trinity. There is an unbroken, continuous relationship of Being between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, so that the full Being of God is understood to exist not only in the Father, but completely in the Son and in the Holy Spirit as well.

subsections.heading: PERICHORESIS
paragraphs: Perichoresis is a carefully developed theological idea that helps us thoughtfully interpret what the Bible teaches about the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit dwelling within one another. The word comes from the Greek word *chora*, meaning "space" or "room," or from *chorein*, meaning "to contain," "to make room for," or "to move forward." It describes a kind of mutual containing or surrounding of realities, sometimes called "coinherence" or "mutual indwelling." It should not be confused with the similar-sounding Greek word for dancing.
── HOW THE IDEA DEVELOPED ──

St. St. Athanasius laid the theological groundwork for this idea while explaining how the Father and the Son dwell within one another. He did this while clarifying Christ's own words to His disciples recorded by St. John, especially "I am in the Father, and the Father is in Me" (John 14:11; also 10:30, 38; 14:10). He deepened the concept of *homoousion* (same Being), which expressed the underlying unity of Being and action between the incarnate Son and God the Father, a unity the entire Gospel depends on.

For St. St. Athanasius, *homoousion* pointed both to the real, distinct identities of the three divine Persons, and to their mutual indwelling within the one Being of God. He understood this as more than just a connection or sharing of qualities between the three Persons. He saw it as a complete mutual dwelling, where each Person remains fully who He is, whether Father, Son, or Holy Spirit, while also being completely present within the other two, just as they are completely present within Him.

St. St. Athanasius never used a specific technical term for this mutual indwelling himself, that came later, but the basic idea already appears in his response to the Arians, who mocked Christ's words "I am in the Father and the Father is in Me" by asking how one could possibly be contained within the other. St. St. Athanasius pointed out that this question wrongly assumes the relationship between Father and Son works like physical objects containing one another. He explained instead that "I am in the Father and the Father is in Me" describes a relationship in which the whole Being of the Father and the whole Being of the Son completely indwell one another, something only conceivable in relation to God Himself, and something we only understand through God's own revelation of Himself.

In his letters on the Holy Spirit written to his friend Serapion, St. St. Athanasius showed that this same mutual indwelling applies equally to the relationship between the Spirit and the Son, and the Spirit and the Father, and so to the whole Trinity. Unless the Being and activity of the Spirit are identical to the Being and activity of the Father and the Son, our salvation would not be secure.

St. Hilary of Poitiers taught much the same thing in the West, based on John 14:10, explaining that the divine Persons fully contain one another as complete Persons, without diminishing each other's honor or glory in any way. He explained that although these divine realities do not exist apart from one another, each still retains its own distinct existence, and they are able to mutually contain one another, so that one continually surrounds, and is surrounded by, the very one it also surrounds. He argued that while this kind of mutual containing makes no sense when applied to physical objects, it is entirely possible with God, who exists both within and beyond all things, containing everything while being contained by nothing.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus was the first to use the verb form of *perichoresis*, originally to describe how the divine and human natures of Christ interacted within the one composite nature, without either nature losing its integrity, though without suggesting that the human nature somehow merged into the divine Nature, and without applying this idea yet to the relationships among the three divine Persons themselves. Later, this concept of *perichoresis* was applied specifically to describe how the three divine Persons dwell within one another, mutually indwelling and coinhering, while still remaining distinct from one another.

Once applied this way, *perichoresis* came to mean the complete mutual containing and indwelling of the three divine Persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, within the one God. Because of this, the term could no longer properly be applied to describe the union of Christ's divine and human natures without seriously distorting the doctrine of Christ.

The earliest known use of the actual word "*perichoresis*" appears in a work on the Holy Trinity attributed to St. Cyril of Alexandria, though its true author remains uncertain. It appears in connection with the key passage John 14:11.

Through this term, St.Cyril of Alexandria expressed the dynamic union and communion of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit within one Being, in such a way that each has His Being within the others and mutually contains the others, without merging or blending together, and without ever being separated from one another, since they are completely equal and identical in divinity and power. Each Person fully contains the one God, both through His relationship with the other two and through His relationship with Himself, since they fully coexist and dwell within one another. Human beings never exist within one another this way, but this is exactly what the divine Persons of the Trinity do.

Since God is Spirit and God is Love, we must understand *perichoresis* in a completely spiritual and deeply personal way, as the eternal movement of love, the communion of love, that the Trinity always is within Himself, and as the same love God actively extends to us through the Holy Spirit, flowing from His shared Being with the Father and the Son. In this way, the Holy Spirit is Himself the personal Love and communion of love shared between the Father and the Son, and is therefore the very foundation of our own communion with God through the love of the Father and the Son.

This teaching matches what theologians like St. Epiphanius of Salamis taught, strongly emphasizing that the shared Being (*homoousion*) applies to the Trinity as a whole. He described the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as three fully real Persons, eternally grounded in, and completely indwelling, one another, while remaining distinct from one another, without ever compromising their complete unity and oneness. Within God's one Being, the three Persons are always exactly who they are, the Father always the Father, the Son always the Son, and the Holy Spirit always the Holy Spirit, each one being fully and truly God.

This also matches the teaching of St. Cyril of Alexandria, who described the living, dynamic mutual indwelling of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit within the essential reality of the Trinity. St. Cyril brought together St. St. Athanasius' emphasis on the one shared Being of the Trinity with St. Gregory of Nazianzus' understanding of a Trinity that is undivided, yet made up of truly distinct, active, and ongoing relationships.

The mystery of *perichoresis* expresses this truth: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons, each with His own unique characteristics, yet they dwell within one another so intimately that these very distinguishing characteristics, instead of dividing them, unite them inseparably. The Father dwells in the Son and the Spirit, the Son dwells in the Father and the Spirit, and the Spirit dwells in the Father and the Son.

The Father is not the Father apart from the Son and the Spirit. The Son is not the Son apart from the Father and the Spirit. The Spirit is not the Spirit apart from the Father and the Son. Each is fully who He is, true God from true God, precisely within the fullness of the other two, who are likewise each true God from true God. Yet within the mystery of their mutual indwelling, they are not three gods, but only one God, the blessed and Holy Trinity.

Perichoresis is not something still or fixed. It is a dynamic reality, describing an eternal movement of love between the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, a love that increasingly flows outward toward us as well. It's also important to understand that perichoresis is not simply a theory or a philosophical guess. It expresses a saving truth: that God Himself is identical with what He reveals and gives us in Jesus Christ and in the Holy Spirit. This assures us that what God is toward us in Christ and in His Spirit is exactly who He eternally and inherently is within Himself.

Together with the idea of *homoousion*, the concept of *perichoresis*, this mutual indwelling of the divine Persons, allows us to understand that the relationships between the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit revealed to us in our salvation reflect the very same eternal relationships within God's own unchanging Being.

So the basic idea of *perichoresis* grows out of joyful faith in Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior, and out of worship and gratitude for God's saving love as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who reconciles us to Himself and draws us into communion with Him. At the same time, *perichoresis* describes such an intimate reality within God's own life that we can only try to put it into words with reverence, humility, and awe, fully aware of how limited and inadequate our language is when trying to describe the mystery of God's oneness and threeness revealed to us.

We could never even attempt this without God's Word becoming flesh in Jesus Christ, and without His gracious willingness to speak to us using human ways of thinking and human language.
