But because of that union, His humanity became, and remains, the effective means of our justification and sanctification, all the way to the end of time. Within this truth lies a hint toward understanding the sacraments themselves.

Just as Christ's humanity carried divine life and became the means of making people holy, the sacraments too became the effective channels of the sanctification He purchased through His death. Just as our Lord was Himself the visible sign of God, being truly God in the flesh, the sacraments became visible signs of the grace, truly grace itself, that He won for us.

If humans were simply angels, or pure spirits, there would have been no need for our Lord to use human nature or physical things to communicate divine realities to us. But because we are made of both matter and spirit, body and soul, we function best when we encounter the material world as a window into spiritual reality. From the earliest days of a child's life, a mother's affectionate touch is never simply about the physical sensation itself. It communicates something profoundly beautiful and invisible: a mother's love. It isn't really the physical object or action itself that we value, but what that action points to and represents.

subsections.heading: SACRAMENTS AND SALVATION
paragraphs: We've all seen roadside signs that simply say, "Jesus saves." This is entirely true, but the real question is: how does He save us? What real connection do we, living in the twenty-first century, actually have with our Lord Jesus Christ, who walked the earth in the first century? Do we connect with Him only by reading about Him? If that were the whole story, our relationship with Him would be barely closer than the one we might have with Plato. If our Lord Jesus Christ is merely a memory of someone who lived centuries ago, it becomes genuinely difficult to see how His influence on us today could differ meaningfully from that of Socrates or Buddha.

The answer to how our Lord actually saves us is found in the sacraments. Christ's divine life is communicated to us through His Church, His mystical body, in essentially the same way His divine life was communicated while He walked physically on earth. Just as He once used His own human nature as the instrument carrying His divinity, and used physical materials to convey His grace, such as clay and water in the healing of the man born blind (John 9:11), He now uses other human beings (priests) and physical materials (water, bread, wine, oil) as instruments to communicate that same divine life, or grace, to us today.

Every sacrament has an outward, visible sign. In baptism, this is water. In the Eucharist, it's bread and wine. But each sacrament also has a specific form, meaning words carrying spiritual significance that accompany the physical elements when the sacrament is given. Three things, then, are absolutely required for something to be a true sacrament: it must have been instituted by our Lord Jesus Christ Himself; it must involve an outward, visible sign; and it must genuinely carry the power to convey the grace purchased for us through Christ's suffering, death, and resurrection.

Calvary functions like a vast reservoir of divine life and grace. From this single reservoir flow seven distinct channels of sanctification, each meeting people at different stages of their spiritual journey. Each of these seven channels is a sacrament, through which the power of the risen Christ is given to souls through real, effective spiritual contact.

This divine grace flows into the soul whenever we receive the sacraments, unless we ourselves place an obstacle in its way, much like water won't flow from a faucet if we hold our hand directly in front of it. But a faucet in a house has no power to quench thirst on its own, unless it's connected to a reservoir and a working pipeline behind it. In the same way, the sacraments don't confer grace like magic symbols working automatically. They convey real grace only because they remain genuinely connected to the risen Christ, through the ongoing work of the Holy Spirit, of whom our Lord said, "He will take of what is Mine and declare it to you" (John 16:14).

subsections.heading: THE SEVEN HOLY SACRAMENTS
paragraphs: 1. The Sacrament of Holy Orders (Priesthood). 2. The Sacrament of Baptism. 3. The Sacrament of Confirmation. 4. The Sacrament of the Eucharist. 5. The Sacrament of Repentance and Confession. 6. The Sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick. 7. The Sacrament of Matrimony.
(Adapted from *These Are the Sacraments*, by Fulton J. Sheen and Yousuf Karsh.)

subsections.heading: A COMMON QUESTION
paragraphs: Question: The word "mystery" appears throughout Scripture with several different meanings. How do these meanings differ from the Church's use of the word "sacrament"?

Answer: Scripture actually uses the word "mystery" in two distinct senses. The first refers to mysteries of knowledge, secrets or hidden truths that God reveals to us. The second refers to mysteries of grace, invisible spiritual gifts granted by the Holy Spirit, which we know as the sacraments.
── MYSTERIES OF KNOWLEDGE ──

"The secret of the Lord is with those who fear Him" (Psalm 25:14). "Surely the Lord God does nothing, unless He reveals His secret to His servants the prophets" (Amos 3:7). "Then the secret was revealed to Daniel" (Daniel 2:19). "To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God" (Luke 8:10). "We speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, the hidden wisdom which God ordained before the ages for our glory" (1 Corinthians 2:7). "Though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge... but have not love, I am nothing" (1 Corinthians 13:2). "Having made known to us the mystery of His will" (Ephesians 1:9). "That I may open my mouth boldly to make known the mystery of the gospel" (Ephesians 6:19). "The mystery which has been hidden from ages and from generations, but now has been revealed to His saints" (Colossians 1:26). "Meanwhile praying also for us, that God would open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ" (Colossians 4:3). "The knowledge of the mystery of God, both of the Father and of Christ" (Colossians 2:2). "Great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh" (1 Timothy 3:16).
── MYSTERIES OF GRACE ──

The word "sacrament" combines the Latin word *sacer*, meaning holy, with the Greek word *mysterion*, meaning a secret rite. Over time, "sacrament" came to describe something sacred and mysterious, carrying real spiritual power, a power transmitted through physical instruments and actions understood as channels of divine grace, established through rituals that Christ Himself instituted. St. Augustine defined a sacrament simply as "the visible form of an invisible grace" (*Encyclopedia Britannica*, Volume 26, page 834).
"A man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh. This is a great mystery, but I speak concerning Christ and the Church" (Ephesians 5:31-32).
"Around the throne were twenty-four thrones, and on the thrones I saw twenty-four elders sitting, clothed in white robes; and they had crowns of gold on their heads" (Revelation 4:4).
The Sacrament of Priesthood

subsections.heading: THE SACRAMENT OF PRIESTHOOD
paragraphs: The Sacrament of Priesthood is the sacrament through which a bishop lays his hands on a chosen candidate, so that the Holy Spirit may descend upon that person and grant him one of the priestly ranks. Through this act, the ordained person receives real authority to carry out the ministry of the Church, whether administering the sacraments, teaching, or other forms of service. This process is called the "laying on of hands," or ordination.

subsections.heading: THE ORIGIN OF THIS SACRAMENT
paragraphs: Our Lord Jesus Christ Himself instituted this sacrament when He chose twelve of His followers and set them apart for ministry: "He called His disciples to Him, and from them He chose twelve whom He also named apostles" (Luke 6:13). He gave them real authority to forgive and to withhold forgiveness of sins: "He breathed on them, and said to them, 'Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained'" (John 20:22-23). Notice that this happened before Pentecost, so this particular gift of the Holy Spirit was specifically the gift of ordination.

Only to these apostles did He say, "Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19), and only to them did He entrust the mystery of His own Body and Blood in the Eucharist.

subsections.heading: THE HONOR OF PRIESTHOOD
paragraphs: St. Paul wrote, "No man takes this honor to himself, but he who is called by God" (Hebrews 5:4), and, "Let the elders who rule well be counted worthy of double honor" (1 Timothy 5:17). The priesthood carries such honor because it involves three things.
── A DIVINE CHOICE, CALL, AND APPOINTMENT ──

"Then He appointed twelve, that they might be with Him and that He might send them out to preach and to have power to heal sicknesses and to cast out demons" (Mark 3:14-15). "And when it was day, He called His disciples to Himself, and from them He chose twelve whom He also named apostles" (Luke 6:12-13). "You did not choose Me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain" (John 15:16). "After these things the Lord appointed seventy others also, and sent them two by two before His face into every city and place where He Himself was about to go" (Luke 10:1). "As they ministered to the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, 'Now separate to Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.' Then, having fasted and prayed, and laid hands on them, they sent them away" (Acts 13:2-3).
── FAITHFULNESS AND STEWARDSHIP ──

"Who then is that faithful and wise steward, whom his master will make ruler over his household, to give them their portion in due season? Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes" (Luke 12:42-43). "Let a man so consider us, as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Moreover it is required in stewards that one be found faithful" (1 Corinthians 4:1-2).
── CONSECRATION AND SANCTIFICATION ──

Our Lord Jesus Christ said, "For their sakes I sanctify Myself, that they also may be sanctified by the truth" (John 17:19). To sanctify means to set apart, or consecrate. Our Lord consecrated Himself for the work of ministry and redemption. In the same way, every rank of the priesthood is consecrated for ministry, following the example of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Great High Priest.

subsections.heading: THE ORDER OF DEACONS
paragraphs: ── 1. EPSALTOS (HYMNIST, CANTOR) ──

The role of the *Epsaltos* is clear from the title itself: to learn and sing the Church's hymns and praises. This rank is mentioned in some of the earliest Church canons: "Chanters also must be blessed by the bishop." Children are often ordained into this rank, echoing the Psalm, "Out of the mouth of babes and infants You have ordained strength" (Psalm 8:2). The reasoning behind ordaining children this way is to attach them closely to the Church early on, allowing them to grow up nourished by the Orthodox faith and its rites, so they become firmly rooted in the faith, holding to it with real spiritual depth and holiness, echoing the Psalm, "But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God... I will praise You forever" (Psalm 52:8-9).
── 2. ANAGNOSTIS (READER, LECTOR) ──

The reader's role is to carry out the daily Scripture readings in church, especially the Epistles. He must read accurately, without mistakes, so the congregation can clearly understand what is read. After the Commemoration of the Saints, readers recite the names of the Patriarchs who have fallen asleep in the Lord, as the deacon says, "Let those who read recite the names of our fathers the Patriarchs who have fallen asleep; O Lord, repose their souls and forgive us our sins." Readers may also deliver sermons to the congregation, as reflected in their ordination service: "Lord, show Your face to Your servant standing before You, to know by Your holy words to preach Your laws to Your people, teach them Your pure words for their rescue and salvation," though this requires specific permission from the bishop or priest. Readers are also responsible for leading the congregation's psalms and responses during the Liturgy and other occasions.
── 3. EPIDEACON (SUB-DEACON) ──

The sub-deacon's responsibilities include keeping heretics and false teachers from entering the church, lighting the church's lamps, maintaining the church's books, preparing the censer, organizing the worshippers, and assisting or standing in for the deacon when needed. These duties come in addition to those already carried out by the reader.
── 4. DEACON (SERVANT) ──

The deacon's role includes reciting all the liturgical responses during services. Historically, only the bishop, priest, deacon, or archdeacon, along with believing kings who had been anointed with chrism, were permitted to enter the sanctuary. The deacon may carry the chalice and distribute the precious blood of the Lord to the congregation during communion. He reads the Holy Gospel during the Liturgy, and may teach or preach with the bishop's or priest's permission. The deacon also assists the priest more broadly, visiting members of the congregation, including widows, orphans, and the sick.

If a man is ordained a deacon before marrying, he does not marry afterward. If he was already married when ordained and his wife later passes away, he remains unmarried afterward, just as priests do in the same situation. If a deacon chooses to marry after ordination, he forfeits his rank.
── 5. ARCHDEACON (LEADER OF DEACONS) ──
The archdeacon leads all the ranks of deacons, oversees their needs, and assigns their specific duties.

subsections.heading: QUALIFICATIONS FOR DEACONS
paragraphs: St. Paul wrote, "Deacons must be reverent, not double-tongued, not given to much wine, not greedy for money, holding the mystery of the faith with a pure conscience. But let these also first be proved; then let them serve as deacons, being found blameless... Let deacons be the husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own houses well" (1 Timothy 3:8-9,12).

The twelve apostles themselves established the standard for ordaining the first seven deacons, requiring men who were "of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom" (Acts 6:3). Although this is the smallest of the priestly ranks, St. Paul still praised it highly, writing, "Those who have served well as deacons obtain for themselves a good standing and great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus" (1 Timothy 3:13). It's also worth remembering that the first Christian martyr, St. Stephen, was himself a deacon, and it was he who saw heaven opened and the Lord Jesus standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:55-56).

subsections.heading: THE ORDER OF PRIESTS
paragraphs: ── 1. PRIEST, ELDER, PRESBYTER ──

This is the first and most essential priestly rank. A priest has the authority to administer every sacrament of the Church, with the sole exception of the laying on of hands and ordination, which remains reserved for the bishop or someone above him. He teaches the people God's word, explains Church doctrine and rites, and leads them toward righteousness. "For the lips of a priest should keep knowledge, and people should seek the law from his mouth; for he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts" (Malachi 2:7). He serves as a father to his spiritual children, caring for them with compassion, tenderness, and love, deeply invested in their salvation, and serving them humbly, just as our Lord washed the feet of His own disciples.
── 2. HEGUMEN, SENIOR PRIEST, ARCHPRIEST ──

This is simply a promotion within the priesthood, not a separate ordination. If more than one priest serves in the same church, the priest with the longest tenure, or the one most active and knowledgeable, is promoted to hegumen. The other priests then defer to him as the primary person responsible for that church.
── 3. CHORBISHOP (BISHOP OF A VILLAGE) ──

This rank first appeared toward the end of the third century in Asia Minor, as dioceses expanded and Church leaders preferred not to split them into smaller, separate territories. The Council of Nicea in AD 325 included fifteen chorbishops from Asia Minor and Syria. This rank later disappeared from the Coptic Church, until Pope Shenouda III revived it, ordaining several monks as chorbishops to assist bishops and metropolitans in overseeing especially large dioceses. His Holiness later promoted most of these men to full bishops or diocesan bishops.

This rank sits close to the rank of bishop, since the candidate is a monk, carries the title "Anba," wears a headpiece very similar to a bishop's, holds authority to ordain the various ranks of deacons, sits as a member of the Holy Synod, and is mentioned by name in liturgical prayers and hymns just as a bishop would be.

subsections.heading: THE ORDER OF BISHOPS
paragraphs: ── 1. BISHOP, OVERSEER, EPISCOPOS ──

This is the highest full rank of the priesthood. Bishops are distinguished from priests by holding the complete fullness of priesthood, including the authority to lay hands on and ordain every deaconal and priestly rank within their diocese.
── 2. METROPOLITAN (BISHOP OF A LARGE CITY) ──
This is a further promotion from the rank of bishop. A metropolitan is named before ordinary bishops in every Church rite.
── 3. PATRIARCH, POPE, ARCHBISHOP ──

The Patriarch holds the highest rank within the episcopacy and carries the greatest governing authority within the priesthood. He serves as the leader of the entire Church, including all bishops and metropolitans. The Patriarch stands as the direct successor of the apostles and serves as a living symbol of the Church's unity. He alone holds the right to ordain bishops, accompanied by at least one other bishop, and to promote bishops to metropolitans. He also holds the sole right to prepare the Holy Chrism (*Myron*). He presides over the sessions of the Holy Synod, the Church's highest governing authority.

subsections.heading: QUALIFICATIONS FOR BISHOPS
paragraphs: St. Paul wrote, "A bishop must be blameless, as a steward of God, not self-willed, not quick-tempered, not given to wine, not violent, not greedy for money, but hospitable, a lover of what is good, sober-minded, just, holy, self-controlled, holding fast the faithful word as he has been taught, that he may be able, by sound doctrine, both to exhort and convict those who contradict" (Titus 1:7-9).

He also wrote, "A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, temperate, sober-minded, of good behavior, hospitable, able to teach; not given to wine, not violent, not greedy for money, but gentle, not quarrelsome, not covetous... not a novice, lest being puffed up with pride he fall into the same condemnation as the devil. Moreover he must have a good testimony among those who are outside, lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil" (1 Timothy 3:2-3,6-7).
── A COMMON QUESTION ──
Question: Scripture requires that a bishop be "the husband of one wife" (1 Timothy 3:2). Why, then, do we ordain bishops exclusively from celibate monks?

Answer: First, it's worth clarifying that individual believers don't personally ordain anyone. The Pope alone ordains bishops; others simply offer recommendations. Second, St. John Chrysostom explained that St. Paul was not establishing marriage as a strict requirement for bishops, but was instead ruling out anyone who had married more than once, since he wanted the most pure and modest candidates available. Since the option of celibacy and monastic life is fully open within the Church, bishops today are ordained specifically from celibate monks who have never married at all. It's also worth noting that the Book of Revelation, the only prophetic book in the New Testament, refers to bishops as "angels," and our Lord Himself said that angels "neither marry nor are given in marriage" (Matthew 22:30).

At the Council of Nicea in AD 325, it was decided that ordinary priests should be married, given the nature of their pastoral work, which often involves entering people's homes and helping resolve family matters. Even so, if a priest becomes a widower, he does not remarry, since he serves as a spiritual father to all the women in his congregation, and a father cannot marry one of his own daughters.

subsections.heading: CHRIST AND THE RANKS OF THE PRIESTHOOD
paragraphs: Our Lord Jesus Christ personally carried out actions that became the very foundation of each Church rank.

The *Epsaltos*, the hymnist, is required to learn and sing the Church's hymns. Our Lord Himself sang a hymn with His disciples before going to the garden of Gethsemane: "And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives" (Matthew 26:30).

The *Anagnostis*, the reader, is primarily responsible for reading Scripture aloud during the Liturgy. Our Lord Himself performed this role when He entered the synagogue and stood up to read (Luke 4:16).

The *Epideacon*, the sub-deacon, is primarily responsible for keeping order within the church. Our Lord did the same when He drove out the money changers and merchants from the temple (Matthew 21:12).
Among the deacon's duties is pouring water for the priest to wash his hands at the start of the Liturgy. Our Lord poured water into a basin Himself and washed His disciples' feet (John 13:5).

The priest's central role is consecrating the bread and wine during the Divine Liturgy and giving communion to the congregation. Our Lord did exactly this on the night of the Last Supper (Mark 14:22-26).

The hegumen's role involves providing for the practical needs of the church's services. Our Lord did something very similar when He told Judas, "What you do, do quickly" (John 13:27); the other disciples assumed, since Judas held the money box, that the Lord had sent him to buy what was needed for the feast, or to give something to the poor (John 13:29).

The bishop serves as shepherd of his flock. St. Peter refers to our Lord Jesus as "the Shepherd and Overseer of our souls" (1 Peter 2:25), and our Lord said of Himself, "I am the good shepherd" (John 10:14).
Only the Pope holds the authority to ordain bishops, just as our Lord alone breathed on His apostles and gave them the authority to bind and loose sins (John 20:22-23).

So in Christ, we find nearly every priestly rank already lived out, in all its variety, so that every person, whatever role they hold, however small it might seem, can find in Him a genuine example to follow, knowing that no rank is truly lowly, since the Lord Himself lived it out and blessed it with His own example.
"The Lord has sworn and will not relent: 'You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek'" (Psalm 110:4).
The Order of Melchizedek

subsections.heading: THE ORDER OF MELCHIZEDEK
paragraphs: The word "priest" first appears in Scripture in connection with Melchizedek: "Then Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine; he was the priest of God Most High" (Genesis 14:18). He blessed Abraham (Genesis 14:19), and Abraham in turn gave him a tithe of everything (Genesis 14:20).

A major theme running through the Book of Hebrews is the contrast between the Levitical priesthood of the Old Testament and the priesthood our Lord Jesus Christ established, following the order of Melchizedek. Several points here are worth noting.

Melchizedek is given no genealogy in Scripture, and nothing is ever said of his death. He is described as being "without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God, remains a priest continually" (Hebrews 7:3). His name is translated "king of righteousness," and he is also called "king of Salem," meaning "king of peace" (Hebrews 7:2). He receives a tithe from Abraham, implying that his rank stands above Abraham's, and by extension, above Abraham's own descendants, the Levites (Hebrews 7:4,9). Notice also the connection between Melchizedek's priesthood and the bread and wine he brought out, foreshadowing the Eucharist.

St. Paul explicitly declares that our Lord Jesus Christ is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, the order of bread and wine, even though Christ was born from the tribe of Judah rather than the tribe of Levi (Hebrews 7:14-17). The Apostle explains, "If perfection were through the Levitical priesthood (for under it the people received the law), what further need was there that another priest should rise according to the order of Melchizedek, and not be called according to the order of Aaron? For the priesthood being changed, of necessity there is also a change of the law" (Hebrews 7:11-12).

This change was fulfilled at the very moment the high priest tore his own robes during our Lord's trial (Mark 14:63), and when the veil of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom, at the moment our Lord breathed His last (Mark 15:38).

subsections.heading: THE PRIESTHOOD OF THE NEW TESTAMENT
paragraphs: Our Lord acted as a priest according to the order of Melchizedek when He took bread and wine, blessed them, and gave them to His disciples, saying, "This is My body" and "This is My blood." Our Lord is called a High Priest according to this same order of Melchizedek (Hebrews 3:1; 5:10; 6:20; 4:14-15). The very title "High Priest" implies that other priests exist within this same order of bread and wine, with Christ standing as their Chief High Priest. This becomes clear from our Lord's own words to His disciples: "Do this in remembrance of Me" (Luke 22:19), referring directly to the Eucharist.

This is the priesthood of the Gentiles, foretold in several Old Testament prophecies: "For from the rising of the sun, even to its going down, My name shall be great among the Gentiles; in every place incense shall be offered in My name" (Malachi 1:11). "Then they shall bring all your brethren for an offering to the Lord out of all nations... And I will also take some of them for priests and Levites, says the Lord" (Isaiah 66:19-21). "In that day there will be an altar to the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt" (Isaiah 19:19).

This altar clearly cannot be a pagan altar, since Scripture describes it explicitly as an altar "to the Lord." Nor can it refer to a Jewish altar, since Jewish law forbade offering sacrifices anywhere outside Jerusalem, which is exactly why the Israelites needed to leave Egypt in the first place, as recorded in Exodus, since they couldn't offer sacrifices to the Lord in a foreign land. Even today, Jewish communities have synagogues around the world, but no altar anywhere, since the site where the Jerusalem temple once stood is now occupied by a mosque, part of why the conflict in the Middle East remains so complicated.

St. Paul affirms this new altar directly: "We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat" (Hebrews 13:10), referring to the Eucharist and to Jews who had not accepted Christ. Our Lord also gave us instructions concerning this altar: "Leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift" (Matthew 5:24).

subsections.heading: THE SPIRITUAL PRIESTHOOD OF ALL BELIEVERS
paragraphs: King David wrote, "Let my prayer be set before You as incense, the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice" (Psalm 141:2). "I will offer to You the sacrifice of thanksgiving" (Psalm 116:17). "Offer the sacrifices of righteousness" (Psalm 4:5). David was not himself a priest descended from Aaron, yet his worship is described as spiritual incense and sacrifice. This is exactly what the spiritual priesthood of all believers refers to. St. Paul describes the Philippians' generous gift in the same way, calling it "a sweet-smelling aroma, an acceptable sacrifice, well pleasing to God" (Philippians 4:18).

This is why St. Paul urges us, "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your reasonable service" (Romans 12:1). "Let us continually offer the sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of our lips, giving thanks to His name. But do not forget to do good and to share, for with such sacrifices God is well pleased" (Hebrews 13:15-16).

It's no surprise, then, that Revelation describes our Lord Jesus Christ as having "made us kings and priests" (Revelation 1:6). We are obviously not literal kings wearing crowns and sitting on thrones, and in the same way, we are not literal priests either, but priests in this spiritual sense described above. This spiritual priesthood belongs equally to both men and women, and it never cancels out the specific New Testament priesthood established according to the order of Melchizedek. The same pattern existed in the Old Testament as well, where the congregation's own spiritual priesthood never replaced the distinct Levitical priesthood.

This is why St. Peter wrote, "You are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, His own special people, that you may proclaim the praises of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light" (1 Peter 2:9), echoing what God had already told the Israelites: "You shall be to Me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation" (Exodus 19:6).

subsections.heading: THE REBELLION
paragraphs: St. Peter wrote, "There were also false prophets among the people, even as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies... and bring on themselves swift destruction" (2 Peter 2:1). This warning applies directly to the issue of priesthood. The Book of Numbers records the story of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, who, together with 250 leaders of the community, rose up against Moses and Aaron, saying, "All the congregation is holy, every one of them, and the Lord is among them. Why then do you exalt yourselves above the congregation of the Lord?" (Numbers 16:3). They rebelled against the distinct Levitical priesthood, wanting to extend this honor to everyone equally. As a result, "the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up, with their households and all the men with Korah, with all their goods" (Numbers 16:32).

In the New Testament, St. Jude describes certain heretics as having "perished in the rebellion of Korah" (Jude 11). This applies directly to Protestants who reject the New Testament priesthood and the Eucharist.

subsections.heading: A COMMON QUESTION: CALLING PRIESTS "FATHER"
paragraphs: Question: Our Lord said, "Do not call anyone on earth your father, for One is your Father, He who is in heaven" (Matthew 23:9). Why, then, do we call priests "father"?

Answer: These particular words were spoken specifically to the disciples, not to the entire crowd listening. Our Lord often addressed certain teachings to His disciples alone, which is exactly why St. Peter once asked Him, "Lord, do You speak this parable only to us, or to all people?" (Luke 12:41).

Spiritual fatherhood is well supported throughout Scripture. In the Old Testament, Elisha the prophet called his teacher Elijah "my father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its horsemen!" (2 Kings 2:12), and King Joash later addressed Elisha the very same way (2 Kings 13:14). King David called Saul "my father" (1 Samuel 24:11) out of respect for their age difference and because Saul remained the Lord's anointed king. Job the righteous said, "I was a father to the poor" (Job 29:16).

In the New Testament, St. Paul wrote, "To Timothy, my true son in the faith" (1 Timothy 1:2), "To Timothy, my beloved son" (2 Timothy 1:2), "You therefore, my son, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus" (2 Timothy 2:1), "To Titus, my true son in our common faith" (Titus 1:4), and, "I appeal to you for my son Onesimus, whom I have begotten while in my chains" (Philemon 10). Should Timothy, Titus, or Onesimus have objected, "You're not really our father, since we're not supposed to call anyone on earth our father"? Clearly not.

St. Paul also described Timothy as having served the gospel alongside him "as a son with his father" (Philippians 2:22), and instructed him, "Do not rebuke an older man, but exhort him as a father" (1 Timothy 5:1), showing real respect for age and treating an older man as a father figure. St. Stephen likewise addressed his own accusers, saying, "Men, brethren, and fathers" (Acts 7:2).

St. Paul wrote to the Galatians, "My little children, for whom I labor in birth again until Christ is formed in you" (Galatians 4:19), and told the Corinthians, "As my beloved children I warn you. For though you might have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel... For this reason I have sent Timothy to you, who is my beloved and faithful son in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 4:14-15,17).
St. John wrote, "My little children, these things I write to you, that you may not sin" (1 John 2:1), and, "I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in truth" (3 John 4).

subsections.heading: A COMMON QUESTION: RECEIVING BLESSINGS THROUGH A PRIEST
paragraphs: Question: Why do we receive a blessing through another human being, the priest? Isn't God alone the true source of blessing?

Answer: Absolutely, God is the source of every genuine blessing, as St. James wrote, "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and comes down from the Father of lights" (James 1:17). But God has always chosen to use human beings as channels through which His blessings reach others.

Noah blessed his sons (Genesis 9:26-27). Isaac blessed his sons (Genesis 27:27-29), and St. Paul confirms, "By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning things to come" (Hebrews 11:20). Jacob, in turn, blessed Joseph's sons (Genesis 48:20; Hebrews 11:21). God told Abraham, "You shall be a blessing" (Genesis 12:2). Elijah became a blessing within the widow's household (1 Kings 17), and Elisha blessed the household of the Shunammite woman (2 Kings 4). Scripture also records, "The Lord blessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake" (Genesis 39:5). Simeon the elder blessed both the Virgin Mary and Joseph (Luke 2:34). St. Paul asks, "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?" (1 Corinthians 10:16).

In fact, as Christians, we are all called to actively bless others: "Love your enemies, bless those who curse you" (Matthew 5:44). "Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse" (Romans 12:14). "Not returning evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary, blessing" (1 Peter 3:9).
"A woman shall not wear anything that pertains to a man, nor shall a man put on a woman's garment, for all who do so are an abomination to the Lord your God" (Deuteronomy 22:5).
The Question of Women's Ordination

subsections.heading: IN THE BEGINNING
paragraphs: Scripture tells us, "God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them" (Genesis 1:27). Both Adam and Eve were equally created in God's image. Neither received more of that image than the other. Scripture therefore begins by affirming the equality of the sexes. As persons, as human beings, as spiritual beings standing before God, men and women are completely equal.

Despite this equality, the second chapter of Genesis gives a more detailed account of how the two were created, revealing some differences in their God-given roles. God did not create the man and woman at the exact same moment. He created Adam first, and Eve afterward, for a specific purpose. By creating Adam first, God established headship as His intended structure for human relationships (Genesis 2:20). If God had intended something different, He could easily have formed Adam and Eve together at the same time and said, "It is not good that man or woman should be alone; I will make them helpers comparable to each other." Instead, God shaped a structure in which the man holds a particular kind of authority.

God also prepared Adam for this role before creating Eve, by having him name the living creatures (Genesis 2:19-20). Naming carries real significance elsewhere in Scripture too. When the Israelites conquered the land across the Jordan, they showed their authority by renaming the rebuilt cities (Numbers 32:38). Pharaoh Necho asserted authority over Eliakim by renaming him Jehoiakim (2 Kings 23:34), and the chief of the eunuchs renamed Daniel and his three friends (Daniel 1:7). In the same way, after God brought Eve to Adam, Adam gave her the name "woman" (Genesis 2:23).

Even the manner of the woman's creation reflects this pattern. Woman was formed from a rib taken from the man's side, suggesting a close, dependent relationship. Man's creation carried with it a kind of leadership role; woman's creation carried with it a role of support for that leadership. Because of this, the original creation, before the fall, laid the groundwork for this structure of headship, which God still called "very good."

subsections.heading: THE FALL OF HUMANITY
paragraphs: When Eve was cleverly tempted and deceived in the Garden of Eden, she acted on her own rather than seeking Adam's guidance, eating the forbidden fruit and then leading her husband into sin as well (Genesis 3:6). Through Eve's lead, the whole created order became corrupted by sin, even though its underlying structure remained intact. Even so, Adam, as the one meant to lead, was held ultimately responsible. It was only after he too ate the fruit that "the eyes of both of them were opened" (Genesis 3:7).

Both the man and the woman received God's judgment for their rebellion. Along with death, they were now destined to live out their lives marked by suffering and pain. Part of God's judgment on Eve, and by extension on all women, introduced real tension into the relationship between men and women: "Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you" (Genesis 3:16). This same word "desire" appears again shortly after, describing sin's desire to overpower Cain: "Sin lies at the door, and its desire is for you, but you should rule over it" (Genesis 4:7).

So God's words to Eve point to a new tendency in women to seek control over men, even while men would, in practice, often rule over women, sometimes harshly. Throughout history, this has produced an ongoing tension between the sexes, with women seeking control and men exercising authority, often poorly. Before the fall, real harmony existed between man and woman. Through sin, tension and conflict entered this relationship for the first time. Adam and Eve lost their relationship with God, symbolized by their hiding among the trees, and their relationship with one another, symbolized by covering themselves with clothing. Through the cross, this original harmony is restored, though the pattern of headship established at creation is not erased.

subsections.heading: WAS PATRIARCHY A CULTURAL ACCOMMODATION IN THE OLD TESTAMENT?
paragraphs: Some argue that women couldn't serve as priests in Old Testament Israel simply because the surrounding culture wouldn't have allowed it. But this overlooks the fact that many of Israel's neighboring nations actually had both men and women serving as priests within their own religions. Others suggest Israelite women were excluded from priesthood specifically to prevent the kind of immorality associated with pagan priestesses. This argument has no real scriptural basis, and it also implies, without any real proof, that women are inherently more prone to sexual immorality than men. In reality, the surrounding culture of the time would have easily accepted women priests in Israel.

The actual reason women in Israel were not ordained as priests had nothing to do with surrounding culture. It came from the pre-fall principle of headship, which reserved spiritual leadership within corporate worship specifically for men.

Deborah, a married woman, stands out as a clear exception to this pattern (Judges 4:4), but she is the exception that proves the rule. Besides being a prophetess, Deborah also served as a judge over Israel. The biblical narrator makes his point clear by highlighting the failure of Israelite men at the time, too fearful to step into leadership themselves. Notice, for example, how Deborah confronts Barak, the military commander of Israel's army, over his own reluctance to lead. After relaying God's command that he engage Sisera's army in battle, Barak replies, "If you will go with me, then I will go; but if you will not go with me, I will not go!" (Judges 4:8). Deborah responds, "I will surely go with you; nevertheless there will be no glory for you in the journey you are taking, for the Lord will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman" (Judges 4:9).

It seems that the Lord raised up this remarkable, faith-filled woman specifically to shame the men of Israel for their own lack of faith, the very quality essential to leadership within God's holy nation. So this story is really meant to rebuke unfaithful men for failing to lead, not to establish a new standard replacing male headship. Scripture elsewhere describes the rule of women as a sign of God's judgment against a sinful nation: "As for My people, children are their oppressors, and women rule over them. O My people! Those who lead you cause you to err, and destroy the way of your paths" (Isaiah 3:12).

subsections.heading: WAS PATRIARCHY A CULTURAL ACCOMMODATION IN THE NEW TESTAMENT?
paragraphs: Some argue that our Lord Jesus Christ couldn't have ordained women as apostles, since the culture of His time simply wouldn't have allowed it without prematurely endangering His ministry. This argument effectively accuses our Lord of quietly accommodating the injustice women faced in His day. But how could this possibly be true, when our Lord Himself asked, "Which of you convicts Me of sin?" (John 8:46)? Sin surely includes any form of gender injustice.

Suggesting that Christ's choice of male apostles was simply a concession to the "male-dominated" culture of His time doesn't hold up. The Gospels show us clearly that our Lord was never afraid to break social customs whenever they conflicted with truth and Scripture. Against strong cultural expectations, He ministered to Gentiles, spoke openly with a Samaritan woman, healed people on the Sabbath, and ate with tax collectors and sinners. He directly confronted the social injustices of His day, speaking against unjust divorce and remarriage, driving out those who exploited others in the temple, and openly criticizing religious leaders for their hypocrisy.

While the Jewish Talmud claimed it would be better to burn the Torah than teach it to a woman, our Lord Jesus Christ freely taught women, including them among His listeners and using illustrations and images that would have been familiar to them (Matthew 13:33; Luke 15:8-10). At a time when men typically avoided even placing coins directly into a woman's hand to prevent physical contact, our Lord touched women to heal them and allowed them to touch Him in return (Luke 7:38). He even welcomed a group of women to travel alongside Him and His disciples (Luke 8:1-3).

Everything about our Lord's life and teaching shows that He never bowed to cultural pressure when moral truth was at stake. He openly condemned the scribes and Pharisees, and anyone else who bent scriptural truth to fit their own cultural norms, calling them "hypocrites" (Matthew 15:7). The "cultural argument" ultimately fails to explain why Scripture never establishes a precedent for women holding headship roles in worship, in either the Old or New Testament.

In how our Lord treated women, we see Him genuinely elevate their standing and treat them with a level of compassion and respect they had rarely, if ever, experienced before. Yet even so, our Lord never elevated women into positions of authority over men. None of the twelve apostles He personally selected were women.

Our Lord could easily have chosen six men and their wives together as apostles, since the wives of the apostles often traveled alongside them (1 Corinthians 9:5). He did not. He could have chosen at least one of the women actively involved in His ministry, who traveled with Him and financially supported Him and His disciples (Luke 8:1-3). He did not. He could have ordained His own blessed mother, who already carried the divine honor of being called "blessed among women" (Luke 1:28). He did not. He could have chosen Mary Magdalene, the very woman He personally commissioned to announce His resurrection (John 20:1-18). He did not. He could have ordained the Samaritan woman, who overcame several cultural barriers, being five times divorced, living unlawfully with a man, and being a Samaritan, to become a remarkably successful evangelist. He did not.

By never appointing a woman as an apostle, our Lord effectively confirmed the pattern already established in the Old Testament, even as He broke from His surrounding culture in so many other ways. If breaking this particular pattern would have genuinely served His mission, it seems clear He would have done so, just as He did elsewhere. It doesn't hold up to argue that this same countercultural Lord suddenly became culturally conditioned specifically on this one point.

In the same way, suggesting that St. Paul's own instructions limiting women's authority over men were merely concessions to the anti-women attitudes of his time ignores Paul's own clearly stated reasoning, and effectively accuses him of real theological inconsistency and hypocrisy. St. Paul wrote, "I do not permit a woman to teach or to have authority over a man, but to be in silence" (1 Timothy 2:12). His stated reason follows immediately: "For Adam was formed first, then Eve, and Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived, fell into transgression" (1 Timothy 2:13-14).

St. Paul, in restricting women from teaching authority, gives us his actual reasoning directly. He never cites cultural or social conditions specific to Ephesus, where Timothy served as bishop, or to New Testament times generally, as the basis for this instruction. Whatever cultural pressures may have existed in Ephesus, whether Gnosticism, occult practices, worship of the mother-goddess Diana, mysticism, or early feminist movements, St. Paul instead grounds his instruction in a theological reason tied to the original creation order. His stated reasoning was that Adam was formed first, and that Adam was not deceived, while the woman was. St. Paul points directly back to the pre-fall creation pattern of headship, reaffirmed after the fall as well. By grounding his instruction in God's own arrangement at creation, rather than in the customs of his own time, St. Paul rules out the idea that this instruction was simply a product of his particular culture or era.

Those who try to explain away St. Paul's words as mere cultural accommodation are effectively suggesting that he either misunderstood or misapplied the Old Testament simply to avoid the discomfort of confronting unjust cultural norms directly. But how could this possibly describe the same Paul who wrote, "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28)? Just a few verses before the passage in question, St. Paul insists, "I am speaking the truth in Christ and not lying" (1 Timothy 2:7).

St. Paul also wrote, "Let your women keep silent in the churches, for they are not permitted to speak; but they are to be submissive, as the law also says" (1 Corinthians 14:34). So St. Paul's reasoning for restricting headship authority to men was never rooted in culture. He clearly understood the lasting, permanent validity of the creation principle of male headship.

St. Paul applies this same reasoning elsewhere, when addressing the practice of head coverings: "For a man indeed ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but woman is the glory of man. For man is not from woman, but woman from man. Nor was man created for the woman, but woman for the man. For this reason the woman ought to have a symbol of authority on her head, because of the angels. Nevertheless, neither is man independent of woman, nor woman independent of man, in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 11:7-11).

This instruction is not weakened or contradicted by St. Paul's earlier mention of women prophesying (1 Corinthians 11:5). Scripture itself distinguishes between the office of pastor and the gift of prophecy: "He Himself gave some to be apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, and some pastors and teachers" (Ephesians 4:11). The gift of teaching and the gift of prophecy are fundamentally different from one another (Romans 12:6-7).

Prophesying involved directly relaying divine revelation, with content that was not the prophet's own to shape (1 Corinthians 14:29-31). A prophet or prophetess never spoke on their own initiative, but only as they were "moved by the Holy Spirit" (2 Peter 1:21). This left little room for personal interpretation in the actual message delivered. This is exactly why the early Church was instructed, "Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge. But if anything is revealed to another who sits by, let the first keep silent" (1 Corinthians 14:29-30).

An elder or priest, by contrast, retains a real degree of personal freedom in how he communicates and teaches, even while the essential content of doctrine remains fixed and unchanging. He is expected to actively engage his own reasoning and reflection in this task.

It's also worth noting, in light of how God's revelation unfolded progressively, that the gift of prophecy was initially an extraordinary, temporary spiritual gift, tied specifically to the beginning of the age of the Holy Spirit and the spread of the Gospel to the whole world. Both men and women shared in this gift at the very start of this new era, fulfilling Old Testament prophecy (Joel 2:28-32; Acts 2:17-21). This kind of extraordinary spiritual gift marked a unique moment at the dawn of this new spiritual age, and is not part of the Church's normal, ongoing ministry today.

The claim that St. Paul contradicts himself, allowing women to prophesy in one place (1 Corinthians 11:5) while instructing them to remain silent in church elsewhere (1 Corinthians 14:34-35), doesn't really hold up. There's no clear evidence that women were prophesying specifically inside formal church gatherings. St. Paul's instruction is that prophets, not prophetesses specifically, are to speak within the church (1 Corinthians 14:29-33). Immediately after giving this instruction, he tells women to remain silent in the churches (1 Corinthians 14:34-35). It seems highly unlikely that someone of St. Paul's theological stature would flatly contradict himself within the space of just a few sentences.

subsections.heading: BIBLICAL OBSTACLES TO WOMEN'S ORDINATION
paragraphs: Scripture consistently teaches that women are not to be ordained as elders or priests. At least three lines of evidence support this. The first concerns the specific qualifications required for the office of priest or bishop. The second concerns the process of replacing Judas among the apostles. The third involves a direct scriptural prohibition against women serving as pastors.
── 1. QUALIFICATIONS FOR ELDERSHIP ──

The specific qualifications given for pastors or elders strongly imply that these roles are meant for men (1 Timothy 3:1-7; Titus 1:5-9). A bishop is required to be "the husband of one wife" (1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:6). He must also be someone who "rules his own household well," since this is treated as a prerequisite for overseeing the Church: "For if a man does not know how to rule his own house, how will he take care of the church of God?" (1 Timothy 3:4-5). According to Scripture, managing the household is primarily the man's responsibility, not the woman's, since the man is considered the head, under Christ: "The head of woman is man" (1 Corinthians 11:3).

This becomes even clearer when we look at the similar qualifications given for deacons: "Let deacons be the husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own houses well" (1 Timothy 3:12). This leaves little doubt about who is meant to manage the household. For consistency, the similar language used for pastors must likewise be understood as referring to men.
── 2. THE REPLACEMENT OF JUDAS ──

The Book of Acts records that the 120 male and female disciples gathered in the upper room sought guidance on replacing Judas. Notably, they turned to Scripture for direction, appealing to the Psalms: "Let another take his office" (Acts 1:20; Psalm 109:8).

Notice the qualifications given for candidates: "Therefore, of these men who have accompanied us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John to that day when He was taken up from us, one of these must become a witness with us of His resurrection" (Acts 1:21-22).

Why did these 120 believers, men and women together, put forward only two men as candidates, with no women considered? Was it because there were no qualified women present? Was there no woman among them whose heart (Acts 1:24) was acceptable to God for this apostolic role? Certainly not. There were clearly capable women among these 120 disciples, since all of them, men and women alike, were filled with the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. The complete absence of any woman candidate, including the Virgin Mary herself, is no accident. The reason women were excluded as candidates, even though some undoubtedly met the other qualifications listed in verses 21-22, was specifically their gender. The disciples gathered in the upper room were "with one accord" (Acts 1:14) in choosing a male replacement.
── 3. THE DIRECT PROHIBITION ──

The third reason women are not ordained as priests or bishops is that Scripture directly prohibits it. Writing to Timothy about how believers should conduct themselves "in the house of God, which is the church of the living God" (1 Timothy 3:15), St. Paul stated plainly, "I do not permit a woman to teach or to have authority over a man, but to be in silence" (1 Timothy 2:12), and, "Let your women keep silent in the churches, for they are not permitted to speak; but they are to be submissive, as the law also says... for it is shameful for women to speak in church" (1 Corinthians 14:34-35).

subsections.heading: DEACONESSES IN THE CHURCH
paragraphs: In the early Church, deaconesses assisted the apostles, and later bishops and priests, with various areas of service. Deaconesses were chosen from among older women, most often widows who had been married only once. St. Paul wrote, "Do not let a widow under sixty years old be taken into the number, and not unless she has been the wife of one man, well reported for good works: if she has brought up children, if she has lodged strangers, if she has washed the saints' feet, if she has relieved the afflicted, if she has diligently followed every good work" (1 Timothy 5:9-10).

One notable example of a successful deaconess is Phoebe, whom St. Paul commends to the Romans: "I commend to you Phoebe our sister, who is a servant of the church in Cenchrea, that you may receive her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints, and assist her in whatever business she has need of you; for indeed she has been a helper of many and of myself also" (Romans 16:1-2).

Since the thirteenth century, the formal service of consecrated deaconesses had largely faded within the Coptic Church. But recognizing the pressing need for women's service within the Church, Pope Shenouda III revived this role, consecrating a large group of deaconesses (who match the criterias outlined by the Apostolic Constitution) to serve the churches of Cairo on the Feast of Pentecost in 1981. This consecration does not involve the laying on of hands or formal ordination.
"Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow" (Psalm 51:7).
The Sacrament of Baptism

Baptism is the Holy Sacrament through which we are born again by being immersed in water three times in the name of the Holy Trinity: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Sacrament of Baptism has the primacy among the Seven Holy Sacraments for it is the door through which the individual enters the Church (as a congregation) and is given the right to partake of the rest of the Sacraments.

E Institution of The Sacrament: Lord Jesus Christ instituted this Sacrament after His blessed resurrection, having completed our redemption and having made salvation available, He said to His disciples, “All authority has been given to Me in heaven and on earth. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Mt 28:18-19), and “He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who does not believe will be condemned” (Mk 16:16). Thus baptism is necessary for salvation as the Lord indicated, “Most assuredly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the Kingdom of God” (Jn 3:5) E How Exactly Does Baptism Save Us? Salvation simply means remission of sins and it is written, “Without shedding of blood [death] there is no remission” (Heb 9:22). Salvation is made available through the redemptive death of Lord Jesus Christ on the cross. In order to have a share in this salvation, we must share the death and resurrection of the Lord. Therefore, St. Paul said, “That I may know Him and the power of His resurrection and the fellowship of His suffering being conformed to His death” (Phil 3:10). Unless a person undergoes such death, he/she will not be saved! Now how can we undergo such death? How can we share the death of the Lord? The answer is “Through Baptism”. St. Paul said, “Or do you not know that as many of you were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death? Therefore we were buried with Him through baptism into death” (Rom 6:3-4). It is our death and burial with the Lord through baptism that saves us and makes us share the glories of His Resurrection. St. Paul affirms, “For if we have been united together in the likeness of His death [baptism], certainly we shall be in the likeness of His resurrection… now if we died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with Him” (Rom 6:5-8). The salvation that began with our death and burial with Lord Jesus through baptism continues to be effective in us also through death. We obtain salvation through death and our bodies must always remain dead in relation to worldly lusts. For as long as the body is dead to sin, salvation lives in it, but when carnal lusts rise from this death, we become liable to lose our salvation since salvation is only attained through death.

Hence St. Paul exhorts us saying: “Reckon yourselves to be dead indeed to sin, but alive to God in Christ our Lord. Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body that you should obey it in its lusts.” (Rom 6:11-12). · “If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.” (Rom 8:13) · “Those who are Christ’s have crucified the flesh and its passions and desires.” (Gal 5:24) · “I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Gal 2:20) · “For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” (Col 3:3) · “Always carrying about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus.” (2 Cor 4:10) · “Therefore put to death your members which are on earth: fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry.” (Col 3:5) “He who has died has been freed from sin.” (Rom 6:7) ààThe salvation that we obtained through baptism continues with us through death. Thus we pray saying, “O, who tasted death in the flesh in the ninth hour for our sake, we sinners, put to death our carnal lusts, O Christ, our God, and deliver us” (From the prayer of the 9th hour – Coptic Book of Hours).

E Symbols of Baptism in The Old Testament: 1. It is written in the Holy Book of Genesis, “The Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters” (Gen 1:2). This is both a symbol and a prophecy about the work of the Holy Spirit in baptismal water to give it its saving efficacy. 2. St. Peter interpreted the story of Noah’s ark and the flood (Gen 7) as a symbol of baptism, he said, “The divine longsuffering waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being prepared, in which a few, that is, eight souls, were saved through water. There is also an antitype which now saves us – baptism (not the removal of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God), through the resurrection of Jesus Christ” (1 Pet 3:20-21) àà Notice the link between baptism and salvation through the resurrection of the Lord. 3. St. Paul interprets the commandment of circumcision (Gen 17) as a symbol of baptism, he said, “You were also circumcised with the circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the sins of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, buried with Him in baptism, in which you also were raised with Him through faith in the working of God who raised Him from the dead” (Col 2:11-12) ààNotice the link between baptism and salvation (through the resurrection of the Lord) for God said about the child who is not circumcised that he will be “cut off from his people, he has broken My covenant” (Gen 17:14). Likewise, a child who is not baptized cannot enter the Kingdom of God (Jn 3:5) 4. The relation between the ark, the circumcision, the saving resurrection of the Lord, and baptism goes even further. Notice that St. Peter emphasizes that only eight souls were saved from the evil world through the water of the flood. Also notice that God ordered that children must be circumcised on the eighth day. Now the Lord’s resurrection took place on the first day of the week (Jn 20:1) that is the eighth day from the previous week. The number eight represents the new life and eternity. In fact number eight is the only number (from 1-10) that does not have a beginning and end (8), which is basically the definition of eternity. 5. St. Paul interpreted the story of crossing the sea (Ex 14) as a symbol of baptism, he said, “All our fathers were under the cloud, all passed through the sea, all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Cor 10:1-2). The sea was a symbol of the baptismal water that draws its saving efficacy from the precious blood of our Lord (no wonder its called the Red Sea), the cloud was a symbol of the Holy Spirit who works through the baptismal water, and Pharaoh was a symbol of the devil who is destroyed by the cross of Lord Jesus through the water of baptism. 6. The Priesthood was not given to Aaron and his sons except after being washed with water (Ex 29:4), also the laver of bronze and it’s water set between the tabernacle of meeting and the alter (Ex 30:18) was a symbol of the spiritual cleansing effect of baptismal water. 7. The sacrifice of Elijah the Prophet was accepted after pouring water on it three times (1 Kgs 18:34). Moreover, Elijah himself was not taken up to heaven until he crossed the waters of the Jordan river (2 Kgs 2:8). The same happened with the Israelites who went into the Promised Land after going through the waters of the Jordan (Joshua 3). In the Holy Book of Revelation we read about “a sea of glass” (Rev 4:6) before the throne of God. The point is that we must go through the waters of baptism to reach heavenly Promised Land and enjoy the company of God.

E The Baptism of St. John The Baptist: No pre-Pentecostal baptism can be equated with Christian baptism. This not only includes St. John the Baptist’s but also the disciples’ baptisms during the life of the Lord on earth (Jn 4:2). These baptisms were preparatory ones, just for repentance, as St. John said, “I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance, but He who is coming after me is mightier than I … He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire” (Mt 3:11). The redemption had not yet been accomplished; the specific relationship of baptism with the cross and the blood of the Lord had not yet been established. Moreover, the gift of the Holy Spirit was not yet available (Jn 7:37-39). On the day of Pentecost no exceptions were allowed for those who may have received St. John’s baptism, St. Peter said, “Let every one of you be baptized” (Acts 2:38) The Holy Book of Acts tells us of a specific incidence where some believers at Ephesus were only baptized with St. John’s baptism so St. Paul asked, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” They replied, “We have not so much as heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.” He wondered, “Into what then were you baptized?” So they said, “Into John’s baptism” Then St. Paul explained, “John indeed baptized with a baptism of repentance, saying to the people that they should believe on Him who would come after him, that is on Christ Jesus.” So when they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. (Acts 19:1-5)

E The Effectiveness of Baptismal Water: It may be objected, “What does mere water do when a person is immersed in it?” One might just as well ask, what does water do when poured into the boiler? The water in the boiler can do nothing of and by itself, nor can the water in the baptistery, but when the water in the boiler is united with the mind of an engineer, it can drive an engine across a continent or a ship across the sea. So too, when water is united with the power of the Holy Spirit, it can give regeneration and spiritual cleansing. Those who think that the effectiveness of baptism depends on the water alone bring to mind the story of Naaman (2 Kgs 5), the commander of the Syrian army, who was a leper. This man came to Elisha the Prophet to be healed from leprosy so he told him, “Go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh shall be restored to you, and you shall be clean” (2 Kgs 5:10). Naaman was insulted and became furious; he said angrily, “Are not the Abanah and the Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? Could I not wash in them and be clean?” (2 Kgs 5:12). His servants, however, said to him, “My father, if the prophet had told you to do something great, would you not have done it? How much more then, when he says to you, ‘Wash and be clean’?” (2 Kgs 5:13). So Naaman went down and dipped in the Jordan and he was healed! Likewise, if the blind man from birth had questioned the words of Lord Jesus about washing in the pool of Siloam (Jn 9:11), he would have remained blind. Our Lord emphasized the relation between the water and the Spirit (Jn 3:5-6) thus baptismal water is not to be considered mere water for “There are three that bear witness on earth: The Spirit, the water, and the blood; and these three agree as one. (1 Jn 5:7)

E Immersion Vs Sprinkling: To baptize (Gr. Baptizo) literally means to immerse or to put into. Therefore, the Orthodox Church baptizes by triple immersion, “in the name of the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit” (Mt 28:19). Baptism by immersion is supported also by the following biblical examples: · “Both Philip and the eunuch went down into the water, and he baptized him. Now when they came out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught Philip away” (Acts 8:38-39). If baptism were by sprinkling, St. Philip could have just brought water to the chariot and sprinkled it on the eunuch. · St. Paul said, “We were buried with Him through baptism” (Rom 6:4), and “Buried with Him in baptism” (Col 2:12). The only way a person is buried in baptism is through complete immersion. · St. Paul said, “According to His mercy He saved us, through the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5), St. Ananias said to St. Paul (Saul), “Be baptized, and wash away your sins” (Acts 22:16). Baptism is also called “washing” in (1 Pet 3:18-21; Eph 5:26). To wash a piece of cloth you need to completely immerse it in water. àà Because baptism is a very important condition for salvation (Mk 16:16; Jn 3:5) the Church allows baptism by sprinkling only in the case where immersion is prevented by a medical condition and there is a risk that the person would die without being baptized. For example, a newborn with a fatal health condition that is kept in an incubator cannot be immersed three times in water, so the Church allows sprinkling in this instance. Moreover, if there was no priest available, any Orthodox Christian (male or female) can perform the baptism by anointing the baby with water three times saying, “I baptize you in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit”. If the baby lives, baptism is not repeated and the child just needs to be anointed with the Holy oil. E Why Do We Baptize Infants? 1. Baptism is essential for salvation and without it a person cannot enter the Kingdom of God, “Most assuredly I say to you, unless a person is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the Kingdom of God” (Jn 3:5). Infants are no exception since they are born with the corrupt nature due to the original sin. Therefore, infants are baptized to insure their salvation. 2. Circumcision was a symbol of baptism (Col 2:11-13). Now if God commanded that infants enter in the Old Covenant with Him, should we prevent them from entering in the New Covenant? 3. Crossing the Red Sea was also a symbol of baptism (1 Cor 10:1-2). Undoubtedly, infants crossed the sea with their parents so why should today’s infants be prevented from being baptized? 4. St. Peter said to the people on Pentecost, “Be baptized… and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is to you and to your children” (Acts 2:38-39). This is a clear implication that children are accepted in baptism. 5. Holy Scripture records several occasions where families and entire households were baptized together (Acts 16:14-15, 33; 1 Cor 1:16). This is another implication that children were baptized. 6. There is not a single biblical verse that supports the prevention of infants’ baptism. On the contrary, our Lord said, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not forbid them; for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Mt 19:14), and “Take heed that you do not despise one of these little ones, for I say to you that in heaven their angels always see the face of My Father who is in heaven” (Mt 18:10)

E One Baptism: The Sacrament of Baptism is performed once and is not repeated as we say in the creed, “we confess one baptism for the remission of sins”. Since baptism is a spiritual birth so a person is born (baptized) once and since baptism is death with the Lord and the Lord died once so a person dies with the Lord (baptized) once. Thus St. Paul said, “one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph 4:5)
E FAQ:
Q: If baptism is necessary for salvation, were the people of the Old Testament baptized?

A: Baptism was not a condition for salvation in the Old Testament, but it was only instituted as a condition in the New Testament, “He who believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mk 16:16). The reason is that baptism’s saving efficacy is linked to the death of Lord Jesus Christ and the Lord had not yet died in the Old Testament. Had baptism existed in the Old Testament, people would have had to be baptized in order to be saved. Nevertheless, the people of the Old Testament practiced the symbol of baptism available to them at such time, namely circumcision (Col 2:11-13). They also kept the Passover, which was a symbol of our Lord (1 Cor 5:7)
Q: What is the fate of infants who die without being baptized?

A: Lord Jesus Christ said, “Most assuredly, I say to you, unless one is born again, he cannot see the Kingdom of God” (Jn 3:3), and “Most assuredly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (Jn 3:5). These infants inherited the corrupt nature due to the original sin, “we were by nature children of wrath” (Eph 2:3) and St. Paul affirms that corruption does not inherit incorruption (1 Cor 15:50). Therefore, these infants cannot enter nor see the Kingdom of God. One may object, “They didn’t do anything wrong!” Well, they didn’t do anything right either. The early Church fathers agree that these infants will not enter the Kingdom of God (based on the words of the Lord) but concerning suffering and punishment the most probable and most acceptable opinion is that they will not suffer since they did not commit any personal sin (St. Gregory the Theologian). God said, “the uncircumcised male child, who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin, that person (that child) shall be cut off from his people; he has broken My covenant” (Gen 17:14). Someone may ask, “What about God’s mercy?” God’s mercy is full of justice and His Justice is full of mercy. So trust in the merciful justice of our God and don’t worry about this subject. “The voice of the Lord is over the waters; the God of glory thunders; the Lord is over many waters.” (Ps 29:3)
Baptism in the Holy Gospels

The Holy Bible is far from silent on the subject of baptism. Many clear and straightforward verses are spread over the whole range of the New Testament from the Holy Gospels to the Holy Epistles. In what follows we shall, by the grace of God, examine the meaning of baptism as recorded in the Holy Gospels. “Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I have commanded you.” (Mt 28:19-20) The key term in this commission is “make disciples”. “Going” is the prerequisite for making disciples, “baptizing” and “teaching” are the means of making disciples. It is very significant that baptism is distinguished from the category of “all things” that the believers must be taught to observe. This is especially important in view of the common Protestant heresy that baptism is just one of the “good works” of Christian life and that it is a mere act of obedience comparable to the many other acts of obedience that we are to perform simply because God has commanded them. If this is so, why is baptism alone singled out for specific mention, and why is it separated from “all that I have commanded you”? The way the commission is worded suggests that baptism has a unique importance in the process of disciple making. We can agree that the term “all things” does refer to the good works belonging to Christian life, but the term is comprehensive “all things” and baptism is not included in it. The clear implication is that baptism is not meant to be placed in the category of good works; it has a meaning distinct from any act of obedience expected of a Christian and an importance far beyond that of any of these acts. This unique importance of baptism is revealed by the following passage where baptism is mentioned but where it would be out of place if it were just another good work, “There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all” (Eph 4:4-6). This passage lists the seven fundamental bases for Christian unity. Isn’t it striking the company that baptism keeps? If baptism is relatively insignificant or even if it has equal significance with other Christian commands and duties, then of all such duties why should it be singled out and ranged here alongside items that occupy a much more lofty sphere of importance? Its companions are the three Persons of the Trinity, the Church (one body), heaven (one hope), and faith (the one body of doctrines which are believed). How can Protestants fail to see the significance of baptism being included here in some sense comparable in importance at least to faith itself? (See Heb 6:1-2 for a similar listing). More light is shed on the nature of this uniqueness in the record of one divinely directed instance of implementing the commission; St. Philip & the eunuch (Acts 8:26-40). It is written that St. Philip “preached Jesus to him” (v.35). This is the one word summary of his preaching “Jesus”. The only recorded response is the eunuch’s cry “Look! Water! What prevents me from being baptized?” (v.36). We cannot avoid the conclusion that the evangelistic preaching of Lord Jesus Christ includes the imperative of baptism. In terms of the commission in (Mt 28:18-19), baptism is something taught before conversion with view to becoming a disciple, while “teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you” follows conversion and deals with the details of Christian life. The element in the text itself that confirms the unique importance of baptism is the expression “in the name” (Gr. eis to onoma). In the biblical world, a person’s name was not just an arbitrary means of identification but was considered to be intrinsically related to the person himself, representing his qualities, his character, and his very nature. Thus “the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit” represents the very Persons of The Holy Trinity. So the Lord Jesus Christ commissioned His apostles to baptize people into a specific relation with the Holy Trinity. The phrase “eis to onoma” was a technical term used in the world of Greek business and commerce. It indicates the entry of a sum of money or an item of property into the account bearing the name of its owner. (Albrecht Opeke, ‘Theological Dictionary of the New Testament’) The use of this phrase in (Mt 28:19) indicates that the purpose of baptism is to unite us with the Triune God in an ownership relation. Thus the person being baptized passes into the possession of the Triune God. Such a relationship prepares him/her for the dwelling of the Holy Spirit after baptism (Chrismation). St. Paul said, “Or do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God, and you are not your own? For we were bought at a price; therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God’s” (1 Cor 6:19-20). The price that St. Paul is talking about is the redemptive death of our Lord Jesus Christ and the strong relation between baptism and the death of the Lord is revealed in (Rom 6:3-4; Col 2:11-13). Thus when we are baptized “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” we become God’s own special possession. No wonder baptism is singled out in the commission as having a unique importance. What we know just from this one passage (Mt 28:18-19) warrants the assessment that baptism has a saving significance – a conclusion that will be even more inescapable in view of the other verses to be discussed below. “Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature. He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who does not believe will be condemned.” (Mk 16:16) It is universally accepted that faith is and has always been an essential condition for salvation (Jn 3:16,18,36). What is striking about (Mk 16:16) is that faith and baptism are linked together in this context. If anything at all were going to be put into such a relationship with faith, there are other things that might at first seem to the non-Orthodox Christian more appropriate than baptism.
