Augustine, by contrast, understood the Church as more like a hospital, a place where fallen humanity could gradually recover and grow in holiness through grace.

subsections.heading: THE NATURE OF GRACE
paragraphs: ── ST. AUGUSTINE'S VIEW ──

Augustine believed we are completely dependent on God for our salvation, from beginning to end. One of his favorite verses was, "Apart from Me you can do nothing" (John 15:5). He carefully distinguished between our natural human abilities, given to us simply as part of being human, and the additional, special gift of grace. God does not simply leave us where we are, disabled by sin and unable to save ourselves. Instead, He gives us grace so that we can be healed, forgiven, and restored.

For Augustine, human nature is fragile, weak, and lost, genuinely needing God's help and care in order to be restored and renewed. Grace, in his understanding, is God's generous and completely undeserved attention toward humanity, through which this healing process can even begin. Human nature requires real transformation through this freely given grace of God.
── PELAGIUS' VIEW ──

Pelagius used the word "grace" quite differently. First, he understood grace simply as our natural human abilities themselves. For Pelagius, these abilities were not damaged, disabled, or compromised in any way. God gave them to humanity, and they are meant to be used as they are. When Pelagius spoke of humanity choosing, "through grace," to live sinlessly, he really meant that our natural abilities of will and reason should, on their own, be enough to help us avoid sin. As Augustine quickly pointed out, this is not at all what the New Testament actually means by "grace."

Second, Pelagius understood grace as a kind of outward enlightenment or instruction God provides. He gave examples like the Ten Commandments and the moral example set by our Lord Jesus Christ. In his view, grace teaches us what our moral duties are, but it does not actually help us carry them out. We are simply enabled to avoid sin through the teaching and example of Christ. Augustine argued that this approach essentially reduced God's grace down to mere law and instruction. According to Augustine, the New Testament actually describes grace as God's direct, active assistance to humanity, not just moral guidance from the outside.

So for Pelagius, grace was something external and passive, something outside of us. For Augustine, grace was the real, redeeming presence of God, active within us through our Lord Jesus Christ, genuinely transforming us from the inside.
── HOW EACH UNDERSTOOD GOD'S INVOLVEMENT ──

For Pelagius, God created humanity, gave clear instructions about right and wrong, and then largely stepped back, taking no further active interest in humanity until the final Day of Judgment. On that day, each person would be judged strictly according to whether they had completely fulfilled every moral obligation. Failing to do so would lead to eternal punishment. Pelagius' calls to moral perfection were marked by heavy warnings about the terrible fate awaiting anyone who fell short.

For Augustine, humanity was created good by God, but then fell away from Him. In an act of grace, God Himself came to rescue fallen humanity from this predicament. He actively helps us: healing us, enlightening us, strengthening us, and continually working within us to restore us.

In short, for Pelagius, humanity simply needed to be shown the right path and then left to walk it alone. For Augustine, humanity needed to be shown the right path and then gently helped every step of the way, or the goal could never even be approached, let alone reached.

subsections.heading: THE BASIS OF SALVATION
paragraphs: ── ST. AUGUSTINE'S VIEW ──

For Augustine, humanity is made right with God entirely as an act of grace. Even our good works are really the result of God working within our fallen human nature. Everything leading up to our salvation is a free, undeserved gift from God, given purely out of love for sinners. Through the death and resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, God is able to deal with fallen humanity in this remarkably generous way, giving us what we do not deserve, salvation, and withholding from us what we do deserve, condemnation.
── PELAGIUS' VIEW ──

For Pelagius, humanity is made right with God based on its own merit. Human good works, in his view, come from the fully independent exercise of human free will, fulfilling an obligation God has laid out. Failing to meet this obligation exposes a person to the real threat of eternal punishment. In this view, our Lord Jesus Christ contributes to salvation only by showing us, through His actions and teaching, exactly what God expects of us. When Pelagius spoke of "salvation in Christ," he really meant "salvation through imitating Christ's example."

It's clear, then, that Pelagianism and Augustine's theology represent two fundamentally different ways of understanding how God and humanity relate to one another. The Council of Carthage in AD 418 sided firmly with Augustine's views on grace and sin, and condemned Pelagianism without reservation. (Adapted from *Christian Theology: An Introduction* by Alister E. McGrath.)

subsections.heading: A NOTE OF CAUTION
paragraphs: St. Augustine's arguments against Pelagius were later used as a starting point for several other heresies, including Salvation by Grace Alone, Predestination, and Eternal Security. Because of this, his anti-Pelagian writings should always be read and understood in contrast to Pelagius' own actual views, so they are not taken out of context or pushed further than Augustine himself intended.
"By the grace of God I am what I am, and His grace toward me was not in vain; but I labored more abundantly than they all, yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me" (1 Corinthians 15:10).
Grace in the Orthodox Perspective

subsections.heading: GRACE AND FREE WILL
paragraphs: Is a person saved by their own works, or by God's grace? Many people have gone too far defending one side or the other, and ended up mistaken. As a general principle, the Orthodox approach to any theological debate tends to find the balanced middle ground between two extremes.

This particular controversy reached its peak in the sixteenth century, when medieval Roman Catholicism placed heavy emphasis on good works as necessary to please God. As a result, many people lived in constant uncertainty and fear about their salvation. This distorted picture of Christianity helped fuel the Protestant Reformation, as its leaders rebelled and redefined grace and justification in very different terms. Much of the foundation for these Protestant teachings came from a particular reading of St. Augustine's writings against Pelagius, combined with a misreading of St. Paul's letters to the Romans and Galatians. Indeed, St. Paul's letters do contain, as Scripture itself warns, "things hard to understand, which those who are untaught and unstable twist to their own destruction" (2 Peter 3:16).

subsections.heading: GRACE AS A GIFT
paragraphs: By definition, grace is a gift. Yet St. Paul pleaded with the Corinthians "not to receive the grace of God in vain" (2 Corinthians 6:1). Speaking about his own life, he said, "His grace toward me was not in vain; but I labored more abundantly than they all," meaning more than the other apostles (1 Corinthians 15:10). So even though grace is truly a gift, we must not receive it and then let it go to waste. St. Paul urged Timothy, "Do not neglect the gift that is in you" (1 Timothy 4:14). In the parable of the unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:23-35), notice that the servant actually lost the free gift his master had given him, because of his own evil actions afterward.
── AN EXAMPLE: AUTHORITY OVER DEMONS ──

Our Lord Jesus Christ gave His disciples the gift of authority over unclean spirits. He said, "Behold, I give you the authority to trample on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall by any means hurt you" (Luke 10:19). When the disciples reported back, "Lord, even the demons are subject to us in Your name" (Luke 10:17), He replied, "I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven" (Luke 10:18). Clearly, the disciples' own weak human nature had no real power over demons. It was only through God's grace that they gained this authority.

Yet on another occasion, the disciples were unable to cast a demon out of an epileptic boy, and privately asked our Lord, "Why could we not cast him out?" (Matthew 17:19). He answered, "This kind does not go out except by prayer and fasting" (Matthew 17:21). So should this authority over demons be seen as a free gift from God, or as something earned through human effort, prayer and fasting? It is genuinely a gift from God, yet this gift is never meant to be received and left unused (2 Corinthians 6:1).

Scripture says, "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all" (2 Corinthians 13:14). This is a real partnership between two parties actively working together, the Holy Spirit and the human person, as St. Paul said, "We are God's fellow workers" (1 Corinthians 3:9). God will not save anyone unless their own free will actually responds to His grace: "Today, if you will hear His voice, do not harden your hearts" (Hebrews 3:8). At the same time, good works alone can never save a person either. This is exactly why the Church teaches us to pray during the midnight prayer, "In my works, apart from grace, I shall have no salvation."

The Holy Spirit is fully able to save and redeem us, but He will not do this alone, without our participation. He wants us to actively take part with Him in managing our own lives. This is what it means to have communion with the Holy Spirit. Given that God genuinely desires everyone's salvation, and given that the heresy of predestination has already been rejected, we should ask: if grace alone did all the work, why would both righteous people and evil people even exist? If salvation depended purely on grace acting alone, there would be no sinners left on earth at all. The simple fact that even one unrepentant sinner exists is clear proof that grace alone does not save anyone without their own participation.
── AN EXAMPLE: JOSHUA AND MOSES ──

Did the people defeat Amalek because of Joshua's fighting, or because of Moses' prayer? Joshua led the army into battle while Moses stood on a hilltop, holding up his hands in prayer (Exodus 17:11). Focusing on only one of these two, while ignoring the other, would be a mistake. Joshua alone, no matter how hard he fought, could never have defeated Amalek without Moses' prayers securing God's help. At the same time, Moses' prayer never meant the army could afford to fight half-heartedly. Fighting, representing human effort, and prayer, representing God's grace, worked together side by side. They were never separate from one another.
── AN EXAMPLE: DAVID AND GOLIATH ──

How did David defeat Goliath? David placed his trust entirely in God, telling Goliath, "I come to you in the name of the Lord of hosts... for the battle is the Lord's, and He will give you into our hands" (1 Samuel 17:45-47). Yet David also personally chose five smooth stones from the stream, ran quickly toward the battle line to meet Goliath, placed a stone in his sling, and struck skillfully. He then had to draw Goliath's own sword to finish the task. Every one of these actions was genuine human effort. Even so, Scripture credits the victory to God, not to David's skill. There must always be real striving and effort on our part, yet in the end, success itself belongs to God.

subsections.heading: GRACE AND FREE WILL WORKING TOGETHER
paragraphs: Free will is itself a gift from God, and salvation is also a gift from God. God's gifts never contradict or cancel each other out. So the work of the Holy Spirit within us does not erase our free will. We remain able to respond to His work, to actively participate with Him, and to be led by Him, but we are equally able to resist and refuse His work within us. St. Stephen told the Jewish leaders, "You always resist the Holy Spirit" (Acts 7:51).

St. Paul instructs us, "Do not quench the Spirit" (1 Thessalonians 5:19), and, "Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God" (Ephesians 4:30). Grace genuinely offers us help, but we retain the real option to accept or reject it. If we choose to actively participate with the Holy Spirit, we will, by God's grace, grow toward true holiness, in proportion to how fully we respond and submit. But if we refuse, grace will never force this growth upon us against our will. The great Divine Physician stands ready and willing to heal, but He still asks each of us, "Do you want to be made well?" (John 5:6).

subsections.heading: GRACE AND SPIRITUAL WARFARE
paragraphs: In Ephesians 6:10-18, we find real wrestling, real spiritual struggle, and real effort, using the full armor of God. God's spiritual weapons carry real power, but if we never actually use them, we will still be defeated. Notice too that among these spiritual weapons are righteousness, prayer, supplication, and watchfulness, all of which require real effort on our part. St. Peter wrote, "Resist him [the devil], steadfast in the faith" (1 Peter 5:9). We are called to resist the devil, to strive, to stand firm and courageous, yet never relying on our own human ability alone. Instead, we resist him while remaining firmly grounded in faith. This verse holds both realities together: real effort in resisting the devil, and the faith that this effort ultimately depends on.

This striving is never a purely personal effort, separate from God's own work within us. It is always a combination of both, exactly as St. Paul described his own ministry: "To this end I labor, striving according to His working which works in me mightily" (Colossians 1:29). This is the same striving he called for when rebuking the Hebrews: "You have not yet resisted to bloodshed, striving against sin" (Hebrews 12:4), and in his instruction to Timothy: "Fight the good fight of faith" (1 Timothy 6:12).

Pope Shenouda III once said that in spiritual warfare, we conquer through our weakness, not our own strength. God told St. Paul, "My strength is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9), and King Solomon wrote, "God gives grace to the humble" (Proverbs 3:34). So we should resist the devil with everything we have, yet still hold to our Lord's teaching, "Do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing" (Matthew 6:3). In other words, we should never take personal credit for any victory, but attribute every success entirely to God.
── AN EXAMPLE: GIDEON'S ARMY ──

There is a beautiful story in the Book of Judges that illustrates this truth well. As Gideon prepared to fight the Midianites, he gathered a massive army of thousands of soldiers. But the Lord told him, "The people who are with you are too many for Me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel claim glory for itself against Me, saying, 'My own hand has saved me'" (Judges 7:2). So God had Gideon reduce the army all the way down to just three hundred men, telling him, "By the three hundred men who lapped I will save you" (Judges 7:7).

Something similar happened to St. Paul. Because of the abundance of revelations he had received, and to keep him from becoming prideful, God gave him "a thorn in the flesh" (2 Corinthians 12:7). When Paul begged the Lord three separate times to remove it, the Lord told him instead, "My grace is sufficient for you, for My strength is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). As Scripture says, "We have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellence of the power may be of God and not of us" (2 Corinthians 4:7).

subsections.heading: A COMMON QUESTION
paragraphs: Question: St. Paul wrote, "It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy" (Romans 9:16). Does this mean human will and effort play no real role in salvation?

Answer: This cannot possibly be what St. Paul meant. The very same person who wrote "not of him who runs" also said of himself, "I have finished the race" (2 Timothy 4:7), and, "I press toward the goal" (Philippians 3:14). St. Paul also tells us, "Do you not know that those who run in a race all run, but one receives the prize? Run in such a way that you may obtain it" (1 Corinthians 9:24), and, "Let us run with endurance the race that is set before us" (Hebrews 12:1). He continues, speaking of himself, "Therefore I run thus: not with uncertainty" (1 Corinthians 9:26).

St. Paul truly ran and pressed forward, even though he was filled with the Holy Spirit and grace worked through him more powerfully than through almost anyone else. He still genuinely needed to run, to press on, and to finish the race, to fight the good fight, exactly as he said, "His grace toward me was not in vain; but I labored more abundantly than they all" (1 Corinthians 15:10). And yet, he never took personal credit for this effort, immediately adding, "Yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me" (1 Corinthians 15:10).

It is entirely true that salvation is "not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy." But we should ask: toward whom does God actually show this mercy? It is toward those who genuinely will and genuinely run. Consider St. Paul's related words: "Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase" (1 Corinthians 3:7). It is entirely true that God alone gives the growth, but growth to what? To the plant that has actually been planted and watered. We cannot use the truth that "neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters" as an excuse to stop planting and watering altogether, foolishly waiting for growth to appear on its own. As King Solomon wrote, "He who observes the wind will not sow, and he who regards the clouds will not reap" (Ecclesiastes 11:4).

The right approach is to plant and water diligently, while still crediting all growth to God. In the same way, we must run and strive with real effort, while still attributing our success entirely to God's mercy and grace, echoing St. Paul's own words: "It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy" (Romans 9:16).
"Whom He foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son" (Romans 8:29).
Predestination in the Orthodox Perspective

subsections.heading: ST. AUGUSTINE AND PREDESTINATION
paragraphs: Grace is a gift, not a reward. This idea is foundational to St. Augustine's theology. If grace were a reward, people could effectively purchase their own salvation through good works, earning their redemption outright. Augustine believed this was completely at odds with what the New Testament actually teaches about grace. Insisting that grace is truly a gift protected against these flawed theories of salvation, and there was real wisdom in this insight.

But on closer examination, this same insight had a darker side. As the Pelagian controversy grew increasingly bitter, the more troubling implications of Augustine's doctrine of grace became clearer. If grace is truly a gift, then God must remain free to offer it, or withhold it, without being obligated by anything outside Himself. If grace were given because of some outside factor, it would stop being a true gift and would simply become a reward for a particular action or attitude. For Augustine, grace only remains truly gracious if it is purely and only a gift, reflecting nothing but the giver's own generosity.

But this gift is not given to everyone. It is particular, given only to some, not because it isn't offered to all, but because not all accept it. Augustine's defense of God's graciousness, resting on the belief that God must remain free to give or withhold grace, ultimately led him to affirm that grace is particular rather than universal.

When this idea is combined with Augustine's teaching on sin, its full weight becomes clear. All of humanity is contaminated by sin and unable to break free on its own. Only grace can set people free. Yet since grace is not given to everyone equally, only some will actually be saved, specifically, those to whom grace is given. Augustine was careful to insist that this did not mean some people were predestined to damnation. Rather, God had simply chosen some out of fallen humanity as a whole. These chosen individuals were truly predestined for salvation. The rest, according to Augustine, were not actively condemned to damnation; they simply were not chosen for salvation.

Even so, as his critics pointed out, choosing to save some inevitably meant choosing not to save others. This exact question resurfaced with new intensity during the ninth-century predestination controversy, when the Benedictine monk Godescalc of Orbais, also known as Gottschalk, developed a doctrine of "double predestination" similar to what would later appear in Calvinism. Following his own logic to its conclusion, Godescalc argued that if God had truly predestined some people to eternal damnation, it made no sense to say Christ died for them, since His death would have accomplished nothing for their unchangeable fate. Wrestling with this troubling implication, Godescalc proposed instead that Christ died only for the elect, meaning His saving work was deliberately limited only to those already predestined to benefit from it.

Most ninth-century theologians reacted to this idea with real disbelief and rejected it. Even so, it would later resurface within Calvinism. (Adapted from Alister E. McGrath, *Christian Theology: An Introduction*.)

subsections.heading: THE UNIVERSAL SAVING WILL OF GOD
paragraphs: Scripture repeatedly affirms that God genuinely desires the salvation of everyone: "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live" (Ezekiel 33:11). "God our Savior... desires all men to be saved" (1 Timothy 2:4). "God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have eternal life" (John 3:16). "He Himself is the propitiation for our sins, and not ours only, but also for the whole world" (1 John 2:2). "Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature" (Mark 16:15).

subsections.heading: HUMAN FREE WILL
paragraphs: Scripture equally affirms that people possess genuine free will: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing; therefore choose life" (Deuteronomy 30:19). "If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land; but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be devoured by the sword" (Isaiah 1:19-20). "If anyone desires to come after Me, let him deny himself" (Matthew 16:24). "If you want to enter into life, keep the commandments" (Matthew 19:17). "If you want to be perfect, go sell what you have and give to the poor" (Matthew 19:21). "Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and dine with him, and he with Me" (Revelation 3:20). "How often I wanted to gather your children together... but you were not willing!" (Matthew 23:37). "You are not willing to come to Me that you may have life" (John 5:40). Our Lord's parable of the wedding feast describes a king who invited guests, "and they were not willing to come" (Matthew 22:2-3). And of Christ Himself, Scripture says, "He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him" (John 1:11).

subsections.heading: GOD'S FOREKNOWLEDGE
paragraphs: Through His divine foreknowledge, God already knows what will happen in the future. He knows who will use their free will to pursue righteousness and goodness, and He equally knows who will misuse that same free will to choose evil and disobedience. God's foreknowledge never interferes with the free will He has given us.

It's also important to distinguish between God's universal saving will and His foreknowledge concerning those who ultimately reject Him. In other words, God genuinely wants every person to be saved, even while He already knows that some will freely choose the wrong path.

subsections.heading: PREDESTINATION: THE ORTHODOX UNDERSTANDING
paragraphs: St. Paul wrote, "All things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called according to His purpose... for whom He foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son" (Romans 8:28-30). Notice carefully that St. Paul says this applies to those who love God, not simply to those whom God loves. This distinction matters, because our love for God depends on our own response, not solely on God's initiative. In the same way, he wrote, "Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man the things which God has prepared for those who love Him" (1 Corinthians 2:9), again saying "those who love Him," not simply "those whom He loves," since our salvation ultimately depends on how we respond to God's grace.

Because of this, we understand God's predestination for salvation as flowing not from His own arbitrary will (since God genuinely wants everyone to be saved), but from His divine foreknowledge: "Whom He foreknew, He also predestined." This same understanding appears in St. Peter's words: believers are "elect according to the foreknowledge of God" (1 Peter 1:2). The key distinction to hold onto is the difference between God's will and God's foreknowledge.
── EXAMPLE: JACOB AND ESAU ──

Scripture says, "Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated" (Romans 9:13). Both Jacob and Esau were genuinely called to salvation, since God loves everyone equally and shows no favoritism (Deuteronomy 10:17). But God, in His foreknowledge, already knew how each of these two men would freely respond to His call. Esau was "hated," or rejected, only because God foreknew he would choose wrongly and live wickedly. Jacob was "loved," or accepted, because God foreknew he would embrace the faith of Abraham and serve God's purposes. God's foreknowledge never overrode either man's free will. This is exactly why St. Paul immediately asks, "What shall we say then? Is there unrighteousness with God? Certainly not!" (Romans 9:14).

The same principle applies to St. Paul himself. Even though he once persecuted the Church, God already knew he would repent, and had chosen him even before his birth: "God, who separated me from my mother's womb and called me through His grace" (Galatians 1:15). Paul's earlier persecution of the Church is itself clear evidence of real free will, since God's foreknowledge of his future calling clearly never interfered with his freedom to choose evil beforehand.
── EXAMPLE: THE POTTER AND THE CLAY ──

Scripture says, "Does not the potter have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?" (Romans 9:21). The potter, representing God, certainly has the power to shape the clay however He chooses, into a vessel of honor or of dishonor. But this potter is also wise and just. It would be absurd for a wonderful, workable lump of clay to fall into the hands of such a wise potter, only for him to deliberately shape it into something dishonorable. On the other hand, if the clay itself is flawed and genuinely unfit to become a vessel of honor, the potter may be forced by the clay's own poor condition to shape it into something less honorable instead. Everything depends on the actual condition of the clay itself, since the potter's genuine intention is for every vessel to become one of honor.

Consider this related passage: "Look, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are you in My hand, O house of Israel! The instant I speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up, to pull down, and to destroy it, if that nation against whom I have spoken turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I thought to bring upon it. And the instant I speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant it, if it does evil in My sight so that it does not obey My voice, then I will relent concerning the good which I said I would benefit it" (Jeremiah 18:6-10).

This passage makes clear that God, the Potter, remains genuinely willing to change His course if a person turns away from evil and earnestly seeks their own salvation. The story of Nineveh is a perfect example of this in action.
── THE PROBLEM WITH THE PROTESTANT VIEW OF PREDESTINATION ──

The Protestant teaching of predestination and election implies real injustice and favoritism. It can lead sinners into despair, feeling that any effort toward repentance is pointless if they've already been predestined as vessels of dishonor and damnation. It can also lead the righteous into carelessness and spiritual laziness. This view leaves many important questions unanswered:

1. Why would God give the world His commandments at all, if people's salvation or damnation were already predetermined? 2. Why would the devil bother tempting the elect, if their salvation is already guaranteed? 3. On what basis could reward even make sense for the elect, if they never truly had a choice in their own destiny? 4. Why would God punish someone who was predestined for ruin from the very beginning?
This understanding of predestination, as taught by Calvinist Protestants, leads to real confusion, and stands in direct tension with God's love, God's justice, and human free will.
"For many walk, of whom I have told you often, and now tell you even weeping, that they are the enemies of the cross of Christ: whose end is destruction" (Philippians 3:18).
Would a Believer Perish?

subsections.heading: CAN A BELIEVER BE LOST?
paragraphs: According to the teaching of "Eternal Security," a true believer can never be lost. Most Protestants hold that salvation comes by grace alone, understood as God's free gift, and therefore guaranteed once received. In what follows, we will examine this teaching in light of Scripture.

subsections.heading: 1. THE CUT-OFF BRANCH
paragraphs: In his letter to the Romans, St. Paul compares the Jews who did not believe to natural branches broken off an olive tree, and the Gentiles who believed to a wild olive branch grafted in to take their place: "If some branches were broken off, and you, being a wild olive tree, were grafted in among them, and with them became partaker of the root and fatness of the olive tree" (Romans 11:17). He then tells the Gentiles, "You will say then, branches were broken off, that I might be grafted in. Well said. Because of unbelief they were broken off, and you stand by faith" (Romans 11:19-20). St. Paul is clearly speaking to believers who are now grafted into the tree and share in its root and richness.

Now consider what he says next to these same believers: "Do not be haughty, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, He may not spare you either. Therefore consider the goodness and severity of God: on those who fell, severity; but toward you, goodness, if you continue in His goodness. Otherwise, you also will be cut off" (Romans 11:20-22). Why would there be any reason for fear, if salvation were truly guaranteed no matter what? The closing words, "you also will be cut off," are a direct warning that these believers could perish if they fail to continue in God's goodness.

This matches what our Lord Himself said: "I am the true vine, and My Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in Me that does not bear fruit He takes away" (John 15:1-2), and, "If anyone does not abide in Me, he is cast out as a branch and is withered; and they gather them and throw them into the fire, and they are burned" (John 15:6). A believer who remains unfruitful will certainly perish.

subsections.heading: 2. APOSTATES AND HERETICS
paragraphs: Heretics and apostates were once genuine believers who later abandoned the true faith and were lost. St. Paul wrote, "Some will depart from the faith, giving heed to deceiving spirits and doctrines of demons" (1 Timothy 4:1). Those who follow such deceiving spirits are certainly lost, as Galatians 5:20-21 makes clear. But the phrase "will depart from the faith" itself proves they were genuinely believers to begin with.

In the Book of Revelation, we read about the teaching and practices of the Nicolaitans, which our Lord hates (Revelation 2:6,15). These Nicolaitans followed Nicolas, one of the seven deacons named in Acts 6:5. Nicolas met every qualification the apostles required for deaconship, being "of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom" (Acts 6:3), and yet he later fell away and was lost.

Another example is Demas, St. Paul's own coworker, mentioned warmly in his letters: "Luke the beloved physician and Demas greet you" (Colossians 4:14), and, "Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you, as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, Luke, my fellow laborers" (Philemon 23-24). Demas was clearly a genuine believer and a preacher alongside Paul. But consider what later happened to him: "Demas has forsaken me, having loved this present world" (2 Timothy 4:10). Demas effectively became an enemy of God, since "friendship with the world is enmity with God" (James 4:4).

In the parable of the sower, our Lord described those who fall away: "The ones on the rock are those who, when they hear, receive the word with joy; and these have no root, who believe for a while and in time of temptation fall away" (Luke 8:13). Those who fall away in temptation clearly have no salvation left. Yet our Lord Himself said they had "received the word with joy" and "believed for a while," a period that could stretch on for years.

St. Paul also wrote, "Let no one deceive you by any means, for that day will not come unless the falling away comes first" (2 Thessalonians 2:3). In such a large-scale falling away, many genuine believers will certainly be lost (Hebrews 6:4-6). Scripture also says of the beast from the sea, "It was granted to him to make war with the saints and to overcome them" (Revelation 13:7). The word "saints" here clearly means believers, yet they lost everything because they failed to overcome, since "he who overcomes shall inherit all things" (Revelation 21:7).

St. Peter wrote, "For if, after they have escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the latter end is worse for them than the beginning. For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than having known it, to turn from the holy commandment delivered to them" (2 Peter 2:20-21). Those who had "escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ" were clearly true believers, yet they were lost because they turned away from what they had received.

subsections.heading: 3. WILLFUL SIN AFTER KNOWING THE TRUTH
paragraphs: In his letter to the Hebrews, St. Paul writes to "holy brethren, partakers of the heavenly calling" (Hebrews 3:1), those who are "partakers of Christ" (Hebrews 3:14), and who, "after being illuminated, endured a great struggle with sufferings" (Hebrews 10:32). He even tells them, "Therefore, brethren, having boldness to enter the Holiest by the blood of Jesus" (Hebrews 10:19).

But then he warns them: "If we sin willfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a certain fearful expectation of judgment, and fiery indignation which will devour the adversaries" (Hebrews 10:26-27). This is a direct warning to these very "holy brethren" that willful, unrepented sin leads to being lost.

He continues: "Of how much worse punishment, do you suppose, will he be thought worthy who has trampled the Son of God underfoot, counted the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified a common thing, and insulted the Spirit of grace?" (Hebrews 10:29). The phrase "by which he was sanctified" proves this person was genuinely a believer, sanctified by Christ's own blood. And the phrase "insulted the Spirit of grace" directly contradicts the idea of so-called "Irresistible Grace," since St. Stephen told the Jewish leaders, "You always resist the Holy Spirit" (Acts 7:51).

The Book of Acts also records the story of Ananias and his wife Sapphira, two believers who sinned willfully and were struck down as a result (Acts 5). Scripture says, "Great fear came upon all the church and upon all who heard these things" (Acts 5:11). If the apostles had taught that salvation is guaranteed no matter what a believer does, what reason would there have been for such great fear?

subsections.heading: 4. THE DISOBEDIENT PEOPLE IN THE WILDERNESS
paragraphs: St. Paul continues his warning to the "holy brethren, partakers of the heavenly calling," saying, "Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: Today, if you will hear His voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion, in the day of trial in the wilderness" (Hebrews 3:7-8). What happened on that day of rebellion, and what does it mean for us? Those who rebelled and provoked the Lord were the disobedient Israelites in the wilderness of Sinai. The Lord said of them, "I swore in My wrath, they shall not enter My rest" (Hebrews 3:11).

Had these people, who perished and whose bodies fell in the wilderness, not already been saved once? St. Paul answers, "For who, having heard, rebelled? Indeed, was it not all who came out of Egypt, led by Moses?" (Hebrews 3:16). The Lord had freed them from slavery and parted the Red Sea for them, and they crossed it as a symbol of baptism: "All were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea" (1 Corinthians 10:2). And yet, despite all of this, they perished in the wilderness and lost their salvation.

The Apostle warns these same "holy brethren," saying, "Let us therefore be diligent to enter that rest, lest anyone fall after the same example of disobedience" (Hebrews 4:11), and, "Therefore, since a promise remains of entering His rest, let us fear lest any of you seem to have come short of it" (Hebrews 4:1).

This example also brings to mind Lot's wife, who was rescued from the destruction of Sodom, yet perished just outside the city. This is exactly why our Lord said, "Remember Lot's wife" (Luke 17:32). As Scripture reminds us, "All these things happened to them as examples, and they were written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. Therefore let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall" (1 Corinthians 10:11-12).

subsections.heading: 5. JUDAS ISCARIOT
paragraphs: Judas was one of the twelve disciples personally chosen by our Lord (Matthew 10:4). He was given authority over unclean spirits, able to cast them out and heal every kind of sickness and disease (Matthew 10:1). He was given knowledge of the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 13:10-11). He left everything to follow the Lord (Matthew 19:27), and was even promised a throne alongside the other disciples to judge the tribes of Israel (Matthew 19:28). He did not turn away with the crowd who abandoned Christ over His teaching on the Eucharist (John 6:66).

This same Judas, the chosen disciple, the believer, the miracle worker, who felt genuine remorse when our Lord was condemned and confessed his sin before the chief priests (Matthew 27:3-4), was ultimately lost. Scripture even calls him "the son of perdition" (John 17:12), not only for betraying Christ, but because he lost all hope and took his own life. We cannot argue that Judas was never truly a believer simply because our Lord once called him "a devil" (John 6:70), since Christ also called Peter "Satan" on one occasion (Mark 8:33), and Scripture reminds us that even demons "believe and tremble" (James 2:19).

subsections.heading: 6. LACKING GOOD WORKS
paragraphs: St. James wrote, "What does it profit, my brethren, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can faith save him?" (James 2:14). This "brother" who has faith is clearly described as a believer, yet this same believer, if he lacks good works, will not be saved by that faith alone. James also wrote, "Therefore, to him who knows to do good and does not do it, to him it is sin" (James 4:17), and, "The wages of sin is death" (Romans 6:23).

subsections.heading: 7. LACKING LOVE
paragraphs: In 1 Corinthians 13:1-3, Paul describes someone who speaks the tongues of men and angels, has the gift of prophecy, understands every mystery, has faith strong enough to move mountains, gives everything to feed the poor, and even gives his own body to be burned. This is clearly a description of an extraordinary believer. Yet Paul says that without love, this same believer is nothing, and will ultimately be lost.

This should remind us of the angel of the church in Ephesus (Revelation 2:1-7). He was without question a genuine believer, described as a star held in the right hand of the Lord Jesus (Revelation 1:20; 2:1). He worked hard, showed patience, and refused to tolerate evil (Revelation 2:2). He endured and did not grow weary (Revelation 2:3). And yet, because he had abandoned his first love (Revelation 2:4), even though he remained a believer, he was told to repent and return to his first works, or else face losing his place altogether (Revelation 2:5).

subsections.heading: CONCLUSION
paragraphs: It's clear from all of this that the doctrine of "Eternal Security of the Believer" does not hold up and stands in real tension with Scripture. All of the elect are indeed believers, but not every believer remains among the elect.
"A wise man fears and departs from evil, but a fool rages and is self-confident" (Proverbs 14:16).
Confidence in Salvation

subsections.heading: CONFIDENCE IN SALVATION
paragraphs: Salvation depends on the grace of God: "By grace you have been saved" (Ephesians 2:8). But it also depends on how our free will responds to God's call: "Have a walk worthy of the calling with which you were called" (Ephesians 4:1), and, "If you would hear His voice, do not harden your hearts" (Hebrews 3:8, 15). So when we talk about confidence in our salvation, we really need to talk about two different things: confidence in God, and confidence in ourselves.

subsections.heading: CONFIDENCE IN GOD
paragraphs: A believer should place unlimited trust and hope in God. Since God's mercy has no limit, our hope in that mercy should have no limit either. Hope is one of the three great virtues named in 1 Corinthians 13:13, and like any virtue, it grows within a person until it reaches its full measure. Perfect hope has no room for doubt and rests on complete certainty. It is grounded in faith in God's own nature, in how He has dealt with us in the past, in the infinite worth of His precious blood, and in His faithful promises. God's mercy, compassion, forgiveness, and love are all without limit. His blood is sufficient to forgive the sins of the entire world, from the beginning of time to the very end, not just once, but endlessly.

subsections.heading: CONFIDENCE IN OURSELVES
paragraphs: Even though we should place unlimited trust in God, we should never place that same trust in our own free will, which can still turn toward evil. "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us" (1 John 1:8). It would be foolish (Proverbs 14:16) to assume we have somehow moved past sin entirely, living a renewed, sanctified life in which sin is no longer possible for us. We are not stronger than those who fell before us. If anything, we may stand on lower ground than they did before their own fall.

St. Paul wrote, "It is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted the heavenly gift, and have become partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, if they fall away, to renew them again to repentance" (Hebrews 6:4-6). Have we, who confidently expect to reach the Kingdom, actually attained the level these people once had? And yet even they, who had received such extraordinary gifts, fell away and were lost, compared by Scripture to land that is "rejected and near to being cursed, whose end is to be burned" (Hebrews 6:8).

St. Paul also wrote, "I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest, when I have preached to others, I myself should become disqualified" (1 Corinthians 9:27). This is the same great saint who was chosen from his mother's womb and called by grace (Galatians 1:15), who was caught up into paradise itself (2 Corinthians 12:4). Even he disciplined his own body out of concern that he might be disqualified. And we are talking about self-confidence!

subsections.heading: THE CONDITIONS FOR GENUINE CONFIDENCE
paragraphs: St. John wrote, "If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God, and whatever we ask we receive from Him, because we keep His commandments and do the things that are pleasing in His sight" (1 John 3:21-22). The condition here is clear: our own conscience must have nothing to accuse us of, meaning we are not doing anything our hearts would rightly condemn.

St. John also wrote, "Little children, abide in Him, that when He appears, we may have confidence and not be ashamed before Him at His coming" (1 John 2:28). But what does it actually mean to abide in our Lord Jesus Christ? St. John explains: "He who says he abides in Him ought himself also to walk just as He walked" (1 John 2:6), and, "Whoever abides in Him does not sin" (1 John 3:6). After reading these verses, who among us would dare claim they are truly abiding in the Lord in this complete sense? And if we cannot honestly say this, how can we claim full confidence?

Finally, St. John wrote, "Love has been perfected among us in this: that we may have boldness in the Day of Judgment; because as He is, so are we in the world" (1 John 4:17). We should ask ourselves honestly: have we actually reached this kind of perfect love? Do we love the Lord with all our heart, mind, strength, and thought? Do we live in this world the way our Lord Himself lived in it? If we can truly say yes, then we are blessed indeed, and we can have real confidence.

subsections.heading: PASSAGES THAT NEED CLARIFICATION
paragraphs: ── 1. "NO ONE SHALL SNATCH THEM OUT OF MY HAND" (JOHN 10:27-28) ──

Our Lord said, "My sheep hear My voice, and I know them, and they follow Me, and I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish; neither shall anyone snatch them out of My hand" (John 10:27-28).

First, notice these people are called "sheep," meaning they belong to the group who will stand at our Lord's right hand on the day of judgment, since the "goats" will stand on His left (Matthew 25:32-33). They hear the Lord's voice and follow Him, meaning they keep His commandments, and "they will by no means follow a stranger, but will flee from him" (John 10:5). This kind of sheep will certainly never perish.

Second, being held in the Lord's hand does not mean the sheep have lost their own free will. In the Book of Revelation, we read of the seven angels, meaning bishops, of the churches being held in the Lord's right hand (Revelation 1:16,20). The phrase "right hand" represents the Lord's power (Psalm 118:15-16). Yet one of these very angels had fallen and needed to repent (Revelation 2:5), another had a reputation for being alive while actually being dead (Revelation 3:1), and a third was lukewarm, on the verge of being spit out of the Lord's mouth, and was described as wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked (Revelation 3:16-17). No one can forcibly snatch a sheep out of the Lord's hand, but the sheep themselves remain free to wander away. As St. Paul warns, "Therefore let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall" (1 Corinthians 10:12).
── 2. "SEALED WITH THE HOLY SPIRIT" (EPHESIANS 1:13-14) ──
St. Paul wrote, "Having believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the guarantee of our inheritance" (Ephesians 1:13-14).

St. Paul also told the same Ephesians, "Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption" (Ephesians 4:30), and told the Thessalonians, "Do not quench the Spirit" (1 Thessalonians 5:19). It's also possible to blaspheme against the Holy Spirit, meaning to refuse repentance entirely, and never receive forgiveness (Mark 3:29), since doing so "insults the Spirit of grace" (Hebrews 10:29). This is exactly why the Church teaches us to pray humbly, echoing King David's words, "Do not take Your Holy Spirit from me" (Psalm 51:11).
── 3. NAMES WRITTEN IN THE BOOK OF LIFE (REVELATION 21:27) ──

St. John wrote, "There shall by no means enter it [the Heavenly Jerusalem] anything that defiles, or causes an abomination or a lie, but only those who are written in the Lamb's Book of Life" (Revelation 21:27). Our Lord told His disciples, "Rejoice because your names are written in heaven" (Luke 10:20). St. Paul wrote of "my fellow workers, whose names are in the Book of Life" (Philippians 4:3).

Even so, having our name written in the Book of Life is not, by itself, an unconditional guarantee of salvation. The Lord told Moses, "Whoever has sinned against Me, I will blot him out of My book" (Exodus 32:33). Notice that Judas was among the disciples whose names were written in heaven (Luke 10:20), as was Demas, St. Paul's own coworker (Philemon 24), and both were ultimately lost. We are called to overcome in order to keep our names written in that book: "He who overcomes shall be clothed in white garments, and I will not blot out his name from the Book of Life" (Revelation 3:5).
── 4. "HE WHO PROMISED IS FAITHFUL" (HEBREWS 10:23) ──

Scripture says, "Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for He who promised is faithful" (Hebrews 10:23). God is indeed completely faithful to His promise of salvation, and we should have real confidence in that promise.

But concerning ourselves, it is also written, "Therefore, since a promise remains of entering His rest, let us fear lest any of you seem to have come short of it" (Hebrews 4:1). Indeed, "If we deny Him, He also will deny us" (2 Timothy 2:12). This is exactly why we are told, "Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling" (Philippians 2:12), and, "Conduct yourselves throughout the time of your stay here in fear" (1 Peter 1:17).
In the end, we should hold complete confidence in God, while at the same time heeding the warning, "Do not be haughty, but fear" (Romans 11:20).
"How shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?" (Hebrews 2:3).
Salvation in the Orthodox Perspective

subsections.heading: THE BLOOD OF CHRIST AND SALVATION
paragraphs: Salvation is only available through the blood of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ: "Without shedding of blood there is no remission" (Hebrews 9:22). The Passover lamb was itself a symbol pointing forward to Christ: "For indeed Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed for us" (1 Corinthians 5:7). Through the blood of that lamb, the Israelites were saved from death: "Now the blood shall be a sign for you on the houses where you are, and when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and the plague shall not be on you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt" (Exodus 12:13). Through Christ's precious blood, our sins are forgiven, and we enter into a new covenant with God: "This is My blood of the new covenant, which is shed for many for the remission of sins" (Matthew 26:28).
── FURTHER BIBLICAL REFERENCES ──

"Shepherd the church of God which He purchased with His own blood" (Acts 20:28). "Having now been justified by His blood, we shall be saved from wrath through Him" (Romans 5:9). "In Him we have redemption through His blood" (Ephesians 1:7; Colossians 1:14). "In Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been made near by the blood of Christ" (Ephesians 2:13). "Having made peace through the blood of His cross" (Colossians 1:20). "Not with the blood of goats and calves, but with His own blood He entered the Most Holy Place once for all, having obtained eternal redemption" (Hebrews 9:12). "How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God" (Hebrews 9:14). "Therefore, brethren, having boldness to enter the Holiest by the blood of Jesus" (Hebrews 10:19). "Of how much worse punishment, do you suppose, will he be thought worthy who has trampled the Son of God underfoot, counted the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified a common thing, and insulted the Spirit of grace?" (Hebrews 10:29). "To Jesus the Mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling that speaks better things than that of Abel" (Hebrews 12:24).

Christ's blood "speaks better things" than Abel's because Abel's blood cried out for vengeance, as God told Cain, "The voice of your brother's blood cries out to Me from the ground" (Genesis 4:10). Christ's blood, by contrast, cried out for forgiveness: "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do" (Luke 23:34).

"Now may the God of peace... through the blood of the everlasting covenant, make you complete in every good work to do His will" (Hebrews 13:20-21). "You were not redeemed with corruptible things... but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot" (1 Peter 1:18-19). "There are three that bear witness on earth: the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and these three agree as one" (1 John 5:8). "The blood of Jesus Christ His Son cleanses us from all sin" (1 John 1:7). "To Him who loved us and washed us from our sins in His own blood" (Revelation 1:5). "You were slain, and have redeemed us to God by Your blood" (Revelation 5:9). "These are the ones who came out of the great tribulation, and washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb" (Revelation 7:14). "And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb" (Revelation 12:11).

subsections.heading: HOW THIS PLAYS OUT IN SCRIPTURE
paragraphs: The sins of the people in the Old Testament were not actually forgiven until the day of Christ's crucifixion. Every Old Testament sin was, in a sense, merely "put away" for the time being, as the prophet Nathan told King David, "The Lord also has put away your sin; you shall not die" (2 Samuel 12:13). Notice he did not say, "has forgiven your sin," since "without shedding of blood there is no remission" (Hebrews 9:22). Because of this, paradise remained closed to even the righteous people of the Old Testament until the day Christ shed His blood on the cross and sins were finally remitted. The phrase "put away" means the sin was transferred, so to speak, from a person's own account to the account of the Savior, to be paid for later.

In the same way, when our Lord told the paralytic, "Your sins are forgiven you" (Luke 5:20), He was effectively giving him a promise of forgiveness, a kind of check that would only be cashed on the cross. This applies to every instance of forgiveness and salvation mentioned before the crucifixion, including the sinful woman, the tax collector, Zacchaeus, and others.

subsections.heading: THE CONDITIONS FOR SALVATION
paragraphs: Our Lord said His blood was shed "for many" (Matthew 26:28), yet in reality, only a few are actually saved (Matthew 7:13-14). This sad reality exists because salvation comes with certain real conditions:
1. Faith. 2. The saving sacraments: baptism, confirmation, repentance and confession, and the Eucharist. 3. Good works.
Each of these deserves its own separate discussion, but first a few clarifications are needed.

Baptism, confirmation, and the Eucharist did not apply to the people of the Old Testament, since these sacraments draw their saving power specifically from Christ's blood and the work of the Holy Spirit, both realities belonging to the New Testament. Even so, the people of the Old Testament had symbols pointing toward these sacraments, such as circumcision serving as a symbol of baptism (Colossians 2:11-12).

These conditions for salvation apply specifically to normal, responsible adults. Whenever these conditions come up, people naturally raise all kinds of edge cases to question them. For example, individuals with significant mental disabilities and infants lack the intellectual capacity to understand and personally believe, so the condition of faith, in this specific sense, does not apply to them in the same way.

The sacrament of the priesthood is what administers these saving sacraments to us, and so plays a major role in our salvation. While we don't personally need to become priests ourselves to be saved, we do genuinely need priests for our own salvation, since they serve as "stewards of the mysteries of God" (1 Corinthians 4:1).

subsections.heading: SALVATION AS THE STORY OF A WHOLE LIFE
paragraphs: St. Paul wrote, "The message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God" (1 Corinthians 1:18). In the Orthodox understanding, salvation covers the whole of life. It isn't a single historical event confined to one moment in the past. As Scripture addresses the subject of salvation, an Orthodox Christian sees it in at least three dimensions:

I believe that I have been saved, having put on our Lord Jesus Christ in baptism. I believe that I am being saved, growing in Christ through the sacramental life of the Church. I believe that I will be saved, by God's mercy on the Last Day of Judgment.

The story of our salvation begins with faith, repentance, and baptism: "He who believes and is baptized will be saved" (Mark 16:16). "Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins" (Acts 2:38), a remission that covers both original sin and every actual sin committed before baptism. Baptism gives us salvation, forgiveness, and new spiritual birth. In baptism, we are buried together with Christ (Colossians 2:12), dying and rising with Him into a new life (Romans 6:4): "Knowing this, that our old man was crucified with Him, that the body of sin might be done away with, that we should no longer be slaves of sin" (Romans 6:6). Through baptism, we become children of God and members of His body, the Church. As St. Paul wrote, "As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ" (Galatians 3:27).

In the sacrament of confirmation, we receive the gift of the Holy Spirit: "You have an anointing from the Holy One" (1 John 2:20), and we become a temple of the Holy Spirit: "Do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God?" (1 Corinthians 6:19). As we respond to the Spirit's work within us, we grow spiritually and bear the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22-23).

Even so, we still sin after being baptized and confirmed. "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us" (1 John 1:8). Even though our nature has been renewed, we did not become incapable of error. The nature we receive in baptism is pure, yet still capable of sin, just as Adam's nature was before the fall. The gift of new birth we receive in baptism does not erase our free will. Even so, there's a real difference between someone who sins while never having been baptized, living a life given over to wickedness, and someone who sins after baptism. This second person still has the Holy Spirit within them, ready to convict and lead them back to repentance. Their sin remains temporary, unless they personally choose, through their own free will, to reject repentance entirely, insulting the Spirit of grace (Hebrews 10:29) and so blaspheming against the Holy Spirit (Luke 12:10).

Through repentance and confession, we continue being saved: "Unless you repent you will all likewise perish" (Luke 13:3,5). "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9). We also receive salvation through the Holy Eucharist, as the priest declares during the Divine Liturgy that it is "given for us salvation, remission of sins, and eternal life to those who partake of it," echoing Christ's own words, "Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life" (John 6:54).

Our life on earth serves as a genuine test of our faith: "Now for a little while, if need be, you have been grieved by various trials, that the genuineness of your faith, being much more precious than gold that perishes, though it is tested by fire, may be found to praise, honor, and glory at the revelation of Jesus Christ" (1 Peter 1:6-7). Indeed, "We must through many tribulations enter the kingdom of God" (Acts 14:22).

We also remain engaged in real spiritual warfare: "We do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this age, against spiritual hosts of wickedness in the heavenly places" (Ephesians 6:12). "Be sober, be vigilant, because your adversary the devil walks about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour" (1 Peter 5:8). Our Lord said, "He who endures to the end will be saved" (Matthew 10:22), and, "He who overcomes shall inherit all things" (Revelation 21:7).

St. Paul wrote, "Lest, when I have preached to others, I myself should become disqualified" (1 Corinthians 9:27), which is exactly why he also urges us, "Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling" (Philippians 2:12). St. Peter likewise exhorts us, "Conduct yourselves throughout the time of your stay here in fear" (1 Peter 1:17). The final outcome of our life and our struggle will only be revealed on the Last Day: "You, who are kept by the power of God through faith for salvation, ready to be revealed in the last time" (1 Peter 1:5). This is exactly why our Lord said, "Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life" (Revelation 2:10).
Since this spiritual struggle continues throughout our entire life, salvation truly is the story of a whole life, not a single isolated moment.
"Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen" (Hebrews 11:1).
Faith in the Orthodox Perspective

subsections.heading: FAITH IN THE ORTHODOX PERSPECTIVE
paragraphs: For Orthodox Christians, being justified by faith is a living, ongoing reality, not a fixed, one-time event. Faith is alive and continuous. It is never something frozen at a single moment in time. Christians do not experience true faith only once, at some critical turning point, and then expect that single moment to cover the rest of their lives. Genuine faith is not simply a decision made once. It is an entire way of life (*The Orthodox Study Bible*).
In what follows, we will look closely at the characteristics of saving faith:
1. Sound faith: apostolic faith, one faith, biblical and traditional faith. 2. Loving faith. 3. Working faith. 4. Faith that endures to the end.

subsections.heading: SOUND FAITH
paragraphs: Scripture states plainly that whoever follows a heresy will not be saved: "The works of the flesh are evident, which are: adultery, fornication... dissensions, heresies... and the like, of which I tell you beforehand, just as I also told you in time past, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God" (Galatians 5:19-21). "There will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies" (2 Peter 2:1). "Whoever transgresses and does not abide in the doctrine of Christ does not have God... If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house nor greet him; for he who greets him shares in his evil deeds" (2 John 9-11). "Now I urge you, brethren, note those who cause divisions and offenses, contrary to the doctrine which you learned, and avoid them" (Romans 16:17). "Reject a divisive man after the first and second admonition, knowing that such a person is warped and sinning, being self-condemned" (Titus 3:10-11).

Several other verses stress how important sound doctrine truly is: "Rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith" (Titus 1:13). "Speak the things which are proper for sound doctrine" (Titus 2:1). "In doctrine showing integrity, reverence, incorruptibility, sound speech" (Titus 2:7-8). "Hold fast the pattern of sound words which you have heard from me" (2 Timothy 1:13). "Take heed to yourself and to the doctrine. Continue in them, for in doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you" (1 Timothy 4:16). "For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires, because they have itching ears, they will heap up for themselves teachers" (2 Timothy 4:3). "A bishop must be blameless... holding fast the faithful word as he has been taught, that he may be able, by sound doctrine, both to exhort and convict those who contradict" (Titus 1:7-9). "You will be a good minister of Jesus Christ, nourished in the words of faith and of good doctrine which you have carefully followed" (1 Timothy 4:6).

A quick note on terminology: heresy is defined as a religious belief that opposes the accepted teachings of a Church, or the outright rejection of the doctrines of an established Church (Webster's New World Dictionary).
── APOSTOLIC FAITH ──

Our Lord told the apostles, "He who hears you hears Me, he who rejects you rejects Me" (Luke 10:16). In other words, rejecting the sound apostolic faith, preserved within the Orthodox Apostolic Church, is really rejecting our Lord Jesus Christ Himself. St. Paul defended this same apostolic faith fiercely: "If we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel to you than what we have preached to you, let him be accursed. As we have said before, so now I say again, if anyone preaches any other gospel to you than what you have received, let him be accursed" (Galatians 1:8-9).

The direct connection between this sound apostolic faith and salvation becomes clear in St. John's description of the heavenly Jerusalem: "Now the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them were the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb" (Revelation 21:14). St. Paul likewise wrote of the Church "having been built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ Himself being the chief cornerstone" (Ephesians 2:20). In short, without this sound apostolic faith, there is no salvation.
── ONE FAITH ──

The saving apostolic faith is a single, unified faith, as St. Paul wrote: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism" (Ephesians 4:5). Unity is an essential mark of sound faith. This is why we confess belief in one holy, catholic (meaning universal), and apostolic Church. Salvation is found only within this Church, where this one sound faith is genuinely practiced: "The Lord added to the church daily those who were being saved" (Acts 2:47). "If he refuses to hear the church, let him be to you like a heathen and a tax collector" (Matthew 18:17).
── BIBLICAL AND TRADITIONAL FAITH ──

This sound apostolic faith rests on both Holy Scripture and the Holy Tradition of the Apostolic Church together. Further detail on this relationship can be found in the earlier section of these notes on Scripture and Tradition.

subsections.heading: LOVING FAITH
paragraphs: Faith is the essential first step toward salvation, and it is itself a great virtue. St. Paul wrote, "Without faith it is impossible to please Him" (Hebrews 11:6). Even so, love is described as greater still: "And now abide faith, hope, love, these three; but the greatest of these is love" (1 Corinthians 13:13). St. Paul also wrote, "Though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing" (1 Corinthians 13:2).

What does this love, greater than faith itself, actually look like? "Love suffers long and is kind; love does not envy; love does not parade itself, is not puffed up; does not behave rudely; does not seek its own; is not provoked; thinks no evil; does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices in the truth; bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things" (1 Corinthians 13:4-7). It's no surprise, then, that genuine love is really expressed through good works, as St. John wrote: "Let us not love in word or in tongue, but in deed and in truth" (1 John 3:18), and, "This is the love of God, that we keep His commandments" (1 John 5:3).

Consider these related verses as well: "Let us consider one another in order to stir up love and good works" (Hebrews 10:24). "Remembering without ceasing your work of faith, labor of love" (1 Thessalonians 1:3). "God is not unjust to forget your work and labor of love" (Hebrews 6:10). "In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails anything, but faith working through love" (Galatians 5:6).
This last verse leads us naturally into the next mark of saving faith: working faith.

subsections.heading: WORKING FAITH
paragraphs: Without good works, faith is considered dead. "Faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead" (James 2:17). "Faith without works is dead" (James 2:20). "As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also" (James 2:26).
The conclusion here is direct: dead faith cannot save anyone.

Faith is made complete through good works: "By works faith was made perfect" (James 2:22). Faith is shown through good works: "Show me your faith without your works, and I will show you my faith by my works" (James 2:18). And justification comes through both faith and works together: "You see then that a man is justified by works, and not by faith only" (James 2:24).
This last verse stands as clear, direct evidence that the Protestant teaching of salvation by faith "alone" cannot be correct.

subsections.heading: FAITH THAT ENDURES TO THE END
paragraphs: Sound faith (apostolic, unified, biblical, and traditional), loving faith, and working faith must all endure to the very end, or salvation itself can still be lost: "He who endures to the end will be saved" (Matthew 10:22). "For we have become partakers of Christ if we hold the beginning of our confidence steadfast to the end" (Hebrews 3:14). "Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life" (Revelation 2:10). "Whose house we are if we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of the hope firm to the end" (Hebrews 3:6). "We desire that each one of you show the same diligence to the full assurance of hope until the end" (Hebrews 6:11).

subsections.heading: IN SUMMARY
paragraphs: As an Orthodox Christian, whenever you read the word "faith" in Scripture, understand that it refers to sound, loving, working faith that endures to the end.
Consider this example: it is written, "Without faith it is impossible to please Him" (Hebrews 11:6). This verse should really be understood this way:

Without sound faith (apostolic, unified, biblical, and traditional), it is impossible to please Him. Without loving faith, it is impossible to please Him. Without working faith, it is impossible to please Him. Without faith that endures to the end, it is impossible to please Him.
"Without faith, sound, loving, and working, and enduring to the end, it is impossible to please Him" (Hebrews 11:6).
Faith vs. Works

subsections.heading: FAITH VERSUS WORKS
paragraphs: For most of Church history, salvation was understood as covering the whole of life. Christians believed in Christ, were baptized, and were nurtured in their salvation within the Church. The core doctrines of the faith centered on the Holy Trinity, the Incarnation of the Son of God, and the atonement.

In sixteenth-century Western Europe, and even somewhat before, the Reformers raised a genuinely valid concern: a widespread understanding had developed that salvation depended on human merit through good works, rather than on God's grace and mercy. In response, "justification by faith alone" (*Sola Fide*, Latin) became the rallying cry of Protestant salvation teaching.

For the Orthodox East, this entire Reformation debate arrived as somewhat late and unfamiliar news. Why this sudden, sharp division between faith and works? The matter had already been settled since apostolic times: final salvation is granted by God's mercy to righteous men and women, and those baptized into Christ are called both to believe in Him and to do good works. A debate framed as "faith versus works" had simply never existed in Orthodox thought before.

For Orthodox Christians, faith is living, dynamic, and continuous, never fixed or limited to a single point in time. It is not something a Christian exercises only once, at one critical moment, expecting that single moment to cover the rest of their life. True faith is not merely a decision made once. It is an entire way of life. This is exactly why the modern evangelical question, "Are you saved?" tends to give an Orthodox believer real pause.

One final difficulty Orthodox Christians have with this teaching is the word "alone." Justification by faith, on its own, poses no real problem. But justification by faith "alone" raises a direct objection, since it contradicts Scripture itself: "You see that a man is justified by works, and not by faith only" (James 2:24) (*Orthodox Study Bible*).

subsections.heading: FAITH AS THE FIRST STEP TOWARD SALVATION
paragraphs: Our Lord Jesus Christ said, "If you do not believe that I am He, you will die in your sins" (John 8:24), and, "He who believes and is baptized will be saved" (Mark 16:16). Faith truly is the first step toward salvation, but it is never the only one. Scripture sometimes uses this first step to represent the entire process that begins with it, but this doesn't mean it's the only step involved.
── EXAMPLE 1: SIMEON THE ELDER ──

Simeon the elder took the infant Jesus into his arms and said, "Lord, now You are letting Your servant depart in peace, according to Your word, for my eyes have seen Your salvation" (Luke 2:29-30). Simeon had not yet actually witnessed the Lord's saving work, which would only take place through the shedding of His blood on the cross some thirty-three years later. He had only witnessed the Incarnation and birth of the Lord. But because this Incarnation was the first crucial step leading toward salvation, Simeon could confidently say, "my eyes have seen Your salvation."

Here, the Incarnation, as the first step of salvation, is used to represent the entire process. But does this mean we are saved merely by Christ's birth alone? Certainly not, since Scripture says, "Without shedding of blood there is no remission" (Leviticus 17:11; Hebrews 9:22).
── EXAMPLE 2: THE PHILIPPIAN JAILER ──

St. Paul and St. Silas told the Philippian jailer, "Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household" (Acts 16:31). How could his entire family be saved simply through his own faith? Does one person's faith save someone else?

The real meaning is that the jailer's faith served as the first step toward his own salvation, and this first step then led naturally to his family embracing the same faith, becoming the starting point for the salvation of the whole household. This becomes clear in the verses that follow: "Then they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house... And immediately he and all his family were baptized" (Acts 16:32-33). The jailer's faith was the first step toward his household's salvation, and Scripture uses it to represent the whole process, but this doesn't erase the other necessary steps that followed: their own faith and their own baptism.
── EXAMPLE 3: ZACCHAEUS ──

Our Lord told Zacchaeus, "Today salvation has come to this house" (Luke 19:9), after Zacchaeus promised to repay four times what he had wrongfully taken from others. This statement means that Zacchaeus' repentance was the first step toward the salvation of his entire household, not the only step required. Every individual within that household still needed to personally repent and believe. This was also simply a promise, pointing forward to the salvation that would later become fully available through Christ's blood on the cross.
── EXAMPLE 4: JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH AND WORKS ──

St. Paul wrote, "Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God" (Romans 5:1). St. James wrote, "You see then that a man is justified by works, and not by faith only" (James 2:24). St. Paul is using the first step, faith, to represent the entire process that begins with it, namely justification. St. James, meanwhile, clarifies that this first step alone is not the whole story.
── EXAMPLE 5: ST. PAUL'S OWN TESTIMONY ──

St. Paul recounted that our Lord appeared to him and said that people would "receive forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those who are sanctified by faith in Me" (Acts 26:18). On another occasion, describing this same vision, Paul said he remained obedient to this heavenly calling and declared to everyone "that they should repent, turn to God, and do works befitting repentance" (Acts 26:19-20).

In the first account of this vision, the first step, faith, is used to represent the whole process of sanctification. But in the second account of that same vision, it becomes clear that faith alone is not the only step, and must be followed by further steps: repentance, turning to God, and genuine good works.
── EXAMPLE 6: CALLING ON THE NAME OF THE LORD ──

St. Paul wrote, "Whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved" (Romans 10:13). Someone might read this and assume that simply believing is all that's required. But our Lord Himself said, "Not everyone who says to Me, 'Lord, Lord,' shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of My Father in heaven" (Matthew 7:21). Faith is clearly the first step, and it must be followed by genuinely keeping the commandments.
── EXAMPLE 7: THE WISE AND FOOLISH VIRGINS ──

After the parable of the wise and foolish virgins, our Lord said, "Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour in which the Son of Man is coming" (Matthew 25:13). Let's apply this directly to the foolish virgins in the story. "Watching" was their first step toward being ready, but it was never meant to be the only step, even though it's the only one our Lord explicitly names. The full sequence would have looked like this: first, watch; second, realize you're out of oil; third, ask the wise virgins for help; fourth, take their advice and go quickly to buy oil; fifth, return before the bridegroom arrives and shuts the door.

Suppose these virgins had assumed that "watching" alone was the only step needed for salvation, and did nothing else but stay awake and wait. Wouldn't they still rightly be called foolish? In the same way, anyone who treats faith as the only step toward salvation is, in Scripture's own words, called foolish: "But do you want to know, O foolish man, that faith without works is dead?" (James 2:20).

Separating works from faith is like separating the spirit from the body. The result, in both cases, is death: "For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also" (James 2:26). It's worth noting that St. James compares good works to the spirit, and faith to the body, not the other way around.

subsections.heading: CONCLUSION
paragraphs: Anyone who preaches faith alone, without works, as the way of salvation is, in Scripture's own words, a fool, and is in fact preaching death: "Do you not know, O foolish man, that faith without works is dead?" (James 2:20). Indeed, "What does it profit, my brethren, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can faith alone save him?" (James 2:14).

In truth, genuine faith is itself a kind of work. When the Jewish crowds asked our Lord, "What shall we do, that we may work the works of God?" He answered them, "This is the work of God, that you believe in Him whom He sent" (John 6:28-29).
