But outside are dogs and sorcerers and sexually immoral and murderers and idolaters, and whoever loves and practices a lie” (Rev. 22:14–15). Thus, the book of Revelation affirms that none shall eat of the Tree of Life but those who are victorious, who held fast to God’s commandments in their lives on earth, who partake of eternal life in the heavenly kingdom. But the heart that is lukewarm in its love hungers, and needs to be fed from the Lord, the Tree of Life.
Did Adam and Eve lose their hope of salvation after hearing the judgment that resulted from their disobedience?

Although the wages of sin is death, God declared His mercy on them and their descendants through the descent of His only begotten Son, the Incarnate, and the gift of salvation through His crucifixion, resurrection, and ascension to heaven. They heard God’s words to the serpent: “and I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her Seed. He shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise His heel” (Gen. 3:15).
Do you know who you are?

We humans often feel small in our own eyes and are aware that we are tiny creatures in the midst of a huge universe in all its grandeur. We appear for a little while and walk the earth like shadows until we vanish. We stumble because of a small stone; we die, or are beset by some tiny microbe that leaves us languishing in our beds for long years, longing for death but unable to find it. Human beings are weak creatures: for the sake of some small despicable lust we can forget our dignity, squander our prosperity, destroy our families, and perhaps lose everything — even though we know it is nothing more than a temporary fleeting pleasure.

Do you wish to know who you really are? You are the subject of God’s love, the recipient of His care and concern, so much so that it might appear He has forgotten the whole world for your sake. When He created you, “God saw everything that He had made, and indeed it was very good” (Gen. 1:31). He looks upon you and sees in you His image and likeness. In you is a mind; you have free will; He has given you the gift of being capable of love, and being drawn towards the Creator who satisfies you, and who imprints His own nature upon you. He rejoices in you. He created heaven and earth to pass away some day (Matt. 24:35), but you He created immortal to live forever. Behold then, your soul, which God values above the whole world, as He said: “what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, and loses his own soul?” (Mark 8:36).
What did sin do to me?

By my own will, I chose separation from God that I might have my own autonomous existence far away from the deep ocean of God’s love. This is Adam’s first sin, and indeed our every sin. I separated my soul from its source of happiness, satisfaction, and life, only to fall under the yoke of sin, only to come under the sway of sin’s oppression. By my own will I chose sin, and it gave me all that it has, against my will — what does sin have except deprivation, oppression, death, etc.?
Deprivation. It took away satisfaction and deprived me of Paradise, it expelled me from peace, joy, and true knowledge.
Injustice. The law of sin is nothing more than confusion and oppression.

Death. Sin is the soul being deprived of God, the giver of life; this is what became of the human soul, by its own free will. The image deviated from its origin; its beauty was destroyed, its nature corrupted, its authority ended, and its ability to commune with God the source of its life was lost.

Humans became perturbed and terrified. In vain they tried to submit themselves to their God in their own way. Adam tried correct his error by himself, but in so doing, he only affirmed his desire to be independent of God and for his own autonomy. Thus, he compounded the consequence of his error with more consequences. He fashioned for himself a garment made of fig leaves, but the leaves shriveled and served only to emphasize his nakedness. It became necessary for God to intervene to erase the consequences that had come upon the humans by their own will. Should God forgive, even at the expense of justice? How then would infinite justice be upheld? But how could God’s love abandon humanity to eternal destruction? Thus, a process of reconciliation between God and humanity was necessary in which God would pay the price of sin without surrendering His justice, and justice would be fulfilled by the depths of His love.

St. Macarius the Great the Great says, “The things of grace are attended by joy, peace, love, and truth … But the forms of sin are disordered, and have nothing of love or joy towards God.” He also says, “For the soul in itself is neither of the nature of the Godhead, nor of the nature of the darkness of wickedness, but is a creature intellectual, beauteous, great, and wonderful, a fair likeness and image of God. It was through the transgression that the wickedness of the passions of darkness entered into it.”

Also, St. Augustine says, “As for the human being, whose nature inclines both to the nature of angels and to that of animals, God created him so. If he submits to his Creator as his true master and reverently keeps His commandments, he attains fellowship with the angels and partakes of blessed everlasting immortality, impervious to death. But if he defies the Lord his God by exercising his free will in arrogance and disobedience, he will submit to death, live as a slave to desire, and be condemned to eternal death.” He also says:
“Oh, my misery! … Darkness has prevailed over me; and although You are the Light, I veil my face from You!
“Oh, my misery! … I am afflicted by many wounds; and although You are the Comforter, the giver of peace, I flee away from You!
“Oh, my misery! … I am overwhelmed by a host of follies; and although You are the Truth, I do not seek Your counsel!
“Oh, my misery! … My ways of going astray multiply; and although You are the Way, I turn away from You!
“Oh, my misery! … With many blows, death defeats me; and although You are the Life, I stay far from You!

“Oh, my misery! … I fall into evil and banality many times; and although You are the Word through which all things were made, I separated myself from You, the One without whom I would not exist! O my King the Word; O my God the Word; O Light, the Creator; the Way, the Truth, and the Life … O You who dispel darkness, evil, straying, and death …

“O Light: without You, all would find themselves in dark night. O Way: without You, there would be nothing but going astray. O Truth: without You, there would nothing but falsehood. O Life: without You, all would be encompassed by death.”

Now that sin devastated all of human nature, what was God to do? It is unthinkable that He should stand by passively watching His beloved. He had already planned our salvation and a means for us to attain forgiveness of sin, return to divine righteousness, and flee to rest in His divine embrace. What, then, is this thing, sin? How does the Holy Trinity impact upon it? How did He equip humanity to understand it and deal with it? How was this achieved? And how can we ourselves receive this grace? All this leads us to talk about our need for salvation, and for the divine Savior.
Source: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Fr. Tadros Y. Malaty (2023), Book 2: Christian Dogma.
The Fall of Humanity — Part 2
How should God react to humanity’s disobedience of the divine commandment?

Humans desired the world, and so their being in the presence of God became a matter of mere words and expressions. Sin became habitual in people’s lives. Although we feel its bitter weight as a burden at times, at other times we return and submit to it with all our essence, inclination, will, and energy. As the apostle Paul says, “For I know that in me (that is, in my flesh) nothing good dwells; for to will is present with me, but how to perform what is good I do not find. For the good that I will to do, I do not do; but the evil I will not to do, that I practice. Now if I do what I will not to do, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me” (Rom. 7:18–20). How, then, should God respond to this human state? Does He still love us? And what must we do in order to renew our nature, which we corrupted by our own will? Is God occupied with His heavenly glories, or will He condescend to deal with us? Will He free us from the dominion of sin to which we willingly gave ourselves over?

I ask God, my God: “O Love, do You still love humans, and long to return them to Your bosom? We humans are unable to ascend to You, for we are drowning in our sins and weaknesses. Will You descend to us, O Holy One?
“O eternal and immortal Love, behold, heaven yearns to learn the mystery of Your wisdom that is full of love. Will You proclaim to us and to heaven the mysteries of Your love?
“Now my God, behold, our lives are corrupted, and we need the One who will renew our nature and liberate us from our eternal death. What will You do for us, O absolute unlimited love?”

St. Cyril the Great says, “God in his love to man provided for us a way of salvation and of life. For believing in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and making this confession before many witnesses, we wash away all the filth of sin, and are enriched by the communication of the Holy Spirit, and made partakers of the divine nature, and gain the grace of adoption.”

For faith in the Holy Trinity is a divine revelation by which the believer experiences the ultimate divine love, and enters into a personal experience of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The true believer finds in the Trinity the fulfilment of every inner need. Our faith in the Trinity touches our lives and being, for we have no life within us without experiencing the love of the Holy Trinity for us, and the works that result from this ultimate love. St. Gregory of Nazianzus says, “To the churches I shall bestow my tears. Through all the vicissitudes of my life God has led me to this point. Tell me, Logos of God, whither now? Towards the unshaken seat, I pray, where is my Trinity, and that united brightness by the faint reflections of which we are now upraised.”
Why was it not enough for God that humans repent of sin?

It was not worthy of God to have warned Adam of the judgment that would result from his eating the fruit of the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil, and then simply take back that judgment when Adam transgressed. St. St. Athanasius says, “For as I said earlier, by the law death thereafter prevailed against us [because of transgression], and it was impossible to escape the law, since this had been established by God on account of the transgression. And what happened was both truly absurd and improper. It was absurd, on the one hand, that having spoken, God should prove to be lying: that is, having legislated that the human being would die by death if he were to transgress the commandment, yet after the transgression he were not to die but rather this sentence dissolved. For God would not be true if, after saying that we would die, the human being did not die.”

St. St. Athanasius adds, “But repentance would neither have preserved the consistency of God, for he again would not have remained true if human beings were not held fast by death, nor does repentance recall humans from what is natural, but merely halts sins. If then there were only offence and not the consequence of corruption, repentance would have been fine.” Repentance alone could never restore humanity to that state of purity it had enjoyed from the beginning, nor could it heal human nature of the nature of incorruption that afflicted it as a result of sin.

This can be likened to someone who goes out into icy weather without sufficient clothing and then comes down with a terrible cold. When he visits his doctor, would it be appropriate treatment for the doctor merely to advise him not to go out in the cold weather again without warm clothing? Clearly not. First, she must treat his infection, and only after that should she resort to advising him not to repeat his error.

If God cannot take back the sentence of death upon humanity, and if our repentance is not enough because it cannot by itself heal the corruption of our nature, then His mercy demands that He take up our human nature through the incarnation in order to renew us and take away from us the sentence of death with which we had been justly condemned.
What is the divine economy for our salvation?

After humanity fell into sin God revealed to Adam and Eve His divine economy for the salvation of His beloved humanity: the Holy Trinity’s plan and work for our salvation; one divine work wherein each Hypostasis has His distinct role in attaining our salvation. The Lord Christ proclaimed the love of God the Father saying, “For God so loved the world that He gave his only begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should nor perish but have everlasting life” (John 3:16). The apostle Paul reveals the love of the Son saying, “Who loved me and gave himself for me” (Gal. 2:20). And the Lord Christ reveals the role of the Holy Spirit in our salvation saying, “He will take what is Mine and declare it to you” (John 16:14).
How does the Holy Trinity cooperate to work in us?

In one divine essence of the Holy Trinity and three distinct Hypostases, all of God’s work expresses His boundless love for humanity; yet it is the cooperative work of the Holy Trinity. As Pope St. Athanasius says, “The Father does all things through the Word in the Holy Spirit. Thus the unity of the holy Triad is preserved.” All divine works are divine gifts granted by the Father, through His Only Begotten Son, by His Holy Spirit.

St. Cyril of Alexandria says, “For the Son does not say that God the Father works separately and by Himself regarding things that are, and that He Himself again likewise works apart from the Father … for so the Creator would be two and not One, if Either work apart and separately … if it were possible that Either should work apart and separately with regard to things that are, as we said before, … the Son will not be speaking the truth, when He says, I am in the Father and the Father in Me (John 14:10).”

St. Ambrose says, “Because you have been baptized in the name of the Trinity, in all that we have done the mystery of the Trinity has been preserved. Everywhere the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one operation, one sanctification … How? God [the Father], who anointed you, and the Lord sealed you, and placed the Holy Spirit in your heart. Therefore, you have received the Holy Spirit in your heart.”

St. John Chrysostom says, “Do you see this love surpassing all expression, all conception? Who was the aggrieved one? Himself. Who first sought the reconciliation? Himself. ‘And yet,’ says one, ‘He sent the Son, He did not come Himself.’ The Son indeed it was He sent; still not He alone entreated, but both with Him and by Him the Father; therefore he said, that, ‘God was reconciling the world unto Himself in Christ’ (2 Cor. 5:19): that is, by Christ.”

We can say with St. Basil the Great, that the divine work or God’s love for humanity is manifested in three types of creation that complement each other, performed by the Holy Trinity: “We find three creations mentioned in the Scripture; the first, the transition from non-existence into existence; the second, the change from worse to better; and the third, the resurrection of the dead. In these you will find the Holy Spirit co-operating with the Father and the Son … Now, man is created a second time through baptism, ‘for if any man is in Christ, he is a new creature’ (2 Cor. 5:17).”
What is the role of each Hypostasis in my life?
The love of God the Father for me: He created me as the greatest creation on earth.
His divine providence embraces me.
He makes all things work for my good.
His Fatherhood is always kind, even when I am being chastened.
With love and wisdom, He grants me the gifts I need.
He grants me the free gift of salvation.
His divine embrace welcomes me.
The grace of the only Son saves me: His names and titles declare His love for me.
He was incarnate for my sake.
He suffered for my sake.
He was crucified for my sake.
He resurrects me with Him.
He raises me to His heavens.
He grants me new life.
The communion of the Holy Spirit: He grants me the revelation of the Holy Scriptures.
He offers me fellowship with God.
He grants me the spirit of adoption by the Father (the new birth of baptism).
He restores the divine image in my nature.
He grants me the forgiveness of sins.
He enlightens my mind.
He grants me membership in the Church, the Body of Christ.
He gives me the power of victory over sin, death, and Satan, and raises my heart up to heaven.
Why was humanity sentenced: “you shall surely die”?

Death is the natural consequence of sin that humanity reaps from willingly committing sin. In foolishness, humanity implanted itself into the cycle of death, and the loving God would not compel humanity to refrain from sin nor stop sin from taking its natural course.

In ancient times, the Gnostics were so offended by scripture passages that spoke of God being angry or repenting that they rejected the Old Testament altogether. But the real cause of their being offended was that they interpreted these passages literally rather than spiritually. Origen says that references to God that employ human analogies of God (anthropomorphisms) such as the wrath of God cannot be interpreted literally. “If you hear of the anger of God and his wrath, do not suppose that anger and wrath are passions of God. The purposes of using this way of speaking are for converting and bettering the infant, since we also use a fearful expression with children, not from an actual state of mind but because of a purpose to cause fear. If we maintain what is kindly for the soul in our expression toward the babe, and we show the affection which we have for it, since we have not altered ourselves nor changed for the conversion of that one, we lose him and make him worse. So then it states that God is also said to be angry and wrathful in order that you can convert and become better. And he is truly neither angry nor wrathful, but you experience the effects of anger and wrath when you are in unbearable pains because of evil, whenever he disciplines by what is called the anger of God.”
How did sin corrupt humanity’s vision of God?

By falling into disobedience, human understanding was corrupted and became closed to seeing God in His love. Instead, humanity saw God as harsh. Job the Righteous, in his moments of weakness under the heavy burden of his trials and the counsel of his friends, saw God as harsh and said to Him, “Your hands have made me and fashioned me, an intricate unity; yet You would destroy me … And will You turn me into dust again? … If my head is exalted, You hunt me like a fierce lion, and again You show Yourself awesome against me. And increase Your indignation toward me; You renew your witnesses against me. Why then have You brought me out of the womb? … Cease! Leave me alone, that I may take a little comfort” (Job 10:8–20).

The heart that is corrupted by sin sees God in his judgment as an unjust judge, reaping what He has not sown, and gathering where He has not scattered seed (Matt. 25:24). He has no sympathy for human weakness nor consideration for our shortcomings. He prepares eternal life for a rare few chosen saints and concocts untold suffering for the multitude of sinners. Do not many modern philosophies attempt to reject this kind of God? In response to these kinds of rejections, some clergy concede this harshness of God, but argue that this God bears no relation to the reality of human affairs, thinking that in so doing, they are resisting the wave of atheism.

My brothers and sisters, no one truly denies the existence of God, not even atheists, for deep down in their souls they feel Him. But in their mindset, they see Him as a harsh and unjust God, and so they fight Him and try to be rid of Him. That is why what we need today is not so much to prove the existence of God as to testify about God’s love for humanity in our practical lives.
What does the story of the tunics of skin signify?

After the fall, God clothed Adam and Eve in tunics of skin (Gen. 3:21). These leather tunics indicate that a blood sacrifice was offered as a ransom for human sin, standing in place of Adam and Eve in receiving the sentence of death, and covering their nakedness. Subsequently, each generation learnt from the generation before it to offer blood sacrifices, so that it is rare to find a religion whose rites do not include the shedding of blood. Through the generations, this idea sometimes became corrupted — some even came to sacrifice their own children.

In the fullness of time, humanity received the written law from Moses’s hands, which law required blood sacrifices because “without the shedding of blood there is no remission” (Heb. 9:22). Blood sanctifies all; and without it, nothing and no one — even if he be high priest — can be sanctified to the Lord: “For when Moses had spoken every precept to all the people according to the law, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying, ‘This is the blood of the covenant which God has commanded you.’ Then likewise he sprinkled with blood both the tabernacle and all the vessels of the ministry. And according to the law almost all things are purified with blood, and without shedding of blood there is no remission” (Heb. 9:19– 22).
How did the blood sacrifices prepare us for the sacrifice of the New Testament?

The blood sacrifices that God showed to Adam and whose details were clarified in the Book of Leviticus are incapable, by themselves, of manifesting God’s love for sinful humanity. Humanity needs to return to the life of holiness, without which no one can see God or come into contact with Him. Humanity needs a conciliator capable of mediating between God and His children.

We needed the incarnation of the Son, the Word, the second Hypostasis. In His profound love for us, this incarnate God came forth, carrying our death in His body. But who can accept such a thing? The mind is incapable of comprehending the depths of God’s love for it. How could God the Word become flesh when his divinity fills all things? The Lord says, “[Am I not] the Lord, and there is no other God besides me? A just God and a Savior; there is none besides Me” (Isa. 45:21), and “you shall know no God but Me; for there is no savior besides Me” (Hos. 13:4).

My Savior loves me; my Intercessor with the Father. He took flesh for my sake and died as an atoning sacrifice for my sins (1 John 2:1–2). This is the salvation offered by the Son, by the cooperation of the Holy Trinity, each Hypostasis completing the others, each Hypostasis proclaiming God’s love for us.
What is the promise of divine salvation and the prophesy of the coming of the Savior after many generations?

The divine promise was repeated, for example, to Abraham, when God said to him: “In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18); and to David the prophet and king: “I will set up your seed after you, who will come from your body, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for My name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever” (2 Sam. 7:12–13); and to Ahaz: “the Lord Himself will give you a sign: Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a Son, and shall call His name Immanuel” (Isa. 7:14).
What does reconciliation with God mean?

St. Cyril says that the sacrifice of our Lord Jesus Christ did not reconcile us only to the Father, but also to the Son. He Himself is the Hypostasis who reconciles us, for we have sinned against Him.
Source: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Fr. Tadros Y. Malaty (2023), Book 2: Christian Dogma.
BOOK 18

The study of Jesus Christ, the incarnate Word of God. It examines His divine and human realities, His teachings, miracles, death, resurrection, ascension, and His role as Savior and Lord of all creation.
Heresies Concerning the Nature of our Lord Jesus Christ

subsections.heading: CHRISTOLOGY: UNDERSTANDING THE PERSON OF JESUS CHRIST
paragraphs: "But who do you say that I am?" (Matthew 16:15)
INTRODUCTION
Every Christian must answer the question that our Lord Jesus Christ asked His disciples: "But who do you say that I am?" (Matthew 16:15).
The answer to this question is not merely academic—it lies at the very heart of the Christian faith.
Christology is the study of the Person of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Soteriology (Greek: Soteria, meaning "salvation") is the study of His saving work.
These two subjects cannot be separated.
WHO CHRIST IS DETERMINES WHAT HE IS ABLE TO ACCOMPLISH.
If Christ is not truly God and truly Man, then salvation itself is impossible.

Throughout history, the Church defended the apostolic faith against heresies that distorted the truth about Christ. Guided by the Holy Spirit, the Holy Fathers preserved the faith once delivered to the saints.

subsections.heading: 1. THE ARIAN HERESY
paragraphs: WHO WAS ARIUS?
Arius (c.250–336) taught that our Lord Jesus Christ was not truly God, but merely the highest and greatest of God's creatures.
Although Arius placed Christ above every other creature, he still insisted that the Son was created and therefore not equal with the Father.
This teaching directly contradicted the apostolic faith.
ST. St. Athanasius' RESPONSE
St. St. Athanasius recognized that Arius' teaching destroyed the Gospel itself.
KEY PRINCIPLE
Only God can save.
Every creature requires salvation.
Therefore, no creature can save another creature.
His argument can be summarized as follows:
• No creature can redeem another creature.
• Arius claimed that Jesus Christ is a creature.
• Therefore, according to Arius, Jesus Christ cannot redeem humanity.
Yet Scripture and the Church proclaim that Jesus Christ IS our Savior.
St. St. Athanasius also argued:
• Only God saves.
• Jesus Christ saves.
• Therefore, Jesus Christ is God.
If Christ were merely a creature, Christians would be guilty of worshiping a creature rather than God. Such worship would be idolatry.
Christians rightly worship Jesus Christ because He is God incarnate.
QUOTE
"The Christology of Jehovah's Witnesses, also, is a form of Arianism; they regard Arius as a forerunner of Charles Taze Russell, the founder of their movement."
— Encyclopedia Britannica, Vol. 1, p. 550

subsections.heading: 2. THE APOLLINARIAN HERESY
paragraphs: WHO WAS APOLLINARIUS?
Apollinarius of Laodicea (c.310–390) strongly opposed Arius but introduced another error.
He taught that our Lord Jesus Christ did not possess a complete human nature.
According to him, the Divine Logos replaced Christ's human rational soul or mind.
As a result, Christ possessed:
• A human body • A divine mind
—but not a complete human nature.
Apollinarius believed this protected Christ's sinlessness because he viewed the human mind as the source of sin.
WHY WAS THIS DANGEROUS?
If Christ did not assume complete humanity, then complete humanity could not be saved.
The Holy Fathers understood that salvation requires Christ to heal every aspect of human nature by assuming it completely.
ST. GREGORY OF NAZIANZUS

"If anyone has put their trust in him as a human being lacking a human mind, they are themselves mindless and not worthy of salvation. For what has not been assumed has not been healed; it is what is united with His divinity that is saved… Let them not grudge us our total salvation, or endue the Savior only with the bones and nerves and mere appearance of humanity."
KEY PRINCIPLE
"What has not been assumed has not been healed."
Because Christ assumed our complete humanity, He redeemed our complete humanity.

subsections.heading: 3. THE NESTORIAN HERESY
paragraphs: WHO WAS NESTORIUS?
Nestorius (c.390–451), Patriarch of Constantinople, rejected the title "Theotokos" (Mother of God) for the Virgin Mary.
Instead, he proposed:
• Christotokos ("Mother of Christ") • Anthropotokos ("Mother of Humanity")
Nestorius argued that Mary gave birth only to the human Jesus, into whom the Divine Logos later descended.
This divided Christ into two separate natures rather than confessing one nature incarnate of our Lord.
WHY THE CHURCH REJECTED THIS
The Church teaches that the Virgin Mary gave birth to the Incarnate Word of God, not merely to a human subject (or thing) later united with God.
Calling Mary "Theotokos" does not mean she originated Christ's divinity.
Rather, it proclaims that the One born from her is truly God incarnate.
SCRIPTURE
"How did this happen to me, that my Lord's mother should visit me?" (Luke 1:43)
"The Holy One who is to be born of you will be called the Son of God." (Luke 1:35)
ST. CYRIL OF ALEXANDRIA

"Hail to Mary, Mother of God, majestic treasure of the whole world, the lamp unquenchable, the crown of virginity, the scepter of Orthodoxy, the indestructible temple, the dwelling of the illimitable, mother and virgin. Hail to you who contained Him, who cannot be contained, in your holy virginal womb..."

subsections.heading: 4. THE EUTYCHIAN HERESY
paragraphs: WHO WAS EUTYCHES?
Eutyches (c.375–454) reacted strongly against Nestorianism.
While Nestorius divided Christ's natures, Eutyches went to the opposite extreme.
He claimed that Christ's human nature was absorbed into His divine nature:
"...as a drop of vinegar in the ocean."
This teaching denied Christ's true humanity.
Because he accepted only one nature after the Incarnation, this teaching became known as Monophysitism.
The Church rejected this teaching because Christ remains fully God and fully Man, without confusion, without change, without division, and without separation.

subsections.heading: SUMMARY
paragraphs: ARIANISM Denied Christ's divinity. Condemned at the Council of Nicaea (325 AD).
APOLLINARIANISM Denied Christ's complete humanity. Condemned at the Council of Constantinople (381 AD).
NESTORIANISM Separated Christ's divine and human natures, denying the hypostatic union. Condemned at the Council of Ephesus (431 AD).
EUTYCHIANISM Denied Christ's humanity by claiming it was absorbed into His divinity. Condemned at the Council of Chalcedon (451 AD).

subsections.heading: WHY THIS MATTERS
paragraphs: These debates were never merely philosophical arguments.
They concern the very heart of the Gospel.
• If Christ is not truly God, He cannot save us.
• If Christ is not truly Man, humanity cannot be healed.
• If His divinity and humanity are separated, there is no true Incarnation.
• If His humanity disappears into His divinity, then He is no longer one of us.
The Orthodox faith proclaims that our Lord Jesus Christ is one incarnate nature and hypostasis, fully God and fully Man.
Through His Incarnation, death, and resurrection, He has united humanity to God and opened the way to eternal life.

subsections.heading: FINAL REFLECTION
paragraphs: "But who do you say that I am?" (Matthew 16:15)
The Nature of our Lord Jesus Christ

subsections.heading: CHRISTOLOGY: THE HYPOSTATIC UNION OF THE TWO NATURES
paragraphs: OUR FAITH CONCERNING CHRISTOLOGY
Our Lord Jesus Christ is God Himself, the Incarnate Logos, who took to Himself a complete manhood.
His Divine Nature is united with His Human Nature in a complete Hypostatic (personal) Union without mingling, confusion, alteration or separation.
Furthermore, the unity between the two Natures occurred without transmutation. Thus neither the Divine Nature transmutes to the Human Nature, nor did the Human Nature transmute to the Divine.

subsections.heading: 1. WITHOUT MINGLING, CONFUSION, ALTERATION, OR SEPARATION
paragraphs: Without mingling — as in the case of wheat and barley or salt and sugar.
Without confusion — as in the case of wine and water or tea and milk.

Without alteration — as in the case of chemical union: Carbon dioxide consists of Carbon and Oxygen, and the nature of both changes when they are combined; each loses some of its properties that distinguished it before this unity. In contrast, no change occurred to the Divine or Human Nature as a result of their unity.
Without separation — for His Divinity parted not from His Humanity for a single moment nor a twinkling of an eye.
THE UNION IN THE WOMB

The Divine Logos was united with the Human Nature (body & spirit) that He took from Virgin Mary by the action of the Holy Spirit: The Holy Spirit purified and sanctified the Virgin so that the Child to whom she gave birth would not inherit the original sin.
This unity between the Two Natures (Human & Divine) took place from the first moment of the Holy Pregnancy.
As a result of this unity between both Natures (Divine & Human) inside the Virgin's womb, One Nature (entity) was formed out of both: "The ONE Nature of God, the Incarnate Logos."
KEY PRINCIPLE

The Term "One Nature" does not refer to either of the Two Natures (Divine & Human), but it refers to the result of the union of Both Natures into this One Nature which is "the Nature of the Incarnate Logos." The term "Two Natures" implies division or potential separation.

Human language is inadequate when it comes to describing this union, but here are two illustrations. These examples are intended to clarify some aspects of the union but they are not perfect, just like our human language. The imperfections are put between brackets { }.

subsections.heading: 2. TWO ILLUSTRATIONS
paragraphs: A) THE UNION BETWEEN IRON & FIRE

In the union of iron and fire, the iron is not changed into fire or the fire into iron. They are both united without mingling, confusion, or alteration. {At a certain temperature the iron will change and extinguishing the fire will separate them.}
B) THE UNION BETWEEN THE HUMAN SPIRIT & BODY
The nature of the human spirit unites with the physical earthly nature of the body without mingling, confusion, alteration, or transmutation. {They will separate by death and then they reunite.}

This union of the two natures (spirit & body) results in ONE nature that is the human nature. The term ONE here doesn't refer to either of the two natures (spirit – body) but it refers to the result of this union of BOTH natures into this ONE human being.
Therefore, just as we say that the person is ONE nature consisting of two elements (spirit & body), we can also say about the Incarnate Logos that He is ONE entity of two natures (Divine & Human).

The union of the spirit & body is a hypostatic one. So is the union of the Divine Logos & the Human Nature in the virgin's womb. A hypostatic, real, self-essential union — not a mere connection that separates, as Nestorius claimed.

Although a person is formed of two natures (spirit & body), nobody refers to him/her as two. All the person's acts are attributed to this ONE nature, not to the spirit alone or the physical body alone. Similarly, all the acts of Christ should be attributed to Him as a whole, not to His Divine Nature independently or to His Human Nature independently.

subsections.heading: 3. IN A NUTSHELL
paragraphs: Our Lord Jesus Christ has One Nature composed of Two Natures:
1. The Divine Nature of the LOGOS. 2. The Human Nature that He took from Virgin Mary.
The Human Nature is composed of Two+ Elements:
a) Human Spirit. b) Human Body.
The Divine Nature of the LOGOS is united with every element of the Human Nature without mingling, confusion, alteration, transmutation, or separation.

As a result of this Hypostatic Union, One Entity is formed out of Both (Divine & Human) Natures. This is the "One Nature Of God, The Incarnate Logos." When we refer to this ONE NATURE, we are referring to this ONE ENTITY that resulted from the union of BOTH the Divine and Human Natures.

subsections.heading: 4. WHAT HAPPENED ON THE CROSS?
paragraphs: Our Lord Jesus Christ died on the cross. Death means that His Human Spirit was separated from His Human Body.
The Divine Logos remained united with BOTH the spirit and the body after their separation. Hence, His Divinity parted not from His Humanity.
This explains why the body was not corrupted in the grave, and it also explains how the spirit was able to return to the body when the Resurrection took place.

subsections.heading: 5. ARE WE MONOPHYSITES?
paragraphs: The Oriental Orthodox Churches (Coptic, Syrian, Armenian, Ethiopian, and Indian) are 'Miaphysites.'

There is a difference between the 'Monophysites' who believe in One Single Nature (Divine) of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the 'Miaphysites' who believe in One United Nature or One Composite Nature (Divine & Human) of our Lord Jesus Christ.
KEY PRINCIPLE
We do not believe in a Single Nature, but we believe in One Incarnate Nature of the Logos.

subsections.heading: 6. OUR FAITH CONCERNING THE ONE WILL AND ACT
paragraphs: Naturally, since we believe that after the union of the Divine and Human Natures, One Nature (entity) resulted — namely, the Nature of the Incarnate Logos — we also believe in One Will and One Act for the Incarnate Logos.
There is no contradiction or conflict between the will and the act of the Two Natures; what the Divine Nature chooses is undoubtedly chosen by the Human Nature.
SCRIPTURE

Our Lord Jesus Christ said, "My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me, and to finish His work" (John 4:34). This proves that His will is the same as the Father's. Certainly, the Divine Logos has the same will as the Father since He is one with Him in the Godhead. Thus, it must be that the Nature of the Incarnate Logos has One Will that is not different from the Father.
In fact, sin is nothing but a conflict between man's will and God's. But our Lord Jesus Christ said, "Which of you convicts Me of sin?" (John 8:46), proving His One will with the Father.

If there were no unity between the will of the Divine Logos and His Human Nature, internal conflict would have resulted. Far be it from Him! How then could the Lord Jesus Christ be our guide and our example?

The complete righteousness that marked the life of our Savior was due to the unity of His Divine and Human will. Also, the crucifixion was the choice of both the Divine and Human will. Had it not been one will, it would not have been said that He died by His own will for us. And since the will is one, the act is also one.
NOTE

The human nature actually consists of three elements: the body, the spirit and the soul. As St. Paul said, "May your whole spirit, soul, and body be preserved blameless" (1 Thessalonians 5:23). Only two are mentioned above for simplicity. But we need to understand that our Lord had a FULL human nature.

subsections.heading: 7. DID THE DIVINE NATURE (OF THE LOGOS) SUFFER?
paragraphs: ST. CYRIL OF ALEXANDRIA — FIRST LETTER TO NESTORIUS

"For thus we say that He both suffered and rose again, not as though God the Word suffered in His own Nature either stripes or piercings of nails or the other wounds (for the Godhead is Impassible because It is also Incorporeal), but since that which had been made His own body suffered these things, He again is said to suffer for us, for the Impassible was in the suffering Body. In like manner do we conceive of His Death too. For the Word of God is by Nature Immortal and Incorruptible and Life and Life-giving: but since again His own Body by the grace of God (as Paul saith) tasted death for every man, Himself is said to have suffered death for us, not as though He had experienced death as far as pertains unto His own Nature (for it were distraction to say or think this) but because (as I said just now) His flesh tasted death. Thus too when His Flesh was raised, the Resurrection again is said to be His, not as though He fell into decay (not so!) but because His Body again was raised. Thus shall we confess One Christ and Lord; not as if co-worshipping a man with the Word, that a fantasy of severance be not privily brought in, by saying with [syn] but as worshipping One and the Same, because not alien to the Word is His Body with which He sits with the Father, not as though two sons sit with the Father but One in union with His own Flesh. But if we reject the Personal Union as either impossible or as uncomely, we fall into saying, Two sons; for we must needs sever and say that the one is man by himself, honoured with the title of son; by Himself again, the Word of God, having of Nature both the Name and Fact of Sonship."

St. Cyril is saying that the Divine Nature is Impassible and Immortal BUT since the body is mortal and possible AND the Divine Nature was united with this mortal and possible body, THEREFORE the Logos is "said" to have suffered pain, "said" to have suffered death. St. Cyril emphasizes "not as though He had experienced death as far as pertains unto His own Nature."
ST. CYRIL'S ANATHEMA #12

"Whosoever shall not recognize that the Word of God suffered in the flesh, that he was crucified in the flesh, and that likewise in that same flesh he tasted death and that he is become the first-begotten of the dead, for, as he is God, he is the life and it is he that giveth life: let him be anathema."

St. Cyril's emphasis is "in the flesh." He is not saying that the Divinity (after the union) suffered pain or died, but that the Logos suffered and died "in the flesh." The Divine Nature is united with the Human nature without alteration; IT remained Impassible after the union, yet the suffering is "ascribed" to IT.
NESTORIUS' COUNTER-ANATHEMA

We can appreciate more what St. Cyril is saying when we read Nestorius' counter Anathema: "If any one, in confessing the sufferings of the flesh, ascribes these also to the Word of God as to the flesh in which he appeared, and thus does not distinguish the dignity of the natures; let him be anathema."

St. Cyril is saying that the sufferings of the flesh are "ascribed" to the Word of God because the Logos was united with the flesh (not because the Divine Nature suffered). Nestorius, on the other hand, who wants to separate the two natures, finds fault in this ascription.

Notice that NEITHER St. Cyril nor Nestorius is saying that the Divine Nature suffered in Itself. St. Cyril is saying that the Logos suffered "in the flesh," and Nestorius is saying that the Logos "never suffered at all."
KEY PRINCIPLE

The Logos is Impassible (does not suffer physical, emotional, or psychological pain), yet He took a complete human nature (with emotions and a personality etc.). Thus the prophecy of Isaiah the prophet, "it pleased the Lord to bruise Him; He has put Him to grief" (Isaiah 53:10), is fulfilled in the Incarnation of the Logos.

subsections.heading: 8. THE EXAMPLE OF THE LORD'S CIRCUMCISION
paragraphs: This is a Feast to the Lord because the Lord (the Incarnate Logos) accepted circumcision. He was circumcised in the flesh.
No one can say that the Divine Nature was circumcised, yet the circumcision of the flesh is ascribed to the Divine Logos because He was united Hypostatically with this flesh.
The same applies to His death and suffering: He suffered and died in the flesh, yet remained Impassible and Immortal.
THE PATTERN
The Logos is Spirit, yet He took flesh, and circumcision is ascribed to Him.
The Logos is Immortal, yet He took flesh, and death is ascribed to Him.
The Logos is Impassible, yet He took flesh, and suffering is ascribed to Him.

This does not in any way decrease or minimize the suffering of the Lord, because we say (with St. Cyril) suffering was "in the flesh" and it was "ascribed to Him." We maintain that the Divine attributes are NOT altered by the Incarnation.
GROWING "IN THE FLESH"
Also, in the fraction prayer of the Lord's feasts, we say about the Incarnate Logos that "He grew little by little," as it was written: "And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature" (Luke 2:52).

Obviously, the Divine Logos, who is Spirit, does not increase in stature. And the Divine Logos, who is "the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24), does not increase in wisdom (the divine Nature is Immutable; it does not change).

However, the increase in wisdom and stature "are ascribed" to the Divine Logos, since the Divine Nature was united with the human nature in the Incarnation, and thus the Divine Logos (who is Immutable) increased in wisdom and stature "in the flesh."

subsections.heading: CLOSING
paragraphs: "Always be ready to give a defense to everyone who asks you a reason for the hope that is in you." (1 Peter 3:15)
Biblical Defense of Our Faith

subsections.heading: THE ONE NATURE AND THE INCARNATION
paragraphs: It is impossible to say that the Virgin Mary gave birth only to the Divine Nature, since she gave birth to a visible child. It is equally impossible to say she gave birth only to a Human Nature, since that would take us back into the Nestorian heresy. And she did not give birth to "a Divine Nature and a Human Nature" as though these were two separate things, since that would mean she had two sons: one who is God, and one who is merely a man. Our Lord Jesus Christ is not two Sons, one being the Son of God, the Divine Word, who deserves worship, and the other being merely a man who does not.

As St. St. Athanasius put it, Christ does not have two natures such that we worship one and not the other. He is instead one single reality, before whom we bow down in a single act of worship. So our worship is never directed at the Divine Nature apart from the Human Nature. There is no separation between them, and all worship is given to the one incarnate God. This is why we worship this newborn Child, saying, "Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, who was born of the Virgin, have mercy upon us."

A helpful way to grasp this comes from how Scripture itself describes marriage. Origen, reflecting on Genesis and Christ's own teaching that "they shall no longer be two, but one flesh," noted that this union of husband and wife is actually a weaker echo of an even deeper union: the union between the Word of God and the human nature He took on, which is more truly "one flesh" than any marriage could ever be. Two distinct people come together in marriage and become, in Scripture's own words, one flesh. Our minds can still tell the husband and wife apart as two individuals, yet from God's own perspective, the perspective we are called to adopt, they are declared to be one. As our Lord said of marriage, "What God has joined together, let not man separate" (Matthew 19:6), and St. Paul later applies this same "one flesh" language directly to Christ and the Church, calling it "a great mystery" that speaks of Christ Himself (Ephesians 5:31-33).

If this is true even of the union between husband and wife, how much more should we refuse to mentally split apart the union between the Divine Word and the human nature He assumed? Just as a husband and wife remain genuinely two, yet are truly declared and treated as one flesh, the divine and human natures of Christ remain fully what they are, yet come together as one united reality. To insist on mentally separating what God Himself has joined, in marriage or in the Incarnation, is to work against the very language Scripture uses to describe both mysteries.
Scripture consistently supports this in speaking of Christ:
• "That Holy One who is born will be called the Son of God" (Luke 1:35).
• "For unto us a Child is born, unto us a Son is given... His name will be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God" (Isaiah 9:6).
• "Behold, the virgin shall be with child, and bear a Son, and they shall call His name Immanuel," which means "God with us" (Matthew 1:23).
• "But why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" (Luke 1:43). Notice that the Virgin Mary is called "Mother of God" while she was still pregnant.
• "When the fullness of time had come, God sent His Son, born of a woman" (Galatians 4:4).
• "Great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh" (1 Timothy 3:16).

subsections.heading: THE ONE NATURE AND REDEMPTION
paragraphs: Believing in the one united reality of the Incarnate Word matters deeply for our salvation. Redemption requires a sacrifice of infinite worth, sufficient to forgive the sins of every person throughout all of history. Since these sins were committed against an infinite God, they require an infinite atonement. If we were to say that only the Human Nature was crucified and suffered disgrace, while the Divine Nature merely worked miracles from a distance, then this infinite atonement would be entirely impossible.

St. Paul wrote, "For had they known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory" (1 Corinthians 2:8). He did not say, "they would not have crucified the man Jesus Christ." His choice of the phrase "Lord of glory" affirms the one united reality of Christ, and shows why this truth matters for our redemption. Our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified in His body, His Human Nature, which was fully united with the Divine Word as one reality. This union is the very foundation of our salvation.

In the same way, St. Peter said the Jews killed "the Prince of Life" (Acts 3:15), using language that points to the Divine Nature even while describing the death of the Human Nature, showing once again their union as one reality.

Our Lord Jesus Christ Himself never separated His two natures. He said, "I am the First and the Last. I am He who lives, and was dead, and behold, I am alive forevermore" (Revelation 1:17). The One who died is the very same One who is the First and the Last. Again, there is no separation, only one united reality.

Scripture affirms this repeatedly: "He who did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all" (Romans 8:32). "For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son" (John 3:16). "He loved us and sent His Son to be the propitiation for our sins" (1 John 4:10). The One who was sacrificed is the only begotten Son, the Divine Word, the second Person of the Holy Trinity. Scripture never says that God sacrificed merely "His Human Nature," even though it was truly His human body that died on the cross. This is clear evidence of Christ's one united reality.

Likewise, it is written, "He has delivered us from the power of darkness and translated us into the kingdom of the Son of His love, in whom we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of sins. He is the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:13-14). When Scripture speaks of forgiveness through Christ's blood, it attributes this directly to the Divine Word, described here as the very image of the invisible God. This, too, points to the one united reality of Christ.

subsections.heading: DID THE DIVINE WORD SUFFER?
paragraphs: The Divine Nature, by its own nature, cannot suffer. But when the Human Nature underwent suffering, it did so while fully united with the Divine Word. The Holy Fathers explained this using the image of a red-hot iron. When a blacksmith strikes red-hot iron with a hammer, he is really striking both the iron and the fire that has penetrated it. The iron, representing the Human Nature, bends and is changed by the blow, while the fire, representing the Divine Nature, remains untouched, even though it appears to bend along with the iron. Even so, because the two are so fully united, suffering that truly belongs to the Human Nature can rightly be spoken of as belonging to the Divine Nature as well, without dividing the two, since there is no separation between them.

St. Paul said, "Shepherd the Church of God which He purchased with His own blood" (Acts 20:28). Here St. Paul attributes blood to God, the Divine Nature, even though God is Spirit (John 4:24) and it was truly the blood of Christ's Human Nature that was shed. As explained above, once the two natures are united, they form one single reality, and it is to this one united reality that Scripture refers.

subsections.heading: THE ONE NATURE AND THE TITLE "SON OF MAN"
paragraphs: The title "Son of Man" clearly points to the Human Nature of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as "Son of God" points to His Divine Nature. Yet on several occasions, our Lord used the title "Son of Man" while clearly meaning "Son of God," which itself proves the one united reality that results from their union.

He told Nicodemus, "No one has ascended to heaven but He who came down from heaven, that is the Son of Man who is in heaven" (John 3:13). Of course, it is the Divine Word who is in heaven even as this very conversation takes place on earth. Yet our Lord applies the title used for His human side to describe what is true only of His divine side, showing their union as one reality.

Likewise, He asked, "What then if you should see the Son of Man ascend where He was before?" (John 6:62). Clearly, the One who was previously in heaven is the Divine Word. Yet our Lord speaks of the Human Nature in a way that only makes sense of the Divine Word, because of their unity as one reality.

Our Lord also said, "For the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath" (Matthew 12:8). Since "Son of Man" points to the Human Nature, and "Lord of the Sabbath" points to the Divine Word, combining them in a single statement is further evidence of their union into one nature.

Also, "The Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins" (Matthew 9:6). No one can forgive sins except God alone, which is exactly why the Jewish leaders accused Him of blasphemy (Matthew 9:3). Yet in this verse, our Lord, using the human title "Son of Man," was pointing to the one united reality of the Incarnate Word.

And finally, "The Son of Man will come in the glory of His Father with His angels, and then He will reward each according to his works" (Matthew 16:27). Since "His Father" and "His angels" point to the Divine Nature, and since judging the world belongs to the Divine Nature alone, using the title "Son of Man" here again shows the union of the two natures into the one nature of the Incarnate Word.

subsections.heading: OTHER EXAMPLES
paragraphs: St. John wrote, "No one has seen God at any time. The only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, He has declared Him" (John 1:18). The Divine Word made the Father known once He became incarnate at the appointed time. Could we say it was merely His Human Nature that made the Father known? No, since St. John specifically says it was the only begotten Word who did this. Yet we also know it was truly the man Jesus Christ who revealed the Father, again showing the one united reality after the union.
Our Lord said, "Before Abraham was, I AM" (John 8:58). He did not say, "My Divine Nature existed before Abraham," but simply said, "I AM," affirming the complete unity and oneness of His nature.

St. Paul, speaking of the Israelites in the wilderness of Sinai, wrote, "They drank of that spiritual rock that followed them, and that rock was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4). The Israelites were in Sinai roughly fourteen centuries before our Lord's birth. How could Christ have been present with them, providing water, unless St. Paul was referring to the Divine Word? Yet the Divine Word was not called "our Lord Jesus Christ" until the Incarnation. Because of the one united reality, the apostle did not separate the two, and freely spoke of the eternal existence of our Lord Jesus Christ, the man, even before His birth. In the same way, he wrote, "Let us not tempt Christ, as some of them also tempted, and were destroyed by serpents" (1 Corinthians 10:9). Concerning Moses the prophet, Scripture also says he considered "the reproach of Christ" to be greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt (Hebrews 11:26).

The angel told St. Joseph that Mary would give birth to a son, and that he should name Him Jesus, "for He will save His people from their sins" (Matthew 1:21). Only God can save people from their sins, yet the angel attributes this act directly to the man Jesus, proving once again the one united reality of the human and divine natures. The same can be said of every miracle our Lord performed.
"Have I been with you so long, and yet you have not known Me, Philip?" (John 14:9).
Lord Jesus Christ & the Father

I) Our Lord Jesus Christ The Logic and Wisdom of The Father: The Greek word ‘Logos’ is derived from the verb ‘Lego’, which means ‘speak – say’, from which also the English word ‘Logic’ derives. Logic doesn’t simply mean pronunciation but it means ‘Reasonable Pronunciation’. Therefore, the word ‘Logos’ refers to God’s Pronounced Logic or Reason. Since the Lord Jesus Christ is God’s Logic (Reason), then He is not created, for how could God create logic (reason) for Himself? With what Logic (Reason) would He do that? Is it conceivable that there was a time when God was illogical or unreasonable? Hence, the Lord Jesus Christ is from the same substance of the Father existing in Him before the time. Therefore, St. John said, “In the beginning was the Word (Logos), and the Word (Logos) was with God, and the Word (Logos) was God” (Jn 1:1). He also said, “For there are three that bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word (Logos), and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one” (1 Jn 5:7). Our Lord Jesus Christ, the Incarnate Logos, is the Second Hypostasis (Person) of the Holy Trinity. He is the Hypostasis of Reason and Wisdom. St. Paul said about Him, “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor 1:24), “In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col 2:3). II) Our Lord Jesus Christ The Son of God The Father: St. John said, “The Word (Logos) became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth” (Jn 1:14). There are two different types of son-ship to God, the first is the Son-ship of our Lord Jesus Christ and the second is

a) The son-ship of humans: God said, “ I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against Me.” (Isa 1:2) · Isaiah the Prophet said, “You, O Lord are our Father.” (Isa 63:16) · God said, “Israel is My son, My firstborn” (Ex 4:22) and “My son, give Me your heart.” (Prov 23:26) · We pray to God saying, “Our Father in heaven …” (Mt 6:9)

E This son-ship is due to: 1. Creation: “But now, O Lord, you are our Father; we are the clay, and You our potter; and all are the work of Your hand” (Isa 64:8). God said to Job, “Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? … When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God (Heavenly creatures) shouted for joy? (Job 38:4-7). 2. Faith: “But as many as received Him, to them He gave the authority to become children of God, even to those who believe in His name” (Jn 1:12). 3. Love: “ Behold what manner of love the Father has bestowed on us, that we should be called children of God!” (1 Jn 3:1). 4. Adoption / Salvation: “We ourselves groan within ourselves, eagerly waiting for the adoption, the redemption of our body” (Rom 8:23). St. John said, “Beloved, now we are children of God; and it has not been revealed what we shall be” (1 Jn 3:2). Even though we are called children of God, this is an honor that we do not deserve. Our Lord Jesus Christ said, “When you have done all those things which you are commended, say, ‘we are unprofitable servants’” (Lk 17:10). On the other hand, St. Paul said about our Lord Jesus Christ that He, “being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but made Himself of no reputation, taking the form of a servant, and coming in the likeness of men” (Phil 2:6-7). The difference is clear then between the Son-ship of the Divine Logos who is equal with God and the son-ship of His creatures.

b) The Son-ship of our Lord Jesus Christ: 1. The Testimony of the Father Himself: It was revealed during our Lord Jeuss Christ’s Baptism, “This is My beloved Son in whom I am well pleased” (Mt 3:17; Lk 3:22) and during His Transfiguration, “This is My beloved Son. Hear Him!” (Mk 9:7). Moreover, the Father said to the Son, in the Holy Book of Psalms, “You are My Son, Today I have begotten You” (Ps 2:7). St. Paul marveled at this declaration and said about our Lord Jesus Christ, “For to which of the angels did He ever say: You are My Son, Today I have begotten You?” (Heb 1:5). E Obviously, this Son-ship is different from our son-ship to God due to the revelations and glory that accompanied the Father’s testimony. If this were an ordinary son-ship, what is the need for all the miracles that took place during the Baptism and Transfiguration of our Lord Jesus Christ, and why would St. Paul appeal to (Ps 2:7) in order to prove that the Lord Jesus Christ is above the angels, if His Son-ship was like ours? 2. The Son-ship of our Lord Jesus Christ is the goal of writing the Holy Gospels: St. Mark starts his Holy Gospel by saying, “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (Mk 1:1). St. John said, “Truly Jesus did many other signs in the presence of His disciples, which are not written in this book; but these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in His name” (Jn 20:30-31). E This is definitely not a regular son-ship like ours for many signs and miracles support it, also accepting and believing in it gives people life. 3. Believing in this Son-ship needed explanation & evangelization: This is quite obvious from the conversion of the Ethiopian Eunuch who needed St. Philip’s explanation of Holy Scripture to reach his conclusion: “I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God” (Acts 8:37). If this were a creature’s son-ship what was the need for the explanation and evangelization? 4. This Son-ship confused Satan: Satan was very suspicious and asked our Lord twice during the temptation saying, “If You were the Son of God…” (Mt 4:3). He may have also spoken through the Jews during the Crucifixion saying, “If You are the Son of God, come down from the cross” (Mt 27:40). E With every question there is a miracle involved, either to transform the stones into bread, or to jump from the pinnacle of the temple, or to come down from the cross. If the Son-ship in question were like ours why then did Satan ask for miracles to prove it? 5. Many miracles declare it: This was obvious after our Lord Jesus Christ’s death, “So when the centurion and those with him, who were guarding Jesus, saw the earthquake and the things that had happened, they feared greatly, saying, ‘Truly this was the Son of God!’” (Mt 27:54). Also, our Lord asked the man who was born blind, “Do you believe in the Son of God?” (Jn 9:35) and he replied “Lord I believe” and he worshiped Him. After our Lord Jesus Christ had walked on the water, “those who were in the boat came and worshiped Him, saying, ‘Truly You are the Son of God’” (Mt 14:33). Likewise, Nathanael was astonished when our Lord Jesus Christ saw him under the fig tree without being physically present. He said, “Rabbi, You are the Son of God!” (Jn 1:49). E This Son-ship was revealed through many miracles that led people to testify and worship our Lord. Surely, this is not a regular son-ship like ours. 6. The Jews understood the theological meaning of this Son-ship: It was written, “Therefore the Jews sought all the more to kill Him, because He not only broke the Sabbath, but also said that God was His Father, making Himself equal with God” (Jn 5:18). They even told Him, “For a good work we do not stone You, but for blasphemy, and because You being a Man, make Yourself God” (Jn 10:33). They also said to Pilate, “We have a law, and according to our law He ought to die, because He made Himself the Son of God” (Jn 19:7). E It is very clear that this Son-ship that deserved death and was considered blasphemy by the Jews is not the same as the one Isaiah the Prophet mentioned, “You, O Lord are our Father” (Isa 63:16). à St. St. Athanasius the Apostolic marveled at the Arians’ denial of the Divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ saying that even the Jews who crucified Him understood the meaning of His words. 7. Our Lord Jesus Christ was called “THE” Son: Our Lord Jesus Christ said, “If the Son makes you free, you shall be free indeed” (Jn 8:36). St. John the Baptist said, “The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into His hand. He who believes in the Son has everlasting life; and he who does not believe the Son shall not see life” (Jn 3:35-36). St. John said, “We have seen and testify that the Father has sent the Son as Savior of the world” (1 Jn 4:14). Also, “He who has the Son has life; he who does not have the Son of God does not have life” (1 Jn 5:12). E Clearly, this Son-ship which is referred to by just “the” is different from any other son-ship. A Son-ship that gives those who believe in it everlasting life. St. Paul said, “when the fullness of time had come, God sent His Son, born of a woman” (Gal 4:4), and “Great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh” (1 Tim 3:16). The Divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ is pretty obvious here. 8. Our Lord Jesus Christ was called “The Only-Begotten” Son: St. John said, “No one has seen God at any time. The only begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father, He has declared Him” (Jn 1:18), “God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have everlasting life” (Jn 3:16), “He who does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God” (Jn 3:18), “We beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father” (Jn 1:14), “God has sent His only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through Him” (1 Jn 4:9). E This title distinguishes our Lord Jesus Christ from all others sons of God who were called as such through creation, faith, love and adoption. Also, note the relation between Him and salvation, glory, and life. St. Paul said that God has spoken to us “by His Son, whom He has appointed heir of all things, through whom He also made the worlds; who being the brightness of His glory and the express image of His person” (Heb 1:3). Indeed, the only begotten Son has declared the Father to us. III) Our Lord Jesus Christ’s Declarations Concerning His Divinity (relation with the Father): · “I and My Father are one.” (Jn 10:30) “He who has seen Me has seen the Father.” (Jn 14:9) · “Believe Me that I am in the Father and the Father in Me, or else believe Me for the sake of the works (miracles) themselves.” (Jn 14:11) “All things that the Father has are Mine.” (Jn 16:15) · “You, Father, are in Me, and I in You.” (Jn 17:21) · “For as the Father raises the dead and gives life to them, even so the Son gives life to whom He wills.” (Jn 5:21) “All should honor the Son just as they honor the Father.” (Jn 5:23) E St. Paul said about our Lord Jesus Christ, “in Him dwells the fullness of the Godhead bodily” (Col 2:9). This dwelling is a Hypostatic (Personal) one, like the dwelling of the light in the sun, the dwelling of the heat in the fire, or the dwelling of the reason in the mind. E Therefore, “We believe in One Lord Jesus Christ, the Only Begotten Son of God, begotten of The Father before all ages; Light of Light, true God of true God, begotten not created, of one essence with the Father, by whom all things were made; who for us men and for our salvation came down from heaven, and was incarnate of the Holy Spirit and of Virgin Mary, and became man, and He was crucified for us under Pontius Pilate, suffered and was buried. And the third day He rose from the dead, according to the Scriptures, ascended into the heavens; He sits at the right hand of His Father, and He is coming again in His glory to judge the living and the dead, whose kingdom shall have no end.” (The Creed). Thomas answered and said to Him, “My Lord and My God!” (Jn 20:28)
Lord Jesus Christ & God's Attributes

subsections.heading: OMNISCIENT (ALL-KNOWING)
paragraphs: To be omniscient means to know everything — every thought, motive, and hidden intention in every person, past, present, and future — without needing to learn, observe, or be told. Nothing is hidden from an omniscient being.

God is Omniscient: Solomon prayed, "Give everyone according to all his ways, whose heart You know, for You, only You, know the hearts of all men" (1 Kgs 8:39). "The Lord weighs the hearts" (Prov 21:2) and "The Lord tests the hearts" (Prov 17:3); David said the same (Ps 7:9; 44:21). The Lord said, "I, the Lord, search the heart, I test the mind, even to give every man according to his ways" (Jer 17:10), and Jeremiah repeated this (Jer 11:20). St. Paul said, "We speak, not as pleasing men, but God who tests our hearts" (1 Thess 2:4).

Our Lord Jesus Christ is Omniscient: He said, "All the Churches shall know that I am who searches the minds and hearts. And I will give to each one of you according to your works" (Rev 2:23) — and He demonstrated this again and again, not by observing behavior but by reading unspoken thoughts directly. He knew the thoughts of the Jews who accused Him of blasphemy when He forgave the paralytic's sins (Mt 9:4), the thoughts of those who claimed He cast out demons by Beelzebub (Mt 12:25), and the thoughts of the Pharisees (Lk 6:8-9). He knew the thoughts of His disciples on many occasions (Lk 9:46-47; Mt 16:7-8), the thoughts of the Pharisee who invited Him to his house (Lk 7:39-40), the doubt of St. Thomas before it was spoken (Jn 20:27), the past of the Samaritan woman (Jn 4:18), the story of the fig tree and Nathanael (Jn 1:47-50), the matter of the fish and the coin (Mt 17:27), and that St. Peter would deny Him (Lk 22:34). Indeed, "He knew all men, and had no need that anyone should testify of man, for He knew what was in man" (Jn 2:24-25).
Conclusion: Only God is Omniscient and knows the hearts of men (1 Kgs 8:39), yet Christ declares that He Himself searches minds and hearts (Rev 2:23). Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ is God.

subsections.heading: OMNIPOTENT (ALL-POWERFUL)
paragraphs: To be omnipotent means to have unlimited power — the ability to do anything consistent with one's own nature, with no external force able to restrain or overpower.

God is Omnipotent: "O Lord God of hosts, who is mighty like You, O Lord? You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, You still them" (Ps 87:8-9). "I am Almighty God" (Gen 17:1). "Behold, God is exalted by His power" (Job 36:22). "Seek the Lord and His strength" (Ps 105:4). "May God Almighty bless you" (Gen 28:3). "The Lord strong and mighty" (Ps 24:8). "He alone spreads out the heavens, and treads on the waves of the sea" (Job 9:8).

Our Lord Jesus Christ is Omnipotent: Isaiah prophesied, "His name will be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God" (Is 9:6). Christ showed this same power over the very things God alone controls: "He arose and rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, 'Peace, be still!' And the wind ceased and there was a great calm" (Mk 4:39) — echoing Ps 87:8-9 above. "He came to them walking on the sea" (Mk 6:48) — echoing Job 9:8 above. St. Peter wrote, "Jesus our Lord, as His divine power has given to us all things that pertain to life" (2 Pet 1:3).

Conclusion: Only God is Almighty, ruling the raging sea and walking on its waves — and Christ was called Mighty God, ruled that same sea, and walked on its waves. His authority was further evident through innumerable miracles over sickness, demons, and nature itself (Mk 15:33; Lk 23:44-45). Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ is God.

subsections.heading: OMNIPRESENT (ALL-PRESENT)
paragraphs: To be omnipresent means to be fully present everywhere at once — not spread thin or divided across space, but wholly present in every place simultaneously, with nowhere His presence fails to reach.

God is Omnipresent: "Where can I go from Your Spirit? Or where can I flee from Your presence? If I ascend into heaven, You are there; if I make my bed in hell, behold, You are there. If I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there Your hand shall lead me, and Your right hand shall hold me" (Ps 139:7-10).

Our Lord Jesus Christ is Omnipresent: He said, "Where two or three are gathered together in My name, I am there in the midst of them" (Mt 18:20) — present fully with every such gathering, not partially, and not by sending some fraction of Himself. He said, "I am with you always, even to the end of the age" (Mt 28:20). And He told Nicodemus, "No one has ascended to heaven but He who came down from heaven, that is, the Son of Man who is in heaven" (Jn 3:13) — claiming to be in heaven at the very moment He spoke on earth.

Conclusion: Only God is Omnipresent. Our Lord Jesus Christ is in the midst of any two or three who gather in His name — in multiple places at the same time (consider how this happens every Sunday). He told Nicodemus He was in heaven even as they spoke. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ is God.

subsections.heading: ETERNAL (WITHOUT BEGINNING OR END)
paragraphs: To be eternal means having no starting point and no ending point — existing outside of time itself, rather than simply living a very long time within it.

God is Eternal: "Thus says the Lord, 'I am the First and I am the Last; besides Me there is no god'" (Is 44:6). "I am He, I am the First, I am also the Last" (Is 48:12). "I am He. Before Me there was no God formed, nor shall there be after Me" (Is 43:10).

Our Lord Jesus Christ is Eternal: "I am the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End, says the Lord who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty" (Rev 1:8; see also Acts 1:11; Rev 22:20). "Do not be afraid; I am the First and the Last. I am He who lives, and was dead, and behold, I am alive forevermore" (Rev 1:18). "Behold, I am coming quickly... I am the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End, the First and the Last" (Rev 22:12-13). St. Paul wrote, "He (Christ) is before all things, and in Him all things consist" (Col 1:17). Christ says, "I am the Root and Offspring of David" (Rev 22:16) — how could He be both His offspring and His root, unless He existed before David in some sense while also descending from him? "The Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has prevailed" (Rev 5:5). Micah prophesied of the Bethlehem-born ruler "whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting" (Micah 5:2). Most directly, Christ told the Jews, "Before Abraham was, I AM" (Jn 8:58) — applying God's own name from Exodus 3:14 to Himself. The angel Gabriel said, "Of His Kingdom there will be no end" (Lk 1:33). And Christ prayed, "O Father, glorify Me together with Yourself, with the glory which I had with You before the world was" (Jn 17:5).

Conclusion: Only God, according to Isaiah, is the First and the Last. Christ declares in Revelation that He is the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End, the Alpha and the Omega — the only logical conclusion being that Christ and God are one. He is also unchangeable, "the same yesterday, today, and forever" (Heb 13:8), just as only God is unchangeable, "with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning" (Jam 1:17). Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ is God.

subsections.heading: LORD
paragraphs: In the Old Testament, the title "LORD" is reserved uniquely for God — the One to be worshipped and served, and no other.

God is LORD: "I am the Lord, that is My name; and My glory I will not give to another" (Is 42:8). "I am the Lord your God... you shall know no God but Me" (Hos 13:4). "The Lord your God is God of gods and Lord of lords" (Deut 10:17). "I am the Lord, and there is no other; there is no God besides Me" (Is 45:5). "You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him only you shall serve" (Lk 4:8).

Our Lord Jesus Christ is LORD: This exact title is applied to Him throughout the New Testament, often in worship. "Many will say to Me in that day, 'Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in Your name?'" (Mt 7:22). St. Stephen's dying words were, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" (Acts 7:59). The repentant thief said, "Lord, remember me when You come into Your Kingdom" (Lk 23:42). St. Paul wrote of "One Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things" (1 Cor 8:6). St. Thomas confessed, "My Lord and my God" (Jn 20:28). He is named "King of Kings and Lord of Lords" (Rev 19:16; also Rev 17:14). Christ said, "The Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath" (Mt 12:8), and instructed His disciples to say, "The Lord has need of it" (Mk 11:3). St. Paul wrote that "every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord" (Phil 2:11). The angel at the tomb said, "See the place where the Lord lay" (Mt 28:6), and Revelation ends, "Even so, come, Lord Jesus!" (Rev 22:20-21). The disciples said, "Lord, even the demons are subject to us in Your name" (Lk 10:17), and recognized Him at the shore: "It is the Lord!"— knowing it was the Lord even without asking (Jn 21:7, 12). The angels announced, "There is born to you this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord" (Lk 2:11), and Zacchaeus addressed Him, "Look, Lord, I give half of my goods to the poor" (Lk 19:8).

Conclusion: Only God is Lord, yet Christ was called by this title constantly, in worship and confession. This very title confused the Pharisees when Christ asked them, "If David calls Him [the Christ] 'Lord,' how is He his Son?" (Mt 22:45). Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ is God.

subsections.heading: GLORIFIED
paragraphs: Glory here refers to the honor, praise, and radiant majesty that belongs to God alone — He explicitly states He will not share it with any other being.
God is Glorified: "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory" (Is 6:3). God says plainly, "My glory I will not give to another" (Is 42:8).

Our Lord Jesus Christ is Glorified: Scripture directs this same glory toward Him. "Grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To Him be the glory both now and forever. Amen" (2 Pet 3:18). "In all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen" (1 Pet 4:11). "To God our Savior, who alone is wise, be glory and majesty, dominion and power, both now and forever. Amen" (Jude 25). "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and riches and wisdom, and strength and honor and glory and blessing!" (Rev 5:12). "Blessing and honor and glory and power be to Him who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb, forever and ever!" (Rev 5:13).

Conclusion: God declares plainly that He will not give His glory to another. Since Scripture gives glory to Christ as well, Christ cannot be "another" separate from God. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ is God.

subsections.heading: HOLY
paragraphs: Holiness means moral perfection — complete separation from sin, being intrinsically and essentially good rather than merely well-behaved.
God is Holy: "There is none who does good, no, not one" (Ps 14:3). "Who shall not fear You, O Lord, and glorify Your name? For You alone are holy" (Rev 15:4).

Our Lord Jesus Christ is Holy: "That Holy One who is to be born will be called the Son of God" (Lk 1:35). "You denied the Holy One and the Just, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you" (Acts 3:14). He is described as one "who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners" (Heb 7:26), and one "who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in His mouth" (1 Pet 2:22). Christ Himself said, "These things says He who is holy, He who is true" (Rev 3:7), and challenged His accusers, "Which of you convicts Me of sin?" (Jn 8:46) — a challenge no one could answer. Even the demons recognized this, crying out, "I know who You are — the Holy One of God!" (Mk 1:24).

Conclusion: Only God is Holy, yet Christ is also Holy. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ is God. (This sheds light on why Christ answered the rich young man, "Why do you call Me good?
