No one is good but One, that is, God" (Mt 19:17) — the Jews used "good teacher" as a routine title for rabbis, so Christ was really asking whether the young man meant it as mere routine or as recognition of His divinity. Christ never denied His own goodness; He said elsewhere, "I am the good shepherd," Jn 10:11.)

subsections.heading: IMMUTABLE (UNCHANGEABLE)
paragraphs: To be immutable means not changing — in character, promise, or nature — over time. God is not inconsistent, does not evolve, and does not shift with circumstance.
God is Immutable: "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and comes down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning" (Jam 1:17).
Our Lord Jesus Christ is Immutable: "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever" (Heb 13:8; see also Heb 1:8-12) — His nature and identity remain fixed and constant, exactly as God's do.

subsections.heading: IN A NUTSHELL
paragraphs: Across eight distinct attributes — each one Scripture assigns to God and God alone — the same attribute is shown to belong just as fully to our Lord Jesus Christ: 1. He is Omniscient (All-Knowing) 2. He is Omnipotent (All-Powerful) 3. He is Omnipresent (All-Present) 4. He is Eternal (Without beginning or end) 5. He is LORD 6. He is Glorified 7. He is Holy 8. He is Immutable (Unchangeable)

Since these attributes cannot belong to two separate beings without dividing what Scripture treats as exclusive to God, the conclusion drawn is that our Lord Jesus Christ is God. "Believe the works, that you may know and believe that the Father is in Me, and I in Him" (Jn 10:38).
Lord Jesus Christ & God's Works

subsections.heading: 1. CHRIST SENDS THE HOLY SPIRIT
paragraphs: ── GOD IS SPIRIT ──
"God is Spirit" (John 4:24). "Now the Lord is the Spirit" (2 Corinthians 3:17).
── GOD POURS OUT AND SENDS HIS SPIRIT ──

"I am the Lord your God and there is no other... I will pour out My Spirit on all flesh" (Joel 2:27-29). "O Lord, how manifold are Your works! You send forth Your Spirit, they are created" (Psalm 104:24-30). St. Paul wrote, "God, who has also given us His Holy Spirit" (1 Thessalonians 4:8). "I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes" (Ezekiel 36:27).
── CHRIST HIMSELF POURS OUT AND SENDS THE HOLY SPIRIT ──

St. Peter said on the Day of Pentecost, "This Jesus God has raised up, of which we are all witnesses. Therefore, being exalted to the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, He poured out this which you now see and hear" (Acts 2:32-33). Our Lord Himself said, "When the Helper comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, He will testify of Me" (John 15:26). "If I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you; but if I depart, I will send Him to you" (John 16:7). "He breathed on them, and said to them, 'Receive the Holy Spirit'" (John 20:22).
Conclusion: God is Spirit, and only God can pour out and send His own Spirit. Yet our Lord Jesus Christ does exactly this. The natural conclusion is that our Lord Jesus Christ is God.

subsections.heading: 2. CHRIST AS CREATOR AND SUSTAINER OF ALL THINGS
paragraphs: ── GOD IS THE CREATOR ──
"In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1). "I am the Lord who makes all things" (Isaiah 44:24).
── CHRIST IS THE CREATOR ──

"All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made that was made" (John 1:3). "He was in the world, and the world was made through Him" (John 1:10). "Through whom also He made the worlds" (Hebrews 1:2). "For by Him all things were created that are in heaven and that are on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things were created through Him and for Him" (Colossians 1:16). "One Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and through whom we live" (1 Corinthians 8:6).
── MIRACLES INVOLVING CREATION ──
Feeding the five thousand and the four thousand (Luke 9:10-17; Matthew 15:32-38). Turning water into wine (John 2:7-8). Creating sight for the man born blind (John 9).
Conclusion: God the Father created everything through His own Wisdom, His Word, His Reason, and God and His Wisdom are one and the same. Therefore, our Lord Jesus Christ is God.

subsections.heading: 3. CHRIST AS GIVER OF LIFE
paragraphs: ── GOD IS THE GIVER OF LIFE ──
"I, even I, am He, and there is no God beside Me; I kill and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39). "The Lord kills and makes alive; He brings down to the grave and brings up" (1 Samuel 2:6).
── MIRACLES OF RAISING THE DEAD ──
The daughter of Jairus (Mark 5:35-42). The son of the widow of Nain (Luke 7:11-17). Lazarus (John 11).
── CHRIST'S OWN DECLARATIONS ──

"I am the bread of life" (John 6:35). "If anyone eats from this bread, he will live forever" (John 6:51). "And I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish" (John 10:28). "I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in Me, though he may die, he shall live. And whoever lives and believes in Me shall never die" (John 11:25-26). "As the Father raises the dead and gives life to them, even so the Son gives life to whom He will" (John 5:21). "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (John 14:6).

Conclusion: When our Lord Jesus Christ raised the dead, He did so simply by commanding the dead person to rise. This stands in contrast to the saints, who prayed to God asking for the dead to be raised (2 Kings 4:33; Acts 9:40). Death itself had no power over Him, and He rose again on the third day. Indeed, "In Him was life" (John 1:4). Since only God is the giver of life, and our Lord Jesus Christ gives life in this same way, our Lord Jesus Christ is God.

subsections.heading: 4. CHRIST AS FORGIVER OF SINS
paragraphs: ── GOD FORGIVES SINS ──

"Bless the Lord, O my soul: who forgives all your iniquities" (Psalm 103:2-3). "The Lord God, merciful and gracious, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin" (Exodus 34:6-7). "If You, Lord, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? But there is forgiveness with You" (Psalm 130:3-4).
── CHRIST FORGIVES SINS ──
He forgave the paralytic (Matthew 9:2; Mark 2:5; Luke 5:20). He forgave the sinful woman (Luke 7:48). He forgave the repentant thief on the cross (Luke 23:43).

Conclusion: Only God can forgive sin, since sin is ultimately committed against Him: "Against You, You only, have I sinned, and done this evil in Your sight" (Psalm 51:4). When our Lord Jesus Christ forgave the paralytic, the Jewish leaders objected, asking, "Who can forgive sins but God alone?" (Mark 2:7). Our Lord responded, "That you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins," and then told the paralytic, "Arise, take up your bed, and go to your house" (Mark 2:10). Therefore, our Lord Jesus Christ is God.

subsections.heading: 5. CHRIST AS JUDGE
paragraphs: ── GOD IS THE JUDGE ──

Abraham called God "the Judge of all the earth" (Genesis 18:25). "The Lord shall judge the people" (Psalm 7:8). "He shall judge the people righteously" (Psalm 96:10). "He shall judge the world with righteousness" (Psalm 96:13). "God Himself is Judge" (Psalm 50:6). "Rise, O Judge of the earth; render punishment to the proud" (Psalm 94:2). "How will God judge the world?" (Romans 3:6).
── CHRIST IS THE JUDGE ──

"For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ" (2 Corinthians 5:10). "The Son of Man will come in the glory of His Father with His angels, and then He will reward each according to his work" (Matthew 16:27; see also Matthew 25:31-46). "The Lord Jesus Christ, who will judge the living and the dead" (2 Timothy 4:1). "I am coming quickly, and My reward is with Me, to give every one according to his work" (Revelation 22:12). "All the churches shall know that I am He who searches the minds and hearts, and will give to each one of you according to your works" (Revelation 2:23).
Conclusion: Only God is the true Judge, yet our Lord Jesus Christ is also the Judge. Therefore, our Lord Jesus Christ is God.

subsections.heading: 6. CHRIST AS SAVIOR
paragraphs: ── GOD IS THE SAVIOR ──
"I am the Lord your God... there is no savior besides Me" (Hosea 13:4). "There is no other God besides Me, a just God and a Savior; there is none besides Me" (Isaiah 45:21).
── CHRIST IS THE SAVIOR ──

St. Peter said of our Lord, "Nor is there salvation in any other, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved" (Acts 4:12). "You shall call His name Jesus, for He will save His people from their sins" (Matthew 1:21). "For the Son of Man has come to save that which was lost" (Matthew 18:11). The Samaritans declared, "This is indeed the Christ, the Savior of the world" (John 4:42). "This is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners" (1 Timothy 1:15).

Conclusion: Since sin is committed against God, who is infinite, it requires an infinite atonement. Only God, who is infinite, is able to provide this kind of salvation. Since the Lord Jesus Christ is able to save in this way, the Lord Jesus Christ is God.

subsections.heading: 7. CHRIST DEMANDS DEVOTION AND ACCEPTS WORSHIP
paragraphs: ── CHRIST DEMANDS EXTRAORDINARY DEVOTION ──

"He who loves father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me. And he who loves son or daughter more than Me is not worthy of Me. And he who does not take his cross and follow after Me is not worthy of Me. He who finds his life will lose it, and he who loses his life for My sake will find it" (Matthew 10:37-39).
── CHRIST ACCEPTS WORSHIP ──

Our Lord accepted worship from the man born blind (John 9:38), from St. Peter (Luke 5:8), from His disciples (Matthew 14:33; 28:17; Luke 24:52), from the woman with the flow of blood (Mark 5:33), from the women after the Resurrection (Matthew 28:9), from the wise men (Matthew 2:11), and from the angels (Hebrews 1:6; Revelation 5:8-9). Notice too that the angels are repeatedly called "His angels" (Matthew 13:41-42; 24:30-31; Revelation 22:16).

Conclusion: No mere human being could rightly ask for this kind of devotion or accept worship without committing a grave sin. Our Lord even encouraged people to pray directly to Him, saying, "Whatever you ask in My name, that I will do" (John 14:13). Notice too that angels are called "His angels," even though they are truly God's angels: "Bless the Lord, you His angels" (Psalm 103:20). Likewise, the Kingdom is called "His Kingdom" (Luke 23:42; 2 Timothy 4:1), even though it is truly God's Kingdom: "God, who called us into His own Kingdom" (1 Thessalonians 2:12). Therefore, our Lord Jesus Christ is God.
"There will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies" (2 Peter 2:1).
Things Hard to Understand (Holy Gospel of St. John)

subsections.heading: DIFFICULT VERSES AND THEIR TRUE MEANING
paragraphs: In his second letter, St. Peter says plainly that some parts of St. Paul's writings, and of Scripture in general, are "hard to understand." He warns that people who are "untaught and unstable" twist these passages, bringing about their own destruction. St. Peter urges us to guard against falling away from firm faith, and instead to "grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ."

He wrote: "Account that the longsuffering of our Lord is salvation, as also our beloved brother Paul, according to the wisdom given to him, has written to you, as also in all his epistles, speaking in them of these things, in which are some things hard to understand, which those who are untaught and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do also the rest of the Scriptures. You therefore, beloved, since you know these things beforehand, beware lest you also fall from your own steadfastness, being led away with the error of the wicked; but grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ" (2 Peter 3:14-18).

Notice two things here. First, Scripture is not always self-explanatory. Some passages are genuinely difficult, which is exactly why Holy Tradition matters so much. Second, even though these passages are hard, and even though many who misread them were simply uneducated, St. Peter still says clearly that they twisted these passages "to their own destruction." As St. Paul warned earlier, those who fall into heresy will not inherit the kingdom of God (Galatians 5:19-21). So neither the difficulty of these passages nor the ignorance of those who misuse them excuses the resulting error. The Arians misread many difficult verses to support their heresy. With the grace and knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ, we will now walk through the traditional Orthodox understanding of several of these verses.
Here are the verses we will examine:

1. "My Father is greater than I" (John 14:28) 2. "I am the true vine, and My Father is the vinedresser" (John 15:1) 3. "That they may know You, the only true God" (John 17:3) 4. "I am ascending to My Father and your Father, and to My God and your God" (John 20:17) 5. "The Son can do nothing of Himself, but what He sees the Father do" (John 5:19) 6. "The Father who dwells in Me does the works" (John 14:10)

It's striking that Arians and Jehovah's Witnesses often quote verses from the Gospel of John, a Gospel written specifically to prove Christ's divinity, in an attempt to deny it. It's equally striking how powerfully the Coptic Orthodox Church has always refuted these claims, never shying away from the difficult verses. In fact, the Church has believers read the most debated verse, "My Father is greater than I" (John 14:28), every single day during the prayer of the third hour, and reads "I am ascending to My God and your God" (John 20:17) during every Resurrection Liturgy.

What follows draws heavily on the writings of the Church Fathers found in the Nicene and Post-Nicene collections, along with lectures given by Pope Shenouda III to theology students in Cairo in 1994 and 1995. St. St. Athanasius wrote seven separate lectures on Proverbs 8:22 alone, and St. Augustine wrote twenty pages on John 5:19.

subsections.heading: 1. "MY FATHER IS GREATER THAN I" (JOHN 14:28)
paragraphs: When the Church Fathers refuted the Arian misreading of this verse, they first established, elsewhere, the full divinity and equality between the Father and the Son. Then they examined the actual context in which this verse was spoken: "You have heard Me say to you, 'I am going away and coming back to you.' If you loved Me, you would rejoice because I said, 'I am going to the Father,' for My Father is greater than I" (John 14:28).

Our Lord said this just before going to the garden to be betrayed by Judas, before being arrested by the Jewish authorities, before being struck across the face by an officer (John 18:22), before being whipped and mocked by Roman soldiers (John 19:1,3), and before carrying His cross to Golgotha to be crucified alongside criminals (John 19:17-18). Psalm 22, which describes His sufferings on the cross, says of Him, "I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised of the people. All those who see Me laugh Me to scorn" (Psalm 22:6-7). Isaiah the prophet likewise wrote, "He has no form or comeliness; and when we see Him, there is no beauty that we should desire Him. He is despised and rejected by men" (Isaiah 53:2-3), and, "He was led as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before its shearers is silent, so He opened not His mouth" (Isaiah 53:7).

St. Paul wrote that our Lord Jesus Christ "did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but made Himself of no reputation, taking the form of a servant, and coming in the likeness of men. And being found in appearance as a man, He humbled Himself and became obedient to the point of death, even the death of the cross" (Philippians 2:6,8). So our Lord was referring to the humble, servant-like form He had taken on in His Incarnation. He was essentially telling His disciples, "If you loved Me, you would rejoice that I am going to the Father, going to the glory that was hidden during My time on earth, since My Father is greater than this human nature I have taken on."

St. Augustine even said that the Holy Spirit is likewise greater than Christ's servant-form, and that Christ Himself, in His divine form, is greater than His own human form. Scripture also says of our Lord, "You made Him a little lower than the angels" (Psalm 8:5), and St. Paul writes, "We see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, for the suffering of death crowned with glory and honor, that He, by the grace of God, might taste death for everyone" (Hebrews 2:9). The Divine Word, who shares fully in the Godhead of the Father and the Holy Spirit, emptied Himself and appeared even lower than the very angels He had created. It's no surprise, then, that He would tell His disciples to rejoice that He was going to the Father, since the Father was never incarnate, only the Divine Word was.

St. Ambrose pointed out that since no one has ever seen the Father directly, as Scripture says, "No one has seen God at any time. The only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, He has declared Him" (John 1:18), every appearance of God recorded in the Old Testament was really an appearance of the Divine Word. This is why Abraham received God's promise of blessing from the Divine Word, sometimes called the "Angel of the Lord" (Genesis 22:15). This may be exactly why our Lord said, "Your father Abraham rejoiced to see My day, and he saw it and was glad" (John 8:56). St. Paul adds, regarding this same promise, "For when God made a promise to Abraham, because He could swear by no one greater, He swore by Himself" (Hebrews 6:13). So "My Father is greater than I" cannot refer to Christ's Divine Nature, since otherwise the Angel of the Lord, the Divine Word, would have had to swear by God the Father in Genesis 22:17, rather than by Himself.

In the story of Samson, Manoah asked the Angel of the Lord for His name (Judges 13:17), and He replied, "Why do you ask My name, seeing it is Wonderful?" (Judges 13:18), echoing Isaiah 9:6. Manoah then said to his wife, "We shall surely die, because we have seen God" (Judges 13:22).

subsections.heading: 2. "I AM THE TRUE VINE, AND MY FATHER IS THE VINEDRESSER" (JOHN 15:1)
paragraphs: The Arians argued that since Christ is the vine and the Father is the vinedresser, Christ cannot share the Father's divine nature, since a vine and the one who tends it are not the same kind of thing. They pointed to the further statement, "I am the vine, you are the branches" (John 15:5), and reasoned that since the branches share the very same nature as the vine, this must mean Christ is created, just like us.
── THE REFUTATION ──

Here, our Lord is really describing the Church as His body, with believers as His members. St. Paul wrote, "You are the body of Christ, and members individually" (1 Corinthians 12:27), and, "Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?" (1 Corinthians 6:15), and, "He put all things under His feet, and gave Him to be head over all things to the church, which is His body" (Ephesians 1:22-23). We are not branches of His divine nature. Rather, because He took on a human nature like ours, we became His members: "Inasmuch then as the children have partaken of flesh and blood, He Himself likewise shared the same, that through death He might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil" (Hebrews 2:14).

St. Augustine explained that since a vine and its branches share one nature, and since Christ's own divine nature is different from ours, He became human so that, in His human nature, He could become the vine, allowing us, who are also human, to become branches of that same vine. So our Lord is really calling His human nature "the vine." The Father, in turn, is called "the vinedresser" in exactly the same sense as when Christ said, "My Father is greater than I" (John 14:28). The Father is also called the vinedresser because He is the One who sent the Word for our salvation: "For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish" (John 3:16). The Church itself is also described as the Father's gift to the Son. In John chapter 17, our Lord refers to believers as "those You have given Me" seven separate times, which is exactly the sense in which the Father is the vinedresser.
── A FEW FURTHER OBSERVATIONS ──

In the parable of the fig tree (Luke 13:6-9), the keeper wanted to dig around and fertilize the tree itself to help it bear fruit. But regarding the vine, our Lord instead says, "Every branch in Me that does not bear fruit He [the vinedresser, the Father] takes away; and every branch that bears fruit He prunes, that it may bear more fruit" (John 15:2). St. John Chrysostom observed that while a tree's root usually needs more care than its branches, Christ says nothing here about tending the root itself, only about tending the branches, showing that He needs no outside help, while the disciples need a great deal of help from the vinedresser.

Our Lord also said, "You are already clean because of the word which I have spoken to you" (John 15:3). St. John Chrysostom pointed out that here Christ presents Himself as the one tending the branches, saying "I have cleansed you," even though earlier He said it was the Father who does this. There is no real separation between the Father and the Son in this work.

St. Augustine added that, to prevent anyone from thinking a branch could produce even a small amount of fruit on its own, Christ immediately adds, "Without Me you can do nothing" (John 15:5). Even though the vinedresser prunes a branch that bears little fruit so it can bear more, a branch that doesn't remain attached to the vine, drawing life from its root, can bear no fruit at all on its own. And although Christ could not have been "the vine" without becoming truly human, He also could not have given this kind of grace to the branches unless He were also truly God.
── CONCLUSION ──

The analogy of the vine, the vinedresser, and the branches is not describing the divine relationship between the Father and the Son. It's describing our relationship with the Father and the Son within the Church. Looking closely at Christ's words, we see that both the Father and the Son actively tend the Church, and we are called members of our Lord Jesus Christ precisely because He shared fully in our human nature through the Incarnation.

subsections.heading: 3. "THAT THEY MAY KNOW YOU, THE ONLY TRUE GOD" (JOHN 17:3)
paragraphs: The Arians claimed that in this verse, our Lord Jesus Christ was declaring that only the Father is truly God.
── HOW THE WORD "GOD" IS USED ──

Scripture uses the word "God" in more than one way. Sometimes it refers specifically to God the Father: "For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son" (John 3:16). Other times it refers to the Holy Trinity as a whole: "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1). This verse describes the whole Trinity, since Scripture also says of the Son, "All things were made through Him" (John 1:3), and of the Holy Spirit, "You send forth Your Spirit, they are created" (Psalm 104:30).
── WHY "ONLY" AND "ALONE" DON'T MEAN EXCLUSION ──

Scripture describes the Father as the One "who alone has immortality, dwelling in unapproachable light, whom no man has seen or can see" (1 Timothy 6:16). Does this mean the Son, of whom it is said, "In Him was life" (John 1:4), lacks immortality? Or that the Holy Spirit is excluded from immortality? Certainly not. Likewise, Scripture says of our Lord Jesus Christ, "Nor is there salvation in any other" (Acts 4:12). No one would seriously argue this verse excludes the Father and the Holy Spirit from our salvation, especially given passages like Matthew 28:19.
── CONCLUSION ──

Our Lord was speaking about the oneness of God, referring to the entire Godhead, including Himself and the Holy Spirit. Notice that He said, "That they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent" (John 17:3). But who is this Jesus Christ, whom the Father sent? He is the Word of God, the Wisdom of God, God made flesh.

subsections.heading: 4. "I AM ASCENDING TO MY FATHER AND YOUR FATHER, AND TO MY GOD AND YOUR GOD" (JOHN 20:17)
paragraphs: St. Augustine explained that Christ did not say "our Father," meaning the Father belongs to Him and to us in two different senses: by nature, He is Christ's Father; by grace, He is ours. Likewise, Christ did not say "our God," but rather "My God" and "your God," again in two different senses: My God, whom I am also under, as man, because of the Incarnation, and your God, between whom and you I stand as Mediator.

St. John Chrysostom similarly explained that the Father belongs to Christ and to us in different ways. He noted that God is the God of the righteous in a different sense than He is the God of everyone else, and this difference is even greater between the Son and us. When Christ said, "Go to My brethren and say to them" (John 20:17), He deliberately clarified the difference so no one would assume this implied equality. He was about to sit on His Father's throne, while His disciples would only stand beside it. So while Christ truly became our brother in His human nature, He remains far greater than us in honor, more than words can express.
── CONCLUSION ──

This verse, which the Arians hoped would undermine our belief in Christ's divinity, actually supports and strengthens it. It also helps us understand Christ's words on the cross, "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" (Matthew 27:46). The Father is His God in a different sense than He is ours. This shows that Christ's divinity did not prevent His human nature from truly suffering. There was still no separation between His two natures; He simply meant that He had been left to endure the pain.

subsections.heading: 5. "THE SON CAN DO NOTHING OF HIMSELF" (JOHN 5:19) AND "THE FATHER WHO DWELLS IN ME DOES THE WORKS" (JOHN 14:10)
paragraphs: The Arians argued that these verses show the Son is inferior to the Father, having less authority, less majesty, and less ability.
── THE CONTEXT OF JOHN 5:19 ──

Responding to the Jewish leaders who accused Him of breaking the Sabbath, our Lord said, "My Father has been working until now, and I have been working" (John 5:17). He was essentially telling them, "When I healed the paralyzed man at the pool of Bethesda on the Sabbath, My Father was working through Me at that very moment. So if you accuse Me of breaking the Sabbath, you are really accusing the Father." Scripture then records, "Therefore the Jews sought all the more to kill Him, because He not only broke the Sabbath, but also said that God was His Father, making Himself equal with God" (John 5:18). It was at this point that Christ said, "The Son can do nothing of Himself, but what He sees the Father do" (John 5:19), showing the complete agreement in will between the Father and the Son.
── ON BEING, SEEING, AND BEING ABLE ──

Drawing on the teaching of St. Augustine, we can understand this more deeply. For the Son, "being" and "being able" are the very same thing. This is not true for us. For a human being, existing and being capable of something are two separate realities, since a person can exist and yet be unable to do what they want, or exist in such a way that they can do what they want. So for us, existing and having ability are genuinely distinct.

But this is not true of God. God's very being and His power are not two separate things. Whatever belongs to Him, and whatever He is, is fully one with Him, because He is God. He does not exist one way and have ability in another way; His being and His ability exist together, since His willing and His doing are always united. Because the Son's power comes from the Father, the Son's very being also comes from the Father, and because the Son's being comes from the Father, the Son's power comes from the Father as well. In the Son, power and being are not separate: His power to act is the very same thing as His being.

Because the Son comes from the Father, He said, "The Son can do nothing of Himself." This is not because His power is somehow less, but because He is not "Son" independently of the Father, and therefore His ability is not independent of the Father either. In other words, "The Son can do nothing of Himself" really means the same thing as saying, "The Son does not exist independently of Himself, that is, apart from the Father." Since He is truly a Son, He was begotten, and since He was begotten, He comes from the One who begat Him.

Even so, the Father begat Him fully equal to Himself. Someone might ask how something eternal could beget something else that is also eternal. Think of it like a flame that produces light: the flame that generates the light exists at the very same moment as the light itself. The flame does not exist before the light in time. From the very moment the flame begins, the light begins as well. Show me a flame that exists without light, and I will show you God the Father existing without the Son.

In the same way, when Christ says, "The Son can do nothing of Himself, but what He sees the Father do," this means that the Son's "seeing" the Father and His being begotten of the Father are actually the same reality. His seeing and His very being are not separate things, just as His power and His being are not separate things. Everything the Son is, He is from the Father. Everything the Son can do, He can do because of the Father. Because what He can do and what He is are one and the same, entirely from the Father.
── IN SUMMARY ──

Whatever the Father does, the Son also does, and the Holy Spirit also does. The work of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit can never truly be separated, because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not three Gods, but one God (Genesis 1:1; Psalm 104:30; John 1:10).
"Some will depart from the faith, giving heed to deceiving spirits and doctrines of demons" (1 Timothy 4:1).
Things Hard to Understand (Holy Gospel of St. Matthew)

subsections.heading: MORE DIFFICULT VERSES AND THEIR TRUE MEANING
paragraphs: Here are the verses we will examine in this section:

1. "But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, but My Father only" (Matthew 24:36), and "But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father" (Mark 13:32). 2. "O My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will" (Matthew 26:39). 3. "All things have been delivered to Me by My Father" (Matthew 11:27), "All authority has been given to Me in heaven and on earth" (Matthew 28:18), "The Father loves the Son and has given all things into His hand" (John 3:35), and "As the Father has life in Himself, so He has granted the Son to have life in Himself, and has given Him authority to execute judgment also, because He is the Son of Man" (John 5:26-27). 4. "To sit on My right hand and on My left is not Mine to give, but it is for those for whom it is prepared by My Father" (Matthew 20:23).

subsections.heading: 1. KNOWING THE LAST DAY (MATTHEW 24:36; MARK 13:32)
paragraphs: Arius argued that since the Son does not know the day of judgment, He cannot be equal to the Father.
── THE SON DOES KNOW THE LAST DAY ──

He is the Word, the Logic and Reason of God the Father, "in whom are hidden all treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3), so of course He knows. He knows the day and hour because it is His own day, the day when He will come in glory to judge the world (Matthew 25:31-32; 2 Corinthians 5:10). It makes no sense for Him to know the day of His own suffering in advance (Matthew 26:2) and yet somehow not know the day of His glorification. Since "the world was made through Him" (John 1:10), He naturally knows when this world will end, because He is the One who created it. Since "all things were made through Him" (John 1:3), including time itself, He also knows the end of time. He is the Beginning and the End (Revelation 22:13), so He knows the beginning and end of all things. He also said, "Nor does anyone know the Father except the Son" (Matthew 11:27). Since knowing the Father is a far greater thing than knowing the timing of the Last Day, and since He clearly knows the greater thing, He surely knows the lesser one as well. He also said, "All things that the Father has are Mine" (John 16:15), which would include knowledge of that day.
── GOD SOMETIMES HIDES HIS KNOWLEDGE ──

Scripture shows that God sometimes speaks or acts as though He does not know something, even though He truly knows everything. He asked Adam, "Where are you?" and "Who told you that you are naked? Have you eaten from the tree of which I commanded you that you should not eat?" (Genesis 3:9,11). He asked Cain, "Where is Abel your brother?" (Genesis 4:9). Regarding Sodom and Gomorrah, He said, "I will go down now and see whether they have done altogether according to the outcry against it that has come to Me; and if not, I will know" (Genesis 18:21). He told Abraham, "Now I know that you fear God" (Genesis 22:12).

In the same way, our Lord asked, "Who do men say that I, the Son of Man, am? And who do you say that I am?" (Matthew 16:13-15). He asked about Lazarus, "Where have you laid him?" (John 11:34). He asked the paralyzed man, "Do you want to be well?" (John 5:6). He asked Philip, "Where shall we buy bread, that these may eat?" (John 6:5). And He asked Peter three times, "Do you love Me?" (John 21).

To those who are lost, He will say, "I do not know you" (Luke 13:25-27). This clearly does not mean actual ignorance, since He follows it by saying, "Depart from Me, all you workers of iniquity" (Luke 13:27). He plainly knows exactly who they are and what they have done. What He means is, "You do not deserve to be known by Me" (compare Matthew 10:33).
── WHY DID CHRIST SPEAK AS THOUGH HE DIDN'T KNOW? ──

Our Lord spoke this way in order to discourage His disciples from pressing Him further with questions. He told them, "Take heed, watch and pray; for you do not know when the time is" (Mark 13:33), notice He said "you," not "we." When He said that the Son does not know the day (Mark 13:32), He meant that the Son does not know it in the sense of knowledge meant to be revealed and shared. This verse does not actually exclude the Son, or the Holy Spirit, who "searches the deep things of God" (1 Corinthians 2:10), from truly knowing the timing of that day.

subsections.heading: 2. WAS OUR LORD AFRAID OF DEATH? (MATTHEW 26:39)
paragraphs: ── OUR LORD WAS NOT AFRAID OF DEATH ──

He Himself said, "Do not be afraid of those who kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do" (Luke 12:4). How could He, of all people, be afraid of death? He also said, "I am the resurrection and the life" (John 11:25), and He already knew He would rise on the third day (Matthew 16:21). Why would He fear something He knew He would overcome?

When St. Peter told Him, "Far be it from You, Lord; this shall not happen to You!" (Matthew 16:22), our Lord sharply rebuked him, saying, "You are an offense to Me" (Matthew 16:23). When Peter later tried to defend Him in the garden by attacking a servant with a sword, Christ said, "Permit even this" (Luke 22:51). He also knew exactly the time and place of His arrest, and yet went there anyway: "Jesus therefore, knowing all things that would come upon Him, went forward and said to them, 'Whom are you seeking?'" (John 18:4). He also said, "I lay down My life that I may take it again. No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of Myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again" (John 10:17). These are hardly the words of someone gripped by fear of death.
── THE CUP ──

This cup does not refer to death itself, but to the cup of the curse (Deuteronomy 27, 28) and the cup of God's wrath (Revelation 14:10), which He willingly endured on our behalf. Regarding this same cup, He said to St. Peter, "Put your sword into the sheath. Shall I not drink the cup which My Father has given Me?" (John 18:11).

subsections.heading: 3. THE FATHER GIVING THINGS TO THE SON (MATTHEW 28:18; JOHN 5:27; MATTHEW 11:27)
paragraphs: Our Lord speaks of receiving certain things from the Father. The Arians misread these verses to argue that the Son must be less than the Father, since the one who gives is greater than the one who receives.
── THE REFUTATION ──

Whatever the Son received from the Father, He received in His human nature. And whatever He received in His human nature, He already fully possessed as the Divine Word. In other words, nothing new was actually given to Him. Just as the sun gives light to its own ray, and the ray receives nothing genuinely new, since that light already belongs to the ray's very nature, so it is with the Son. As He said, "All things that the Father has are Mine" (John 16:15), and, "O Father, glorify Me together with Yourself, with the glory which I had with You before the world was" (John 17:5).

subsections.heading: 4. SITTING AT HIS RIGHT AND LEFT (MATTHEW 20:22)
paragraphs: The Arians claimed that since the Father can do something the Son apparently cannot, the Father must be greater.
── THE REFUTATION ──

We should first ask: who is actually prepared to sit at the right and left hand of our Lord Jesus Christ? The answer is: no one. That throne is inaccessible, not only to human beings, but even to the saints, apostles, angels, archangels, and every power in heaven. As St. Paul wrote, "To the Son He says: Your throne, O God, is forever and ever" (Hebrews 1:8). This is exactly why our Lord told James and John, "You do not know what you ask" (Matthew 20:22).

So why does He speak as though someone might actually sit there? He was simply meeting His disciples where they were, at their current level of understanding, and to avoid embarrassing them directly, He gently answered, "It is not for Me to give, but it is for those for whom it is prepared by My Father." No one should ever think our Lord Jesus Christ is somehow unable to give heavenly gifts. He gave His disciples the keys to the gates of heaven and earth (Matthew 18:18), and St. Paul declares that Christ Himself prepared the crown of righteousness for him (2 Timothy 4:8).
"If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house nor greet him; for he who greets him shares in his evil deeds" (2 John 10).
Things Hard to Understand (Holy Epistles of St. Paul)

subsections.heading: FURTHER DIFFICULT VERSES AND THEIR TRUE MEANING
paragraphs: Here are the verses we will examine in this section:

1. "The firstborn of all creation" (Colossians 1:15), "The firstborn from the dead" (Colossians 1:18), "When He again brings the firstborn into the world" (Hebrews 1:6), "That He might be the firstborn among many brethren" (Romans 8:29), and "The beginning of the creation of God" (Revelation 3:14). 2. "Now when all things are made subject to Him, then the Son Himself will also be subject to Him who put all things under Him, that God may be all in all" (1 Corinthians 15:28). 3. "Therefore God also has highly exalted Him and given Him the name which is above every name" (Philippians 2:9), and "God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ" (Acts 2:36). 4. "God, Your God, has anointed You with the oil of gladness" (Psalm 45:7; Hebrews 1:9). 5. "He had offered up prayers and supplications, with vehement cries and tears, to Him who was able to save Him from death, and was heard because of His godly fear" (Hebrews 5:7).

subsections.heading: 1. THE FIRSTBORN OF ALL CREATION (COLOSSIANS 1:15)
paragraphs: The Arians misread the word "firstborn" and claim it means our Lord Jesus Christ was the first created being.
── TWO CREATIONS ──

Scripture describes two creations. The first is the original creation described in Genesis. St. Paul spoke of this old creation when he wrote that "the creation itself also will be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God" (Romans 8:21).

There is also a second, new creation. St. Paul describes it this way: "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new" (2 Corinthians 5:17). "For we are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works" (Ephesians 2:10). "For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails anything, but a new creation" (Galatians 6:15). "Put on the new man which was created according to God, in true righteousness" (Ephesians 4:24).

Our Lord Jesus Christ is the firstborn of this new creation. As St. Paul writes, "Having abolished in His flesh the enmity, that is the law of commandments contained in ordinances, so as to create in Himself one new man from the two, thus making peace" (Ephesians 2:15). How do we ourselves become part of this new creation? We must be born again through water and the Holy Spirit (John 3:5). What happens in this new birth through baptism? "For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ" (Galatians 3:27). "You have put off the old man with his deeds, and have put on the new man who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of Him who created him" (Colossians 3:10).

The word "beginning" in Revelation 3:14 does not describe a place in a chronological sequence. The original Greek word, *arche*, is more accurately translated "source" or "origin," pointing to Christ as the Master of all creation. Our Lord Jesus Christ, as the Beginning, is the very source and foundation of God's creation (John 1:1-3; 1 Corinthians 8:6; Colossians 1:16-17), the creative Word and Wisdom of God.

subsections.heading: 2. THE SON'S SUBJECTION TO THE FATHER (1 CORINTHIANS 15:28)
paragraphs: The Arians claim this verse shows a difference in rank or dignity between the Father and the Son.
── THE REFUTATION ──

Our Lord Jesus Christ represented all of humanity in many ways: in repentance and baptism, fasting, prayer, and death on the cross. He didn't personally need to do any of these things. Even John the Baptist told Him, "I need to be baptized by You" (Matthew 3:14), yet Christ chose to do so anyway "to fulfill all righteousness" (Matthew 3:15).

As the Head of the Church, with us as members of His body, Christ will present our own subjection to the Father on our behalf. This will take place on the Last Day, once every member of His body, the Church, is complete. What is said elsewhere of God being "all in all" (1 Corinthians 15:28) is also said directly of our Lord Jesus Christ: "There is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcised nor uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all" (Colossians 3:11).

subsections.heading: 3. GOD EXALTED HIM AND MADE HIM LORD (PHILIPPIANS 2:9)
paragraphs: St. Paul's words, along with those of St. Luke, mean that God exalted our Lord Jesus Christ and made Him known as Lord and Christ in the minds of those who came to believe in Him. God was revealing what Christ already possessed, not adding something new to Him.

Consider an example. After Jacob received his father's blessing, Isaac told Esau, "Indeed I have made him your master" (Genesis 27:37). Isaac was not actually giving Jacob any new authority. He was simply declaring and revealing what Jacob already had, since God had already said, while both sons were still in the womb, "The older shall serve the younger" (Genesis 25:23).

subsections.heading: 4. "GOD, YOUR GOD, HAS ANOINTED YOU" (HEBREWS 1:9)
paragraphs: The grain offering described in Leviticus 2:4 symbolized the human nature of our Lord. It contained oil mixed within it, and was also anointed with oil on the outside. Oil symbolizes the Holy Spirit, who descended on our Lord at His baptism, the very anointing referred to in Psalm 45 and by the prophet Isaiah: "The Spirit of the Lord God is upon Me, because He has anointed Me to preach good tidings to the poor" (Isaiah 61:1). Our Lord Himself applied this exact passage to Himself (Luke 4:16-21).
This anointing belongs to the human nature of our Lord Jesus Christ. His divine nature anointed His human nature, just as He said, "I sanctify Myself" (John 17:19).

subsections.heading: 5. DID OUR LORD REALLY FEAR DEATH? (HEBREWS 5:7)
paragraphs: The prayers, cries, and tears our Lord offered in the garden, so intense that His sweat became like great drops of blood (Luke 22:44), were not offered to save Himself from death. He was praying instead for believers and for the Church, about whom it was said, "I will strike the shepherd and the sheep will be scattered" (Zechariah 13:7; Mark 14:27).

Our Lord was praying for the faith of His followers, knowing that His death would deeply shake them. This is exactly what He told St. Peter: "Satan has asked for you, that he may sift you as wheat. But I have prayed for you that your faith should not fail" (Luke 22:31-32).
Our Lord Jesus Christ, Savior of the World — Part 1
Why does the Christian Church consider the Old Testament to be an integral part of the Holy Bible?

The Church ties readings from the Old Testament to those from the New Testament in all its liturgical prayers. The Church also firmly resisted the various heretics who attempted to exclude the books of the Old Testament from canon of the Holy Bible.

St. Paul writes, “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness for everyone who believes, for Moses writes this about the righteousness which is of the law: ‘The man that does those things shall live by them.’” (Rom. 10:4–5). The apostle Paul is quoting Moses here: “You shall therefore keep my statutes and my judgments which if a man does he shall live by them” (Lev.18:5). St. John Chrysostom tells us that man can neither live nor be righteous unless he fulfills all the statutes of the law—a feat that we must admit is beyond human ability. If the Jews base their righteousness on adherence to the law, the law itself declares the utter inability of humans to achieve righteousness and life. This leads us to faith in our Lord Jesus Christ who alone among humanity has not broken the law, but is able to make those who believe in Him righteous. This why the apostle Paul does not allow the Jews any excuse, for the law itself declares Christ as the only One who is righteous in the sense of righteousness intended by the law. To reject Him is to reject righteousness, even if one thinks that he is made righteous by the law. St. Clement of Alexandria says, “‘For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness’ (Rom. 10:4), who was prophesied by the law to every one who believes.”

The Jews are proud of the fact that they are the people of God who received the divine law by Moses through angels (Heb. 2:2). But now the incarnate Word Himself has come to us, giving Himself to us, and granted us to be the children of the Father in the waters of baptism through the Holy Spirit. St. Augustine says, “He who gave the law likewise gave grace; but the law He sent by a servant, with grace He Himself came down.”
How was the Old Testament law inadequate without the Lord Christ?

The righteousness of the law was difficult if not impossible to fulfill. Then Christ came, not to offer easy commandments or to make those who believe in Him less diligent; but to bring Himself closer to His believers and to dwell in them; not that they may fulfill the works of the law, but that through His work in them their righteousness might exceed that of the scribes and pharisees, as He said: “unless your righteousness exceeds the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, you will by no means enter the kingdom of heaven”(Matt. 5:20).
Why does St. Paul rebuke his own Jewish race?

St. Paul rebukes the Jews because they neglected the central role they were meant to play, which is to preach the Messiah to which the Old Testament’s symbols and prophecies testify. In other words, their proper task was not to haughtily and vainly engage in foolish disputes against the gentiles, but to preach the faith to them. This is what the apostle Paul meant by saying, “How then shall they call on Him in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in Him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: ‘How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the gospel of peace, who bring glad tidings of good things.’” (Rom. 10:14–15).
What is the chief concern of the Old Testament prophets?

In the passage, “All day long I have stretched out My hands to a disobedient and contrary people” (Isa. 65:2; Rom. 10:21) St. John the Chrysostom finds a description of the Old Testament in general where the Lord has stretched out His arms through the cries of the prophets, declaring His love for them despite their stubbornness and resistance. God is a Father extending His arms to His people, who reject Him as a little child who rejects the embrace of his Father’s love. In these prophetic words (Isa. 65:2), St. Justin Martyr finds a reference to the cross upon which the Lord stretched out His arms and died to embrace all. In the Liturgy of St. Gregory we pray:
“You, O my Master, have turned for me the punishment to salvation.
As a good Shepherd you have sought after that which had gone astray.
As a true Father, You have labored with me, I, who had fallen.
You have bound me with all the remedies that lead to life.
You are He who sent unto me the prophets for my sake, I, the sick.
You have given me the law as a help.
You are He who ministered salvation to me, when I disobeyed Your law.
As a True Light, You have shone upon the lost, and the ignorant.”

Therefore, the law and the prophets are a means granted by God to humanity as part of our preparation for redemption; for the coming of the Redeemer, the Savior, who grants righteousness, and opens the path to heaven.

St. Augustine says, “‘Thus they thought, and erred; for their wickedness blinded them’ (Wisd. Of Sol. 2:18–21). These words apply also to those who, in spite of all these evidences, in spite of such a series of prophecies, and of their fulfilment, still deny that Christ is foretold in the Scriptures. As often as they repeat this denial, we can produce fresh proofs, with the help of Him who has made such provision against human perversity.” The events of the life of Christ were not unforetold. Christ Himself asked us to believe in these prophecies and was constantly affirming, even after His resurrection, that all these things were all written about Him in the books.
First, prophecies about the life of the Lord Christ:
What are the most important prophecies concerning the incarnation of the Word from the seed of King David of the Tribe of Judah?

First: in speaking to the serpent after the fall of Adam and Eve into sin, God announced that the Savior would be born from a woman, saying, “And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her Seed; He shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise His heel” (Gen. 3:15). The Savior was born from a woman and crushed the head of the serpent. Although Satan hounded Christ all the way to the Cross, the Lord Christ crushed his head by rising from the dead and liberating the righteous souls from Hades.

Second: when Jacob blessed his twelve sons, to Judah — the tribe from which Jesus came — he said, “the scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh comes; and to Him shall be the obedience of the people” (Gen. 49:10). “Scepter” here refers to the King’s scepter; and “lawgiver” refers to the one who makes the laws and enforces them such that truth may be established. “Shiloh” is a Hebrew word that more or less means “one who has a scepter” or “the one to whom belongs the kingship,” and this is the meaning employed in the Septuagint’s Greek translation of the word. Thus, this verse is a prophecy about the Lord Christ that refers to Him as “Shiloh,” the King of Kings (Rev. 19:16). Consequently, we can read this verse as follows: “Sovereignty will not be taken away from the tribe of Judah, nor shall the right to judge be taken away from his descendants, until the coming of Christ the King, the Overseer, the true and eternal Judge, to whom all peoples submit.”

Third: “There shall come forth a Rod from the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots. The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon Him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord. His delight is in the fear of the Lord, and He shall not judge by the sight of His eyes, nor decide by the hearing of His ears; but with righteousness He shall judge the poor, and decide with equity for the meek of the earth; He shall strike the earth with the rod of His mouth, and with the breath of His lips He shall slay the wicked. Righteousness shall be the belt of His loins, and faithfulness the belt of His waist” (Isa. 11:1–5). So, the Lord Christ will come from the house of David son of Jesse.
Fourth: “I have made a covenant with My chosen, I have sworn to My servant David: your seed I will establish forever, and build up your throne to all generations” (Ps. 89:3–4).
“His seed [David’s descendants] also I will make to endure forever, and his throne [David’s throne] as the days of heaven” (Ps. 89:29).

“Once I have sworn by My holiness; I will not lie to David: his seed shall endure forever, and his throne as the sun before Me; it shall be established forever like the moon, even like the faithful witness in the sky, amen” (Ps. 89:35–37).

These words about the continuation of David’s reign “forever,” “to all generations”; and about his throne being established “like the days of heaven,” “as the sun before Me,” were not fulfilled except in the person of the Lord Christ who is descended from David.
What are the most important prophecies concerning the birth of the Lord Christ?

First: His birth from a Virgin and that He will be called “Emmanuel.” “Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign: behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a Son, and shall call His name Emmanuel” (Isa. 7:14). God does not only give us a sign or a miracle, but He Himself becomes the sign or the miracle through His birth from a virgin, and His name is “Emmanuel” which means “God with us.”

Second: His birth in Bethlehem. “But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of you shall come forth to Me the One to be Ruler in Israel, whose goings forth are from of old, from everlasting” (Mic. 5:2). This Ruler is eternal; the everlasting One who is born in time is our Savior who was born in Bethlehem.
Third: His flight to Egypt. “When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son” (Hos. 11:1).

“The burden against Egypt. Behold, the Lord rides on a swift cloud, and will come into Egypt; the idols of Egypt will totter at His presence, and the heart of Egypt will melt in its midst” (Isa. 19:1).

Fourth: The anointment of Christ with the Holy Spirit. “The Spirit of the Lord God is upon Me, because the Lord has anointed Me to preach good tidings to the poor; He has sent Me to heal the broken-hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound; to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all who mourn” (Isa. 61:1–2). The Lord Christ was anointed through His incarnation, or was consecrated by the Father for the work of salvation, through which He gives hope to the poor, the broken-hearted, the captives, the prisoners, and those who mourn because of sin, death, and Satan’s reign.
What are the most important prophecies about the Lord Christ’s last week on earth?

First: The Lord Christ’s entry into Jerusalem. “Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! Shout, O daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your King is coming to you; He is just and having salvation, lowly and riding on a donkey, a colt, the foal of a donkey” (Zech. 9:9). The Lord Christ entered Jerusalem humbly, riding on a donkey, and a colt, the foal of a donkey.

Second: The conspiracy to give Him up to the Jewish leaders. “Then I said to them, ‘If it is agreeable to you, give me my wages; and if not, refrain.’ So they weighed out for my wages thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me, ‘Throw it to the potter’—that princely price they set on me. So I took the thirty pieces of silver and threw them into the house of the Lord for the potter” (Zech. 1:12–13). This is a prophecy of Judas’ conspiracy to betray the Lord Christ to the leaders of the Jews in return for thirty pieces of silver; and after that, his regret and attempt to return this small amount to the Jewish leaders. But the Jews refused to take the money, so Judas cast it into the sanctuary and went and hung himself. The Jews used this money to buy a potter’s field in which they could bury strangers, and named this field, “the field of blood” (Matt. 27:3–8).
Third: The suffering of the Lord Christ. “I gave My back to those who struck Me, and my cheeks to those who plucked out the beard; I did not hide My face from shame and spitting” (Isa. 50:6).

“But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised by the people. All those who see Me ridicule Me; they shoot out the lip, they shake the head, saying, ‘He trusted in the Lord, let Him rescue Him; let Him deliver Him, since He delights in Him!’” (Ps. 22:6– 8).

“For dogs have surrounded Me; the congregation of the wicked has enclosed Me. They pierced My hands and My feet; I can count all My bones. They look and stare at Me. They divide My garments among them, and for My clothing they cast lots” (Ps. 22:16–18).
“They also gave me gall for my food, and for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 69:21).

Isaiah described Christ’s sufferings as though he were one of the eyewitnesses of His crucifixion, even though he preceded Christ by more than seven hundred years. For this reason some have called him “The Evangelist Prophet” …

“Who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? For He shall grow up before Him as a tender plant, and as a root out of dry ground. He has no form or comeliness; and when we see Him, there is no beauty that we should desire Him. He is despised and rejected by men, a Man of sorrows and acquainted with grief. And we hid, as it were, our faces from Him; He was despised, and we did not esteem Him.

“Surely, He has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed Him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted. But He was wounded for our transgressions, He was bruised for our iniquities; the chastisement for our peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned, every one, to his own way; and the Lord has laid on Him the iniquity of us all.

“He was oppressed and He was afflicted, yet He opened not His mouth; He was led as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before its shearers is silent, so He opened not His mouth. He was taken from prison and from judgment, and who will declare His generation? For He was cut off from the land of the living; for the transgressions of My people He was stricken. And they made His grave with the wicked but with the rich at His death, because He had done no violence, nor was any deceit in His mouth.

“Yet it pleased the Lord to bruise Him; He has put Him to grief. When You make His soul an offering for sin, He shall see His seed, He shall prolong His days, and the pleasure of the Lord shall prosper in His hand. He shall see the labor of His soul, and be satisfied. By His knowledge My righteous Servant shall justify many, for He shall bear their iniquities. Therefore I will divide Him a portion with the great, and He shall divide the spoil with the strong, because He poured out His soul unto death, and He was numbered with the transgressors, and He bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors” (Isa. 53:1–12).

In the first section of this passage, the prophet Isaiah describes the appearance of the Lord Jesus Christ on the cross, “despised and rejected by men, a Man of sorrows and acquainted with grief. And we hid, as it were, our faces from Him; He was despised, and we did not esteem Him.” He then explains that all this was for our sakes, we the sinners: “He was bruised for our iniquities; the chastisement for our peace was upon Him, and by His stripes (wounds) we are healed.” The prophet also refers to the crucifixion of Christ between two thieves deserving of death, and how “He was numbered with the transgressors” and died on a cross in order to make us righteous: “He shall see the labor of His soul, and be satisfied. By His knowledge My righteous Servant shall justify many, for He shall bear their iniquities.” His burial in the new tomb of a wealthy man, that of Joseph of Arimathea, is prophesied thus: “But with the rich at His death.” Thus, did the prophet describe the sufferings of Christ and the details of the crucifixion as though he had seen them firsthand. He offers us profound insights into the meaning of the salvation to be found in the cross.
What are the most important prophecies concerning the resurrection of the Lord Christ?

The authors of the gospels say that Christ’s tomb in the garden was a new one. This detail tells us that the death of Christ heralds and leads us into Paradise, “where the forerunner has entered for us” (Heb. 6:20). In fact, the newness of the tomb means taking a path that no one has ever taken before, by which we return from death to life; the renewal of our souls. It also means that Christ created this way for us, and by it, abolished corruption. Therefore, by the death of Christ, death for us was transformed into nothing more than a kind of sleep, similar in its characteristics to merely resting. Yet we remain “alive to God” (Rom. 6:11), and we live forever as scripture says. Further, St. Paul in many places describes death as sleep for those who die in Christ. In ancient times, the dread of death cause people to live in terror. But now:
“For You will not leave my soul in Sheol, nor will You allow Your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 16:10).

“Come, and let us return to the Lord; for He has torn, but He will heal us; He has stricken, but He will bind us up. After two days He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live in His sight” (Hos. 6:1–2).
Both these verses are prophecies about the resurrection of Christ, the Lord of Glory; while the second of them adds the detail that the resurrection occurs on the third day.
What are the most important prophecies concerning the Ascension of the Lord Christ to heaven?

“You have ascended on high, You have led captivity captive; You have received gifts among men, even from the rebellious, that the Lord God might dwell there” (Ps. 68:18). This is a prophecy about the ascension of Christ after He had completed His work of salvation; defeated the enemy, the devil; and freed all the souls of the righteous who had been in the clutches of Satan in Hades.
Second, prophecies about the acts of the Lord Christ:
What are the most important prophecies concerning the Lord Christ as a prophet?

“The Lord your God will raise up for you a Prophet like me from your midst, from your brethren. Him you shall hear” (Deut. 18:15). The Lord Christ came, descended from Abraham, like His brethren in flesh, in order to prophecy and teach us about the Holy Trinity.
What are the most important prophecies concerning the Lord Christ as a priest?

“The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at My right hand, till I make Your enemies Your footstool.’ The Lord shall send the rod of Your strength out of Zion. Rule in the midst of Your enemies! Your people shall be volunteers in the day of Your power; in the beauties of holiness, from the womb of the morning, You have the dew of Your youth. The Lord has sworn and will not relent, ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek’” (Ps. 110:1–4). Through the death of the Lord Christ on the cross, His resurrection and ascension to the heavens, He offered Himself as a sacrifice to God the Father and became Himself a priest forever who gives those who believe in Him bread and wine just as Melchizedek offered in the past, but which are His holy Body and Blood.
Third, prophecies about the divinity of the Lord Christ:
What are the most important prophecies about the divinity of the Lord Christ?

In the book of Isaiah the prophet, we read, “For unto us a Child is born, unto us a Son is given; and the government will be upon His shoulder and His name will be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. Of the increase of His government and peace. there will be no end, upon the throne of David and over His kingdom, to order it and establish it with judgment and justice from that time forward, even forever. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will perform this” (Isa. 9:6–7). Of His reign it was said, “the government will be upon His shoulder,” for all the kings of this world are crowned with regal crowns on their heads; but Christ’s reign was upon the wood of the cross which He carried on His shoulder.

Another prophecy is found in the book of Proverbs: “Who has ascended into heaven, or descended?” Who has gathered the wind in His fists? Who has bound the waters in a garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is His name, and what is His Son’s name, if you know?” (Prov. 30:4). These are clear and candid words about God who has authority over wind, water, and earth; but then comes the question, “What is His name, and what is His Son’s name, if you know?” The question here is not merely a question about the name of God the Father or the name of His Son, but is meant to show the impossibility of humans comprehending the nature of God, His transcendence and His limitlessness. What concerns us here is the proclamation of the Son of God who is necessarily God, of one nature with

God the Father. The Jews were puzzled by these questions, bereft of any answer, awareness, or understanding. But we who live at the end of the ages know well and understand by the Holy Spirit that He is God the Father, and that His Son is our Lord Jesus Christ who was incarnate for our salvation.

From this brief sample of the many aspects of the life of the Lord Christ prophesied in the Old Testament we appreciate the importance of prophecies that, hundreds of years before His coming, come close to drawing a full picture of the person of our Lord Jesus Christ, who took flesh in the fullness of time, so that the Jews who rejected Him have no excuse. Therefore, the Old Testament and the prophecies it contains are an essential part of our Holy Bible in which we see Christ by the light of the New Testament, in which we find the accurate fulfillment of these prophecies.
Important Conclusions: 687
God gave the law to the children of Israel in order to curb evil.
The law contains ethical commandments; and the punishment for disobeying these commandments was death.

The law is holy for it is the word of God and His judgments. But it does not make sinners righteous; rather, it condemns them (since all have sinned); it does not forgive sins nor does it heal human weakness.

The Old Testament contains the Torah which represents the legislative aspect, as well as prophecies which represent divine revelations that obscurely point to the Savior in order to prepare humanity to receive Him.
The prophecies cover all aspects of Savior’s life, so that His appearance as a Savior may be a fulfillment of the prophecies.
What are the signs that confirm that the one born of St. Mary is the Messiah, the promised Savior?
The words of the prophet Isaiah that He would be born of a virgin (Isa. 7:14).
The prophecy of Micah the prophet that He would be born in Bethlehem (Mic. 5:2), as the Jews already knew (Matt. 2:4–6).
Malachi prophesied about John the Baptist, who comes in the spirit of Elijah to prepare the way to the Lord (Mal. 3:1; 4:5).
Zechariah the prophet prophesied that He would enter Jerusalem as a king riding on a donkey (Zech. 9:9).
Isaiah the prophet described the suffering of the Savior in some detail (Isa. 53).
David the prophet spoke of the piercing of His hands and feet (Ps. 22:16).
Daniel prophesied the time of His coming (Dan. 9:24–27).
Did anyone know that the one born of the Virgin was the Messiah, the Savior?
The angels testified of Him when they appeared to the shepherds and urged them to worship Him (Luke 2:8–15).

A great star guided the Magi (St. John Chrysostom says that this was an angel in the form of a star) to come and find Him, preaching as they travelled that they were going to worship the King of the Jews. They offered Him gold as to a King; frankincense as to a heavenly High Priest; and myrrh as to the Crucified One who suffers for the salvation of humanity (Matt. 2:1–12).
The Holy Spirit declared the identity of the child Jesus to Simeon the elder and Anna the prophetess (Luke 2:25–38).
St. John the Baptist testified of Him, saying, “Behold! The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:36).

The Father testified of Him when He was baptized in the River Jordan, saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17). He also testified of Him during His transfiguration before three of His disciples (Mark 9).
What are the principal teachings of Christ?
That we comprehend the truth of our life in Christ: that we are the children of God the Father; members of the body of Christ; the temple of God in which the Spirit of God dwells.
That we comprehend the purpose of our lives: which is to experience the promise of heaven; to be elevated by divine grace from glory to glory, awaiting the day of the coming of the Lord with joy.
That we strive with the aid of divine grace that we may walk in the Lord (Col. 2:6) and become an icon of the Lord Christ.

That we be aware of our weaknesses, endure the weaknesses of our brothers and sisters, and pray for their repentance and ours, saying “forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us.”
That we strive to work for the Kingdom of God, so that those who seek the salvation of their souls may be joined to the Church.

That we bear the image of Christ, as Pontius Pilate said that He always smiled but was never seen sniggering; and in certain situations, He was saddened, such as when He wept over Jerusalem which killed the prophets and rejected the Messiah, the Savior.

It befits us to accept the words of the Lord of Glory given that He is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14:6); and to receive the seeds of eternal life that He plants in our hearts so we may enjoy the holy life, joy of the spirit, and eternity. As the apostle says, “having been born again, not of corruptible seed but incorruptible, through the word of God which lives and abides forever” (1 Pet. 1:23).
What are the signs that Jesus Christ performed?

John the evangelist says, “And there are also many other things that Jesus did, which if they were written one by one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that would be written” (John 21:25). Thus, His unseen signs and miracles are innumerable, but here are some of which we know:
He cast out the demons that possessed some people. By so doing, He proclaimed that He sets us free from the devil and all his evil powers.

On many occasions He healed all the sick who came to Him. He healed them with a word from His mouth or a touch from His hands (possibly, with His hands positioned to form a cross). And some were healed merely by touching the hem of His garment, as in the case of the woman who had a flow of blood (Mark 5:25–34). By so doing, He identified Himself as the physician who heals souls and bodies.

He fed a multitude one time with five loaves and two fish (Matt. 14:13–22) and another time with a few little fish (Matt. 15:34). By so doing, He declared that He alone is able to satisfy our souls by His presence in us by His grace.
He walked on water (Matt. 14:25), and by His word, the waves and storms were calmed (Matt. 8:23–27).
He raised the son of the widow of Nain from death (Luke 7:11–17), the daughter of Jairus (Matt. 9:18), and Lazarus who was buried in the tomb for four days (John 11).
Source: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Fr. Tadros Y. Malaty (2023), Book 2: Christian Dogma.
Our Lord Jesus Christ, Savior of the World — Part 2
How does the Lord Christ save us?

Out of His love for us, He was incarnate and became man that He might dwell among us as one of us, and that He might forge a precious friendship with us. St. Cyril the Great says, “Our nature became acceptable in Christ, for we had been expelled because of the rebelliousness of Adam; but now, Christ restores us to the Father.” He also says, “He is the Lamb who offered Himself as a sacrifice for the salvation of humanity from sin and purifies it to be without sin; He guides us to the Father.”

When we broke the commandment of God, He gave us commandments and granted us incomparable capabilities to enable us to keep His commandments. Therefore, He called Himself “the way” (John 14:6). He gave us His life as a model that we long to follow (John 12:26) and granted us His Holy Spirit who guides us in Christ who is the way (John 14:6). St. Cyril the Great says, “It was necessary therefore that the Word of the Father, when He humbled Himself unto emptiness, and deigned to assume our likeness, should become for our sakes the pattern and way of every good work.” He also says, “Why therefore did He make His abode in the wilderness, and fast, and endure, being tempted? The type has regard to us, my beloved: He sets before us His acts as our example, and establishes a model of the better and more admirable mode of life practised among us.”

He suffered, was crucified, and died so that we might consider our suffering as being in fellowship with Him, and so that we might say, “I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20).

Because He rose from the dead and ascended to the heavens, we can say with the apostle Paul: “[He] raised us up together, and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Eph. 2:6). By His resurrection, He proclaimed His victory over the devil, sin, and death. St. Cyril the Great says, “by the Only-begotten Word of God having become man, without ceasing to be that which He was, He glorified the nature of man, in that He did not disdain to take upon Him its meanness, in order that He might bestow upon it His own riches.
How does the death of the Lord Christ on the cross save us from sin, the curse, and death?

The apostle Paul highlights the role of the Lord Christ in the salvation of humanity by comparing Him to Adam, who is considered the head of all humanity according to the flesh. On the other hand, Jesus Christ came from the seed of Adam by His incarnation but became the head of humanity because He is the Almighty, the Giver of divine grace. He unites us with Him as our Head, through our faith.

In Adam, we inherited corruption through sin, condemnation came upon us, and we fell under the judgement of death. But the Lord Christ, because of His love for us, accepted the suffering and death of the cross and came to be subject to the curse; not because of any sin He committed, but in order to unite us with Him, abolish sin, grant us His righteousness to work in us, free us from the curse, and grant us the resurrected life in place of death. In this way, the mercies of God upon us have come to us through His justice. By Him, we live the life of victory and are worthy of the blessed eternal life.

The Holy Bible describes this mystery as “the mystery which has been hidden from ages and from generations, but now has been revealed to His saints. To them God willed to make known what are the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles: which is Christ in you, the hope of glory” (Col. 1:26–27).

“For if by the one man’s offense death reigned through the one, much more those who receive abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness will reign in life through the One, Jesus Christ” (Rom. 5:17).

“There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death. For what the law could not do in that it was weak through the flesh, God did by sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, on account of sin: He condemned sin in the flesh, that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit” (Rom. 8:1–4).
Is this salvation available to all people?

The Lord Christ, the Savior, offered Himself as a sacrifice for everyone. For His part, He offers His grace and His free salvation to all. But our part is to exercise the complete free will he has given us and choose to share in His sufferings with Him, be conformed to His death, and say with the apostle Paul: “That I may know Him and the power of His resurrection, and the fellowship of His sufferings, being conformed to His death” (Phil. 3:10). The Body and Blood of the Lord, given for our sake, support us in attaining this when we commune of them, as the apostle Paul says: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death till He comes.” (1 Cor. 11:26). He also says, “And those who are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.” (Gal. 5:24).
Why did St. Jacob of Sarug call the cross of the Lord Christ “The Divine Chariot”?

After His death on the cross, the body of Christ was buried in the tomb. The cross became a kind of divine chariot bearing the soul of Christ down into Hades, that He may destroy its gates and liberate all those who were held captive and take them to paradise, rejoicing in their victory over the devil and over death. As for the Lord’s divinity, it parted neither from His body nor from His soul. St. Peter says, “For Christ also suffered once for sins, the just for the unjust, that He might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive by the Spirit, by whom also He went and preached to the spirits in prison” (1 Pet. 3:18–19).
How did the Lord Christ come to be crucified when His life, teachings, and miracles testified to His Holiness?

The high priests, scribes, and pharisees hated the Lord Christ because He rebuked them for their false teachings and wicked lives. On their part, they envied Him and therefore wrongly accused Him and condemned Him to death. But the multitudes loved Him, sought Him, listened to Him, and beheld the miracles He performed.
Why does the Orthodox Creed mention that He suffered, was crucified, and was buried?
To affirm that He took real flesh, and not, as some heretics believed, that He did not take a real body, but that He only appeared to people to have done so.
How could He, being God, suffer, be crucified, and be buried?

Because it is God’s good pleasure to redeem humanity. His divinity did not suffer — only His humanity, as He said: “Because I lay down My life that I may take it again. No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of Myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. This command I have received from My Father” (John 10:17–18).
What does it mean that Jesus Christ was crucified for our sake?
