Also in Zechariah: ‘Behold, I bring forth my servant. The Dayspring is his name, because the stone which I have placed before the face of Joshua; upon that one stone are seven eyes’ (Zech. 3:8–9). Also in Deuteronomy: ‘And you shall write upon the stone all this law, very plainly’ (Deut. 17:8). Also in Joshua the son of Nun: ‘And he took a great stone, and placed it there before the Lord; and Joshua said unto the people, Behold, this stone shall be to you for a testimony, because it has heard all the things which were spoken by the Lord, which He has spoken to you today; and it shall be for a testimony to you in the last of the days, when you shall have departed from your God’ (Josh. 24:26–27) … This is the stone in Exodus upon which Moses sat on the top of a hill when Joshua the son of Nun fought against Amalek [Ex. 17:12–13]; and by the sacrament of the stone, and the steadfastness of his sitting, Amalek was overcome by Jesus, that is, the devil was overcome by Christ. This is the great stone in the first book of Samuel, upon which was placed the ark of the covenant when the oxen brought it back in the cart, sent back and returned by the strangers [1 Sam. 6:15]. Also, this is the stone in the first book of Samuel, with which David smote the forehead of Goliath and slew him [1 Sam. 17:49–51]; signifying that the devil and his servants are thereby thrown down—that part of the head, namely, being conquered which they have not had sealed. And by this seal we also are always safe and live. This is the stone which, when Israel had conquered the foreigners, Samuel set up and called its name Ebenezer; that is, the stone that helps [1 Sam. 7:12].”
Why is Jesus called “the Garment of righteousness”?

St. St. Athanasius the Apostolic says, “For we need in this to put on our Lord Jesus (cf. Rom. 13:14), that we may be able to celebrate the feast with Him. Now we are clothed with Him when we love virtue, and are enemies to wickedness, when we exercise ourselves in temperance and mortify lasciviousness, when we love righteousness before iniquity, when we honour sufficiency, and have strength of mind, when we do not forget the poor, but open our doors to all men, when we assist humble-mindedness, but hate pride.”
Why is Jesus called “the Suffering Servant”?
Isaiah the prophet gave us the praise of the Suffering Servant, who is the crucified Christ (Isa. 53).
Why is Jesus called “the Judge”?

Christ identifies Himself as the Judge (John 5:22) who will judge the living and the dead (1 Pet. 4:5); not to terrify them, but to reassure them. He will come to condemn the wicked and to prepare the marriage supper, where the Church will rejoice without any fear of the enemy who opposes her. The wicked will see His eyes as a flame of fire and in His mouth a sharp sword and He will rule them with a rod iron. As for His children, they will see Him as the “King of Kings and Lord of Lords” who protects and glorifies them (Rev 19:9–16).
What is “the Jesus Prayer”?

Let us conclude this survey of the names and titles of Christ by mentioning the effectiveness of the “Jesus Prayer” in our lives. When the believer experiences the power of the name of Jesus, he cries out with blind Bartimaeus, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” (Mark 10:47, Luke 18:38). This prayer is found in the biography of Abba Philemon (6 to 7 century). It is also found in the letters of Saints Barsanuphius and John of Gaza (beginning of the 6 century), Dorotheus of Gaza, and St. John Climacus. The Church employs it as a spiritual practice for her children, with the addition of part of the prayer of the tax collector who beat his chest saying, “God be merciful to me a sinner!” (Luke 18:13).

St. Anthony the Great says, “Do not cease from reciting the name of the Lord Jesus, but hold onto to His name with your mind, repeat it with your tongue, and say in your heart: ‘My Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me; My Lord Jesus Christ help me.’ Also say: ‘I praise You, my Lord Jesus Christ.’”
It was also known to St. Macarius the Great the Great and St. Evagrius.

St. Macarius the Great the Great says, “Be attentive to the name of our Lord Jesus Christ with a remorseful heart and let it pour forth from your lips. Let the name reflect back upon you. Do not bury it in your thoughts only for display, but be alert whenever you cry it out, saying, “O my Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me!” Then, in serenity you shall see His divinity resting in you; He will bring to naught the darkness of pain that is in you; and He shall purify your inner man to be like the purity of Adam dwelling in paradise. This is the blessed name that St. John the Evangelist called, “the light of the world” (John 8:12); the sweetness of which no one can ever have enough and the true “bread of life” (John 6:35).”

Abba Evagrius says, “Tormented by the thoughts and passions of the body, I went to find the Abbot St. Macarius the Great. I said to him: ‘My father, give me a word that I may live by it.’ Then St. Macarius the Great said to me: ‘Attach the rope of the anchor to the rock and, by God’s grace, the ship will cross the diabolic waves of the deceptive sea and the tempest of the darkness of this vain world.’ I said to him: ‘What is the ship, what is the rope, what is the rock?’ The Abbot St. Macarius the Great said to me: ‘The boat is your heart: guard it. The rope is your spirit: attach it to our Lord Jesus Christ who is the rock that has power over all the diabolic waves and surges that the saints are contending with; for is it not easy to say with each breath: Our Lord Jesus, the Christ, have mercy on me; I bless You, my Lord Jesus, help me? And as the fish struggling against the current can be caught unawares, we also, if we patiently persist in faithfully reciting the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, He will snare the devil by his nose (“one pierces his nose with a snare” Job 40:24) because of what he has done to us, and we who are weak shall know that help comes to us from the Lord Jesus Christ.”

And Abba Jacob says, “I once went to Abba Isidore and I found him writing, so I sat by him and noticed that from time to time he raised his eyes to heaven and his lips would move without me hearing any sound; so I said to him, ‘What are you doing, Abba?’ He said to me, ‘Do you not do the same?’ I said to him, ‘No, Abba.’ He then told me, ‘If you do not do that, Abba Jacob, then you have not yet become a monk, not even for a single day.’ And this is what he used to say: ‘My Lord Jesus Christ, help me. My Lord Jesus Christ have mercy on me. I praise You, My Lord Jesus Christ.’”
Source: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Fr. Tadros Y. Malaty (2023), Book 2: Christian Dogma.
BOOK 19

"On the Incarnation of the Word" was written by St. Athanasius the Apostolic in the fourth century AD. It is one of the most treasured writings in the life of the Church, answering a simple but enormous question: why did God become human?

We confess with him one Christ, one composite nature, truly God and truly human, joined together without division and without separation, the same Word who made us come back, in love, to remake us.

This section is a summary of the entire book, broken into its different parts, along with my own commentaries and remarks on each one.
Why St. Athanasius Is Writing This

subsections.heading: WHY ST. ATHANASIUS IS WRITING THIS
paragraphs: St. Athanasius opens by reminding his friend St. Macarius the Great of an earlier work they shared, a treatise called Against the Heathen, in which he had already walked through the errors behind idol worship: how people invented gods out of their own wickedness, and how these idols had no real power. Having laid that groundwork, he now wants to move on to something even more central to the faith: the doctrine of the incarnation, the teaching that God's own Word became human.

He is honest about how controversial this claim is. Jewish readers, he says, dismiss it as a slander against God, since it seems to compromise God's transcendence. Greek philosophers laugh at it outright, since in their thinking, a perfect, unchanging deity could never lower itself into something as messy and limited as human flesh. Yet Christians worship precisely this. St. Athanasius does not try to soften this tension. Instead he leans into it: he tells St. Macarius the Great that the more the world mocks this belief, the more it ends up proving God's power, since God turns what looks like weakness into the very thing that displays his strength.

Before diving into the specific question of the incarnation, St. Athanasius insists on going back even further, to creation itself. His reasoning is that you cannot properly understand why the Word became flesh to save the world unless you first understand that this same Word was the one who made the world in the first place. The Incarnation, in other words, is not God's Plan B. It is the same Creator returning to restore what he originally made.
Bad Explanations for Where the World Came From

subsections.heading: BAD EXPLANATIONS FOR WHERE THE WORLD CAME FROM
paragraphs: Before St. Athanasius can explain how the world is being renewed, he wants to clear away three wrong ideas about how the world came to exist in the first place, since each one, left unanswered, would undercut everything he wants to say about God's power to save.

The first error belongs to the Epicureans, who taught that the universe simply happened by chance, with no plan or intelligence behind it at all. St. Athanasius finds this obviously false just from looking around. If everything really came together at random, he argues, there would be no reason for the world to show the kind of order it does, distinct sun, moon, and earth, distinct hands, eyes, and feet on a human body. Randomness would produce sameness or chaos, not the intricate, differentiated order we actually observe. Order, for St. Athanasius, is itself evidence of a mind behind it.

The second error he attributes to Plato and his followers, who taught that God shaped the world out of matter that already existed independently, matter God himself did not create. St. Athanasius treats this as a subtle insult to God, even though it sounds more reverent than pure chance. If God needs pre-existing material to work with, then God is limited by that material's availability, the same way a carpenter is limited by whatever wood happens to be on hand. A God who depends on outside material to create anything is not really all-powerful. He is, at best, an extremely skilled craftsman working within someone else's constraints.

The third error, which St. Athanasius associates with Gnostic teachers, claims the visible world was made not by the true God at all, but by a separate, lesser being, often called a demiurge, distinct from the Father of Jesus Christ. St. Athanasius rejects this immediately by appealing to Jesus's own words about marriage, where Jesus credits the Creator, without qualification, with making humanity male and female, and to the opening of John's Gospel, which says all things were made through the Word, with no exceptions.
God Made Everything from Nothing, Out of Pure Generosity

subsections.heading: GOD MADE EVERYTHING FROM NOTHING, OUT OF PURE GENEROSITY
paragraphs: Having ruled out the wrong theories, St. Athanasius states the true one plainly. God did not need any pre-existing matter, and nothing about creation happened by accident or blind chance. Out of nothing at all, God brought the entire universe into being simply by speaking through his Word. St. Athanasius backs this up by quoting Genesis, and also an early Christian text called The Shepherd of Hermas, which states plainly that God alone made all things and brought them into existence out of nothing.

St. Athanasius roots this act of creation in God's own character. Since God just is goodness itself, he could never be stingy or withhold existence from anything he might have made. His creative generosity flows naturally from who he is. Out of everything he made, though, God showed a special, extra measure of care toward the human race specifically. He did not simply create people the way he created animals or plants, as passive, unthinking creatures. He made humanity in his own image, giving people an actual share in the reasoning power of his own Word, so that, carrying this inner reflection of the Word within them, they could go on living forever in the blessed happiness of paradise, the true life meant for those who belong to God.

But God, in his foresight, also knew that human free will could bend in either direction, toward good or toward evil. So he built in a kind of safeguard from the very beginning: a specific command, along with the specific place, the garden, where humanity was to live under that command. If people kept the grace they had been given and remained obedient, they would go on enjoying life in paradise, free from sorrow, pain, or anxious care, with the added promise of full incorruption in heaven still to come. But if they broke the command and turned toward evil, they would experience exactly the corruption their own nature was already prone to, being expelled from paradise, and from then on living out their days moving steadily toward death and decay.
Why a Book About Jesus Starts with Adam

subsections.heading: WHY A BOOK ABOUT JESUS STARTS WITH ADAM
paragraphs: St. Athanasius pauses to address a question he expects his reader is already asking. Why does a treatise supposedly about the incarnation of the Word spend so much time discussing where humanity came from in the first place? He insists this is not a detour but essential background. You cannot properly understand why the Savior needed to appear among us, he argues, unless you first understand exactly what had gone wrong with the human race that needed saving.

He reminds St. Macarius the Great that, according to what was said in the earlier treatise, people were only able to hold off natural decay and corruption for as long as they stayed close to God and kept his commandment. Once they turned away from him through disobedience, they naturally began drifting back toward the very nothingness they had originally been created out of. This was not some arbitrary, disconnected punishment handed down after the fact. It was the direct and predictable outcome of humanity cutting itself off from the one power that had been actively holding its underlying mortality in check all along.
Sin Escalates Quickly Once It Starts

subsections.heading: SIN ESCALATES QUICKLY ONCE IT STARTS
paragraphs: St. Athanasius describes, in fairly vivid terms, how things did not simply stop at humanity losing its grip on eternal life. Once that first act of disobedience opened the door, evil did not stay contained to a single mistake. It spread, multiplied, and intensified generation after generation. What began as one act of disobedience in a garden grew, in St. Athanasius's account, into an explosion of violence: theft everywhere, broken families, cities warring against cities, nations rising against nations, and civil unrest tearing apart entire societies. He does not shy away from naming specific categories of sin either, quoting Paul's description in Romans of society turning even against what is understood as the natural order.

The picture St. Athanasius paints throughout this section is one of a downward spiral with no natural floor. Once people lost sight of God as their true reference point, there was nothing internal to stop the slide from getting steadily worse. Each generation, in his telling, did not simply repeat the sins of the last but pushed further past whatever boundaries had existed before, becoming, in his words, insatiable in sinning.
God Faced with a Genuine Dilemma

subsections.heading: GOD FACED WITH A GENUINE DILEMMA
paragraphs: St. Athanasius now lays out what almost reads like a genuine dilemma facing God, phrased with real rhetorical force. On one side, humanity, God's own handiwork, made specifically in his image, was falling apart and heading toward total ruin, with that divine image being steadily effaced through sin and corruption. On the other side, simply allowing this collapse to continue seemed completely unworthy of a God who is supposed to be good.

He pushes the logic further with a pointed question: wouldn't it actually have been better if God had never made human beings at all, rather than making them only to watch them be destroyed afterward? Neglecting his own finished work, he argues, would look like weakness on God's part rather than goodness, since a truly good and powerful maker does not simply abandon what he has made once it runs into trouble. So, in St. Athanasius's framing, simply doing nothing was never really a live option consistent with who God actually is.
Why Simple Repentance Was Not Enough

subsections.heading: WHY SIMPLE REPENTANCE WAS NOT ENOUGH
paragraphs: St. Athanasius takes seriously an obvious, simpler solution someone might propose: what if God had just asked people to repent, and left it at that? He does not dismiss this idea out of hand. He grants that demanding repentance would indeed be a response worthy of God's goodness, in principle. But he ultimately argues it falls short for two distinct reasons, laid out with careful, almost legal precision.

First, repentance alone would fail to properly honor the truth of God's own earlier warning about death as the consequence of sin. If people simply repented and then went on living entirely unharmed, as though nothing had happened, God's own spoken word, that disobedience would lead to death, would effectively have been broken or proven false. Second, and just as importantly, repentance has real limits even on its own terms. It can genuinely stop someone from continuing to commit further acts of sin going forward, but it cannot, by itself, undo or reverse the deeper corruption that has already taken root within human nature as a result of past sin. Repentance addresses future behavior; it does not restore what has already been damaged. St. Athanasius concludes that something more than a simple change of heart was required. Nothing less than the same Word who had originally made humanity in his own image in the first place could actually recreate that damaged image once it had already been ruined.
The Word Takes On a Human Body

subsections.heading: THE WORD TAKES ON A HUMAN BODY
paragraphs: St. Athanasius now begins to reveal his actual answer. The Word, though he had truly never been absent from creation to begin with, since he sustains everything at all times, now comes to visit that same creation in an entirely new and unprecedented way, by actually taking on a real, genuine human body of his own. Seeing humanity trapped and helpless under the weight of death, and watching God's own image within them steadily fading away through ongoing corruption, the Word responds with genuine mercy and takes to himself a body of exactly our own kind and nature.

Crucially, St. Athanasius insists this body was formed within the womb of a virgin, entirely without any human father involved. He is careful to specify that the Word does not merely appear human, the way an actor might put on a costume or a temporary disguise. He genuinely and fully takes on complete human nature, body and soul, for a specific, deliberate purpose: so that by actually dying, in that real human body, on behalf of everyone, he could effectively cancel out the death sentence that had held legal claim over the entire human race since the fall. And by then rising again from that same death, he could reopen the way back to incorruption for every person who shares in that same common human nature he had personally taken on.
Christ's Death Pays a Debt Owed by Everyone

subsections.heading: CHRIST'S DEATH PAYS A DEBT OWED BY EVERYONE
paragraphs: St. Athanasius explains that since the Word himself could never actually die, being immortal and eternal by his very nature, he instead took on a body that genuinely could die in humanity's place. He frames this almost like a financial transaction, in fairly deliberate legal and economic language: because every single person owed an outstanding debt of death as a direct consequence of sin, the Word's offering of his own sinless, untainted body effectively settled that entire collective debt on behalf of everyone joined to him through their shared human nature.

He then offers one of the treatise's most memorable illustrations to help explain how this actually works. He compares it to a king who moves his own royal household into just one single house within a large city under his rule. Once the king himself is physically, personally present and residing there, St. Athanasius argues, the entire surrounding city gains real, tangible extra protection and honor as a direct result, since no enemy or bandit would ever dare attack or plunder the very place where the king himself now personally lives. In exactly the same way, St. Athanasius argues, once the eternal Word took up genuine residence within a single human body, the corrupting, destructive power that death had previously held over humanity as a whole permanently lost its former grip.
Scripture Backs Up This Picture of Christ's Death

subsections.heading: SCRIPTURE BACKS UP THIS PICTURE OF CHRIST'S DEATH
paragraphs: St. St. Athanasius extends his earlier royal analogy one step further. He compares God's saving action to a king who discovers that a city he founded is now under attack, specifically because of the carelessness and negligence of its own inhabitants. Such a king, St. Athanasius points out, does not simply write the city off as a loss. He steps in personally to reclaim and fully restore it, motivated not by the residents' own carelessness, which in fact caused the whole crisis, but by what is fitting and consistent with his own royal character and responsibility as its founder.

Having established this image, St. Athanasius then pauses to ground his entire argument so far directly in Scripture itself, offering a fairly dense string of New Testament quotations pulled from Paul's letters and from the Epistle to the Hebrews. These passages describe Christ dying specifically on behalf of all people, tasting death personally for every single individual, and becoming what Hebrews calls the pioneer, or trailblazer, of a fully resurrected humanity yet to come. St. Athanasius closes the section by drawing out a fitting symmetry: since death itself first entered the world specifically through one man's disobedience, it makes complete sense, he argues, that death would likewise be undone specifically through one man's perfect obedience in return.
The Second Reason: Humans Needed to Actually Know God

subsections.heading: THE SECOND REASON: HUMANS NEEDED TO ACTUALLY KNOW GOD
paragraphs: St. Athanasius now introduces an important second, complementary reason for the incarnation, running alongside the first reason concerning death and corruption. Even setting aside the specific problem of death entirely for a moment, he argues that human beings were, from the very beginning, never naturally equipped on their own to fully know or comprehend their own Creator. This limitation was simply built into the difference between an infinite, uncreated God and finite, created beings.

To bridge this natural gap, God had given humanity a real share in his own divine Image, meaning his own Word, so that by perceiving and reflecting on this inner likeness planted within them, people could come to genuinely know the Father through it, and go on to live the truly happy and blessed life this knowledge of God makes possible. But people badly squandered this remarkable gift. Rather than recognizing God correctly through the divine Image already present within their own nature, they instead invented physical idols to worship, eventually sank into worshiping demons outright, and turned to practicing magic and astrology as substitutes for genuine knowledge of the true God. St. Athanasius stresses that none of this happened because God had somehow hidden himself away from humanity. The knowledge of God had always remained genuinely available and accessible to them the whole time.
God's Patience Before Sending His Son

subsections.heading: GOD'S PATIENCE BEFORE SENDING HIS SON
paragraphs: Even once people had already turned away toward idol worship, St. Athanasius makes clear that God did not immediately resort to the most drastic option of sending his own Word directly, in person. Instead, St. Athanasius describes several earlier, progressively more direct attempts God made to patiently reach people first. The order and beauty visible within creation itself, he suggests, should have been more than enough, if people had only looked at it carefully and thoughtfully, to point them back toward its true Maker on their own.

When this natural approach failed to reach large numbers of people, God then sent the law and the prophets, human teachers people could relate to and trust more directly and personally, precisely so people could come to learn about God's nature and character through fellow human beings they were already inclined to listen to. St. Athanasius is careful to insist that these prophets were never intended only for the Jewish people exclusively, but were meant to serve as something like a holy school of moral and spiritual instruction offered to the entire world. Despite all of this patient, escalating effort on God's part, St. Athanasius laments that most people nevertheless remained thoroughly distracted by immediate pleasures and were further led astray by ongoing demonic deception at work in the world around them.
Why God Could Not Simply Stay Silent

subsections.heading: WHY GOD COULD NOT SIMPLY STAY SILENT
paragraphs: St. Athanasius argues forcefully that it would ultimately have been beneath God, and inconsistent with his own character, to simply allow this ongoing situation to continue indefinitely without any further direct intervention. He presses the underlying logic with a pointed rhetorical question: what possible point could there have been in making humans specifically in God's own image to begin with, if that very image was simply going to be permanently ignored, lost, and forgotten forever afterward?

He develops this argument further through another political analogy, comparing God to a human king whose own subjects have gradually drifted away and begun serving someone else instead. Such a king, St. Athanasius points out, does not simply give up his territory and walk away without a fight. He typically sends warning after warning, then personal messengers, and finally, if all else genuinely fails, comes in person himself as an absolute last resort. In exactly the same way, St. Athanasius argues, God's own creatures could never have been capable of restoring his damaged image within themselves, since they themselves were, after all, only copies of that image to begin with, not its original source. Angels could not accomplish this task either, since even they, unlike humanity, were never actually made in God's own image in the first place. Only the true, original, and unmade Image of the Father, meaning the Word himself, genuinely possessed the necessary standing and capability to renew and restore that same image within fallen humanity.
Like Restoring a Faded Painting

subsections.heading: LIKE RESTORING A FADED PAINTING
paragraphs: St. Athanasius offers what has become one of his single most famous and frequently quoted illustrations in the entire treatise. He asks his reader to imagine a portrait originally painted onto a wooden panel, which has since become dirtied, damaged, and badly faded through the passage of time. To properly restore such a portrait, he explains, the actual original subject of that portrait needs to personally return and sit for the artist all over again, so that the very same likeness can be freshly redrawn directly onto that same original wooden panel, rather than simply discarding it and starting over on an entirely new one.

In exactly the same way, St. Athanasius explains, the Son, who is himself the true and perfect Image of the Father, comes back specifically to the very same human nature he had originally shaped in his own likeness at creation, in order to lovingly renew and restore that same faded likeness once again from within. He goes on to explain more precisely why simply relying on creation's natural witness, or on human teachers alone, was ultimately no longer sufficient at this later stage. People had already persistently ignored both of these earlier paths for so long and so thoroughly that something far more direct and immediately visible was now genuinely required to reach them. Since ongoing demonic deception had already thoroughly confused and clouded people's minds and souls from within, and since human teachers were simply incapable of perceiving or directly addressing that deep inward corruption the way the Word himself uniquely could, only the Word's own direct, personal presence could possibly reach deeply enough to actually fix the real underlying problem at its source.
Meeting People Wherever Their Attention Had Wandered

subsections.heading: MEETING PEOPLE WHEREVER THEIR ATTENTION HAD WANDERED
paragraphs: St. Athanasius compares the Word's overall strategy in the incarnation to that of an unusually kind and patient teacher who, when some of his students simply cannot yet grasp more advanced material right away, deliberately comes down to meet them at their own current level first, teaching them through simpler, more accessible lessons before gradually working back up toward deeper truths. Since people's scattered attention and devotion had already wandered off in so many different directions by this point, some toward worshiping nature itself, some toward worshiping other human beings, some toward demons, and some toward the spirits of the dead, the Word deliberately takes on a genuine human body specifically so that he can meet people wherever their attention already happened to be fixed, and then gently but firmly redirect that same misplaced devotion back toward its proper and true object.

St. Athanasius argues that whatever specific object of devotion people had wrongly become fixated on beforehand, the Word's own visible works and actions while personally present in the body would eventually and unmistakably reveal him as genuinely superior to all of it. He exposes false gods as powerless, casts out demons with clear and visible authority, and ultimately rises from the dead himself, an act which, among many other things, thoroughly exposes the fundamental emptiness of worshiping the merely dead as some kind of substitute for the living God.
Becoming Visible So People Could Eventually See the Invisible

subsections.heading: BECOMING VISIBLE SO PEOPLE COULD EVENTUALLY SEE THE INVISIBLE
paragraphs: Building directly on the previous section's argument, St. Athanasius explains that since people's minds and attention had already become so thoroughly fixated on physical, visible things, the Word deliberately chose to make himself visible too, specifically so that he could gradually and patiently draw people's attention toward himself, first simply as a man among other men, and only afterward, through his own distinctive works and actions, progressively reveal himself as something far greater than a mere man.

He connects this overall strategy to Paul's own striking language in Ephesians about Christ's love somehow reaching into and filling every possible dimension, height, depth, breadth, and length all at once. St. Athanasius argues that the Word's ongoing presence now genuinely touches every single part of creation in a comprehensive way: above, through his original work in creation itself; below, through his humble human birth; in the depths, through his subsequent descent among the dead; and across the whole breadth of the world, through his continuing, ongoing work in it even now. St. Athanasius also makes a point of noting that Christ deliberately did not rush immediately toward his death and resurrection the very moment he first arrived among us. He instead first spent a substantial amount of time performing visible works and actively teaching, precisely so that people would have real opportunity to come to recognize him as genuinely more than merely human, well before his full identity would eventually be conclusively revealed and confirmed through his subsequent resurrection.
Fully Present in a Body, Yet Never Confined by It

subsections.heading: FULLY PRESENT IN A BODY, YET NEVER CONFINED BY IT
paragraphs: St. Athanasius now directly addresses a fairly subtle theological worry that a careful reader might reasonably raise at this point: did the Word becoming human somehow trap, limit, or confine him in some way, the same way an ordinary human soul is generally confined to acting only through its own single physical body at any given time? He argues quite firmly and directly that this was simply not the case for the incarnate Word. Even while genuinely, fully present and personally active within a specific human body, the Word remained, at that very same time, also fully present and active throughout the entire rest of the universe simultaneously, continuing to sustain, order, and govern absolutely everything exactly as he always had, without any interruption or diminishment whatsoever.

To help illustrate this fairly difficult and paradoxical point, St. Athanasius compares the Word to the physical sun, which is genuinely able to shine down and directly touch the earth below without ever itself becoming dirtied, diminished, or corrupted in any way by whatever it happens to touch or illuminate. In exactly the same way, he argues, the Word's genuine presence within a specific human body never actually limited, lowered, or diminished him in the slightest. If anything, quite the opposite was true: his presence there actively made that particular human body holy and sanctified, all without ever changing, altering, or lowering his own unchanging divine nature in any way.
── COMMENTARY ──

This is exactly how we understand the union of divinity and humanity in Christ: not two separate things loosely stitched together, and not the divine nature swallowed up or hidden by the human one, but one living Christ, one nature of the Word made flesh, fully God and fully human at once, without confusion and without change. This is the confession St. Cyril of Alexandria defended so fiercely against Nestorius, and it remains dear to our hearts to this day. Christ was never divided. He was never two. He is one Lord, one Savior, whole and undivided, and that wholeness is exactly what makes it possible for him to save us completely.
How Christ's Human Actions Reveal His Divine Identity

subsections.heading: HOW CHRIST'S HUMAN ACTIONS REVEAL HIS DIVINE IDENTITY
paragraphs: St. Athanasius offers his readers a helpful and fairly practical framework for correctly interpreting Gospel passages that describe Jesus doing seemingly very ordinary things, such as eating food, growing physically tired, or being born as an infant. These particular passages, he explains, accurately describe what was genuinely, truly happening to his real, authentic human body throughout his earthly life. But standing right alongside these entirely ordinary human experiences, Christ's specifically miraculous works, healing every conceivable kind of illness and disease, decisively casting out demons, restoring sight to a man born completely blind, transforming ordinary water into wine, walking directly on top of the sea, and feeding thousands of people from just a small handful of available food, all clearly reveal that this particular man was no ordinary human being at all.

St. Athanasius insists that these kinds of miraculous actions are simply not the sort of things any purely human being could ever accomplish entirely on their own power. Taken together, then, Christ's fully authentic human experiences on one hand, and his unmistakably divine actions on the other, work side by side throughout the Gospel narratives to jointly reveal both essential realities at once: a genuinely real human body experiencing real human limitations, and the divine Word himself actively working through and within that same body at the very same time.
── COMMENTARY ──

It helps to read the Gospels with this in mind. When Jesus gets tired at a well, or hungry in the desert, that is not a contradiction of his divinity, it is simply his real, genuine humanity showing itself honestly. And when he heals a man born blind or feeds a crowd from a handful of bread, that is his divine power shining through that same human life. These are never two separate people taking turns. It is always the one Christ, acting as who he truly is: God who has genuinely become human, without ceasing for a moment to be God.

St. Cyril would later put this beautifully when he insisted we should never split Christ into "one who does the human things" and "another who does the divine things." There is only ever the one Lord Jesus Christ, and everything Scripture says of him, hunger and miracles alike, is said of that same single, undivided Person.
Even Creation Itself Testified at the Cross

subsections.heading: EVEN CREATION ITSELF TESTIFIED AT THE CROSS
paragraphs: St. Athanasius points specifically to the striking events surrounding Christ's crucifixion, unusual darkness covering the sky in the middle of the day, and the earth itself visibly shaking, as further compelling evidence supporting his overall claim about Christ's genuine divine identity. He argues that if the natural created order itself reacted with such dramatic, visible awe and disturbance at the death of this one particular man, this fact itself must be understood as creation actively bearing witness that something far greater than merely an ordinary human death was actually taking place at that specific moment.

Having now thoroughly established, through both Christ's fully human life and his unmistakably miraculous works discussed across the preceding several sections, that Christ is genuinely and truly God the Word himself, St. Athanasius signals clearly to his reader that he is now finally ready to turn his full attention toward what will become the central, defining event of the entire remaining treatise: the actual nature, meaning, and ultimate purpose behind Christ's death itself.
Summing Up Why Only Christ Could Do This

subsections.heading: SUMMING UP WHY ONLY CHRIST COULD DO THIS
paragraphs: St. Athanasius pauses here to briefly review and consolidate the substantial ground he has already carefully covered across the treatise so far. Only the one who had originally made humanity entirely out of nothing in the first place could genuinely recreate it now. Only the one who is truly the authentic Image of God could properly restore that same damaged image within others. Only the one who is Life itself, in his own essential nature, could actually give genuine immortality to otherwise mortal beings. And only the eternal Word himself could properly and effectively teach the whole world the truth about the Father.

He then turns his attention specifically toward the actual practical mechanics of exactly how Christ's saving death functions. Because a genuine debt of death was owed collectively on behalf of absolutely everyone, Christ, having already thoroughly demonstrated his authentic divine identity through his many miraculous works described in earlier sections, subsequently offered his own body up to death specifically in humanity's place, thereby canceling that long-standing collective debt once and for all, while simultaneously revealing his own body afterward as genuinely incorruptible, standing as the very first example and guarantee of the resurrection promised to everyone else who follows after him. St. Athanasius pauses here almost apologetically to explain directly why he keeps circling back repeatedly to restate broadly similar ideas from slightly different angles throughout the treatise: because this particular subject matters so profoundly, he explains, he would much rather risk some noticeable repetition than risk accidentally leaving out anything genuinely important along the way.
Why Christ Didn't Simply Die Quietly, in Private

subsections.heading: WHY CHRIST DIDN'T SIMPLY DIE QUIETLY, IN PRIVATE
paragraphs: St. Athanasius raises a genuinely reasonable objection someone reading carefully might naturally ask at this point: if Christ's death needed to happen specifically on behalf of all humanity, why not simply arrange for a peaceful, private death instead, rather than enduring the public humiliation and violence of crucifixion specifically? He answers that an ordinary, private death would have wrongly suggested that Christ's own body was inherently weak in exactly the same way ordinary human bodies are naturally weak, gradually breaking down over time the way sickness and age eventually overtake absolutely everyone in the natural course of things.

But Christ, St. Athanasius insists, was never actually weak in that particular sense, since he is himself the very source and origin of all life. So it made complete sense, he argues, that death would instead need to come to him specifically from an outside source, meaning through other people's deliberate actions against him, rather than arising naturally through his own gradual internal decline the way it does for everyone else. St. Athanasius adds that although Christ genuinely did experience things like ordinary hunger, entirely consistent with his having taken on a fully real human body, he never actually suffered from disease or any kind of natural physical breakdown or decay, since neither of those things would have been consistent or fitting with who he truly was in his deeper nature.
Why Christ Didn't Avoid His Enemies Either

subsections.heading: WHY CHRIST DIDN'T AVOID HIS ENEMIES EITHER
paragraphs: St. Athanasius anticipates yet another closely related objection a careful reader might reasonably raise: if Christ genuinely could have simply avoided death altogether by successfully hiding from those actively plotting against him, why didn't he choose to do exactly that instead? He explains that this too would have been fundamentally inconsistent with who Christ truly is. Just as it would have been genuinely wrong for Life itself to directly end his own body's life through his own personal action, it would have been equally wrong for him to actively flee or hide from the death that others were already fully intending to inflict on him regardless.

Instead, St. Athanasius explains, Christ deliberately allowed that particular death to come to him entirely from an outside source, so that once it actually arrived and made contact with him, it could subsequently be completely and permanently undone from within his own body, once and for all. St. Athanasius adds a further, quite practical point here as well: if Christ's own body had ever fallen seriously ill in the ordinary way human bodies naturally do, this would have badly undermined people's overall confidence in his demonstrated power to heal others of their own various illnesses, since it would understandably look as though he somehow could not even manage to protect his own body from precisely the same kinds of weaknesses he was simultaneously curing in everyone else around him.
Why the Death and Resurrection Both Needed Public Witnesses

subsections.heading: WHY THE DEATH AND RESURRECTION BOTH NEEDED PUBLIC WITNESSES
paragraphs: St. Athanasius argues that if Christ had instead died quietly in some hidden, private location, and only afterward simply claimed to have risen from the dead without any prior verification, no genuinely reasonable person would have found this claim believable, since there would have been absolutely no reliable way to independently confirm that he had actually died in the first place. Resurrection, he points out, only carries any real meaning or weight if a genuine, clearly verifiable death has actually come before it.

This is precisely why, St. Athanasius argues, it mattered so significantly that Christ's death took place publicly and openly, with numerous clear, reliable witnesses present, in much the same way his earlier miracles, such as healing the blind man or turning water into wine, had also deliberately taken place out in the open, before witnesses, rather than in private or in secret. Without genuine public witnesses present for both the death itself and the subsequent resurrection, St. Athanasius points out, the disciples could never have gone on to preach the reality of the resurrection with any real confidence or credibility afterward, and he notes that even with reliable witnesses actually present at the time, many people still stubbornly refused to believe the accounts regardless.
Why Christ Accepted a Death Chosen by His Enemies

subsections.heading: WHY CHRIST ACCEPTED A DEATH CHOSEN BY HIS ENEMIES
paragraphs: St. Athanasius considers whether Christ ought to have instead arranged for some easier or more conventionally dignified form of death for himself, rather than specifically accepting crucifixion, a particular method of execution chosen deliberately by his own enemies precisely because of how thoroughly disgraceful and humiliating it was intended to be. He argues that if Christ had instead personally selected his own preferred method of death, this choice might have reasonably suggested that he was only actually capable of overcoming that one specific kind of death, leaving open the troubling possibility that some other, different form of death might potentially have defeated or overcome him instead.

By deliberately accepting whatever particular death his enemies happened to choose to inflict on him, precisely because it was specifically intended to be maximally humiliating and disgraceful, Christ thereby demonstrated total, comprehensive power over death in absolutely every possible form it might conceivably take. St. Athanasius compares this directly to a genuinely skilled wrestler who deliberately allows his opponents to be freely chosen for him by interested onlookers, rather than carefully selecting easier opponents for himself in advance, specifically in order to prove his clear superiority beyond any possible reasonable doubt or lingering suspicion. He also notes, almost as an aside, that this particular form of execution happened to leave Christ's body physically undivided and intact, unlike beheading would have, a specific detail whose deeper significance he goes on to explain more fully in the following section.
Why Specifically the Cross

subsections.heading: WHY SPECIFICALLY THE CROSS
paragraphs: St. Athanasius offers three distinct, carefully connected reasons explaining why crucifixion specifically, rather than any other conceivable form of death, was the particularly fitting and appropriate choice in this case. First, since Scripture explicitly describes anyone hung directly on a tree as thereby bearing a curse, Christ's death specifically on a wooden cross allowed him to personally take on and absorb the very curse that humanity had originally earned for itself through sin, fulfilling this scriptural pattern quite literally and directly.

Second, since crucifixion by its very physical nature stretches a person's arms outward in opposite directions, this specific physical detail vividly and visibly pictured Christ actively drawing both Jewish and Gentile people toward himself simultaneously from two entirely opposite directions, ultimately uniting both groups together as one within his own single body. Third, since crucifixion by its very nature physically lifts a person upward into the open air above the ground, and since Scripture separately describes hostile spiritual powers as specifically operating within that same air above the earth, Christ's death occurring in precisely that particular location both symbolically and, in St. Athanasius's account, quite genuinely and actually broke the specific power those same hostile spiritual forces had previously held over humanity's path toward heaven.
Why the Third Day, Specifically

subsections.heading: WHY THE THIRD DAY, SPECIFICALLY
paragraphs: St. Athanasius carefully explains why Christ's resurrection specifically occurred neither too soon after his death, nor too long afterward either. If he had risen again immediately, right after dying, people might have reasonably doubted whether he had genuinely and fully died at all in the first place. But if, on the other hand, too much additional time had been allowed to pass instead, natural decomposition would have inevitably begun setting in, and people might then have reasonably suspected some kind of substitution or elaborate trick had taken place, rather than accepting it as a genuine resurrection of that very same original body.

Three days, St. Athanasius argues, struck exactly the right careful balance between these two competing concerns: enough elapsed time to fully and convincingly prove that death had truly and completely occurred, but not so much additional time that the body's genuine continuing identity could reasonably be called into serious question by skeptical observers. This specific timing also conveniently meant that the resurrection was publicly announced while the very same original witnesses who had personally seen Christ die, including even his own hostile enemies, were still readily present and available nearby to potentially confirm or dispute exactly what had actually happened.
How the Cross Changed the Way Christians Relate to Death

subsections.heading: HOW THE CROSS CHANGED THE WAY CHRISTIANS RELATE TO DEATH
paragraphs: St. Athanasius now shifts his overall approach noticeably, moving from sustained logical argument toward direct observation of the world immediately around him. He points out that before Christ's coming, even genuinely devout and faithful believers had generally viewed death itself with real, palpable dread and fear, and people commonly mourned their dead as though they had been lost forever with absolutely no hope of any future recovery or restoration. But after the resurrection had taken place, Christian believers, including even quite young people, reportedly began facing death with startling, unprecedented courage, with some even actively and willingly embracing martyrdom outright rather than deny their newfound faith under pressure or threat.

St. Athanasius takes this dramatic and widely observable shift in overall attitude as strong, compelling evidence that something genuinely real must have actually changed regarding death's underlying power over humanity, since fear of death is such a deeply ingrained, seemingly universal human instinct that overcoming it this completely, this consistently, and this widely across an entire community of believers would surely require some kind of truly extraordinary underlying cause to adequately explain it.
An Invitation to Test the Claim for Yourself

subsections.heading: AN INVITATION TO TEST THE CLAIM FOR YOURSELF
paragraphs: St. Athanasius directly and pointedly challenges any skeptical readers he might have: if you still genuinely doubt that death has truly lost its former power and grip, simply look carefully at how many Christians, both young and old alike, have willingly and even eagerly faced death for the sake of their faith without displaying any real fear. He compares this directly to a fireproof material that can only genuinely prove itself to be fireproof once someone actually goes ahead and tests it directly, firsthand, by placing it in an actual flame.

In exactly the same way, he argues, anyone who remains doubtful about Christianity's specific claims regarding death's defeat ought to actually test those claims personally by genuinely adopting the Christian faith themselves, rather than simply continuing to speculate about it abstractly from a safe intellectual distance. He notes that many people who had previously mocked these very same claims eventually came to sincerely believe them after all, and that some of these former skeptics even went on to become martyrs themselves later, following their own personal conversion to the faith.
The Evidence Points Back to One Clear Cause

subsections.heading: THE EVIDENCE POINTS BACK TO ONE CLEAR CAUSE
paragraphs: St. Athanasius argues that this widespread pattern of Christian fearlessness specifically in the face of death simply cannot be adequately explained away as merely some vague, generic cultural trend with no specific identifiable cause behind it. It has, he insists, one clear, specific, and directly identifiable cause: namely the actual cross and subsequent resurrection of Christ himself. He compares this directly to the way sunrise is obviously and immediately understood as the clear explanation whenever darkness suddenly and dramatically gives way to full daylight.

In exactly the same way, he argues, when death, something people have always instinctively and universally feared throughout all of human history, is suddenly and consistently held in genuine, casual contempt by ordinary believers coming from every different age group and social background imaginable, the resurrection of Christ specifically, and nothing else besides it, stands out as by far the most reasonable and adequate available explanation for such an unusual, remarkably consistent, and widely observed pattern of behavioral change.
If He Weren't Alive, None of This Would Be Happening

subsections.heading: IF HE WEREN'T ALIVE, NONE OF THIS WOULD BE HAPPENING
paragraphs: St. Athanasius argues that the ongoing, currently visible effects of Christ's continuing ministry are themselves strong, compelling evidence that he remains genuinely alive and actively at work even now, rather than being merely a distant memory of someone who lived and died long ago in the past. He points specifically to the ongoing, day-by-day reality of people actively converting to Christianity from literally every nation, of adulterers genuinely abandoning their former immoral ways of life, and of various established forms of idol worship steadily losing their former grip and influence over people, all of which, in his own account, are actively happening specifically through the continuing name and influence of Christ himself.

He argues that dead people simply do not retain this particular kind of ongoing, active influence over the behavior and choices of the living. Since something is clearly and demonstrably still actively at work in the world around him, and doing so quite specifically and consistently through Christ's own name, this fact itself, St. Athanasius argues, points directly back toward the underlying reality of his continued, ongoing life.
Even the Old, Rival Gods Seem to Recognize Christ Is Alive

subsections.heading: EVEN THE OLD, RIVAL GODS SEEM TO RECOGNIZE CHRIST IS ALIVE
paragraphs: St. Athanasius makes a deliberately ironic argument here, specifically directed against religious skeptics of his own time. He points out that if the various spirits and false gods people had previously worshiped are genuinely still alive and actively powerful in their own right, and yet these same spirits and gods consistently retreat, visibly lose their power, and fall completely silent specifically whenever confronted with Christ's name, then, by strict logical consequence, it should actually be those older, rival gods, rather than Christ himself, who ought to be considered the truly dead and genuinely powerless ones by comparison.

He points specifically to the widespread abandonment of magic, superstition, and traditional idol worship happening broadly throughout the Roman world of his own time, attributing this large-scale shift specifically to ongoing Christian influence, and argues that this particular pattern of continuing, actively demonstrated influence is fundamentally inconsistent with whatever people would normally expect to associate with something genuinely dead and entirely powerless.
You Don't Have to See Him to Know He's Real

subsections.heading: YOU DON'T HAVE TO SEE HIM TO KNOW HE'S REAL
paragraphs: St. Athanasius directly addresses the fairly natural objection that no one today can simply point directly to Christ's risen body as final, conclusive proof of the resurrection. He responds that God has always been properly and primarily recognized throughout history through his ongoing works and actions rather than through any kind of direct, unmediated physical sight, since God himself remains, by his very nature, fundamentally invisible to human eyes. He compares this directly to a person who has been blind since birth, who can nevertheless remain genuinely confident that the sun truly exists, simply by directly feeling its warmth on their skin, even without ever having actually seen it with their own eyes.

In exactly the same way, he argues, skeptics who genuinely cannot yet bring themselves to fully believe are still fully capable of observing Christ's ongoing, continuing effects at work within the lives of genuine believers all around them, as real, tangible, and directly available evidence in its own right. St. Athanasius closes out this extended section of the treatise by noting that even evil spirits themselves, according to the various Gospel accounts, reportedly and immediately recognized and visibly feared Jesus throughout the course of his earthly ministry, a fact he treats as yet further confirmation that Christ's true underlying identity was genuinely never seriously in doubt, even among those figures most inclined and most motivated to actively oppose him.
